10135-the-great-english-short-story-writ:
This first volume of The Great English Short-Story Writers, in the Reader's Library of 1910, opens with introductory essays by William J. Dawson and Coningsby W. Dawson on the evolution of the short story. The tales that follow trace the form from its beginnings.

Readers meet Defoe's Apparition of Mrs. Veal, Hogg's Mysterious Bride, Irving's Devil and Tom Walker, Hawthorne's Dr. Heidegger's Experiment, Poe's Purloined Letter, and Stockton's Story of Seven Devils. The volume is a compact history of the English short story, told through its masterpieces. The essays alone make it a useful history of the form.
1025-essays-political-economical-and-phi:
Benjamin Rumford, Count Rumford, gathers his essays on politics, economy, and philosophy in this first volume. Rumford, an American-born scientist and administrator, wrote on heat, light, workhouses, and the relief of the poor. Rumford, born Benjamin Thompson in Massachusetts, served Bavaria as a minister and scientist.

The essays mix experiment with practical reform, from stoves and kitchens to the management of beggars in Munich. Rumford's clear, useful prose made him a model of Enlightenment science applied to daily life. His essays on workhouses in Munich showed how the poor could be fed, clothed, and set to work.
10355-travels-in-morocco-volume-1:
James Richardson's travels in Morocco, edited by his widow, open in this first volume with an introduction on the Straits of Gibraltar. Richardson, author of works on Central Africa and the Sahara, toured Morocco a few years before his death. The editor stresses the empire's size, its near eight million people, and its wars.

The volume sets the scene for the journey: coasts, towns, rulers, and European rivals France and Spain near Gibraltar. Later chapters will carry the reader inland. Readers get a learned, Victorian-era start to a two-volume portrait of Morocco under pressure from Europe.
10388-a-collection-of-old-english-plays-:
A. H. Bullen edited this first volume of old English plays, issued between 1882 and 1889 in four volumes. Bullen rescued plays that had not been reprinted, and some that had never been printed at all, for students of dramatic literature. His preface promises unknown works by Massinger, Fletcher, and Shirley in later volumes.

This volume holds The Tragedy of Nero, The Mayde's Metamorphosis, The Martyr'd Souldier, and The Noble Souldier. An introduction to Nero laments the lost close of Tacitus' Annals, which would have lit the tyrant's reign. Readers get rare Tudor and Stuart drama, with scholarly notes for modern study.
10561-fine-feathers-ship-s-company-part-:
W. W. Jacobs published this comic tale as the first part of Ship's Company, opening on Bank Holiday with Mr. Jobson waking to a Sundayish feeling. Jobson, an orderly man who hung his trousers on a brass knob for twenty years, finds them gone, replaced by a tailcoat, waistcoat, check trousers, and a tall silk hat. His family means to make a toff of him.

Jobson, draped in a counterpane, searches the house for his clothes, growing alarmed as the joke unfolds. Jacobs writes in brisk, cockney-flavored prose, full of domestic comedy. Readers get a short, funny tale of a sailor's family, pride, and fine feathers.
10636-the-travels-of-marco-polo-volume-1:
Marco Polo, a Venetian merchant of the thirteenth century, spent years traveling through Asia and later told the story of what he saw. This first volume presents the Yule-Cordier edition: Henry Yule's annotated translation, revised by Henri Cordier, with Cordier's later notes added. It is the scholarly standard form of Polo's account in English.

Volume one covers Polo's journey east, the lands he crossed, and the courts, cities, and customs he describes, with notes that explain names, routes, and doubtful points. The text mixes wonder at strange sights with careful detail about trade, rule, and daily life. Readers meet one of the great travel books of the Middle Ages, in an edition built for serious study.
1067-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-volum:
Ulysses S. Grant wrote in his last year to leave his family provided for. He tells his life from his Ohio boyhood through West Point, the Mexican War, and the first years of the Civil War. He covers Fort Donelson, Shiloh, and Vicksburg with a plain soldier's eye for ground, men, and supply. Mark Twain published the work.

Grant's modesty is the book's mark: he gives credit freely, owns blunders plainly, and never boasts. His clear prose made the memoirs a bestseller and a classic of American letters. The first volume ends with the Union cause gaining ground and Grant rising to command.
10781-deserted-sailor-s-knots-part-1:
W. W. Jacobs's Sailors' Knots, published in 1909, is a set of comic tales told by a Thames night-watchman, and "Deserted" is its first story. The watchman, fresh from a row with a lighterman, turns to the most dressy sailor he ever knew: Rupert Brown, named by his mother while his father was at sea. Rupert's fine clothes and airs set the comedy going.

Jacobs lets the watchman tell the tale in broad riverside speech, with jokes at the expense of vanity and sailors' pride. The story stands alone, needing no knowledge of the rest of the book. Readers get a short, funny yarn in Jacobs's best manner, from the docks and pubs of London's river.
10957-the-love-affairs-of-great-musician:
Rupert Hughes wrote this 1903 study of musicians' love lives, the first book on the subject, drawing on newly published letters and lives. Volume one moves from ancient musicians and men of Flanders to Orland di Lassus, Purcell, Stradella, Palestrina, and Bach, then to Haydn, Gluck, Rousseau, and Piccinni. Portions first appeared in The Criterion and The Smart Set.

Hughes uses fresh material, including the identity of Beethoven's Immortal Beloved, Liszt's letters to his princess, Chopin's supposedly burned letters, and Clara Schumann's courtship. He treats love as a force shaping music, not mere gossip. Readers interested in music history will enjoy the anecdotes, while scholars can trace his sources in the new biographies he cites.
1100-king-henry-vi-part-1:
William Shakespeare's first history play opens the Wars of the Roses with the death of Henry V and the loss of his French conquests. The boy king Henry VI reigns in name while his lords quarrel, Joan of Arc rallies France, and the brave Talbot dies betrayed at Bordeaux.

The play moves between London plots and French battlefields, with Joan as both witch and patriot in English eyes. Its verse is young and bold, and its scenes of war still stir. The play sets up the feud of York and Lancaster that runs through the whole sequence.
1115-king-henry-iv-part-1:
Prince Hal, heir to England's throne, wastes his youth drinking with Sir John Falstaff at the Boar's Head, while his father the king faces rebellion from Hotspur and the Percys. William Shakespeare's history play follows Hal from tavern jokes to the field of Shrewsbury, where he kills Hotspur and proves himself.

Falstaff, fat, witty, and gloriously dishonest, steals every scene he enters, and his catechism on honor is famous. The play balances low comedy with high politics and ends with the rebellion broken but not ended. It stands as Shakespeare's most popular history.
11181-captains-all-captains-all-part-1:
W. W. Jacobs opens his Captains All collection with a night-watchman's yarn about old Sam Small, a sailor who grumbles about the sea yet spends his shore pay in a fortnight. When Sam tries to mend his ways, he hunts newspaper advertisements for a comfortable shore berth and competes with seventy-nine other men for one post, earning a black eye for his trouble. The watchman tells it all in thick Thames-side dialect.

Jacobs built his reputation on stories like this one, where seamen's schemes collapse through vanity, drink, or bad luck. The humor is gentle rather than cruel, and the setting is the working waterfront. Readers who enjoy dialect comedy and sea stories will find the collection's tone set firmly here.
11436-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Stories by American Authors, volume one from 1903, collects five short stories: Bayard Taylor's Who Was She, Brander Matthews and H. C. Bunner's Documents in the Case, William Henry Bishop's One of the Thirty Pieces, Rebecca Harding Davis's Balacchi Brothers, and Albert Webster's Operation in Money. Taylor's opener begins with a birthday confession, a friend's eyes asking a question the narrator has fifty times meant to answer. fearing a smile or charitable pity for a passion that seems fantastic.

The volume showcases American short fiction at its most polished, from mystery to finance to circus life. Its authors were leading magazine writers of their day. Readers sampling the period's story craft will find the collection a convenient, varied introduction.
11471-shareholders-deep-waters-part-1:
W. W. Jacobs gives this short tale to his night-watchman, who opens with a sailor's rule: a sailor is safest at sea, and trouble starts ashore. Money, marriage, and drink follow men off the ship, and one poor fellow, the watchman says, was found with six women in court at once.

The title piece turns on shares and a hidden parcel of sixteen pounds, lost by the very man who hid it. Told in the watchman's own rough speech, the story is a comic warning about wages spent, lent, or stowed where no one, least of all the owner, can find them again.
11699-j-s-le-fanu-s-ghostly-tales-volume:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu's first volume of ghostly tales pairs Schalken the Painter, dated 1851, with An Account of Some Strange Disturbances in Aungier Street, dated 1853. Schalken opens on a picture in good preservation, its lights its chief apparent merit, its subject its real value.

A female figure in white, lamp in hand, wears an arch smile suited to a pretty woman at a prank, while the background stays dark. Aungier Street follows two medical students, cousins, who take a haunted house and learn that pen, ink, and paper are cold vehicles for the marvellous. The tales are told best after nightfall, by a fireside.
11951-a-popular-history-of-france-from-t:
François Guizot's History of France opens, in this first of six volumes, with a letter to the publishers describing history as one vast, long drama. Events, Guizot argues, link together according to defined laws, while actors play parts not ready made or learned by heart, but shaped by birth, ideas, and will.

The volume carries that view into the earliest times of France, following kings, peoples, and institutions as they form a nation. Guizot, a historian and statesman, writes for general readers rather than specialists, favoring narrative and character over antiquarian detail. The drama metaphor governs the whole six-volume design.
11971-dialstone-lane-part-1:
Part 1 of W. W. Jacobs's Dialstone Lane opens in the private office of Tredgold and Son, land and estate agents, where Mr. Edward Tredgold looks out through wire blinds at Binchester's peaceful High Street. Tredgold senior, who believed in work for the young, had left early. His son, glad to share his father's views, had passed most of the work to a clerk.

This opening portion establishes the town, the firm, and the young men whose treasure hunt will drive the novel, before the captain, the map, and the Southern Seas expedition take over. As a separate part, it reads as a gentle comedy of office life and seaside respectability, with Jacobs's humor already at work in small evasions and courtesies.
12151-back-to-back-night-watches-part-1:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this comic short story as part of Night Watches, his 1911 Thames-side collection. A night watchman tells it in dockside dialect, as he does all the tales in the book, and the humor comes from plain men tangled in their own schemes.

Mr. Scutts comes home hurt in a small railway accident and takes to his bed, hoping for a payout from the company. Weeks of idleness wear on him, and a chance caller plants the idea of a larger claim. The story turns on Scutts greed, his wife watchful eye, and the slow collapse of a plan that looked easy from a sickbed. It is a small, sharp study of malingering and marital suspicion.
12201-the-money-box-odd-craft-part-1:
Sailormen are not good hands at saving money, says the night watchman who opens The Money-Box, the first tale in W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft of 1909. At sea, with no pub within a thousand miles, sailors talk grandly of saving; ashore, the money melts.

The story follows men paid off who try every scheme to keep their wages: banks, boxes, friends, and pledges, each undone by thirst, generosity, or a sharper friend. Jacobs tells it in dockside dialect, with the watchman toying with a bad shilling on his chain. The comedy is affectionate: men who mean to save and fail in the same ways, year after year. The tale sets the tone for Odd Craft, where small plans meet human nature.
12396-the-star-chamber-an-historical-rom:
W. Harrison Ainsworth published The Star-Chamber, volume one, in 1854 with Tauchnitz at Leipzig. Ainsworth, author of Windsor Castle, sets the romance in Jacobean London, around the hated court of Star Chamber.

Chapters open at the Three Cranes in the Vintry, introduce Sir Giles Mompesson and his partner, and follow a Star-Chamber victim, Jocelyn Mounchensey, through provocation and forged signatures. A mid-book crowd scene has Dick Taverner demand hanging for Puritans and knaves alike. Ainsworth mixes history with melodrama, piling villains, myrmidons, and rescues. The novel is a Victorian historical romance, vigorous and partisan against Stuart tyranny.
1251-le-morte-d-arthur-volume-1:
Thomas Malory gathers the legends of King Arthur in this first volume. The tales tell of Arthur's birth, the sword in the stone, the founding of the Round Table, and the early quests of Lancelot, Gawain, and their fellows. The tales move from Camelot's glory to its first shadows.

Malory's prose, plain and grave, gives the legends their classic English form, and his knights fight, love, and fail by a code of honor. The book has fed poets and novelists for five centuries. This volume opens the great cycle, and it still reads as the heart of Arthurian romance.
12537-account-of-a-tour-in-normandy-volu:
Dawson Turner's first volume of letters from Normandy, London 1820, addressed to the Reverend James Layton of Catfield, investigates the architectural antiquities of the duchy. Observations were collected during three tours, in the summers of 1815, 1818 and 1819, chiefly in the second year, with authorities quoted where Turner did not depend on his own remarks.

Journals of tour companions supplied some facts, Turner admits, without tedious minuteness. Engravings illustrate churches, abbeys and castles along the route. The volume, companion to the second, offers a learned, illustrated tour for readers who wanted Normandy's stones explained, not merely pictured.
12565-an-account-of-the-english-colony-i:
David Collins, judge advocate and secretary of the colony, published this 1798 account of the English colony in New South Wales. It adds remarks on native inhabitants, and particulars of New Zealand from Lieutenant-Governor King's manuscripts. Engravings illustrate the first volume.

Collins opens with a plea for wise severity: punishment should purify, and many now suffering early death might become ornaments of society. The narrative that follows records settlement, convicts, food, government and contact with Aboriginal peoples. The volume is a foundational source for early Australia, written by an official who watched a penal colony struggle toward a colony.
12742-minstrelsy-of-the-scottish-border-:
Walter Scott's Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border, volume one of three, published in 1806, collects historical and romantic ballads from southern Scotland, with a few modern pieces founded on local tradition. Dedicated to Henry, Duke of Buccleuch, the book inscribes tales that celebrated his ancestors' prowess and cheered their halls, in Scott's humble, obliged voice.

After the fall of the house of Douglas, Scott notes, no single chieftain held such supremacy over the borders, as barons who shared the spoil resisted royal power. Ballads of feud, love and war follow, with Scott's notes and introductions. The volume founded Scott's fame and modern ballad scholarship, preserving border song in print.
12886-the-coquette-s-victim-everyday-lif:
Charlotte M. Braeme's The Coquette's Victim, first in the Everyday Life Library, opens in a police court on May 14, where Magistrate Kent, famed for reading faces, meets a case that puzzles him. Drunkards, thieves, and battered wives pass before the bench in the morning's work. A little boy sent on an errand starts the tale's turn.

Later scenes follow a handsome youth of eighteen, home from school covered with honours, whose mother Lady Hildegarde probes his character by the drawing-room fire. Braeme's moral melodrama warns against vanity and flirtation. The novel shows the popular sentimental fiction that filled cheap libraries of its day.
12956-a-history-of-indian-philosophy-vol:
Surendranath Dasgupta's History of Indian Philosophy, volume one, first edition Cambridge 1922, dedicates a lifetime's work to India's great sages, who first formulated freedom's principles and sought truth's ultimate essence. A note on Sanskrit pronunciation likens vowels to Italian, with a approaching o in bond, and a long a approaching a in army. The dedication sets a reverent tone.

A Jain passage shows the scholarship: Digambaras hold original works lost and present texts spurious, with sacred language called Jaina Prakrit and later works Jaina Maharashtri. Glosses, commentaries, and Umasvati's ancient treatise fill the tradition. The volume is a landmark of Indian philosophy in English.
12963-melbourne-house-volume-1:
Melbourne House, volume one of 1865, by the author of The Wide, Wide World, opens a domestic novel of a little girl and her household. A child comes down a flight of stairs as the story begins, and the volume follows family life, servants, and moral growth in a well-to-do American home. The transcriber notes the edition's rough typesetting, with small errors corrected for reading ease.

A mid-book scene finds a servant named June, shy and gliding, unable to sing a camp-meeting song for a visitor named Gary, who has never been to such a meeting. The novel's earnest, sentimental tone marked its author's popular style. Volume one sets up a long family story continued elsewhere.
12984-eugene-field-a-study-in-heredity-a:
Eugene Field: A Study in Heredity and Contradictions, volume one, by Slason Thompson, appeared in December 1901. Thompson argues that Field would have wanted his life told as a quizzing jest, not a straight record of birth and works, and the book tries to catch that odd personality. Portraits, views, and facsimiles illustrate the text.

Field's pranks on his wife, always met with a startled Oh, Eugene, run through the book, as does his spent patrimony, mortgaged to Mr. Gray until no equity remained. The study gives a lively, affectionate portrait of the Chicago humorist and children's poet.
13065-beethoven-s-letters-1790-1826-volu:
Volume one of this two-volume set gathers Ludwig van Beethoven's letters from 1790 to 1826, translated by Lady Wallace from Ludwig Nohl's collection. Added letters to Archduke Rudolph, drawn from Ludwig Ritter von Köchel's collection, sit in date order and are marked with a K. The letters run from the composer's youth to his later years in Vienna.

They cover money troubles, publishers, concerts, patrons, and friends, and they show Beethoven pleading, joking, scolding, and planning new work. A will-like passage speaks of deafness and of death coming before his powers were fully spent. For readers, the letters give the man behind the music in his own urgent voice, with all its pride, warmth, and strain.
13117-the-nests-and-eggs-of-indian-birds:
Allan O. Hume's Nests and Eggs of Indian Birds, volume one, second edition of 1889, was edited by Eugene William Oates after Hume gave up the task. Hume had spent years gathering notes since his first rough draft, and Oates took up the reissue with care. The volume is a work of close field record, species by species.

Entries note nests watched day by day, such as one in a clover-like plant three feet up, where both birds built and five eggs were laid. Another entry describes a small bag nest of thatch-grass flowers, four inches high, set a foot from the ground. The book's worth lies in that patient detail, gathered across India by many hands and set down for future watchers.
1340-autobiography-of-andrew-dickson-whi:
Andrew Dickson White opens his autobiography with his youth, education, and the early years that led to Cornell University. White, a scholar and diplomat, tells how he came to believe in free, nonsectarian learning. White, born in 1832, grew up in Syracuse and studied at Yale and in Europe.

The first volume follows his schooling, travels, and first public work, setting the stage for Cornell's founding. White writes with candour and detail, and the book gives a view of American intellectual life in the mid-nineteenth century. His first volume ends as Cornell takes shape, a university open to any person and study.
13645-the-tatler-volume-1:
Richard Steele launched The Tatler in London in 1709, writing under the name Isaac Bickerstaff. Jonathan Swift and Joseph Addison joined him, and George A. Aitken later edited this volume with notes. Each short number pretends to come from a coffeehouse, a theatre, or a bookseller's shop. The pose let Steele comment on daily life in a lively, sociable voice.

Inside, short essays judge manners, fashion, gambling, duelling, and stage gossip. Some pieces tell small stories sent in by readers. Others praise good sense and good temper over show and spite. Footnotes name the real people behind the jokes and explain old customs. Read together, the numbers give a vivid street-level view of London at the start of the 1700s.
13675-goody-two-shoes-a-facsimile-reprod:
This volume reproduces the 1766 edition of Goody Two-Shoes, with an introduction by Charles Welsh. The tale follows Margery Meanwell, a poor orphan girl who gains a pair of shoes and then learns to read. She teaches village children their letters and grows into a respected schoolmistress. John Newbery first published the story for children in London.

Welsh discusses the book's history and the claim that Oliver Goldsmith wrote it. Washington Irving is cited among those who backed that view. The facsimile keeps old spelling, pictures, and layout, so readers see the book as children once did. Its lessons link kindness, learning, and good fortune. The tale helped shape English children's literature.
1381-poems-volume-1:
George Meredith opens his collected poems with the first volume of his verse: lyrics on love, nature, and the hard lessons of life, written in his dense, aphoristic style. The poems show the novelist as poet, thinking in images of earth, sea, and sky.

Meredith's verse is not easy, but it rewards patience with maxims and music. The volume gathers his early and middle lyrics. It suits readers who know his novels and want the poetry that ran beside them. Meredith's early lyrics reward readers who know his novels. Meredith's verse rewards patience with maxims, images, and music.
13945-sunny-memories-of-foreign-lands-vo:
Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, wrote Sunny Memories of Foreign Lands after a European tour. Volume one, published in Boston in 1854 with designs by Hammatt Billings, collects letters home. Stowe quotes Shakespeare on sharing rare, noteworthy objects seen in travel. Her preface promises sunny memories, not gloomy critique.

Letters describe schools, churches, and society in Britain and on the Continent. A passage on common schools notes little moral training where opportunity for character growth is scant. Stowe writes as a famous American visitor, welcomed and watched. The book suits readers of travel writing and Stowe's life. It shows mid-century America looking at Europe.
14353-the-poems-of-jonathan-swift-d-d-vo:
William Ernst Browning edited this 1910 London volume, the first of a collection of Jonathan Swift's verse. Swift, the Anglo-Irish clergyman and satirist, wrote most of these poems between the late 1600s and the early 1700s.

Odes to patrons and bishops sit beside ballads, petitions, riddles, and mock-heroic pieces on London life, politics, and court gossip. The verse is plain, biting, and often funny, aimed at vanity, faction, and folly. Browning's introduction sets the poems in their order. Readers get Swift the versifier rather than the prose pamphleteer, sharp in short lines and unsparing in judgment.
14431-international-miscellany-of-litera:
This October 1850 number of the International Miscellany gathers literature, art, and science for American readers, with a portrait of Lord Brougham on its opening page. The New York monthly reprinted European material alongside original notes.

Items include a ghost story called The White Lady, reports on Fanny Kemble's London readings, notes on literature in Africa, and Lamartine's apology for his Confidences. Some scanned words were marked unreadable by the transcribers. The issue shows mid-century American taste: curious, improving, and eager for news from London and Paris. Its editors aimed at readers who wanted the world in one monthly parcel.
14549-rule-a-wife-and-have-a-wife-beaumo:
Rule a Wife and Have a Wife, by John Fletcher with Francis Beaumont, appears here in A. R. Walker's edition of their works. The comedy is set among Spanish soldiers and court ladies.

Juan de Castro and Michael Perez recruit companies and praise the giant-like Don Leon. Margarita, brought up a courtier, delights in company and courtship and keeps her husband at a servant's distance. Leon endures her scorn and commands her household in turn. The play is a lively Jacobean comedy of marriage, power, and wit, still funny in its battle of the sexes.
14551-a-catechism-of-christian-doctrine-:
Baltimore Catechism No. 1, prepared by order of the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore and approved in 1885, served first communion classes in American Catholic schools. Cardinal McCloskey and Archbishop Gibbons approved the text.

Short questions and answers cover the Creed, the commandments, and the sacraments in simple form, with prayers and hymns appended. One lesson lists six ends of the Holy Eucharist, from union with Christ to a pledge of everlasting life. The book is the smallest of the Baltimore series, and its plain form taught generations of children. First communicants learned its short answers by heart.
1493-the-legends-of-the-jews-volume-1:
Louis Ginzberg's first volume gathers Jewish legends from Creation to Jacob, retold from rabbinic sources and translated by Henrietta Szold. Chapters follow the first days of the world, Adam and Eve, Noah, Abraham, and Jacob, weaving commentary, parable, and folk tale into a continuous narrative.

Ginzberg's notes trace each legend to its source, giving scholars a map of the tradition while general readers enjoy the stories themselves. The volume opens a vast work of folklore and faith. It remains a standard treasury of Jewish legend, rich in wonder and moral reflection.
1500-king-henry-vi-part-1:
Shakespeare's first history of Henry VI opens after the death of Henry V, with England losing ground in France and quarrels brewing at home. Joan of Arc, called Joan la Pucelle here, leads French forces to victory at Orleans, while English lords, led by Gloucester, Bedford, and York, fall into rival camps.

Battle scenes alternate with court intrigue, and the young king proves too weak to hold his nobles together. The play ends with a truce and a marriage bargain that promises more trouble. It is the start of Shakespeare's Wars of the Roses sequence, rough, stirring, and full of early promise.
1516-king-henry-iv-part-1:
Henry IV, Part 1 balances a king's troubled reign with the riotous life of Prince Hal, who drinks and robs with Falstaff at the Boar's Head in Eastcheap. Rebellion gathers in the north under Hotspur, a fiery young warrior who despises the court's politics and longs for honour in battle.

Hal's road from tavern to battlefield leads to Shrewsbury, where he meets Hotspur face to face and proves himself his father's son. Falstaff's wit runs through the play like a counter-song. It is Shakespeare's most popular history, mixing comedy and war with unmatched energy.
15271-traditions-of-lancashire-volume-1:
John Roby's Traditions of Lancashire, in a fifth edition in two volumes, gathers folk tales and legends of the English county. Steel and wood engravings illustrate the set, and a Verstegan motto on facing sharp judges fronts the first volume. Roby writes with an antiquary's care for old stories.

Tales of ghosts, witches, old halls, and local heroes fill the pages, rooted in Lancashire places and families. The collection helped shape how Victorians saw their own folk past. Readers who love English folk lore will find the volume rich, atmospheric, and full of county character.
15735-history-of-the-negro-race-in-ameri:
The first volume of George W. Williams's history of Black Americans, issued by G. P. Putnam's Sons in New York in 1883. Williams, the first Black member of the Ohio legislature, covers 1619 to 1800. His subtitle promises Negroes as slaves, as soldiers, and as citizens. A sketch of Africa and accounts of Sierra Leone and Liberia open the work.

Williams argues for the unity of the human family before tracing slavery's growth in the colonies. Black soldiers in early wars, and the first steps toward citizenship, get careful record. He writes with pride and with documents, not mere praise. The volume stands as a landmark: the first full history of Black America by a Black scholar.
15777-a-voyage-towards-the-south-pole-an:
The first volume of Captain James Cook's account of his second voyage, in the ships Resolution and Adventure, during 1772 to 1775. Printed in London in 1777, it carries maps, charts, and views drawn by Mr. Hodges. Cook writes as commander, with Captain Furneaux's narrative of the Adventure added. The book stands as a landmark of exploration literature.

Cook sails from England toward the South Pole, seeking a southern continent through ice and storm. Book One follows the passage to the Society Isles, with notes on winds, currents, and island peoples. Hodges' views give readers faces and shores they had never seen. The volume matters for science and seamanship alike: careful, plain, and honest about danger, distance, and doubt.
15997-alfred-russel-wallace-letters-and-:
James Marchant edited this 1916 Cassell volume on Alfred Russel Wallace, the naturalist who worked out natural selection alongside Charles Darwin. Volume one covers Wallace's early years, his letters from 1854 to 1862, the discovery itself, and the full surviving letters between Wallace and Darwin from 1857 to 1881. Plates and a list of Wallace's writings round out the book.

The letters show two busy scientists testing ideas, sharing specimens, and treating each other with care at a turning point in science. Readers also glimpse Wallace's travels, friendships, and home life behind the famous theory. The book suits anyone who wants the human story behind evolution's great debate in the scientists' own words.
16232-the-culture-of-vegetables-and-flow:
Sutton and Sons of Reading published this gardening guide in a sixteenth edition in London in 1921, through Simpkin, Marshall, Hamilton, Kent. Its contents divide the gardener's year into monthly work for vegetables, then rotation of crops, chemistry of garden crops, artificial manures, and the culture of flowers from seeds. Flowering bulbs, flowers all the year round, and pests of plants and flowers, including fungus pests, complete the book.

The guide speaks with a seedsman's practical authority, telling readers what to sow, when to feed, and how to fight disease. Its monthly calendar keeps the busiest gardener on track. Modern gardeners will still find clear, old-fashioned advice for kitchen gardens and flower beds alike.
16363-the-new-york-times-current-history:
This January 23, 1915 volume of New York Times Current History prints Sir John French's own story of the war's opening months. His famous dispatches to Lord Kitchener, secretary of state for war, begin with a first report from the front dated September 7, 1914. French reports that transport from England by sea and rail went in the best order, with each unit arriving well within schedule.

Concentration finished on the evening of Friday, August 21, and the force moved on Saturday to positions chosen for operations requested by the French commander, General Joffre. The dispatches that follow trace retreat, battle, and resolve in a commander's voice. Students of the First World War will find essential, contemporary British evidence.
16370-lameness-of-the-horse-veterinary-p:
J. V. Lacroix, doctor of veterinary science, wrote Lameness of the Horse as number one in the Veterinary Practitioners' Series. The book teaches working vets and horse owners how to find, name, and treat the many causes of a horse going lame, from foot and leg troubles to gait and stance. A transcriber's note records variant spellings and a small list of typographical errors kept in the text.

Its contents order was kept as printed, with authorities cited after the index rather than before it. The manual speaks in a practical, clinical voice, aimed at the stable and the surgery rather than the library. Horse owners, farriers, and veterinary students will find a clear, old-style guide to equine lameness.
16472-through-forest-and-fire-wild-woods:
Edward S. Ellis opens his Wild-Woods Series with this 1891 boys' adventure. Nick and his schoolmates face a lost child, a search party groping in darkness, alarming footprints, bear hunters, and a dinner in the woods. A dog named Bowser proves his worth, and marksmanship, hunting, and forest craft fill the later chapters.

Ellis writes brisk, outdoor tales for boys, with danger kept exciting rather than grim. The forest setting drives every chapter, from school days to a face-to-face meeting with a wild beast. Young readers of old-style adventure will find the book a fast, wholesome yarn of woods life.
16485-a-year-s-journey-through-france-an:
Philip Thicknesse writes home from France and Spain in this first volume of letters, printed in Dublin in 1777. The opening letter, from Calais in June 1775, recalls earlier letters that helped a friend tour France, and promises fresh hints on French manners and customs. Later letters follow the road through French towns toward Spain.

Thicknesse writes as a lively, opinionated traveler, keen on customs, food, and local character. The letter form keeps the book easy to dip into. Readers of eighteenth-century travel will enjoy a frank, chatty guide to France on the eve of revolution.
16702-the-new-york-times-current-history:
This January 9, 1915 volume of the New York Times Current History gathers early war documents and comment on the European war. It prints what Americans said to Europe, with portraits of Charles W. Eliot and James M. Beck. Beck argues the case of Dual Alliance against Triple Entente in a supreme court of civilization, on the British White Paper, the Russian Orange Paper, and the Belgian Gray Paper.

The volume gives readers of 1915 the papers and the pleas as they stood, before later battles rewrote the tale. It mixes official papers with legal argument and American voices. History readers can use it as a first-draft record of how the war was judged in its first months, not as a final verdict.
16994-a-year-s-journey-through-france-an:
Philip Thicknesse wrote this second volume of A Year's Trip across France and part of Spain, printed at Dublin in 1777 by J. Williams. Letter thirty-four, from Nismes, opens with praise for the mistress of the house where Thicknesse lodges. She is a woman of such beauty, elegance, and breeding that he began to suspect the house too fine for any seen outside Paris. He had been directed to the house and recommended to the lady as a lodger.

Thicknesse writes in letters, mixing travel notes, people, and sharp opinions as he moves through France and Spain. His tone is frank, curious, and often tart. The volume gives a lively, 1700s view of southern Europe on the road, useful for travel history and for readers who like letter books with bite.
1705-a-history-of-science-volume-1:
Henry Smith Williams, assisted by Edward H. Williams, opens his five-volume history with the beginnings of science. It moves from prehistoric tools and sky-watching to the organized knowledge of Egypt, Babylonia, and Assyria. Chapters follow the alphabet, early Greek thinkers in Italy, and the schools of Athens.

The volume is written for general readers rather than specialists. It treats science as a long human effort: counting, measuring, healing, and mapping the heavens, each step building on the last. Readers get a clear survey of the ancient world before Greece. They also get a sense of how much of later science rests on work done long before any modern laboratory existed.
17513-st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-:
A full year's run of St. Nicholas, Scribner's illustrated magazine for girls and boys, conducted by Mary Mapes Dodge, fills this fifth volume, from November 1877 to November 1878, published by Scribner and Company in New York. Its contents open with Child-Queen, pictured by Alfred Fredericks, and Chased by Wolves, pictured in full. A jingle about an old person of Crewd and Mollie's Boyhood follow.

As a bound year's volume, the book gathers stories, verses, and pictures that entertained American children through 1878. Readers get a rich sampler of Victorian children's reading, from adventure to nonsense. The volume suits collectors and readers of children's magazine history.
1765-king-henry-vi-part-1:
England is losing its French conquests after Henry V's death, and Talbot, the great English captain, fights on while Joan of Arc rallies the French. The great English captain Talbot fights on while Joan — Joan la Pucelle in the play — rallies the French, and the nobles at home quarrel over power.

The play mixes battle scenes with court intrigue, and its language moves between Talbot's plain soldier's honor and Joan's fierce rhetoric. This early Gutenberg text notes that a better-proofed edition exists elsewhere. The play itself is the same: the start of Shakespeare's long history of a kingdom falling apart from within.
17721-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-:
The Bay State Monthly was a Boston magazine of New England history, life writing, and state progress, and this 1885 issue is the first number of its third volume. Its pages mix short histories, town sketches, and serial fiction, all aimed at readers proud of Massachusetts and its past.

Alongside notes on books and state affairs, the issue runs a long serial tale in which two young men spar over pride, charm, and place. The mix shows how a state magazine of the day taught its readers: a bit of past, a bit of present, and a story to keep them turning pages. It is a fine window on Boston letters in the mid-1880s.
18020-the-wits-and-beaux-of-society-volu:
Grace and Philip Wharton wrote The Wits and Beaux of Society, here in a new 1890 edition with a preface by Justin Huntly McCarthy. The first volume sketches the bright, bold talkers of the courts of Charles II and Louis XIV, with pictures by H. K. Browne and James Godwin.

Readers meet De Grammont and his witty attacks on Mazarin, St. Evremond the handsome Norman, Hortense Mancini, Lord Rochester in his prime, and La Belle Jennings. The Whartons write with gossip, charm, and light scholarship. It is a gay, old-style gallery of wits, best for readers who love court anecdote and high-society sparkle.
18387-the-days-of-bruce-a-story-from-sco:
Grace Aguilar, author of Home Influence and The Vale of Cedars, wrote this story from Scottish history in two volumes, the first published by D. Appleton in New York in 1871. The Days of Bruce tells the story of Robert the Bruce and Scotland's fight for freedom, in the romantic historical manner of Aguilar's day. Aguilar writes with pain and pleasure, since the work was a labor of love.

The tale opens on a wild March evening at the ancient Tower of Buchan, where wind howls round the walls and waves lash below, mingling roar with roar. From that stormy coast the story moves into Bruce's struggle, his followers, and the making of a king. Readers get Scottish history as romance: castles, storms, loyalty, and the long fight that made a nation, told for young readers of the nineteenth century.
1865-north-america-volume-1:
Anthony Trollope's North America, volume one, opens his journal of travels through the United States from August 1861 to May 1862, when he visited every state that had not seceded except California. The book is partly a travel journal and partly a running argument about the Civil War and about American manners.

Trollope discusses Seward's offer to send British troops across Maine, and records what Americans told him about their cause, with the bluntness of a visitor who does not hide his opinions. The volume pairs with the second as a single report from a country at war. It is still read for its vivid, opinionated picture of the North in 1862.
1925-droll-stories-volume-1:
Monks, wives, seneschals, and devils people these ten tales, told in the manner of Rabelais and collected, Balzac says, from the abbeys of Touraine. The Fair Imperia, The Venial Sin, How the Good Man Bruyn Took a Wife, and The King's Sweetheart lead a set of stories told in old French dress.

Balzac writes in the manner of Rabelais, with monks, wives, seneschals, and devils, and with jokes about sins repented and mourning that follows. The tales are bawdy and learned together. Their interest lies in Balzac's play with language: a modern novelist trying on the voice of the sixteenth century, and enjoying it.
19317-gallipoli-diary-volume-1:
General Sir Ian Hamilton wrote this Gallipoli Diary, volume one. It was published in New York in 1920 with pictures and maps. Hamilton commanded the Allied force at the Dardanelles. His diary runs from planning to hard fighting on a narrow peninsula front. A letter from General d'Amade opens the book. It praises the commander's ardour and will.

Hamilton records talks with Lord Kitchener. Kitchener claims one submarine in the Marmora would rout the Turkish garrison. It need only wave a Union Jack. Hamilton notes that Braithwaite must go with him, not his trusted chief of staff Ellison. Readers get a commander's frank, daily account of a famous failed campaign, its hopes, frictions, and costs.
19449-the-north-american-indian-vol-1:
Edward S. Curtis wrote, photographed, and published this first volume of his great series on the Indians of the United States and Alaska, issued in the early nineteen hundreds under the patronage of J. Pierpont Morgan. Frederick Webb Hodge edited the text, and field work underpinned every page.

The volume opens with Apache life, including a pool scene photographed by Curtis, and records tales, customs, and camp life in words and images. Curtis's project, planned in twenty volumes, remains both a landmark of photography and a debated record of Native peoples at a turning point.
19599-troublous-times-in-canada-a-histor:
John A. Macdonald, a veteran of eighteen sixty-six and eighteen seventy, wrote this history of the Fenian raids on Canada. It runs from Irish plots and a Cincinnati convention to landings near Fort Erie and the battle of Ridgeway.

Chapters follow Canadian volunteers, the Toronto naval brigade, and the hurried Fenian evacuation, with state papers on clemency for prisoners. Macdonald writes as a participant, and his book remains a first-hand account of Canada's brush with Irish-American invasion. On the Niagara frontier, companies under Lieutenant-Colonel Robert B. Denison guarded the line near Chippawa.
19612-history-of-dogma-volume-1:
Adolf Harnack wrote this history of Christian dogma, here in its first volume in English translation, edited for the Theological Translation Library. It opens with long prolegomena on how dogma should be studied, then traces the presuppositions behind church teaching.

Harnack follows the early church's message about Christ as teacher, crucified and risen, and shows how that message grew into a canon that drew in apostles and Paul's letters. The work remains a landmark of liberal church history, learned and bold in its judgments. Harnack notes one gospel writer who tells of Jesus only to establish belief that he is the Messiah, the son of God.
19828-reminiscences-of-sixty-years-in-pu:
George S. Boutwell wrote Reminiscences of Sixty Years in Public Affairs, volume one dated 1896. He undertook it at his children's request, he says. Friends like J. Bancroft Davis and William A. Richardson advised him too. He calls the venture open to debate in wisdom. Three fourths of a century of experience stand behind the sketch. Boutwell had been governor, congressman, and treasury secretary.

Few Americans served as long at as many levels. Boutwell helped found the Republican Party and fought slavery early. His memories cover antislavery politics through Reconstruction finance. Volume one carries the first stretch of that career. Memoirs by insiders anchor political history. Boutwell's is unusually long in view and plain in style.
19831-the-rise-and-fall-of-the-confedera:
Jefferson Davis published The Rise and Fall of the Confederate Government in 1881. Volume one of two argues the Confederacy's case after its defeat. Davis protests that ignorant readers call the South revolted provinces. He insists the states held reserved powers under the Union's nature. On his view, the United States forced war to preserve itself. The book is a brief written by the losing president.

Davis wrote to vindicate secession as constitutional action. His volumes mix memoir, documents, and legal argument. Historians read them as the Lost Cause in its author's own words. Little here is neutral, and that is its value. The work shaped Southern memory for generations. It remains essential evidence of how the Confederacy explained itself.
19959-the-mabinogion-vol-1:
The Mabinogion is the great storehouse of medieval Welsh tales. Lady Charlotte Guest translated it from the Red Book of Hergest. Volume one of this later edition adds corrective footnotes. The editor offers more literal renderings of some passages in them. Guest's flowing versions sometimes smooth the Welsh too much. Between text and notes, readers get both story and scholarship.

Guest's translation, finished in the 1840s, introduced Welsh myth to the world. Princes, enchantresses, and giants fill its eleven tales. Arthur appears at its edges, older than the romances made him. Volume one opens a literature few English readers knew. The tales shaped modern fantasy more than most know. Tolkien himself drew on this well.
20014-canada-and-the-canadians-vol-1:
Canada and the Canadians surveys the young Dominion for British readers. Volume one opens on Britain's surprising ignorance of Canada. The mother country knows very little about her finest colony, it asserts. Sober, speculative English emigrants sail out knowing hardly more. Sir Richard Bonnycastle wrote the original survey in the 1840s. This edition carries his portrait of Canada to later readers.

Bonnycastle was a Royal Engineers officer stationed in Canada. He wrote its scenery, society, and prospects with a settler's zeal. The book recruits emigrants while describing the land honestly. Snow, forests, and new towns dominate his first volume. Canadian history keeps returning to Bonnycastle for color. Volume one sets the colonial scene in full.
20153-the-american-journal-of-archaeolog:
The American Journal of Archaeology for 1893 lists scholars from many lands and schools. Alfred Emerson of Cornell appears among its roll of names. So do men from Princeton, Berlin, Athens, and Rome. Archaeology then drew a small, linked world of diggers and scholars.

Journal issues held reports of digs, finds, and debates on old art. Readers could follow new work at Athens or Rome from home. The lists alone show how wide the field's reach had grown. This issue serves those who trace how archaeology became a modern science. Such journals still guide students of the ancient world today.
20241-the-palace-of-pleasure-volume-1:
The Palace of Pleasure, volume one, reprints William Painter's famed Elizabethan tale storehouse. Joseph Haslewood's 1813 edition, in just 172 copies, served as copy here. Proof was checked against British Museum copies of the 1575 edition. Painter's tales gave later playwrights a rich stock of plots.

Shakespeare and others drew stories of love, murder, and fate from Painter. Italian and French tales, Englished by Painter, fill this first volume. Each tale is short, sharp, and full of sudden moral turns. Readers get a key source book of Elizabethan fiction in full. Scholars still use Painter to trace where Elizabethan plots first entered English print.
20452-letters-of-edward-fitzgerald-in-tw:
Edward FitzGerald, the English man of letters best known for his version of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, was also a great letter writer. This first of two volumes gathers his correspondence with friends. The letters are chatty, bookish, and full of East Anglian life.

FitzGerald's memory held fast to stories he heard from others. The dramatic facts of the Fualdès murder at Rodez in 1817, and the famous trial that followed, fastened themselves on his mind for years. He knew all the details told by word of mouth. The letters show that same appetite for people, books, and odd events.
20826-traditions-of-the-north-american-i:
Twelve miles from a great tribe, the author of Traditions of the North American Indians was born. The Pawkunnawkuts, once a vast and warlike nation, had shrunk to some five hundred souls. Their lands had narrowed to a few thousand acres by his birth.

James Athearn Jones gathered tales told at Indian camp fires for these volumes. Myths, legends, and tribal memories fill volume one in the tellers' own vein. Jones wrote them down when such lore was fast being lost. His work, flawed by its age, still keeps early records of native story that might else have vanished from print.
2087-life-and-letters-of-charles-darwin-:
Francis Darwin edits the first volume of his father's life and letters, choosing letters to show Darwin's personal character as well as his work. The chapters follow Darwin's books, since his life was so much a life of research. Francis Darwin, himself a botanist, understood his father's work from the inside.

Letters are kept near chronological order, though Darwin often worked on several subjects at once, mixing experiment with long reasoning. The volume gives a warm, human portrait of the naturalist before fame settled on him. The first volume ends before the Origin storm, so it shows Darwin the young naturalist at work.
20925-history-of-the-united-states-volum:
Quit rent, New Style dates, and words like sedulous fill the glossary of this United States history. Volume one ends its main tale with helps for hard period terms. A land tax that frees a tenant from other dues earns its own clear entry.

Charles and Mary Beard taught America to read its past through work and wealth. Their histories stress farms, trade, and industry beside wars and laws. Volume one runs from first settlements to a young republic's growth. The glossary shows their care for plain readers, keen that no old term should bar the way to the story.
20933-the-natural-history-of-selborne-vo:
Gilbert White cared only to return to Selborne, the village where he was born, this life notes. Oxford gave him livings, yet home and its fields held his heart. He died there June 26, 1793, past his three score and ten.

White's letters on birds, beasts, weather, and gardens form The Natural History of Selborne. Volume one sets his calm, exact watching before the world. Few books have taught so many to look closely at home ground. White's work, first out in 1789, has never left print, a proof of how fresh his Selborne still feels.
2138-the-day-s-work-part-1:
Rudyard Kipling gathers the first part of The Day's Work, stories of engineers, soldiers, and workers across the British Empire. The tales praise duty, craft, and the men who keep machines and borders running. Kipling published The Day's Work in 1898, gathering stories from magazines.

Kipling writes of India and the sea with technical detail and vivid slang, and the stories show his belief in work well done. The collection suits readers who know Kim and want Kipling's shorter, tougher tales. Part one, with engineers and soldiers, shows the empire's working men at their tasks.
21538-souvenir-of-the-george-borrow-cele:
Norwich honoured its famed wanderer in the George Borrow Celebration of July 5, 1913, and James Hooper edited the souvenir. The committee borrowed pictures and writings from many Borrow lovers for the book. Jarrold and Sons of London and Norwich published it at half a crown.

Views show Borrow's birthplace at Dumpling Green, East Dereham, and his old home in Willow Lane. Verses praise the pilgrim of the road, whose trust was his light and truth his load. A. J. Munnings designed the cover, with Borrow and Petulengro above the city. The book preserves a day when a whole city claimed its wild, gifted son.
21615-curiosities-of-literature-vol-1:
Isaac Disraeli gathers essays in Curiosities of Literature, volume one, edited by his son, the Earl of Beaconsfield. The younger Disraeli adds a memoir and notes to this new edition. The publishers promise a mix found nowhere else in so pleasant a form.

Essays range over literary, artistic, and political history, with critical talks and anecdotes. One piece argues that a man's life is full of incidents, most too slight to matter to his kind. The set won great fame on its own, volume by volume. Young and eager seekers after knowledge, the preface says, have always loved these books.
2167-miscellaneous-writings-and-speeches:
Thomas Babington Macaulay's first volume of miscellaneous writings gathers his contributions to Knight's Quarterly Magazine, from his earliest to his latest work. Macaulay had long hoped for such a collection. Knight's Quarterly Magazine gave the young Macaulay his first wide audience.

Born in 1800, a Cambridge scholar and fellow, called to the bar in 1826, and elected for Calne in 1830, he wrote these pieces across a busy public life. The volume shows the young Macaulay's range, from criticism to history and verse. His early essays already show the confident, marching prose that made his history famous.
21817-handy-andy-a-tale-of-irish-life-vo:
Handy Andy, the blundering Irish servant whose mistakes drive the fun, stars in Samuel Lover's tale of Irish life. Lover opens with an address answering critics who called his Irish portraits too kind. A portrait painter by trade, he pleads guilty to taking the best view of his subject. Andy, he grants, is a fellow no gentleman would want in his service, yet he has redeeming natural traits.

This first volume of two sets Andy loose among squires good and bad, with enough villainy to keep the tale moving. Lover writes Ireland with love and laughs at it in the same breath. The book made Andy a byword for cheerful incompetence. Its humor is broad, warm, and rooted in close knowledge of Irish speech and ways.
22131-the-story-of-the-upper-canadian-re:
John Charles Dent wrote The Story of the Upper Canadian Rebellion, published at Toronto in 1885. Volume 1 covers the rising of 1837 and its roots in bad government. Dent quotes the rebels' own plea: they took up arms not to attack others, but to defend themselves. The words come from a letter written by prisoners at Montreal to Lord Durham in 1838.

Dent worked from records, newspapers, and survivors' accounts. He follows William Lyon Mackenzie and the men who marched down Yonge Street. The book judges both rebels and rulers with care. It remains a standard narrative of the rebellion that pushed Canada toward responsible government.
22221-oswald-langdon-or-pierre-and-paul-:
Carson Jay Lee published Oswald Langdon, or Pierre and Paul Lanier, a romance of 1894–1898, in Chicago in 1901. The book reached a fifth edition quickly. Its opening cry, "The Star! The Star! Mother!" sets a tone of wonder and alarm. Young Oswald is haunted by a crime committed in London years before, and he wonders what New York police could know or care about it.

Lee spins the tale across the Atlantic in the years of the Spanish-American War. Brothers Pierre and Paul Lanier share the stage with Oswald in a plot of hidden guilt and pursuit. The novel is a period melodrama, eager, earnest, and long forgotten.
22305-the-naval-history-of-the-united-st:
Volume one of The Naval History of the United States appeared in 1886. It starts long before the United States had a navy at all. The opening scene is set in May 1636, in Long Island Sound.

A stout little sloop of some twenty tons is out on a trading trip. At her helm stands John Gallop, a sturdy colonist and skilled seaman. He earned his bread trading with Native people along the Sound's shores. They, in turn, eagerly sought trade with Plymouth and New Amsterdam. Starting here roots American sea power in small colonial craft, trade, and risk.
22336-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-february:
Buchanan's Journal of Man began with its February 1887 issue, volume one, number one. The editor had watched human progress, he says, for half a century. Assisting that progress was his pleasure and his task.

The journal promised a periscope of progress for its readers. It would cover all that interests the philanthropist. Such a scope took in reform, science, and human welfare. Launching a journal on that promise took confidence and hope. This first issue preserves the start of that venture. Readers can see how a Victorian reform editor framed his mission at the very moment he began.
22414-the-birth-of-yugoslavia-volume-1:
The Birth of Yugoslavia, volume one, tells how a new South Slav state arose. It emerged from the First World War's wreckage of empires. A note on spelling shows the care taken with names.

Names of places and persons follow Croat orthography throughout. That means the Latin alphabet, modified for Serbo-Croatian sounds. This script, with its diacritic marks, was shaped in the early nineteenth century. Such details mattered in a land of many peoples and tongues. The history follows Croats, Serbs, and their neighbors toward union. Readers get a near-contemporary account of Yugoslavia's founding. It explains a new country while its borders were still fresh news.
22488-the-mirror-of-taste-and-dramatic-c:
The Mirror of Taste and Dramatic Censor began with volume one, number one, in January 1810. It was an early American magazine of theatre and taste. Its first essay considers readers who hunt deep erudition.

Those with talent, leisure, and inclination for such hunting are few. Of that number, still fewer could be diverted by light pieces. Casual reading of fugitive essays would not turn them aside. The magazine thus defines its audience and its lighter mission. It promised reviews, criticism, and taste for playgoers and readers. This first number preserves the birth of American dramatic criticism. Scholars can watch a young republic argue about its stage.
2251-king-henry-iv-part-1:
Prince Hal idles in Eastcheap taverns with Falstaff while his father Henry IV faces rebellion from the Percys. King Henry IV, Part 1 cuts between the prince's comic education and Hotspur's hot-blooded revolt, building toward their duel at Shrewsbury. Shakespeare balances tavern prose against the high verse of honor and kingship.

Falstaff's lies about a robbery, his mock-king play, and his battlefield cowardice steal every scene he enters. Hal's growth from wastrel to warrior gives the play its arc. It remains the most popular of the histories, and Falstaff its most quoted creation.
2254-king-henry-vi-part-1:
Young Henry VI inherits a throne he cannot hold, and England's French conquests crumble under quarreling lords. Part 1 introduces Joan of Arc as a warrior maid, Talbot as the doomed English hero, and the first red and white roses plucked in a garden quarrel. Shakespeare's early history is pageant-like, full of battles, sieges, and bold speeches.

Joan's capture and burning close a play that mixes chronicle with legend. The seeds of civil war are planted in every scene of faction. Readers tracing Shakespeare's growth will see his history manner taking shape here.
22718-cathedrals-and-cloisters-of-the-so:
Cathedrals and Cloisters of the South of France, volume 1, is a richly produced travel and architecture book issued by G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1906. The catalog record credits the publisher. It tours the great churches of Languedoc and Provence, town by town, with photographs and close description.

The author protests against treating the old churches as an endless, monotonous procession, differing only in size, style, and age. That, the text insists, is distinctly unfair: these churches have personalities and quirks as real as those of individuals. Cloisters, carvings, and local legends get the same patient attention. The book belongs to the great age of cathedral tourism, when educated travelers crossed France with a Baedeker in one hand and books like this in the other.
22762-history-of-the-rise-of-the-hugueno:
Henry M. Baird wrote History of the Rise of the Huguenots, whose first volume tells how French Protestantism grew under persecution in the sixteenth century. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Baird, an American scholar of French Protestant descent, spent his life on this history.

His preface celebrates the new evidence available to his generation: a rich store of lifelike, trustworthy views of the past. Diplomacy's secrets stand revealed, and official statements may now be tested against the unguarded accounts sent in cipher to foreign courts. Private collections of original documents add their weight. Volume 1 builds from such sources toward the wars of religion. Baird's work remains a standard narrative, learned and openly sympathetic to its subject.
2295-waifs-and-strays-part-1:
O. Henry's Waifs and Strays gathers early stories of New York and beyond, full of clerks, shopgirls, tramps, and con men. Part 1 shows the young master of the twist ending learning his trade: a gift misfires, a stranger turns out to be a friend, and a small kindness changes a life. The city itself is the real hero.

The stories are short, witty, and warm, with O. Henry's famous reversals already in place. Readers new to him can start here and move on to his better-known volumes. The collection is pure entertainment with a kind heart.
2303-legends-and-lyrics-part-1:
The first part of Adelaide Anne Procter's Legends and Lyrics introduces the poet Dickens championed, in verse both devout and domestic. Ballads of saints, legends of charity, and lyrics of home and loss fill the volume, written in a clear, musical style that made Procter a household name in her time. Her poems favor feeling over experiment.

The collection's best pieces still move readers with their directness, especially those on the poor and the outcast. As a record of Victorian popular taste, it is invaluable. Poetry readers will find a voice sincere, graceful, and of its age.
2332-critical-and-historical-essays-volu:
Thomas Babington Macaulay's first volume of Critical and Historical Essays gathers his famous Edinburgh Review pieces on Milton, Machiavelli, and others. The essays made Macaulay's name with their sweep, confidence, and rolling sentences, turning literary criticism into a kind of history. His judgments are bold, his learning wide, and his partisanship open.

Reading these essays is like hearing a great lecturer at full power. Modern scholars dispute many of his verdicts, but his prose still carries readers along. The volume is essential for students of Victorian letters. Macaulay later wrote a great History of England in the same confident style.
23770-mission-furniture-how-to-make-it-p:
H. H. Windsor's Mission Furniture, Part One, appeared in 1909 as a Popular Mechanics handbook, written so readers can understand it. Like the other handbooks in the series, its text and pictures were prepared by experts and revised by the magazine's editor, for home study as well as class use.

Contents give measured plans for a home-made mission chair, a lamp stand, a porch chair, a tabouret, and a Morris chair. Later pieces include a mission library, a candlestick, a lawn swing, a roll-top desk, and a piano bench. Chapters on mission stains, filling oak, wax finishing, and fuming oak teach the Craftsman finish. It remains a usable pattern book for the mission style.
23788-the-posthumous-works-of-thomas-de-:
Alexander H. Japp edited The Posthumous Works of Thomas De Quincey, Volume One, published in London in 1891. Japp worked from the original manuscripts, put into his hands by Mrs. Baird Smith and Miss De Quincey, the author's daughter, and selected for variety and contrast.

The volume leads with Suspiria de Profundis, followed by essays critical, historical, biographical, philosophical, imaginative, and humorous. Japp thanks a friend for help reading the proofs, and dedicates the book to the two women who trusted him with their father's remains. For De Quincey readers, it gathers fugitive pieces that had never before reached print.
24067-hidden-from-the-prudent-the-7th-wi:
Paul Jones, secretary of the Fellowship of Reconciliation, delivered Hidden from the Prudent as the seventh William Penn Lecture at Race Street Meeting House, Philadelphia, on May 8, 1921. Walter H. Jenkins printed the lecture the same year, with Paul Jones's signature as frontispiece.

Jones begins in January 1915, on his first visit to the Ute Indian Reservation in northeastern Utah, driving with the missionary to Ouray for the monthly issue of government rations. That evening, about fifty or sixty Indians sat around the stove in the log store, under flickering lanterns, to hear of God's love for men. Next morning, Albert Cesspouch, blind from trachoma, stood with his blanket around him, his daughter Rosita interpreting, to speak of what had been on his mind since summer.
24311-the-preacher-and-his-models-the-ya:
The Reverend James Stalker, author of Imago Christi, The Life of Jesus Christ, and The Life of St. Paul, gave these Yale lectures on preaching in 1891, published in London by Hodder and Stoughton in 1919. The book takes its epigraph from Augustine. Who makes it possible to say what ought to be said, and as it ought to be said, except him in whose hand are we and our sermons?

A letter from Yale Divinity School, signed by President Timothy Dwight and professors of Hebrew and systematic theology, thanks Stalker for instructive and stimulating lectures in the Lyman Beecher Course. The school rejoices that publication will carry the profit wider. Readers get a classic guide to preaching, through models a preacher may study and follow.
2468-repertory-of-the-comedie-humaine-pa:
This first part of the Repertory of the Comedie Humaine serves as a guide to Honore de Balzac's vast sequence of novels: its characters, families, and recurring figures. The repertory lists who appears where, tracing lives across the novels like a census of a fictional France. For readers lost in Balzac's world, it is an essential map.

The volume's value lies in its system: cross-references turn a sprawling masterpiece into a navigable country. Balzac scholars and devoted readers alike use such guides. The repertory opens the door to the whole Comedie.
24938-the-nursery-july-1873-vol-xiv-no-1:
The Nursery for July 1873, volume fourteen, number one, is a Boston monthly for youngest readers, published by John L. Shorey. Its prose contents run from Look Out for the Engine and Hettie's Chickens to The Little Fortune-Seekers, The Fourth of July Cake, and Prairie Dogs.

One tale, Touch My Chicks If You Dare, pits Bravo, a three-month-old pup, against Downy, a three-day-old chick. Bravo thinks himself a match for any hen, while Downy strayed from its mother for a crumb. Bravo growls and leaps, but Downy minds its crumb. The issue mixes stories, verse, and pictures in the gentle style of Victorian children's magazines.
25092-the-roman-traitor-vol-1:
Henry William Herbert's Roman Traitor, volume one, published in Philadelphia in 1853, is a historical novel set in the last days of the Roman Republic. Its stage is the Rome of Cicero, Cato, and Catiline, where conspiracy, ambition, and loyalty collide as the Republic slides toward collapse.

Herbert fills the story with senators, soldiers, and lovers, including a young couple watched by Catiline himself as intrigue tightens around them. The volume's chapters move from the men and measures of the plot through love affairs, oaths, ambushes, and disclosures. Readers get a melodramatic but vivid picture of Rome on the edge of revolution.
25108-the-south-seaman-an-incident-in-th:
Louis Becke's South Seaman, from his 1901 collection The Tapu of Banderah, recounts an incident from the sea story of Australia in July 1828. The Sydney brig Indefatigable, once the crack trader Calder under Captain Peter Dillon, sails from Chile loaded with wheat and bound for Sydney.

When her crew reaches a Pacific island, they meet Tahitians whose welcome has turned cold. They learn why: escaped convicts from Van Diemen's Land had earlier repaid island hospitality with theft and murder. Becke ties the episode to Dillon's fame as finder of the lost La Perouse relics. He tells it as a vivid slice of the rough early Pacific trade.
25119-the-conquest-of-canada-vol-1:
The Conquest of Canada, volume one, published in New York in 1850 by the author of Hochelaga, compares the English and French races for supremacy in America. The author argues that the two peoples started fairly equal, but built their colonies on opposite plans: New France grew by state direction, New England by its settlers.

French officials, he writes, served France rather than Canada and longed for home, while English settlers raised their own taxes, framed their own laws, and worshipped in their own way. Only in trade did London insist on strict obedience. The volume sets out the contest that would end with Britain's conquest of Canada.
2559-the-forsyte-saga-volume-1:
John Galsworthy opens his great family saga with The Man of Property, the first volume of the Forsyte story. Old Jolyon Forsyte gathers his clan at home, at the opera, and at dinners, while the younger Jolyon, James, and Swithin circle the family's wealth and pride.

At the center stands Soames Forsyte, a solicitor who treats his wife Irene as one more possession, and builds a house to prove it. Galsworthy writes with cool irony about money, marriage, and the Forsytean grip that holds all of them. This volume sets the feud and the passions that will run through the whole saga.
25723-the-voyage-of-the-oregon-from-san-:
One of the crew tells this voyage of the Oregon from San Francisco to Santiago in 1898. The Merrymount Press printed it privately in Boston in 1908. Only one hundred and twenty-five copies were printed. Almost ten years had passed since the nation followed the ship by scanty telegram.

The Oregon hurried around the continent as far as Bahia. Then came two anxious, silent weeks fearing four Spanish cruisers with torpedo boats athwart her course. Tidings of arrival at Jupiter Inlet ended suspense. Off Santiago, after a month of waiting, Cervera's squadron came out to meet a splendid ship.
2578-the-french-revolution-volume-1:
Hippolyte Taine opens his French Revolution volumes with anarchy, the subject of this second volume of his Origins of Contemporary France. Paris up to July 14, the storming of the Bastille, and the months to October 6, 1789 fill the early chapters.

Taine then turns to the Constituent Assembly, its labors, its damage, and its constructions, judging the new order against the old. His method piles documents high, and his verdict is severe. The volume remains a formidable, if partisan, history of how France slid from reform into violent disorder. Readers still turn to it for its mass of detail, even when they dispute its verdict.
2581-the-modern-regime-volume-1:
Hippolyte Taine reaches Napoleon in this fifth volume of his Origins of Contemporary France, the first volume of The Modern Regime. Taine opens with Bonaparte himself, his character, genius, ideas, and passions, before turning to the state he built.

Later books study the new government's institutions, its services, its taxes, and its recovery of social order after revolution. Taine admires Napoleon's energy while judging his system coldly. The volume serves as a searching portrait of the man who remade France, and of the order that outlived him. The volume closes Taine's long inquiry with a hard look at power made permanent.
25900-senatorial-character-a-sermon-in-w:
C. A. Bartol preached this sermon at West Church, Boston, on Sunday, March 15, 1874, just after the death of Charles Sumner. Taking for his text the psalm verse on teaching senators wisdom, Bartol says the pulpit must do more than expound old creeds. Its higher end is to give meaning to the scenes of real life, where speaker and hearer both play a part.

The sermon honors Sumner as a martyr to the right, beaten by brutal force in defiance of parliamentary privilege while Douglas and his peers looked on. Sumner, Bartol says, came back after years of suffering like a witness risen, while his assailant died first in disgrace and remorse. At the same height as Milton in blindness, Sumner stands in Bartol's praise as a senator taught by wisdom and pain.
25911-sea-power-in-its-relations-to-the-:
Captain A. T. Mahan opens his study of sea power in the War of 1812 with the antecedents of the war, from colonial conditions to Jay's Treaty. Printed in London in two volumes, the first sets out how trade, impressment, and embargoes drew America toward war with France and Britain alike. A frontispiece shows the impressment of an American seaman, the grievance at the heart of the quarrel.

Mahan follows the drift to war through Jefferson's time, when the next step, barring some lucky change, seemed likely to be war with both powers at once. The embargo, he argues, failed to bend either foe without firm union at home. The volume lays the ground for the battles of the second book, showing why a young republic took to the sea in anger.
25957-the-contemporary-review-january-18:
The January 1883 Contemporary Review opens volume forty three with Herbert Spencer on the Americans, Edward A. Freeman on university elections, and Franklin Leifchild with a new reading of Hamlet. Panislamism and the Caliphate, the Bollandists, England, France, and Madagascar, and the religious future of the world fill the early pages, with Syrian colonization and the Conservative dilemma to follow.

Later months in the same volume take up French thought, Gambetta, Rossetti's art, the Channel Tunnel and the silver streak, reform, ancient international law, a Russian prison, and democratic Toryism. One essay traces the Bollandists through Oriental history, from the Essenes and monastic roots to Saracen persecution and Arabic numerals reaching Europe. The review gives a full shelf of Victorian debate in one stout volume.
26041-aunt-jo-s-scrap-bag-volume-1:
Louisa M. Alcott gathers old and new stories in Aunt Jo's Scrap Bag, first volume, in a cheaper London edition of 1892 from Sampson Low. Alcott likens her work to grandmothers rummaging piece bags for gay odds and ends to fill stockings hung in a row on Christmas Eve. She hopes little dears in nightcaps and gowns will cry oh with pleasure as they pull out her small gifts.

Contents run from my boys and Tessa's surprises to Buzz, the children's joke, and dandelion tales, with Christmas holidays of 1871 to 1872 to open. One farmyard scene shows Mrs. Cluck hunting Peep, while Peck staggers as if tipsy and Doctor Drake waddles by to call it fits, fatal and past help. Alcott writes with humor, warmth, and a keen eye for child life.
26132-the-apple-tree-the-open-country-bo:
L. H. Bailey's Apple-Tree, first of the Open Country Books, treats a familiar tree as a subject for country living. Opening chapters place the apple-tree itself, ask where there is no apple-tree, and set the tree in the landscape, reading orchard and countryside together.

Bailey's opening list keeps the tree at the center, moving from the tree alone to the tree among fields, roads, and houses. The book gives the apple-tree a standing in the open country beside the farm and the village, in short chapters that join natural history to the look of the land.
2616-memoirs-of-general-william-t-sherma:
William T. Sherman begins his memoirs by dedicating them to his comrades in arms, volunteers and regulars alike. Nearly ten years after the Civil War, he notes, no satisfactory history of it yet exists for the public, and none should be attempted until the government publishes its records.

Sherman then tells his own story, from early service through the war's first campaigns, in plain, forceful prose. The memoir mixes personal recall with documents and argument, and it set the terms for how his campaigns would be judged. It remains a frank, indispensable account by one of the war's most debated generals.
2619-the-home-book-of-verse-volume-1:
Burton Egbert Stevenson edited this first volume of The Home Book of Verse, a two volume set gathering poems for family reading. Part one, Poems of Youth and Age, opens with Keats on the human seasons, then turns to babies and children in verse by Blake, MacDonald, and others.

The anthology ranges across centuries and moods, chosen for warmth and memorability rather than scholarly fashion. Parents, teachers, and poetry lovers will find old favorites beside lesser known gems. The volume works as a fireside book, meant to be read aloud and returned to often.
2647-life-and-letters-of-lord-macaulay-v:
Sir George Otto Trevelyan wrote this life and letters of Lord Macaulay, his uncle, and the second edition adds fresh material gathered in nine months. Trevelyan spared no pains to make the first edition complete, and the new matter enriches the portrait.

This first volume follows Macaulay from boyhood through his rise as historian, essayist, and parliamentarian, told largely in his own letters. The young Macaulay's energy, memory, and ambition leap from the page. The book remains the standard life of the man who wrote England's most famous history. Trevelyan writes as both nephew and historian, fond but unsparing.
2668-the-life-and-adventures-of-baron-tr:
Baron Trenck's memoirs, translated by Thomas Holcroft, open with an introduction on two cousins Von der Trenck, barons of an ancient East Prussian house. Both were adventurous soldiers, and the elder Trenck's life reads like a romance of courts, camps, and prisons.

This first volume follows his early service, his daring escapes, and his clashes with kings and jailers, told in his own vigorous voice. Holcroft's 1892 Cassell translation keeps the swagger and the detail. The book remains a classic of true adventure, stranger than most novels of its age. Prussian courts, Austrian prisons, and battlefield daring fill the early chapters.
