2671-the-complete-writings-of-charles-du:
Charles Dudley Warner's first volume of complete writings gathers My Summer in a Garden, Backlog Studies, and Baddeck. An introductory letter jokes about introductions themselves, calling them pilasters put on a building for looks, flat and often needless.

Warner writes of garden weeds, winter fires, and a trip to Cape Breton with warmth and easy humor. The essays made his name as America's genial companion for the fireside. The volume opens the set with his most loved pieces, and it still reads as a friendly invitation to slow down. Garden, fireside, and seacoast give the volume its threefold charm.
27169-fern-vale-or-the-queensland-squatt:
Colin Munro's Fern Vale, or The Queensland Squatter, volume one of three, published in London in 1862, opens with a preface on ignorance of Australia at home. When Parliament first heard of dismembering New South Wales's northern districts as a refuge for expatriated felons, a noble lord asked where New South Wales was.

Munro argues that English readers still know little of colonial life and manners, as if Australia remained in primitive inanition. The novel that follows takes readers to Queensland squatter country, where settlers build stations and society on a frontier the mother country barely pictures.
27192-political-women-vol-1:
Political Women, volume one, by the author of Royal Favourites, studies the women who threw themselves into the vortex of politics in seventeenth-century France. The author picks political women of the Fronde for study, above all the Duchess de Longueville and her circle, at work in the time of Richelieu's heirs.

The narrative follows their plots, exiles, and influence through five books, showing how salon and court became instruments of state. The volume argues that these women, often dismissed as intriguers, shaped the Fronde's course and deserve a place in political history.
27354-arch-ological-essays-vol-1:
The late Sir James Y. Simpson, physician to the Queen in Scotland and professor of medicine and midwifery at Edinburgh, pursued history and archaeology as refreshment from his anxious medical labours. John Stuart, secretary of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland, edited this first volume of Simpson's collected essays, published at Edinburgh in 1872.

The papers had appeared in the transactions of societies and in scientific journals, where many had grown scarce and hard to reach. Simpson's son put the copies and his father's notes into Stuart's hands, since Simpson himself had meant to reprint them. The volume preserves a busy physician's second life as an antiquary, in permanent form.
27586-the-mentor-the-war-of-1812-volume-:
Professor Albert Bushnell Hart of Harvard wrote this Mentor number on the War of 1812, dated 15 March 1916, volume four, number three, serial number 103, priced at fifteen cents. The Mentor's motto was Learn One Thing Every Day.

Mentor gravures picture Captain James Lawrence, Commodores Stephen Decatur and William Bainbridge, Commodore Oliver Hazard Perry, the Battle of Lake Erie, and General Andrew Jackson. An old song recalls Perry at Put-in Bay on 10 September 1813, and lines from June 1813 mourn Lawrence. The number gives a compact, illustrated lesson on the war's naval heroes. Perry's pennant on the Lawrence fronts the number.
27698-principles-of-political-economy-vo:
William Roscher's Principles of Political Economy, translated by John J. Lalor from the thirteenth German edition of 1877, presents the historical school of economics. This first volume was published in New York by Henry Holt and Company in 1878.

Roscher defines goods, value, wealth, and economy, then sets political economy among related sciences and defends the historical method against abstract systems. Added chapters on paper money, international trade, and protection make the volume a full statement of how economies grow within nations and history. A preliminary essay by L. Wolowski on the historical method opens the volume.
27818-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for August 1845, volume fifty-eight, number three hundred and fifty-eight, gathers essays, fiction, and criticism from the great Tory monthly. Its contents include an essay on punishment, a conclusion on Pushkin, and a new part of Marston, or the Memoirs of a Statesman.

Other pieces offer a letter from London by a railway witness, an essay on priests, women, and families, and notes on the British critics. The issue shows Blackwood's at mid-century: serious, partisan, and wide-ranging across literature, politics, and social questions. The punishment essay takes up the pamphlets of Captain Maconochie on reforming criminals while punishing crime.
28169-memoirs-to-illustrate-the-history-:
Francois Guizot's Memoirs to Illustrate the History of My Time, volume one, London, 1858, covers France from 1807 to 1815. Guizot, later a leading statesman, recalls his entry into Paris society, his lectures on modern history, and his work under the Empire. He meets Chateaubriand, Madame de Stael, and other figures of the age.

The volume moves through the fall of Napoleon, the Restoration, and Guizot's post as secretary-general to the Ministry of the Interior. His account mixes personal memory with political judgement. It gives a first-hand view of France changing rulers and regimes in a few short years.
2833-the-portrait-of-a-lady-volume-1:
Henry James began The Portrait of a Lady in Florence in the spring of 1879, and the novel appeared serially in the Atlantic Monthly and Macmillan's Magazine from 1880. This first volume introduces Isabel Archer, a young American woman of independence and imagination, arriving in England among relatives and admirers. Ralph Touchett, Lord Warburton, and the lively Henrietta Stackpole circle her with advice and affection.

James follows Isabel's education in freedom, as she refuses good offers and chooses her own path through Europe. The prose lingers on conversation, houses, and the small signs by which character shows itself. The volume sets up the great drama of the second half, which turns on what Isabel does with the liberty she has guarded so fiercely.
28720-the-esperantist-vol-1-no-1:
The first number of The Esperantist, the gazette for spreading Esperanto, dated November 1903 and edited by H. Bolingbroke Mudie. Published by the Esperanto Club in London, it sold for fourpence a copy or three shillings a year. Its contents mix language lessons with movement news: an essay on Esperanto by W. T. Stead, a synopsis of grammar, and notes on Esperanto in daily life and shorthand.

The number also prints a translation of Shakespeare's Tempest, an Italian summer sketch, a sailor's life, humorous telegraphy, letters, and an original march with music. It lists the secretaries of Esperanto societies from Bournemouth to Edinburgh. Readers get a lively picture of the young international-language movement at the moment it began organizing in Britain.
2874-personal-recollections-of-joan-of-a:
Mark Twain told the story of Joan of Arc through her fictional childhood friend, the Sieur Louis de Conte, in this first of two volumes. The book opens by quoting Louis Kossuth on Joan's unique distinction, holding supreme command of a nation's armies at seventeen. Chapters follow her girlhood at Domremy, the fairy tree, the pillage of her village, and her voices, including the archangel Michael.

Twain, who counted the book among his most serious works, presents Joan as a plain country girl whose faith and courage carry her toward Orleans. The narrator's affection gives the history an intimate tone. The volume covers her rise from village child to inspired leader, leaving her trial and martyrdom for the second part.
29090-the-complete-poetical-works-of-sam:
This first volume of The Complete Poetical Works of Samuel Taylor Coleridge gathers the poet's verse with full scholarly apparatus. The transcriber's notes explain a careful system: Greek words transliterated between plus signs, Hebrew between pound signs, italics in underscores, and diacritics shown by breve and macron marks. Struck-out words appear in brackets with asterisks.

Coleridge, author of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and Kubla Khan, stands among England's great Romantic poets, and this volume opens the complete record of his poems. Readers get the verse itself, presented with the care of a modern critical edition, in a text that preserves the original's marks and variants. It suits students and lovers of Romantic poetry alike.
29091-the-complete-poetical-works-of-sam:
Ernest Hartley Coleridge edited this first volume of Samuel Taylor Coleridge's complete poetical works, published by the Clarendon Press in two volumes. Volume one gathers the poems, with textual and bibliographical notes, including poems and versions published here for the first time.

Coleridge, the Romantic poet of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and Kubla Khan, appears here in full range: early lyrics, meditative verse, and experiments in meter. The editor's notes track drafts and early versions, showing how poems changed. Readers get a scholarly edition of a major poet, useful both for reading the poems and for studying how they were made.
29425-the-confessions-of-a-caricaturist-:
Harry Furniss published this first volume of confessions in New York and London in 1902 with Harper and Brothers, dated London, December 1901, illustrated throughout. A caricature of Mr. Gladstone opens the volume. Furniss, a leading Victorian caricaturist, tells his life through his art.

Chapters cover confessions of childhood and after, bohemian confessions, confessions as a special artist, and confessions as an illustrator, a serious chapter. A chat between pen and pencil precedes parliamentary confessions. Furniss apologizes beforehand for jokes at friends' expense. Readers get a caricaturist's memoir, witty and self-aware, about drawing the powerful for a living.
295-the-early-short-fiction-of-edith-wha:
Edith Wharton's early stories show a master learning her range before The House of Mirth. Volume One of this ten-volume collection gathers Kerfol, Mrs. Mansey's View, The Bolted Door, The Dilettante, and The House of the Dead Hand. Dates run from 1891 to 1916.

Kerfol, from Scribner's in March 1916, opens with a solitary house a host urges a visitor to buy. Ghosts, marriage bargains, and social traps recur through the set. A bibliography of Wharton's stories and poems accompanies the fiction. The volume suits readers tracing her growth. The stories show Wharton finding the voice of her later novels.
29631-journal-of-a-residence-at-bagdad-d:
Anthony N. Groves, missionary, kept this journal of a residence at Bagdad during the years 1830 and 1831, printed in London in 1832 by James Nisbet of Berners Street. Its spelling keeps period variants, from Mousul and Mosul to piastre and piaster, Shiraz and Sheeraz, as the transcriber notes. Groves writes of individuals, causes, and states of mind, in the manner of Paul and Barnabas narratives.

The journal closes a melancholy portion with satisfactory letters and a friend recovering daily his strength. Its pages give a missionary's view of Bagdad under Ottoman rule. Readers of mission and Middle East history will find a rare, first-hand journal from a city seldom described by English visitors of its day.
29983-st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-:
St. Nicholas Magazine for Boys and Girls, volume five, number ten, is dated August 1878, with a copyright that year by Scribner and Company. Its opening piece is King Cheese, a story of the Paris Exhibition of 1867, by J. T. Trowbridge, told in verse. The tale begins in the lovely land of the Swiss, a land of lakes, icy seas, chamois, chalets, musical boxes, watches, and cheese.

In its old town-hall, the quaint little town of Nulle gathers, amid sleek cattle resting in shadow or pool and dairy-maids carrying pail and stool. The burgomaster calls his fellow citizens, great and small, short and tall, to counsel. Ahead lies a wonderful show, a truly universal fair at Paris, where every country will carry its most beautiful, useful, or rare product. The burghers must choose what Nulle shall send for its honor and profit.
3023-faust-part-1:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe wrote Faust, Part 1, as the first part of his great drama of a scholar who bargains with the devil. Faust, weary of learning, opens a volume and applies himself to translating its sacred lore into his loved German tongue. He pauses at the words In the beginning was the Word, unable to prize the mere word so highly, and renders it instead as sense.

The play follows Faust through the pact with Mephistopheles, the love of Gretchen, and the ruin that follows knowledge and desire. Goethe's verse moves between philosophy, comedy, and lyric, and the translation problem in the opening scene mirrors the whole drama. Faust remains the central work of German literature, inexhaustible in reading.
30415-the-galaxy-january-1877-vol-23-no-:
The Galaxy, a magazine of entertaining reading, volume 23, January 1877 to June 1877, comes from Sheldon and Company in New York in 1877. Churchwell and Teall did the typography, and Smith and McDougal did the electrotyping. The index gives the administration of Abraham Lincoln by Gideon Welles, some old almanacs by Charles Wyllys Elliott, and Alnaschar, 1876, by Bret Harte.

Alfred de Musset and letters of Balzac by Henry James, Jr., applied science by Charles Barnard, art's limitations by Margaret J. Preston, Assja by Ivan Tourguéneff, a ballad of Constance by William Winter, the battalion by J. W. De Forest, beer by S. G. Young, and to Beethoven by Sidney Lanier follow. Cleopatra's soliloquy by Mary Bayard Clarke, an evening party with the Cossacks by David Ker, and the dead star by John James Piatt follow. A dead Vashti by Louise Stockton and drift-wood by Philip Quilibet fill the magazine's pages.
30626-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds Illustrated by Color Photography, volume one, number two, for February 1897, opens with a letter from the president of the National Teachers' Association. Written from the New York Department of Public Instruction, superintendent's office in Albany, on 26 December 1896, the letter praises the serial.

An HTML version offers the original lovely illustrations, and the issue continues the monthly's popular, juvenile bird portraits in color. Volume one, January to June 1897, later bound as a book, shows the series' early form. The February number suits families, teachers, and young naturalists learning birds by picture and plain text.
30651-paris-from-the-earliest-period-to-:
William Walton writes Paris from the Earliest Period to the Present Day, volume one. George Barrie and Son published it in Philadelphia in 1899, with a photogravure of the Seine at Bougival after Julius L. Stewart. Its motto runs in French: it floats without being submerged.

Volume one chapters cover Gallo-Roman and pre-medieval periods, the court and upper classes, and the bourgeois and lower classes. An illustration shows the Martyr of the Merovingian period, after a tapestry by F. Bac. Walton opens by imagining Paris as the most beautiful, witty, wicked, and artistic of towns, then traces its long history in rich detail.
30677-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Put out in Chicago by the Nature Study Publishing Company, this November 1897 issue is number five of volume two of Birds, a monthly serial shown in color photography. Its stated aim was to spread knowledge of bird life, and its pages mix short lives of birds with notes for readers who watched them in the field. The issue opens with a long piece on John James Audubon.

That opening piece praises Audubon's love of nature and fresh style, and retells scenes from his youth, including a cruel monkey killing his mother's parrot Mignonne. The shock, the writer says, helped turn the boy toward birds for life. For modern readers the issue offers both early bird study and a vivid taste of how Americans in the 1890s learned about, drew, and loved wild birds.
30726-cole-s-funny-picture-book-no-1:
E. W. Cole of Melbourne wrote and compiled this children's picture book, first published in 1879 and held here in a reprint billed as the seventy-third edition, totalling 920,000 copies. Cole, born at Woodchurch, Kent, in 1832, ran Cole's Book Arcade, which the book says held more than a million books, new and second-hand. Its full title calls it a family amuser and instructor, meant to delight children and make home happier.

Inside are pictures, choice riddles, games, and pieces of reading for adults as well as children. A note warns that later reprintings changed very little, so the edition numbers can mislead, yet the practice of counting each reprint was kept for interest. It is a lively piece of Australian publishing history, and a window on what families read and played with in the late nineteenth century.
30850-philippine-mats-philippine-craftsm:
Issued by the Bureau of Education in Manila in 1913, this bulletin is number one in the Philippine Craftsman Reprint Series. It reprints material from volume one, numbers three, four, and five, of The Philippine Craftsman, and it was made as a handy manual for teachers. Its purpose was to guide instruction in mat making, an important branch of industrial work in the islands.

Inside are directions for preparing mat materials, with color schemes and details for weaving a number of fine approved Philippine designs. The foreword notes that mats serve for sleeping and other household uses, and that better design and workmanship could make the craft a source of income in thousands of Filipino homes. It is a practical, illustrated record of a living craft and a colonial school program.
30965-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Put out in Chicago by the Nature Study Publishing Company, this December 1897 issue is number six of volume two of Birds, a monthly serial shown in color photography. Its stated aim was to spread knowledge of bird life, and its pages mix short lives of birds with notes for readers who watched them in the field. This issue opens with a report on the Ornithological Congress.

That congress was the fifteenth annual session of the American Ornithologists' Union, held for three days at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, November 9 to 11, 1897. Dr. C. Hart Merriam of the Department of Agriculture presided, with about one hundred and fifty members from nearly all states present. The first paper, by J. C. Merrill, honored Charles Emil Bendire and his work on American birds.
31004-ten-thousand-a-year-volume-1:
Samuel Warren, fellow of the Royal Society, wrote Ten Thousand a Year. It is held here in volume one of a Boston edition from Little, Brown and Company in 1900, printed at the University Press in Cambridge. The publishers' preface says a well-printed edition of this notable story had not been in print in England or America since its original publication in 1841. This edition was reason enough. It includes the author's notes on the many legal topics in the work.

Warren supplied thirty-three notes to the text, marked by numbers in square brackets, with the notes themselves at the end of the document. The volume is inscribed in October 1841 to Emily, a little blue-eyed, laughing image of purity and happiness, as a slight memorial of a father's affection for an only daughter. It is a Victorian novel with a legal mind, restored here with its author's notes.
31188-laramie-or-the-queen-of-bedlam-a-s:
Captain Charles King's 1889 novel, published by J. B. Lippincott in Philadelphia, is a story of frontier army life in the Sioux War of 1876, subtitled Laramie, or the Queen of Bedlam. It opens at a fort where the Platte rushes past under the Engineer Bridge. The smaller Laramie tributary rushes noisily down its stony bed past the commanding officer's house and the surgeon's quarters.

Bare gray-brown slopes shut the horizon south and west, while eastward lies the broad valley and northward a level flat streaked with hoof and wheel tracks to a distant bridge. Through that garrison world of soldiers, families, and frontier danger, King, himself a serving officer, tells a romance of the Sioux war years.
31368-glimpses-of-the-past-history-of-th:
W. O. Raymond's Glimpses of the Past, a history of the River St. John from 1604 to 1784, was published at St. John, New Brunswick, in 1905. Raymond, born and reared on the river's banks, writes in his preface of a lifelong love for its history and its people. The book appeared in connection with the tercentenary of the river's discovery by de Monts and Champlain on June 24, 1604.

Champlain, illustrated in the book as discoverer of the river and father of New France, anchors the early chapters. Later sections follow settlement, conflict, and daily life along the St. John through nearly two centuries. Raymond's local knowledge gives the history a grounded, affectionate quality. Readers of Canadian history will find a detailed regional study, built from a lifetime beside one river.
31616-health-lessons-book-1:
Alvin Davison's Health Lessons, book one, by the professor of biology at Lafayette College, was published by the American Book Company with copyright in 1910. An illustration caption sums up its teaching as exercise, fresh air, and well-chewed food for a strong, healthy body. Its contents move from caring for the health and the parts of the body, through feeding the body, to food and health, in short chapters for schoolchildren.

Davison writes the health textbook of the progressive era, when schools first taught hygiene as a subject. His lessons are practical: how to eat, breathe, exercise, and care for the body day by day. Readers of educational history will find a clear example of early health teaching, and parents will recognize advice that has changed less than one might expect.
31666-recreations-of-christopher-north-v:
Christopher North's Recreations, in a new edition in two volumes, opens with volume one, published by William Blackwood and Sons of Edinburgh and London in 1868. Its contents begin with Christopher in his sporting jacket, in three fyttes, then a tale of expiation, a morning monologue, and the field of flowers. Cottages follows, with an hour's talk about poetry.

The volume continues with Inch-Cruin, a day at Windermere, and the Moors, in a prologue and two flights to Glen-Etive and the coves of Cruachan. North's recreations mix tale, talk, and landscape sketch, and the volume gathers the lighter, reflective side of a writer better known for criticism.
31826-tales-from-blackwood-volume-1:
This first volume of Tales from Blackwood, published by William Blackwood and Sons at Edinburgh and London, gathers stories first printed in Blackwood's Magazine. Its contents include Professor Aytoun's The Glenmutchkin Railway, Vanderdecken's Message Home, The Floating Beacon, Colonna the Painter, J. G. Lockhart's Napoleon, Colonel E. B. Hamley's A Legend of Gibraltar, and William Mudford's The Iron Shroud.

Aytoun's railway tale, from October 1845, sketches the railway mania then in full progress in Glasgow and Edinburgh. Readers get a varied Victorian magazine anthology, mixing humor, sea stories, art, and military legend, in the voice of one of Britain's leading periodicals.
31908-with-the-world-s-great-travellers-:
With the World's Great Travellers, volume one, edited by Charles Morris and Oliver H. G. Leigh and published at Chicago in 1901, gathers first-class travel tales by brilliant men and women. Its preface argues that next to actual travel, reading such stories is the finest aid to broadening views and enlarging useful knowledge of people and the world's ways.

Contents include Harriet Martineau on winter and summer in New England. They also include Charles Morris on Niagara Falls, Henry Latham on New York to Washington in 1866, and pieces on Florida alligators, the Mammoth Cave, and plantation life in war times. Readers get an armchair world tour, from familiar American scenes to tropic and Arctic lands.
32190-the-works-of-alexander-pope-volume:
Volume one of the poetry in this new edition of Alexander Pope's works, published in London by John Murray in 1871, gathers Pope's early verse with scholarly apparatus. The new edition adds hundreds of unpublished letters and other new material, gathered in part by the late John Wilson Croker, with introductions and notes by the Reverend Whitwell Elwin. Portraits and other illustrations accompany the text.

The contents begin with a catalogue of Pope's collected editions, a memorial list of relations and friends, Warburton's advertisement, and an introduction, before the author's preface and recommendatory poems. Translations follow: the first book of Statius's Thebais, Sappho to Phaon and other pieces from Ovid, and January and May and The Wife of Bath from Chaucer. The Temple of Fame and the Pastorals, with a discourse on pastoral poetry, close the volume's main matter.
32271-a-struggle-for-rome-v-1:
Felix Dahn's A Struggle for Rome, volume one of three, translated from the German by Lily Wolffsohn, was published in London by Richard Bentley and Son in 1878. It is a historical romance of the sixth century. Its Geibel epigraph holds that if anything is more powerful than fate, it is the courage which bears it undismayed. Dahn's preface traces the pictures to his studies for The Kings of the Goths and for Procopius of Caesarea, on the migration of nations and the decay of the Roman Empire.

By referring to those works, Dahn writes, readers may tell what details and changes the romance added to reality. In history, the events described filled almost thirty years. For obvious reasons, the long interval had to be shortened, or at least disguised. Readers get a Gothic-Roman epic, where sixth-century history becomes romance, compressed but grounded in scholarship.
32471-stories-pictures-tell-book-1:
Flora L. Carpenter's Stories Pictures Tell, Book One, published in Chicago and New York in 1918, teaches picture study through stories about famous paintings. Carpenter, instructor in drawing at Waite High School in Toledo, Ohio, wrote for teachers who enjoyed picture work with children but lacked time to gather material. Art supervisors assigned picture study in each grade, yet teachers often found much about artists and little about their pictures.

Contents follow the school year. Millet's Feeding Her Birds and Van Dyck's Children of Charles I come in September and October. Raphael's Madonna of the Chair, Reynolds's Miss Bowles, and Bouguereau's Two Mothers and Their Families follow. A review of pictures and artists, with suggestions to teachers, closes the book. Half-tone photographs illustrate each lesson.
32829-a-concise-history-and-directory-of:
A concise history and directory of Norwich for 1811, printed by C. Berry of Dove-Lane in 1810, lists the city's residents, trades, and institutions. The editor's address, dated Norwich, October 19, 1810, notes that nine years had passed since the last directory. Fewer than half the old entries still stood at the same address, so the lists were much augmented and corrected.

Population tables compare the parishes across 1693, 1752, 1786, and 1801, parish by parish. The directory records charitable and public institutions found nowhere else, in alphabetical order corrected to the first vowel. Its trade notes praise the keels and wherries running between Norwich and Yarmouth, carrying fifteen to fifty tons with crews of two. The passage to Yarmouth, thirty-two miles, could be made in five hours.
3295-the-poems-of-emma-lazarus-volume-1:
This first volume of Emma Lazarus's poems holds narrative, lyric, and dramatic verse, with a biographical sketch to open. Epochs, the opening sequence, moves through youth, regret, longing, storm, and surprise, tracing a young poet's growth in five moods. Lazarus, a New York poet of the late nineteenth century, writes with a formal grace learned from older models.

A transcriber's note marks two famous pieces. Sunrise is an elegy to President James A Garfield, who died on 19 September 1881 from a gunshot wound received in July. The New Colossus, her sonnet of welcome, is engraved on the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty. The volume shows the poet before that fame: serious, musical, and already public minded.
33051-momotaro-or-little-peachling-japan:
Momotaro, or Little Peachling, number one in the Japanese Fairy Tale Series published by T. Hasegawa in Tokyo, tells one of Japan's best-loved tales in a small, illustrated book. Long ago, an elderly man headed for the mountains to cut grass, while an elderly woman headed for the river to wash clothes. As she washed, a huge object came crashing and splashing downstream toward her. Using a length of bamboo to draw it near, she found an enormous peach, and splitting it open revealed a child inside.

That child, Momotaro, grows into the peach boy hero who sets out with animal companions to face the ogres of his island tale. Hasegawa's books introduced Japanese fairy tales to Western readers in charming form. This first number is short, bright, and made for reading aloud, and it remains a perfect first meeting with a classic Japanese story.
33433-sketches-of-aboriginal-life-americ:
V. V. Vide's Sketches of Aboriginal Life, American Tableaux number one, presents scenes of Native American life in verse and prose. Its chapter headings, set in Gothic type, and its notes, placed at each chapter's end, frame a work that aims to picture the old ways in tableaux, or living pictures. The book was published by Buckland and Sumner, with standardized punctuation.

The sketches suit readers of early American literature, offering a period view of Native life as white writers imagined it. Their tone is romantic and dated, reflecting the tableaux fashion of their day. For students of representation, they are a revealing source on how aboriginal life was staged for nineteenth-century readers.
3366-a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-1:
William Dean Howells opens A Hazard of New Fortunes with a bibliographical note on his own move. The story was the first fruit of his New York life, begun after a quarter century in Cambridge and Boston ending in 1889. He used his own transition to the commercial metropolis in framing the experience of his supposititious literary adventurer, Basil March.

March, with his wife, is a character Howells employed in some six books, and the note names that history. Part one follows the Marches to New York, to a magazine, and to the hazards of a new fortune in a new city. Readers meeting Howells's New York novel here get its foundation: an editor's household transplanted, and a city waiting to test it.
3371-their-silver-wedding-journey-volume:
William Dean Howells opens the Marches' silver wedding journey in this first volume. The business side insists March needs a rest, noting that both his wife and his doctor want him to travel. It is his sabbatical year besides, the argument runs, and he could file plenty of copy for the magazine. March replies, in the novel's dry opening exchange, by asking whether that is his notion of a sabbatical.

An 1899 edition note cautions that some chapter numbers appear misordered or absent, while assuring readers no text is missing across the three volumes. The journey that follows retraces the wedding trip after twenty-five years. Readers get the Marches older, Europe changed, and a marriage tested by time rather than by novelty.
3375-the-landlord-at-lion-s-head-volume-:
William Dean Howells opens The Landlord at Lion's Head with a bibliographical note on its origin. In dim recesses of consciousness where things have their beginning, he supposes, the novel may be traced to a fact. That fact was a fortnight's sojourn on the western shore of Lake Champlain in the summer of 1891. Across the water in Vermont stood constantly before his eyes a majestic mountain form.

That form, the Lion's Head, gives the novel its place and its landlord. A mountain hotel, a family, and a summer's company grow from that fortnight's view. Readers starting the novel here get its ground first: lake, mountain, and a house built to face both, in Howells's patient, observant prose.
33797-sinister-street-vol-1:
Compton Mackenzie's Sinister Street opens in this first volume, which holds two books: The Prison House and Classic Education. The title, Mackenzie warns in a note dated 1913, is symbolic and bears no heraldic meaning. The novel follows a boy's mind as it moves from childhood toward the unsettled years between boyhood and manhood.

Mackenzie treats that middle stretch as a ferment, when character is undecided and the way of life is still uncertain. School, home, and first hopes shape the young hero in turn. The volume sets up a long coming-of-age story told with close attention to a boy's inner life.
33800-the-mysteries-of-paris-illustrated:
Eugène Sue opens his vast Parisian melodrama in this first volume of The Mysteries of Paris. It is illustrated with etchings by Mercier, Bicknell, Poiteau, and Adrian Marcel in a de luxe edition limited to one thousand copies. Twenty-six chapters move from the tapis-franc and the ogress through the history of La Goualeuse and the Chourineur, an arrest, Thomas Seyton and Countess Sarah, your money or your life, a walk.

Later chapters follow Murphy and Rodolph, a rendezvous, preparations, a bleeding heart, a vault, a sick-nurse, punishment, the Isle Adam, recompense, departure, researches, and the history of David and Cecily. Later chapters also follow a house in the Rue du Temple, four stories, Tom and Sarah, and a ball. Sue's underworld Paris, with its thieves, fallen women, and disguised prince, set the pattern for the city-mysteries genre.
33847-the-history-of-cuba-vol-1:
Willis Fletcher Johnson wrote this history of Cuba, with volume one published in New York in 1920. Johnson, a professor of American foreign relations at New York University, opens with Columbus and the claim that in Cuba the annals of America begin. Early chapters weigh where Columbus first landed and what the island's first peoples were like.

The volume traces discovery, conquest, and the growth of Spanish Cuba in clear, ordered chapters. Johnson writes for a general reader, with maps and pictures to aid the story. It remains a useful early American account of Cuba's first centuries.
33929-dixmude-the-epic-of-the-french-mar:
Charles Le Goffic wrote this account of Dixmude, a stand by French marines in October and November 1914, as part of a series on soldiers' tales of the Great War. The marines held a Belgian town against a German push toward the coast, in weeks when the front was still taking shape. Le Goffic tells the fight as an epic of endurance.

The book follows sailors turned soldiers through mud, shell fire, and close fighting, with officers and men named for their steadiness. It was meant for readers at home who wanted to grasp what the early war cost. The account still reads as a tribute to a small force that held a vital point.
3405-ragged-lady-volume-1:
This first volume of William Dean Howells's novel introduces Clementina Claxon, a country girl called the ragged lady. The story opens on rural roads, where her party must stop and ask at a house set back among pine woods which way to take for South Middlemount. Clementina, sharp tongued and watchful, already shows the pride and humor that will carry her through the book.

Howells follows her from this plain country life toward wider society, with family talk, small humiliations, and early hopes. The volume sets up the questions the second half answers: how far can a poor girl rise, and what will she give up to do it. It reads as a gentle social novel, rich in dialogue and New England detail.
34073-the-new-gresham-encyclopedia-a-to-:
Angelo S. Rappoport, R. F. Patterson, and John Dougall edited this first part of volume one of the New Gresham Encyclopedia, published in London in 1922 by the Gresham Publishing Company. Plates include coloured algae as frontispiece, aeroplane, air-ships, human anatomy, archaeology of stone, bronze, and iron ages, architecture, and bacteria.

Maps in colour cover Africa, Asia, and Australia, and a list of contributors opens the volume. Entries run from A toward amide, with pronunciation guides for the reader. The encyclopedia serves homes and schools with pictures and maps. It remains a handsome record of early twentieth-century knowledge.
3646-the-dwelling-place-of-light-volume-:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, opens his industrial novel with a glacier image for modern life. Bewildered and helpless people, he writes, are torn from the parent rock, crushed, rolled smooth, and left stranded in strange places. So Edward Bumpus is severed from the ancestral ledge, from the firm granite of seemingly stable things, and cast into a new industrial world.

The first volume sets the scene in a New England mill town, where Puritan churches try to compromise with an age of anarchy and produce a medley of rounded towers stained mulberry. Workers, ministers, and owners meet in a town changing fast. The novel suits readers who enjoy large American stories of labor, faith, and the cost of industry.
3662-oscar-wilde-his-life-and-confession:
Frank Harris writes a life and confessions of Oscar Wilde in this first volume, drawing on his own friendship with Wilde. Harris knew Wilde in London at the height of his fame, and he writes about the playwright's wit, his success, and the circles that adored him. This volume covers Wilde's early life, his rise, and the years before his fall.

Harris writes as a partisan friend, defending Wilde and attacking his enemies with equal heat. Readers should weigh his account against other lives, since Harris shapes the story to his own loyalties. The volume suits readers who want Wilde in the voice of a man who knew him, vivid, opinionated, and close to the scene.
3681-mr-crewe-s-career-volume-1:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, opens his political novel with a portrait of Hilary Vane, more often called the Honourable Hilary Vane. Vane, of Camden Street in the hills near Ripton, boasts that he never held an office in his life. Yet he stands as trustee for many people and institutions, deacon of the first church, and a lawyer of such ability that his word moves the state.

This first volume sets the world that the young reformer Mr Crewe will challenge: a small state run by railroads, lawyers, and quiet bargains. Churchill writes New Hampshire politics with the detail of a man who knew it. The volume suits readers who enjoy American political novels, where ideals meet the machine.
3736-a-far-country-volume-1:
Winston Churchill, the American novelist, opens his long novel of modern America with the youth of Hugh Paret. Hugh calls himself a corporation lawyer by accident of environment. He offers his book as the autobiography of a romanticist, a man who took his country as the happy hunting ground of enlightened self interest. The first volume follows him through home, school, and university, tracing how a bright boy learns to want the prizes his age offers.

Churchill writes the inner life as carefully as the outer, weighing motives with frankness and a sharp eye for social climbing. A chance meeting at a mailbox, a twisted smile from a young woman, and the shame that follows show how small moments bend a life. Readers who like serious novels of ambition will find this opening volume a firm foundation for the whole work.
3835-correspondence-of-wagner-and-liszt-:
This first volume gathers the letters of Richard Wagner and Franz Liszt, translated by Francis Hueffer. The correspondence shows a friendship that was also a working alliance, as Liszt at Weimar made his small city a focus of Wagner's fame. Wagner writes with gratitude for the brilliant articles on Lohengrin coming from Weimar, contrasting them with the jealous enmity of Dresden critics who worked to confuse the public.

The letters cover scores, productions, money troubles, and the daily business of getting new music heard. Wagner calls Weimar a blessed asylum where he can breathe freely and ease a troubled heart. Music lovers will find the volume a close view of two great careers in harness, with admiration, advice, and occasional friction all in the writers' own words.
3838-memoirs-of-marguerite-de-valois-que:
Marguerite de Valois, queen of Navarre and wife of the future Henri the Fourth, wrote these memoirs of the French court in the years 1565 to 1582. The publisher's note calls her witty and beautiful, with black sparkling eyes and a saucy vivacity that fills her anecdotes. The first volume follows her youth among the Guises, the Medici, and the great lords whose quarrels would soon drown France in blood.

A central passage shows her mother, Catherine de Medici, excusing the Guise attempt on Admiral Coligny's life as a son's revenge for his father's death. Marguerite records the excuse with grief in her mother's looks and words. Readers who like court memoirs will find a vivid and personal history, told by a queen who watched the wars of religion from inside the palace.
3847-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
Madame de Montespan opens her memoirs with a translator's plea for fairness, since historians took their view from narrow and malicious contemporaries. Her recollections, avowedly desultory and out of order, offer unconscious self portraiture of a court lady whose beauty bewitched a great king and whose sarcasm made duchesses tremble. The first book sets her at court among rivals, queens, and cardinals.

A lottery anecdote shows her luck and nerve, as tickets are registered beforehand and a young queen, tightening a slipping garter, hands Montespan her ticket to hold. Montespan returns her own ticket instead, and her number wins a portrait of the king set in brilliants, to the surprise of the queen mother and the cardinal. Readers who like court comedy will find the opening book sly and sparkling.
3927-prince-zilah-volume-1:
Jules Claretie opens Prince Zilah with a Hungarian prince and a gypsy girl's gift. Andras Zilah looks at the girl and asks what talisman she offered, and she answers with pebbles from the lakes of Tatra, sewn in a little leather bag. Old legends call those lakes the eyes of the sea. There the most beautiful carbuncle in the world lies hidden, guarded by frogs with diamond eyes and lumps of pure gold for feet.

Andras feels more touched than astonished at the superstition, and at an offer Prince Sandor refused with a smile the evening before. The volume sets a prince of old Hungary against Paris society and gypsy faith. Readers who like Claretie's romantic novels will find a first volume of legend, pride, and a gift that carries a fate.
3931-zibeline-volume-1:
Philippe de Massa opens Zibeline with a card game played for a fortune. A debtor, more eager to play to the gallery than to reduce his enormous sum, proposes six hands of bezique at ten francs a point. His opponent agrees at once, a circle forms around the two players, and curiosity runs through the assembly at the exciting match.

Bezique uses four packs of cards, and points may continue indefinitely, but a player must win at least one thousand points at the end of each hand or be said to fail. The volume sets a Paris world of gambling, gallantry, and debt in motion. Readers who like Massa's brilliant romances will find a first volume of wagers, wit, and a hero living beyond his means.
3935-a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-vol:
Andre Theuriet opens A Woodland Queen with an inheritance that may or may not exist. Intercourse has long been broken off between two families, and Julien de Buxieres has placed no reliance on chimerical hopes from his elder kinsman. He receives almost with indifference the official news of the death of Claude Odouart de Buxieres.

By direct line from his late father, Julien becomes the only legitimate heir of the chateau and lands of Vivey. Yet a strong probability remains that Claude made a will in favor of someone within his own circle, and a second missive from Arbillot the notary may settle it. Readers who like Theuriet's country novels will find a first volume of woods, houses, and a young man's uncertain fortune.
3939-the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-ce:
Alfred de Musset opens The Confession of a Child of the Century with a young man undone by jealousy. Hearing nothing from his mistress since his last letter, he asks what she is doing, whether she loves another, and whom he shall love in return. A distant voice answers that two beings who love and embrace, and who are not thou and I, cannot be possible, and calls him a fool.

His friend Desgenais counsels contempt, asking when he will forget that woman, whether she is such a great loss, and why he does not take the first comer and console himself. The narrator answers no, it is not such a great loss, and boasts that he drove her away. Readers who like Musset's Romantic confession will find a first volume of pride, pain, and self deception.
3943-monsieur-de-camors-volume-1:
Octave Feuillet opens Monsieur de Camors with a portrait of an old counsellor near a throne. Had Liberty been mother to this old gentleman, the narrator says, and had he met her in a clump of woods, he would have strangled her. He terms old duffers such ministers as he suspects of liberal views, especially those in favor of popular education.

A more hurtful counsellor never approached a throne, yet luckily, while near it in office, he was far from it in influence. He remains a charming man, gallant and fresh, more gallant than fresh, with habits not too good, haunting the greenroom of the opera. He has two daughters, recently married, before whom he repeats his maxims. Readers who like Feuillet's society novels will find a first volume of reaction, charm, and a family to come.
3947-cinq-mars-volume-1:
Alfred de Vigny opens Cinq Mars with a household divided by loyalty. A guest declares he has just written to his nephew to disinherit him if he has passed over to the Emperor, as report says he has. Another guest, remarkable for knots, ribbons, and tags, wears the black cordon of the Order of Saint Michael. He bows and says all faithful subjects ought to speak thus.

The Marechal answers that Launay deceives himself very much. Persons of their blood are subjects only at their own pleasure, he says. God has caused them to be born as much lords of their lands as the king is of his. Readers who like Vigny's historical romance will find a first volume of pride, conspiracy, and Richelieu's France taking shape.
3954-l-abbe-constantin-volume-1:
Ludovic Halevy opens L'Abbe Constantin with a young man slipping away to a ball he was never invited to. The narrator catches Roger de Puymartin escaping furtively, catches him in the hall, and proposes going home together. Roger answers he is not going home at all, but to the ball at Mrs Scott's, and invites the narrator along.

Neither man has been invited, Roger admits, but he goes with a friend who scarcely knows the Scotts, enough to introduce them. He adds that the narrator has seen Mrs Scott on horseback in the Bois, but not in a low gown, and her shoulders are shoulders which ought to be seen. Readers who like Halevy's comedy will find a first volume of Americans, clergy, and Parisian daring.
3958-a-romance-of-youth-volume-1:
Francois Coppee opens A Romance of Youth with a schoolyard that mocks its own advertisement. The ground is graveled with stones from the river, with a paved gutter where one could gather half a dozen lost marbles, a broken top, and shoe nails. After recreation hours one could gather still more. A solitary sycamore is supposed to justify the illusion of the garden promised in the advertisement.

Trees have common sense, the narrator jokes, so this one should know it is not a garden by itself. It stands at one side of the gymnasium portico, in a rectangle formed by a prison wall bristling with broken bottle glass and three distressing buildings. Readers who like Coppee's schoolboy Paris will find a first volume of childhood, irony, and a tree given an unjust fate.
3963-cosmopolis-volume-1:
Paul Bourget opens Cosmopolis with talkers in Rome, where a man who has studied many languages holds forth at a street corner like the hero of a Russian novel. Montfanon listens with an impenetrable air, a man awaiting the end in religious solitude, for whom nothing gives greater pleasure than the discussion of ideas. He feels with extreme ardor, and is almost pained by the partly ironical dilettanteism of Dorsenne.

Author and monk share common ground, yet their tempers differ, one enthusiastic and one detached. The volume sets up Bourget's international Rome, where French, English, American, and Italian lives cross in drawing rooms and churches. Readers who like Bourget's psychological novels will find a first volume of ideas, faith, and cosmopolitan society.
3968-jacqueline-volume-1:
Th. Bentzon, writing as Madame Blanc, opens her French novel in the home of a deputy to the French Chamber and his daughter Jacqueline. The father loves his home but is rarely in it, absorbed by committee work and reports that keep him from family life.

Into that gap steps a clever stepmother, whose watchful ways set the tone for the household. Jacqueline, bright and keen-eyed, learns to read the adults around her and to hold her own ground. The volume lays the groundwork for the quarrels to come, with Paris politics at the edge of the frame and a young woman's pride at its center.
3972-the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-volume-:
Rene Bazin's diary novel opens in late December 1884 with a young scholar seeking help for his thesis on the Junian Latins. These were poor slaves freed in a way that strict Roman law did not accept, and the puzzle has caught his full interest.

He calls on a teacher named Flamaran, hoping to pull his Latin freedmen out of a scholarly mess. The dated entries mix study, visits, and self-mockery, giving a lively sense of student life in Paris. Readers who enjoy a quiet, witty record of a young mind at work will find the volume a gentle start to a longer story of duty and hope.
3976-fromont-and-risler-volume-1:
Alphonse Daudet opens his Paris novel on the shared landing of a poor family's home, a space that serves as an extra room in summer. Women talk there, children play there, and little Chebe is sent there when her noise grows too much indoors.

From that small stage Daudet widens the view to the business house of Fromont and the people tied to it by work and kin. The volume sets up Risler, Sidonie, and the Fromont family, with Paris trade and tenement life close at hand. Readers meet a world where a firm's fortunes and a family's hopes rise and fall together.
3981-gerfaut-volume-1:
Charles de Bernard's French novel opens at the castle of Bergenheim, where a lady startled by thunder rushes into a great room of polished chestnut wood. Three windows light the long room, and the middle one opens like a door onto a balcony.

The castle sets the stage for a story of love, honor, and rank, as guests and hosts weigh duty against feeling. Bernard builds the scene with care for place and manners, letting the old house itself speak for the world its people inhabit. The volume draws readers into a slow, courtly drama where a glance or a word can carry great weight.
3986-conscience-volume-1:
Hector Malot opens his novel of guilt with Saniel and Glady walking a rain-washed Paris street, where wet asphalt shines like a mirror. Talk turns to a man named Brigard, whom Saniel is said to have wounded by his words.

The volume sets up a rich man's refusal and the strain it puts on a doctor's pride and purse. Saniel, keen and hard-working, faces a world where money and favor decide much, and where one slight can fester. Malot builds the crime story slowly, from talk and slight to the darker acts that conscience will later force its hero to face.
3991-madame-chrysantheme-volume-1:
Pierre Loti, born Louis-Marie-Julien Viaud at Rochefort in 1850, served in the French Navy from 1867 to 1900 and rose to captain. His comrades called the timid young midshipman Loti, after a small Indian flower, and the name stuck to the writer he became.

The first volume of his Japan novel draws on that naval life, setting a French officer among the sights, homes, and customs of a port town. Loti writes as a witness, keen on color and mood, and the book's charm lies in close, firsthand scenes. Readers meet a tale of a brief marriage and a strange land, told with the eye of a sailor abroad.
3996-an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-volum:
Emile Souvestre's Paris journal opens on New Year's Day, when the writer wakes with the new month in mind and turns his thoughts back to the year just buried. While crowds welcome the young sister year, he mourns the old queen wrapped in her winding sheet.

The volume sets the journal's pattern: short dated notes from a top-floor room, mixing city sights with quiet moral thought. New Year gifts, winter streets, and small home scenes each open a brief lesson. Readers who like slow, reflective books will enjoy this gentle start to a Paris diary that finds meaning in ordinary days.
4057-marius-the-epicurean-volume-1:
Walter Pater's philosophical romance opens in the grave early years of Marius, a Roman youth whose mother's death turns feeling into questioning. The death brings his affections and their likely loss into full view, making him a seeker after how to live.

A chapter called The Tree of Knowledge sets the tone, with Latin tags and long, meditative prose. Pater follows Marius through schools, rites, and ideas of the ancient world, weighing Epicurean calm against duty and faith. Readers who enjoy slow, beautiful prose about the life of the mind will find the first volume a rich, demanding start.
4071-monsieur-lecoq-v-1:
Emile Gaboriau's detective novel opens its first volume with Monsieur Lecoq, the young police agent, studying a prisoner. Lecoq doubts that a man could hide his feelings under the humiliating formalities of arrest, formalities that can be pushed to the verge of insult.

Sure that disgrace will make the prisoner revolt, lose self-control, and speak, Lecoq watches for the revealing word. Gaboriau builds the case from small signs, false names, and patient reasoning. Readers who love the roots of detective fiction will enjoy this first volume of a classic French mystery.
4101-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's history of the Mayflower opens its first volume with the Speedwell, the first vessel the Leyden Pilgrims bought for their emigration. The Speedwell carried the originators from Delfshaven to Southampton, to join the Mayflower as her consort.

Her leaks and delays became a deciding factor in the Mayflower's late departure for New England. Ames tells the story from logs, lists, and letters, with care for ships, men, and dates. Readers who want the Pilgrim voyage in full detail will find this volume a solid, scholarly start. Later volumes follow ship, crew, and passengers in turn.
4235-dynevor-terrace-or-the-clue-of-life:
Charlotte M. Yonge, author of The Heir of Redclyffe, set this novel in a terrace of respectable houses where several families live close enough to watch, judge, and marry one another. The first volume opens with Charlotte, a girl of seventeen, and moves through schoolroom memories, farewells, family compacts, and new arrivals.

Yonge's clue of life is a moral one: her characters look for a guiding rule in everyday choices about duty, marriage, and faith. The chapters mix domestic comedy with serious reflection, and the novel rewards readers who enjoy long Victorian family stories told with attention to manners, conscience, and the small crises of provincial life.
4257-andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-mili:
John McElroy, late of Company L of the 16th Illinois Cavalry, wrote this account of fifteen months as a prisoner of the Confederacy. It first appeared in 1879. The opening volume follows his capture and his time in Richmond. It then follows the move to Andersonville.

McElroy describes the crowded stockade and the shortage of food and shelter. He describes the daily struggle to stay alive. He writes as a private soldier rather than an officer, and his detail is concrete. The book was meant to put the prison experience on record while survivors could still speak.
4262-the-golden-bowl-volume-1:
Henry James published The Golden Bowl in 1904. This first volume contains Book First: The Prince. It introduces the Prince, a modern Roman at home in London. He finds by the Thames a stronger image of empire than in contemporary Rome. He drifts through Bond Street shop windows filled with silver, gold, and precious stones.

The volume sets up the marriage at the novel's center. The Prince marries Maggie Verver, daughter of the wealthy American collector Adam Verver. A close friendship with Charlotte shadows the marriage. James works through fine shades of motive and perception. The golden bowl of the title waits as a beautiful object with a hidden flaw.
4401-the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-e:
George Meredith's Arabian entertainment begins in this first volume with Shibli Bagarag, nephew of a barber, sent to shave the enchanted Shagpat. The contents list the thwackings, the story of Bhanavar the Beautiful, the betrothal, and the punishment of Shahpesh the Persian. The genie Karaz, the well of Paravid, and the horse Garraveen follow.

Meredith tells the quest in mock-oriental prose, nesting tale within tale as Shibli gathers the means to break the enchantment. The talking hawk, Goorelka of Oolb, and the lily of the enchanted sea await in later parts. This volume sets the fantastic machinery in motion, with humor and high romance.
4406-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volum:
George Meredith wrote this novel of a father's system for raising a son, and the first volume opens at Raynham Abbey. Its contents list the inmates of the abbey, the fates selecting Richard's fourteenth birthday to try the system, the magian conflict, arson, and Adrian plying his hook. Later chapters bring juvenile stratagems and Daphne's bower.

The system is Sir Austin Feverel's scientific plan to keep his son pure, recorded in aphorisms from The Pilgrim's Scrip. Meredith shows the plan meeting real boys, real girls, and real tempers. The first volume sets the ordeal in motion, with comedy and irony, as theory collides with youth.
4413-sandra-belloni-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni introduces Emilia, a young Italian singer, to the English ladies of Brookfield. The contents open with the Poles' prelude and an expedition by moonlight, then follow Wilfrid's diplomacy and Emilia's first trial in public. She plays the cornet, supplies the key to herself, and continues her performance.

Threats of a crisis in the government of Brookfield follow, with the virtue resident in a tail-coat, and a big drum speeding the march of Emilia's history. Rival clubs and the ladies of Brookfield at school close the book. Emilia's voice, and the English manners around it, set Meredith's comedy in motion.
4421-rhoda-fleming-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's Rhoda Fleming introduces the Kentish family at Queen Anne's Farm, with the might of the money demon and a text from scripture in the contents. The sisters meet, Edward and Algernon appear, and great news from Dahlia sets the plot moving. Mrs. Lovell is introduced, and Robert intervenes.

The book closes with Dahlia not visible and an indicative duet in a minor key. Rhoda, the steadfast sister, watches Dahlia's fall and the family's shame with a clear eye. Meredith's novel of seduction and honor begins here, in Kentish fields and farmhouse talk, before London takes the story over.
4427-evan-harrington-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens above buttons, with the heritage of the son and the daughters of the shears. Evan is a tailor's son, and his sisters dream of gentility while his father's trade hangs over them. On board the Jocasta, the family and the funeral, and a gentleman on the road set the story moving.

Mother and son close the book, after Evan meets the world that will judge him by his birth. Meredith's comedy turns on a single secret: the hero's father cut cloth, while his sisters pass as countesses. This first volume plants the joke and the danger together, with high spirits.
4435-vittoria-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's Vittoria opens up Monte Motterone and on the heights, introducing Signorina Vittoria, the singer who will become a voice of Italian revolution. Ammiani's intercession, a spy, a warning, and Barto Rizzo follow, with a letter closing the book. The Alps frame a story of conspiracy.

Vittoria, an English girl turned Italian patriot, sings for a cause that may cost her life. Meredith sets her among conspirators, soldiers, and lovers, with the mountains above and the Austrian police below. This first volume plants the revolt's hopes, and Vittoria's double life as artist and agent.
4444-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book One of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens with the hero as a subject of contention, a boy fought over by his family. The contents list an adventure on his own account, Dipwell Farm, a taste of grandeur, a dear friend, and a tale of a goose. Harry tells his own story, with energy and humor.

Later books in this volume follow a free life on the road, Janet Ilchester, and an evening with Captain Bulsted. An expedition, the great fog and the fire at midnight, and a voyage bound on the Priscilla follow. Harry's father, a charming adventurer, hovers over the boy's youth, and the novel's comedy of fortune begins.
4453-beauchamp-s-career-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career introduces Nevil Beauchamp as the champion of his country, with uncle, nephew, and baronial views of the present time. A glimpse of Nevil in action follows, with Renee, love in Venice, and an awakening for both. A night on the Adriatic and morning at sea under the Alps close the book.

Nevil, a naval officer of strong feeling, returns to England with ideals that will clash with family, party, and love. Meredith sets his hero's ardor against the baronial world of his uncle, Lord Romfrey. This first volume plants the novel's themes: honor, reform, and the cost of holding fast to principle.
4461-the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-w:
Book One of George Meredith's Tragic Comedians opens with a defense of the word fantastical, scorned by reviewers yet constantly useful. Claimants to the epithet lie outside books and poets, Meredith argues, in nature foremost, wherever sunlight lets her push forth fantastically. Human nature, that wandering ship of drunken pilot and mutinous crew, fits the word no less.

The novel retells the love of Ferdinand Lassalle, socialist orator, and Helene von Donniges, with its brilliance and folly. This first volume sets the pair, their world, and Meredith's ironic tone. Readers meet a heroine and hero who are grand, charming, and fatally theatrical, in a study of love as performance.
4465-diana-of-the-crossways-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways introduces Diana Warwick through diaries and diarists, then an Irish ball in the capital's assembly rooms. The interiors of Redworth and Sullivan Smith follow, with hints of Diana's experiences and what they led to. A scrupulous gentleman who came too late appears.

The book's chapters follow the couple, the crisis, and a practical man and a divining woman learning to respect one another. Diana, brilliant, witty, and Irish, enters London society with a past and a pen. This first volume sets her gifts, her marriage, and her fall from favor in motion, with Meredith's ironic sympathy.
4471-one-of-our-conquerors-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's One of Our Conquerors opens across London Bridge, through the vague to the infinitely little, with old Veuve and a second bottle. A London walk westward follows, with Nataly, a general man of the world, and a professional. Some familiar guests appear, with an inspection of Lakelands.

Skepsey in motion closes the book, with the couple justified of love having sight of their scourge. Victor Radnor, conqueror in business and love, lives with Nataly outside marriage, while his wife lives apart. This first volume sets the novel's grand theme: success, secrecy, and the price paid by a daughter.
4477-lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta opens with love at a school, Lady Charlotte, the tutor, and recognition. Shades of Browny and Matey advance and retire, in Meredith's playful manner, as the old soldier Lord Ormont and young Aminta meet. The contents of later books promise languor, prattlers, and a bruised warrior.

This first volume plants an unequal marriage: a veteran of reputation and a girl of spirit, judged by a society that loves scandal. Meredith's comedy follows their game with sympathy for both. Readers meet the novel's chief players early, and the terms of its long contest between age, youth, and the world's talk.
4483-the-amazing-marriage-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's Amazing Marriage opens with Dame Gossip as chorus, telling of the elopement of the Countess of Cressett with the old buccaneer. Charles Dump the postillion conducts them, and a great county family watches. Dame Gossip's introductory meanderings end in her sudden extinction.

Morning and farewell to an old home follow, with a mountain walk in mist and sunshine, the natural philosopher, and the lady's letter. The amazing marriage itself, between Fleetwood and Carinthia, takes shape through gossip, elopement, and county talk. This first volume sets Meredith's most gossipy comedy in motion.
4489-celt-and-saxon-volume-1:
Book One of George Meredith's Celt and Saxon, published in 1910, opens with an excursion in a Celtic mind. A young Irish gentleman of the O'Donnells, a Patrick, leads the reader into questions of Irish and English character. Mr. Adister, Caroline, and the princess follow, with scenes at the pianos chiefly without music.

A consultation gives opinions upon Welsh women and the Cambrian race, with the miniature, Captain Con, and Mrs. Adister O'Donnell. The captain's cabin, the brothers, and a new character close the book. Meredith's unfinished novel of nations begins here, witty about Celt and Saxon, and fond of its Irish talkers.
4534-sylvia-s-lovers-volume-1:
Elizabeth Gaskell published Sylvia's Lovers in three volumes in 1863, and this file holds the first volume alone. It opens in Monkshaven, a whaling town on the north-east coast of England, at the end of the eighteenth century, when the town held about half its later size. Sylvia Robson, her family, and Philip Hepburn enter the story against a background of Greenland whalers, new cloaks, and homecomings.

Chapters move from the town and the returning sailors to the press-gang, a sailor's funeral, and the slow growth of attraction and rivalry. Gaskell writes with close attention to dialect, work, and family feeling. Readers of this volume get the groundwork of the novel: a small port, a young woman courted by two men, and a war at sea that will soon break into private lives.
4609-the-letters-of-horace-walpole-earl-:
Horace Walpole's letters appear here in the first of four volumes, covering 1735 to 1748, with many letters now first published from the original manuscripts. The volume opens with a preface, advertisements, a letter from Sir Charles Grey linking Walpole with Junius, and a sketch of Walpole's life by Lord Dover. Then come Walpole's reminiscences of the courts of George the First and George the Second.

Those reminiscences move through George the First's reign, the house of Brunswick, the Duchess of Kendal, and the intrigues around Sir Robert Walpole, with Bolingbroke waiting in the wings. Readers get gossip, politics, and portraiture from a master letter-writer, at close range to power. This volume suits readers of eighteenth-century history who like their politics told through personalities, letters, and court talk.
4679-johnson-s-lives-of-the-poets-volume:
Samuel Johnson's Lives of the English Poets appears here in a volume covering Addison, Savage, and Swift, transcribed from the 1888 Cassell edition. Johnson wrote these lives as introductions to a trade edition of poets chosen by booksellers for republication. Sometimes, the introduction notes, they dealt briefly with men the public has long ceased to care about. Richard Savage would be such a man, if Johnson's account had not secured him lasting remembrance.

Johnson published his life of Savage at thirty-five, while his other lives appeared when his age had about doubled. He was very poor when he wrote Savage, and that life holds no less interest than the lives of Addison and Swift between which it sits. Readers get three classic Johnson biographies, sharp in judgement and rich in anecdote, and a fine entry to his Lives as a whole.
4681-frederick-chopin-as-a-man-and-music:
Frederick Niecks wrote Frederick Chopin as a Man and Musician in two volumes, and this file holds volume one, in its third edition of 1902. It opens with prefaces to the first edition of 1888, the second of 1890, and the 1902 edition, then a proem on Poland and the Poles, followed by chapters one through nineteen. Niecks states his method plainly in the first preface.

A novelist, he says, may follow artistic instinct freely, while a biographer is fettered by subject matter. The biographer must accept a compromise between the desirable and the necessary, rather than shape facts into perfect form at the cost of truth. Niecks therefore gives readers facts and his own conclusions, so they can judge for themselves. This volume covers Chopin's Polish roots and early life and work.
4719-wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-cons:
John Richardson opens Wacousta, or The Prophecy, in this first volume of three, with a preface on the earlier history of the country. Shortly after France ceded the Canadas to England, Pontiac, great head of the Indian race of that period, formed a federation of tribes threatening extermination to British posts along the western frontier. Nine posts stood there, and Pontiac used a stratagem to reduce them.

Investing one fort to cut off all communication and hope of succour, he offered terms of surrender that were never kept in honourable spirit. Seven outposts fell, in turn, to confidence in his truth, unlike the noble and generous Tecumseh's dealings with enemies. Detroit and Michilimackinac, now Mackinaw, remained. Readers should start here, since volume one sets the conspiracy, the siege, and the prophecy in motion.
4725-john-lothrop-motley-a-memoir-volume:
Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr., opens his memoir of John Lothrop Motley in this first volume, with a note on its origins. The memoir rests on a biographical sketch prepared at the request of the Massachusetts Historical Society for its Proceedings. Controversies the Society could not enter are treated at length here, with details too long for a customary tribute to a deceased member.

The memoir begins in 1814 to 1827, with birth and early years to age thirteen. Motley's great-grandfather came from Belfast in Ireland to Falmouth, now Portland, Maine, in the earlier part of the last century. He married twice and had ten children, four by the first marriage and six by the last. Holmes calls the whole memoir still but an outline, useful for present need and for a future biographer. Readers get Motley's beginnings, in warm, careful prose.
4797-the-complete-poetical-works-of-perc:
The Complete Poetical Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley, volume one, is the Oxford edition of 1914, edited by Thomas Hutchinson. It includes materials never before printed in any edition of the poems. Its preface says the edition gathers all Shelley's ascertained poems and fragments of verse that have hitherto appeared in print, and this first volume opens that gathering.

Hutchinson worked, as far as possible, on recognising the editio princeps, the first printed edition, as primary textual authority. He was not content to reprint Mrs. Shelley's 1839 recension, or any later editor's, and the text results from a fresh collation of early editions, with rejected readings subjoined in footnotes. Wherever good reason appeared for superseding the first edition, as with Julian and Maddalo, the fact is announced and the substituted exemplar indicated in a prefatory note. Readers get Shelley's poems in a scholarly Oxford text, beginning here with the first volume.
4942-evolution-of-expression-volume-1:
This first volume of Evolution of Expression gathers poems and prose pieces chosen for reading aloud and for training expression. Dickens, Browning, Tennyson, Scott, Wordsworth, Stevenson, and Riley all appear, with pieces ranging from The Tea-Kettle and the Cricket to Lochinvar, The Brook, My Shadow, and The Swing.

The selections suit recitation, elocution practice, and classroom reading, mixing humor, pathos, and adventure in short forms. No editor is named in the record. Teachers and readers who enjoy performing poetry get a ready anthology, where famous names sit beside lesser-known pieces chosen for their speaking quality.
4964-waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since-v:
Walter Scott's Waverley opens, in this first volume, with the author gravely weighing his title and his hero's name. He might have seized a sounding surname from English history or topography, as his predecessors did. Instead he weighs chivalrous names like Howard, Mordaunt, and Mortimer against softer, sentimental sounds like Belmour and Belville.

The choice matters because the novel sends young Edward Waverley from England into Scotland during the Jacobite rising of 1745. Scott's playful preface introduces a romance that will test its hero's loyalties. Readers get the start of the historical novel itself, witty about its own making before the adventure begins.
4998-the-notebooks-of-leonardo-da-vinci-:
Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks, in this first volume, gather the artist's notes on painting, including his thoughts on the Last Supper at Milan. That picture, Vasari says, suffered irremediable injury from decay and reckless restorations in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, yet no Renaissance picture became so well known through copies of every description.

Vasari also notes that Leonardo labored much more by his word than by deed, meaning the manuscripts preserved to this day. The volume shows Leonardo thinking on paper: observing, measuring, and theorizing. Readers get the artist as writer, whose notebooks explain the paintings almost as fully as the paintings explain themselves.
5084-life-and-letters-of-thomas-henry-hu:
Life and Letters of Thomas Henry Huxley, in this first volume, follows the great biologist from 1825 through the early 1860s in dated chapters. The narrative moves from childhood and schooling to voyages, scientific friendships, and the controversies that made Huxley famous as Darwin's bulldog, with illustrations throughout.

Plates include a portrait from a daguerreotype made in 1846, a facsimile sketch called The Loves and Graces, a photograph from 1857, and a view of Marlborough Place from the garden. No editor is named in the record. Readers get Huxley's formation years in his own letters and his family's memoir, a portrait of Victorian science coming of age.
509-the-purcell-papers-volume-1:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu opens his Purcell Papers in this first volume, with a memoir by Alfred Perceval Graves. The memoir traces Le Fanu's Huguenot kin from Normandy to Ireland. Then come four tales: the ghost and the bone-setter, the fortunes of Sir Robert Ardagh, the last heir of Castle Connor, and the drunkard's dream.

Le Fanu writes Irish gothic with humor and dread, in dialect and in plain prose by turns. Ghosts, curses, and drink shape each tale's moral turn. The volume serves as a fine entry to Le Fanu, where a priest's papers open a door on old Ireland's fears.
5197-my-life-volume-1:
Richard Wagner's My Life, volume one of the authorised translation from the German, covers the composer's early years. Part One runs from 1813 to 1842, and Part Two from 1842 to 1850. The volume ends with his Dresden period, while a preface explains that the text was dictated to his wife over several years.

Wagner tells of childhood, training, early operas, and the experiences that shaped his art, in his own vigorous and partisan voice. The volume offers a first-hand foundation for understanding the composer. It pairs naturally with the second volume, which carries the story through his years of exile.
5234-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
The Confessions of Harry Lorrequer, generally attributed to Charles James Lever, opens its first volume with chapters one through ten. Harry, a young Irish soldier, recounts his scrapes with pipe-clay caps, culverins, and Horse Guards regulations, in the comic, anecdotal manner of a regimental mess tale.

This volume covers only the opening adventures, and later volumes carry Harry's confessions forward. Readers get a lively sample of Lever's early humour: military life, practical jokes, and Irish high spirits, told by a hero who confesses everything except, perhaps, his own good sense.
5431-stories-by-foreign-authors-german-v:
This volume gathers German stories in translation, opening with Paul Heyse's The Fury, also known as L'Arrabiata. It begins at dawn over Vesuvius, with mist hanging across the bay toward Naples and the sea lying calm. Other stories in the book include Rudolph Lindau's The Philosopher's Pendulum, Leopold von Sacher-Masoch's The Bookbinder of Hort, and Rudolph Baumbach's The Egyptian Fire-Eater.

E. T. A. Hoffmann's The Cremona Violin and Heinrich Zschokke's Adventures of a New Year's Eve complete the set. Readers get a varied sampler of nineteenth-century German tale-telling, from Italian coastal passion to fantasy and New Year's mischief, all in short, readable form.
5461-the-sisters-volume-1:
Georg Ebers's The Sisters, translated from the German by Clara Bell, begins with a dedication to his friend Eduard von Hallberger. Ebers recalls twenty years of warm, unbroken friendship, with four earlier works published under Hallberger's care. This fifth book, partly written at Hallberger's home, was meant as a special token of thanks.

The romance itself opens in ancient Memphis, where sisters navigate palace life, temples, and the meeting of Greek and Egyptian worlds. Ebers writes with a scholar's eye for place and custom. Readers get the first volume of a historical novel that values family feeling as much as pageantry.
5467-joshua-volume-1:
Georg Ebers's Joshua, translated from the German by Mary J. Safford, opens with the author's preface about finishing the book. Ebers resolved the previous winter to complete it, thinking constantly of the friend he meant to honor with the dedication. That friend, Gustav Baur, died a few months before publication, so the volume appears in his memory.

The romance that follows retells the biblical Joshua story from its Egyptian beginnings, with Hosea among the Hebrews in Pharaoh's land. Ebers brings his study of the ancient Near East to the tale. Readers get the first volume of a scholarly biblical novel, serious in tone and rich in period detail.
5704-the-physiology-of-marriage-part-1:
Honore de Balzac opens The Physiology of Marriage with a teasing dedication and a warning to women readers: they may feel they have already read the book without knowing it.
