This first part treats marriage as a subject for cool, witty analysis, examining husbands, wives, temptation, and the social rules that guard or betray a household. Balzac writes as a moral anatomist, dissecting conduct with irony.

The book's fame rests on its blend of satire and serious observation. Readers meet maxims, cases, and arguments about fidelity, boredom, and power inside marriage, all delivered with Parisian sharpness. It is not a manual of advice in any simple sense. It is a provocative study of how love, law, and custom collide, and it still sparks debate about its claims.
5750-st-george-and-st-michael-volume-1:
Volume one of St George and St Michael opens a historical romance of England in the Civil War years. Early chapters introduce Dorothy and Richard. They also introduce Richard and his father, a witch, a chapter of fools, and preparations. Reflections and an adventure follow, before love and war, Dorothy's refuge, Raglan Castle, and two marquises enter the story. A magician's vault adds a note of mystery.

Readers follow young lovers and divided families through a country split by king and Parliament, with castles, sieges, and old loyalties shaping every choice. The romance favors character and period atmosphere over battle detail, letting household and court scenes carry the history. This first volume sets the lovers' story in motion and leaves their fortunes tied to the war around them.
5808-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part one of Mark Twain's Following the Equator begins the world journey across America to Vancouver and aboard the steamer Warrimo. Chapter headings promise steamer chairs, a captain, a gritty purser, the brightest passenger, remedies for bad habits, a doctor and lumbago, a moral pauper, limited smoking, and remittance men. From the Pacific crossing, the narrative turns toward new costumes, fish, snake, and boomerang stories.

Readers board with Twain's party and settle into shipboard comedy before reaching foreign shores. The part introduces the voyage's method: a maxim from Pudd'nhead Wilson, a diary note, and a joke that tests itself against experience. It suits readers starting Twain's world tour in order, and it stands alone as a lively account of leaving home by rail and sea.
5818-the-gilded-age-part-1:
Part one of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Warner, opens on June eighteenth. The scene is Obedstown, East Tennessee. Squire Hawkins sits on a stile of large blocks before his house, contemplating the morning. The town stands on a mountain top, though nothing in the landscape shows it, on a mountain stretching abroad over the country. From that quiet seat, a saga of speculation, family, and American ambition begins.

Readers meet the Hawkins family and the dream of wealth that will carry them to Washington and beyond. The part sets the novel's tone, mixing frontier humor with satire of land schemes and political hope. It suits readers starting the Gilded Age, since its opening scenes plant the fortunes, follies, and characters that later parts will test.
5826-the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-a:
Volume one of the Diary and Letters of Madame D'Arblay, by Frances Burney, covers 1778 to 1787, with notes by Ward and a preface by Lord Macaulay's essay. A subtitle calls Burney the cream of diarists and memoir writers, and detailed contents trace her first novel's publication and her entry into literary London. The volume follows a young woman writer finding fame, friends, and court life.

Readers meet eighteenth-century London through Burney's sharp, lively letters, where assemblies, authors, and royalty appear as daily news. The diary form gives immediacy, as triumphs and embarrassments arrive without hindsight. It suits readers of Burney, women's writing, and Georgian society, offering a firsthand chronicle that still feels fresh and funny.
5836-sketches-new-and-old-part-1:
Part one of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old gathers early comic pieces, from a preface through My Watch, Political Economy, and The Jumping Frog. Contents continue with Journalism in Tennessee. The Story of the Bad Little Boy and The Story of the Good Little Boy follow. Poems by Twain and Moore, Niagara, Answers to Correspondents, and To Raise Poultry complete the early set. The McWilliamses' experiences follow among further sketches.

Twain offers his humor in short bursts, where a watch, a frog, or a newspaper office becomes a stage for absurd logic. The sketches favor tall talk and deadpan narration, with morals that mock themselves. The part suits readers new to Twain, since each piece stands alone, and fans will enjoy seeing the young humorist's range in one lively volume.
5854-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-vo:
Volume one, part one of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs opens with ancestry, birth, early education, and a clerkship in a grocery store. Sheridan's parents, John and Mary, came to America in 1830, drawn by his father's uncle Thomas Gainor, then living in Albany. Chapters follow Monroe shoes, a journey to West Point, hazing, a fisticuff battle, suspension, a return to clerkship, and graduation.

We meet a future Union general as a boy and cadet, learning discipline the hard way. The memoir's plain, soldierly prose favors incident over reflection, letting schoolboy fights and first appointments stand for character. It suits readers of Civil War memoirs and military biography, offering the opening chapters of a career that would shape the war's later campaigns.
5860-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-:
Part one of Grant's Personal Memoirs, volume one, covers ancestry, birth, boyhood, West Point, and graduation. Later chapters treat army life, causes of the Mexican War, camp salubrity, Corpus Christi, Mexican smuggling, and Spanish rule in Mexico. A trip to Austin, promotion to full second lieutenant, and the army of occupation follow, before the advance across the Colorado and the Rio Grande.

Readers meet Grant before the Civil War, as a young officer learning war in Mexico at Palo Alto, Monterey, Buena Vista, and Vera Cruz. The memoir's plain style favors clear narrative over flourish, letting campaigns speak for themselves. It suits readers of military memoirs and American history, offering the foundation of the general who would later command Union armies.
5966-what-s-mine-s-mine-volume-1:
George MacDonald opens the first volume in a handsome London dining room that feels oddly lifeless. Nothing in it shows genuine choice, only fashion and the custom of its class, from the mirrored oak sideboard to a dozen heavy chairs in fawn morocco. The room sets up a tale about ownership and the self.

The volume's chapters then move outward to a girls' first walk, a village shop, work and wage, the plough-bulls, the fir-grove, and a clan Christmas. Hills, a lake, wolves, and a gulf that divides people all feature.
6095-amelia-volume-1:
Henry Fielding's Amelia, volume one, opens with an exordium and observations on the English constitution, then curious examinations before a justice of the peace. The history sets out into a prison, disclosing further secrets of the prison-house and adventures that befall Mr. Booth there.

Miss Matthews behaves extraordinarily on meeting Booth, and begins her history, raising the question whether a woman can appear to be what she really is not. Fielding, edited here by George Saintsbury, mixes law, love, and prison life. Attention stays fixed on the opening instalment here, while later instalments wait for their own separate treatment.
6123-theological-essays-and-other-papers:
Thomas De Quincey, author of Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, opens his first volume of theological essays with Christianity as an organ of political movement. He notes that forces illimitable in effect are often obscure in their steps, like growth, animal or vegetable, or the hour-hand of a watch.

Judging by past and present change, we know such forces are awake, though immediate appearances suggest sleep. The volume adds Protestantism, Judas Iscariot, Hume's argument against miracles, casuistry, and Greece under the Romans. De Quincey reasons in long, winding sentences about faith, history, and power.
6146-narrative-and-miscellaneous-papers-:
Thomas De Quincey opens his first volume of narrative and miscellaneous papers with The Household Wreck, The Spanish Nun, and Flight of a Tartar Tribe. The Household Wreck begins with the archangel's warning that to be weak is to be miserable, since all weakness is suffering and humiliation.

Beyond all other weakness lies man's frail tenure of enjoyments, his power to protect, even for a moment, the crown of flowers that settles on his haughty brow. De Quincey laments the mutability of all man grasps and the hollowness amid rapture. Coverage in this entry halts at the first collection, leaving the second collection entirely outside its scope.
6169-memorials-and-other-papers-volume-1:
Thomas De Quincey addresses the American editor of his works in Memorials, and Other Papers, volume one, anxious to place these papers in that house's hands exclusively in the United States. He seeks no further emolument, but acknowledgment of services already rendered.

The editor brought together a widely scattered collection, a task De Quincey found insurmountable from nervous depression, and shared American edition profits without solicitation, legal claim, or expectation, on spontaneous motion alone. De Quincey hopes some new papers will hold value for readers of the original series. This entry confines itself to the opening collection, and nothing from the companion collection is brought into it.
6174-pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-:
Parker's first volume of Pierre and His People holds The Patrol of the Cypress Hills, God's Garrison, and A Hazard of the North. The general introduction, written for the 1912 subscription edition, sets each work's relation to himself, its companions, and his literary life's scheme.

Parker wishes God-speed to an edition he hopes will make old friends warmer and new friends more understanding. Most novels and stories, he says, came from incidents or characters he knew, heard intimately, or found in historians. The opening set of tales is the sole subject here, and the later sets are not described in this entry.
6186-northern-lights-volume-1:
Parker's Northern Lights, volume one, holds A Lodge in the Wilderness, Once at Red Man's River, The Stroke of the Hour, and Buckmaster's Boy. Its introduction places the book a generation later than Pierre and His People, when railway, towns, cities, and emigration ended much isolation.

The conditions of Pierre and Shon McGann's days practically ended with the railway's advent, Parker writes, and whole life lost its character of isolation and pathetic loneliness. The account offered here belongs to the first northern collection only, and no later northern collection is folded into it.
6192-mrs-falchion-volume-1:
Parker's Mrs. Falchion, volume one, began in 1892 amid the Pierre stories and finished in summer 1893, written in the days of the three-decker novel. Every Parker novel until 1893 came in two or three volumes, selling more to libraries than to the general public, and this book never appeared serially.

Parker wanted his first novel judged as a whole and taken at a gasp. A Methuen reader opposed publishing it, but Mr. Methuen himself, then called Mr. Stedman, was impressed and gave friendly confidence, certain it would arrest critics and public alike.
6206-the-trail-of-the-sword-volume-1:
The Trail of the Sword, volume one, sets forth the history of Jessica Leveret and Pierre Le Moyne of Iberville, with George Gering and others, across four epochs. The first epoch gives an envoy extraordinary, a renegade's threat, a face at the window, uplifting of swords, fruits of the law, and kidnapping.

Later epochs promise friends in council, a glass darkly, the porch of the world, qui vive, strange people, and escape from the net. Parker writes New France adventure where sword, law, and love cross. The opening trail volume is the only one considered here, and the volumes that follow it are not considered.
6211-the-translation-of-a-savage-volume-:
The Translation of a Savage, volume one, lists his great mistake, a difficult situation, out of the north, in the name of the family, and an awkward half-hour. Its introduction places composition in early autumn 1893 at Hampstead Heath, where Parker often sought an atmosphere conducive to writing.

Hampstead, scarcely invaded by lodging-house keepers, stays essentially residential, with literary and artistic character all its own, like Chelsea. Parker says he has seen more people carrying books at Hampstead than anywhere else in England. This entry addresses the first volume alone, keeping the second and third volumes for their own entries.
6215-the-pomp-of-the-lavilettes-volume-1:
Parker's introduction to The Pomp of the Lavilettes believes the book holds elements justifying consideration, though its first appearance came under less than favorable conditions. It is the only book he ever sold outright, in 1896, to Lamson and Wolffe of Boston.

Mr. Lamson, energetic and enterprising, came to Atlantic City while Parker visited the United States and made a gallant offer for English, American, and colonial book and serial rights. Parker felt he might one day regain control, while immediate phenomenal sale seemed unlikely. Only the opening volume is covered by this entry, while the second volume stands apart for separate coverage.
6219-the-trespasser-volume-1:
Gaston Belward rides toward Ridley Court through foggy London with Jacques Brillon at his side, their horses brought across the sea at foolish cost. Cottagers stare as the pair take the highway past the railway station, and the opening sets a restless man against an old English house he means to claim. In the chapters that follow, Belward tells the story of his life, looks back over his father's past, and meets the enemy who stands in his path.

Parker tells this first part as a tale of search and claim, with a hero who left a wholesome northern life to chase a kingdom of his own. The tone is brisk and romantic, full of horseback travel, sharp talk, and old family pride. What Belward wants, and what it will cost him to take it, drives every scene in this opening volume.
622-the-letters-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Sidney Colvin selects and edits Stevenson's letters to family and friends in this first of two volumes, from the 1906 Methuen edition. Student days at Edinburgh, travels, and early authorship fill the pages, with letters to his mother, Charles Baxter, Mrs. Sitwell, and Colvin himself. Three new letters join this edition.

Stevenson writes with wit, warmth, and restless energy, even in illness and exile. His letters show a writer shaping himself in public and private at once. The volume serves as a rich life in letters, where a beloved author talks straight to those who knew him best.
6224-the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-1:
Captain Robert Moray tells his own story as an officer first in the Virginia regiment and later in Amherst's regiment, looking back on a life shaped by war and intrigue. This opening volume escorts him to a citadel, puts him in charge of the King's magazine, and follows a wager, a sword, and a rat caught in a trap. A dormouse device and Moray's account of his own life round out the start.

Parker frames the tale as a memoir of French Canada in wartime, with spies, soldiers, and proud governors crowding the scene. The first volume sets the board: a young officer, a guarded fortress, and enemies who watch every move. Its pace is that of a yarn told by a man who lived it, plain in voice and rich in incident.
6230-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
No coast in the world matches Jersey for treachery, Parker begins, with rocks seen and unseen and tides that sweep up from southern seas to smash against the Channel Isles. The first volume opens on invasion, as French boats drive for the shore and guards asleep or drunk yield without a fight. Currents scatter the fleet, and the island itself seems to rise against the invaders, as if the sea were its army.

Parker called the book a protest and a deliverance, a break after seven years of writing about Canada. This opening part lays out the two kingdoms of the subtitle, France and Jersey, and the people caught between them. Its scenes run from wild water and rock to quiet island homes, with war as the force that will test every bond.
6237-the-lane-that-had-no-turning-volume:
The English Governor of French Canada comes to Pontiac with a grand retinue, plainly out of his way, because rumours of disloyalty trouble the district. A meeting under the Seigneur has already passed resolutions close to sedition, and only the Cure and the Avocat, speaking in time, cooled the habitants' ardour. The Seigneur parts from them in anger, and the title tale begins with a parish balanced between old France and new rule.

Parker's opening volume sets the whole Pontiac world in motion, with the Governor's visit, a return, redcoats, and a door that will not open. Madelinette, Valmond, and the parish notables move through ten chapters of loyalty tested and secrets kept. It is a tale of a lane with no turning, where a village must choose its road and live with the choice.
6250-michel-and-angele-a-ladder-of-sword:
Parker opens with an old letter feeling, saying this story seems lifted from an ancient cabinet with the faint perfume of bygone days on it. Its roots lie in a true, brief record of Huguenots who fled France for England, kept at the Walloon Church in Southampton. There, in the summer of a year in the 1570s, a widow of Montgomery and her household were admitted to communion, and Angele Aubert married Michel de la Foret.

This first volume imagines the real lives behind those dim records, as a French refugee couple builds a life in Elizabethan England. Court, faith, and flight shape the early chapters, with swords never far from sermons. Parker writes with fond care for his sources, turning a parish register entry into a romance of exile, marriage, and stubborn belief.
6256-donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-eg:
Parker introduces Egypt as his new field after years of writing about Canada. He says the welcome given to Donovan Pasha convinced him the step was wise for his art and his mind. This first volume holds four tales: a lamp held out to burn, the price of a grindstone and a drum, the desertion of Mahommed Selimon, and the reef of Norman's woe. A Mudir bargains over rentals, counting fat years and lean years in piastres per feddan.

These are stories of Englishmen and Egyptians meeting in offices, villages, and river towns, where custom and new rule pull against each other. Dicky Donovan, the small man at the centre of the set, moves through them with wit and nerve. Parker writes Egypt by study as closely as he once wrote Canada by life, and the tales carry the heat, haggling, and humour of the place.
6268-embers-volume-1:
Embers opens with poems of love, travel, and the north, from Rosleen and Mary Callaghan to Kildare, far wandering, and a light heart sought again. The titles run like a map of feeling: no man's land, at sea, eyes like the sea, under the cliff, summer come, and a flower of all the world. A desert calls, a forgotten word waits, and a courier star crosses poems on the world in making, the north trail, and the scarlet hills.

This first volume gathers Parker's verse in a generous run, with woodsmen, pioneers, and a little house among its figures, and a crowning close to end the set. The poems are short, musical, and plain spoken, fond of open country and parted lovers. Read together they show a novelist writing in a second key, where a single image, a hill, a sea, a star, must carry the whole feeling.
6272-a-lover-s-diary-volume-1:
A lover's diary in verse begins with a vision above the din, then love's courage, love's language, and aspiration, leading to a meeting and a nest. Pisgah, a shrine, a torch, and armour follow, with denial, testament, and captivity testing the feeling. A woman's hand, one face seen among many, a mother, and the first sight of the beloved give the sequence its human centre.

This first volume moves from first wonder to sealing and pledge, through fates that laugh and a way of dreams, ending on an accolade, fallen idols, and a poem for Tennyson. Parker writes love as a course of trials, each poem a dated entry in feeling rather than in fact. The verse is earnest and elevated, fond of stars, wings, and shrines, and it trusts one voice to carry a whole courtship.
6275-the-money-master-volume-1:
Peace and plenty is the phrase Jean Jacques Barbille, miller and moneymaster, applies to his home at the height of his career. Pines give warmth in winter and coolness in summer, and oak, ash, and hickory join them. The Beau Cheval river runs wayward past house and mills, now rushing, now silent through long reaches. The land is rugged and bold near at hand, then gentle and spacious farther on.

This first epoch follows the grand tour of Jean Jacques and the rest of a story called tomorrow, told twice over in its titles. A young man leaves Provence with farewells to parents and brothers already dead, and a desire to share the pains of parting he sees around him. Parker opens a long tale of a man who gathers mills, farms, stores, and debts, and calls the gathering peace.
6281-the-world-for-sale-volume-1:
The Druses are up, and a girl in a canoe tries rapids no one has ever run alone, at low water, when every rock has its chance. Osterhaut, the jack of all trades at Lebanon, and Jowett, the horse dealer, watch from the bank with a sportsman's joy and fear. Old Tekewani calls after her, for he ran those rapids himself years ago when his tribe was torn, and has ruled the Blackfeet ever since.

This first book of the novel sets two towns, Lebanon and its neighbour, against each other, with Ingolby, Jethro Fawe, and a whisper from beyond at its centre. A prisoner goes free, fires burn unguarded, and a girl's daring opens a tale of railways, rivalry, and Romany pride. Parker writes the west as a place where a single run of rapids can make or break a reputation.
6289-wild-youth-volume-1:
Askatoon has more character than any other town in the west, Parker says, for its citizens are marked, original, and at times almost bizarre. The place sleeps with one eye open and wakes with both wide, bright and clever by nature rather than by teaching. Nothing shakes it from wholesome control, though now and then a flag of distress goes up, from Patsy Kernaghan the casual to the Young Doctor, the town's intellectual meridian.

This first volume brings the Mazarines taking possession, a girl saying her name is Louise, a man who fought with beasts at Ephesus, and Orlando with an adventure. Two sides to a bargain, things that must happen, a zoological garden, and an oriental way of it follow, with stars in their courses to close. Parker writes wild youth against a shrewd town, where new arrivals test old composure.
6292-no-defense-volume-1:
Goodbye, Dyck, a wild young Irish spirit calls, saying he will meet his friend at the sessions or the assizes, a jest with humour behind it. Dyck Calhoun, a year or two older, is called by his servant Michael Clones the worst and best scamp of them all. He is up to any harmless deviltry, yet above reproach in all relations touched by the commandments. In agitated Ireland, such a man might commit an act that brings him to court.

This first book follows two meetings, a messenger, a quarrel, a duel, and the killing of Erris Boyne, into prison, where mother and daughter wait and a father visits. A letter from Sheila reaches Dyck behind bars. Parker opens a tale of Irish high spirits turning grave, as drinking, gaming, and temptation wear down a young man's resistance until one tavern meeting changes his life for good.
6296-carnac-s-folly-volume-1:
Carnac, Carnac, come and catch me, a young voice calls on a perfect summer day in the wild world behind near woods and far pine and hemlock. The girl's voice laughs, challenges, and decoys, while Carnac chases her by a tumbling stream where his father's logs jam on rocky ledges. Black bearded river drivers with pike poles loose the key logs, and timber tosses down the current as man's purpose seems to avail so little.

This first book runs from childhood days and eleven years passing to Carnac's return, the house on the hill, and his work as manager. Luke Tarboe has an offer, John Grier makes another, a puzzle forms, Denzil tells his story, and Carnac talks with his mother before saying goodbye. Parker opens a Canadian tale of timber, family, and a boy grown into a man of bargains.
6346-cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-vo:
Frances Burney's Cecilia, praised in a January 1783 letter as liked and read as any book ever was, opens with an orphan's secret prayer. Peace to her honoured parents, she prays, as she quits her youth's abode, tears filling her eyes at the last view of her native town. Cecilia Beverley, just twenty-one, comes of rich Suffolk farmers, though her father lived as a private country gentleman, elegance having replaced rapacity in his use of wealth.

This first volume of three follows a journey and a young heiress entering a world of rank. A haughty, affable host half rises from his chair and mistakes her unease for awe at superior consequence. Burney writes society with sharp, comic observation, as Cecilia's fortune draws suitors, guardians, and gossip. The volume sets her course: an orphan with money, manners, and a conscience, learning whom to trust in London life.
636-memoirs-of-extraordinary-popular-del:
Charles Mackay chronicles mass follies in this first volume, from 1841. The Mississippi Scheme, the South Sea Bubble, and Tulipomania lead the set, with relics, prophecies, duels, thugs, and the love of the marvelous. Mackay argues that whole nations, like men, have whims and seasons of madness.

Mackay writes with brisk, moralizing energy, piling anecdote on anecdote. His opening warns that millions can chase one delusion till a newer folly catches them. The book endures as a classic of crowd psychology, still quoted whenever markets, cults, or crazes seize a people.
6417-a-political-and-social-history-of-m:
Carlton J. H. Hayes writes a long textbook, purposely long, to give college courses secure foundations in modern European history from 1500 to 1815. The period is the most complicated and inherently interesting in recorded history, he says in his preface, and a short book could not do it justice. Volume one runs from new national monarchies and the old Holy Roman Empire through city states and northern Europe in 1500.

Commercial revolution, sixteenth century politics, Protestant revolt, Catholic reformation, and sixteenth century culture follow, with absolutism in France, parliament's triumph in England, and world conflict between France and Britain. Hayes notes that Protestants kept much Catholic theology in common, from Trinity to redemption. The book is a survey built for study, with argument, narrative, and society in one frame.
691-the-complete-works-of-james-whitcomb:
James Whitcomb Riley, the Hoosier poet, opens his collected works with a volume that sets his home ground in Indianapolis. Lockerbie Street, his quiet lane of hollyhocks and roses, became a shrine for visiting readers. Riley, born in Greenfield, Indiana, became known as the Hoosier Poet.

The volume gathers early poems and sketches in Riley's warm, homely voice, with dialect pieces beside more formal verse. It introduces a poet who made Indiana childhood, farm life, and small-town feeling into national favourites. His dialect poems, read aloud across America, made him one of the nation's most loved poets.
6910-life-of-her-most-gracious-majesty-t:
Sarah Tytler writes the life of Queen Victoria in two volumes, and this first volume carries an introduction by Lord Ronald Gower. Gower pleads his long friendship through his mother with the Queen, and his own loyalty and affection for his sovereign, as his claim to introduce the work. He recalls a colored chalk study of the Queen's hand by Sir David Wilkie, found by chance at Windsor Castle.

The life that follows traces Victoria from youth toward the throne, in a narrative meant for loyal readers of the Empire. Tytler draws on public record and court memory, while Gower's preface lends the book a personal note. The volume stands as a Victorian portrait of a queen, warm, respectful, and rich in court detail.
6939-old-mortality-volume-1:
The editor's introduction to Old Mortality, perhaps the best of Scott's historical romances, traces its origin to May 1816. Joseph Train, the gauger from Galloway, breakfasted with Scott in Castle Street, bringing a relic of Rob Roy and a parcel of traditions. A letter from Broadfoot, schoolmaster at Pennington, signed in jest Clashbottom, gave Scott his Jedediah Cleishbotham, dominie of Gandercleugh.

Train admired the antiques in Scott's den, above all a portrait of Claverhouse now at Abbotsford. From such scraps Scott built his tale of Covenanters, soldiers, and a divided Scotland. This first volume opens the romance, setting its folk, its faith, and its feud in motion before the battles that the second volume carries on.
6942-the-heart-of-mid-lothian-volume-1:
Walter Scott began The Heart of Mid-Lothian almost before he had finished Rob Roy, as the editor's introduction relates. On November 10, 1817, he wrote to Archibald Constable that talks with Longman had failed, since that firm would not relieve the Ballantynes of worthless stock. Constable, on the spot, could manage the sale his own way, and Scott promised volumes of his best.

The tale itself, second series of Tales of My Landlord, is arranged by Jedediah Cleishbotham, schoolmaster and parish clerk of Gandercleugh. A Burns verse at its head warns Scots that a chiel is among them taking notes and will print them. This first volume opens the Edinburgh story that made the novel famous.
7080-speeches-on-questions-of-public-pol:
John Bright's speeches on questions of public policy, edited by James Thorold Rogers, open this first volume of two with the motto Be Just and Fear Not. The preface values the speeches as examples of public speaking, praising Bright's clear diction, skillful arrangement, vigor of style, persuasive reasoning, and perfect candor. Even those who differ from his theory of the public good, Rogers argues, must grant those gifts.

The editor expects the course of events to drive all who seek influence in public affairs to study speaking as an art. Nothing in English literature, he claims, will serve that study better than Bright. Only this first volume's speeches are described here, as a school of plain, honest, and forceful political speech.
7111-the-land-of-midian-revisited-volume:
Richard Burton revisits the land of Midian in this first volume, telling the plain unvarnished tale of the second expedition. Like the first, it owes all to the liberality and foresight of Ismail the First, Khedive of Egypt. Between December 19, 1877, and April 20, 1878, the officers covered some 2500 miles by sea and land, mapping 600 miles besides by paths.

Burton dedicates the book to his niece Maria Emily Harriet Stisted, who died at Dovercourt on November 12, 1878. A Mother Shipton prophecy heads the volume, promising gold found in a land not now known. The public, Burton notes, will understand one subject has not bred two books: this is the second expedition's own record of an old new land.
7131-the-history-of-the-united-states-fr:
Julian Hawthorne writes the history of the United States from 1492 to 1910. This first volume runs from discovery on October 12, 1492, to the battle of Lexington on April 19, 1775. A Remington painting of the warrior's last ride at Deerfield fronts the book. Contents move from Columbus, Raleigh, and Smith through the freight of the Mayflower and the spirit of the Puritans, to Hudson and Stuyvesant.

Liberty, slavery, and tyranny, Catholic, philosopher, and rebel, and Quaker, Yankee, and king follow. The Stuarts and the charter, fifty years of fools and heroes, and the plains of Abraham and the Stamp Act come next. The passing of the Rubicon and the shot heard round the world close the volume. Hawthorne opens by asking what we mean when we speak of history.
7133-the-great-conspiracy-volume-1:
John Logan opens The Great Conspiracy, its origin and history, with a preface pledging historical accuracy, authentic facts, fair and impartial grouping, and true and just conclusions. He will not mince words nor refrain from calling things by their right names. Nor will he curry favor by fulsome praise on one side or undue denunciation on the other, whether of living or dead. His history traces the conspiracy from obscure birth in the brooding brains of a few ambitious men of the Republic's earliest days.

Through later years of devolution it runs to the evil days of nullification and the bitter, bloody period of armed rebellion. Still more recent and perhaps more sinister developments lie beyond. Only this first part's matter is traced here, as Logan lays the conspiracy's roots in the Republic's youth.
7154-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-1:
Twain's Prince and the Pauper begins, in this first part, with a letter. Hugh Latimer, Bishop of Worcester, writes to Lord Cromwell on the birth of the Prince of Wales, afterward Edward the Sixth. Drawn from national manuscripts preserved by the British government, the letter rejoices in old spelling. The prince so long hungered for has come, with joy in these parts no less than among neighbors at the birth of Saint John the Baptist.

Latimer prays for grace to yield due thanks to the Lord God, God of England, or rather an English God, who has overcome all ill with exceeding goodness. The part that follows sets the Tudor court, the pauper's London, and the exchange of two look alike boys in motion. Only this opening part's matter is traced here.
7193-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-1:
Part One opens with the author's preface, and Twain is frank about his sources. Most of the adventures really happened, one or two were his own, and the rest belonged to boys who were his schoolmates. Huck Finn is drawn from life, while Tom himself is a composite of three boys Twain knew, built on the composite order of architecture.

Twain adds that the odd superstitions in the book were all prevalent among children and slaves in the West thirty or forty years before, at the period of the story. He wrote mainly to entertain boys and girls, yet hoped men and women would not shun the book on that account. This part holds the preface and the tale's first steps.
7242-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part One of Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee opens with a preface that treats harsh old laws with sly care. Twain says the ungentle laws and customs touched in the tale are historical. So are the episodes used to show them, though he does not pretend they all lived in sixth-century England. Later ages had them, and the sixth century, he jokes, would have filled any gap with something worse.

That preface sets the book's method: a modern American mind dropped into Arthur's court, judging old cruelty by later light. Twain warns readers not to take his history too straight, while promising that the satire cuts true. This part holds the preface and the tale's opening bargain with the past.
7253-the-letter-bag-of-lady-elizabeth-sp:
A. M. W. Stirling compiled this first volume of Lady Elizabeth Spencer-Stanhope's letter-bag from the Cannon Hall papers, covering 1806 to 1873 across nearly seventy years of national history. Stirling presents the papers as a sequel and conclusion to two earlier books, Coke of Norfolk and his Friends and Annals of a Yorkshire House. More essentially, they continue a family story told in letters.

Ton, the volume's epigraph warns, is a chameleon whose hue changes with every ray of light, and the letters catch society shifting with fashion and time. Dedicated to Charles G. Stirling, the book lets private correspondence carry public history. Volume One opens the long run of letters.
731-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon opened his great history with Rome in the age of the Antonines, when the empire seemed at its height. He surveys its extent, armies, and wealth. He then traces the turn to cruelty and folly under Commodus, the sale of the empire to Didius Julianus, and the civil wars won by Septimius Severus. Notes by H. H. Milman aid the modern reader.

Gibbon's prose is grand and ironic, and his judgement is severe on tyranny and corruption. This first volume sets the pattern for the whole work: vast learning, clear narrative, and a moral eye on power. It remains the classic English account of Rome's long fall, and the place to start for any reader of the series.
7339-an-account-of-sa-go-ye-wat-ha-or-re:
John N. Hubbard's Account of Sa-go-ye-wat-ha, or Red Jacket, and His People, 1750 to 1830, dedicates itself to Henry G. Hubbard of Middletown, Connecticut, in grateful recollection of pleasant memories and substantial tokens of esteem. Hubbard hopes the pages may interest an occasional leisure hour, and his preface sets his book beside Colonel William L. Stone's Life and Times of Red Jacket, long before the public and valued for its industry and ability.

Stone's extensive work gives Hubbard a foundation, while his own account narrows to Red Jacket and his people across eighty years of change. The book treats a Seneca orator and leader with respect, tracing his world from colonial contact toward removal's shadow. It reads as a nineteenth-century American attempt at fair Indian history.
7382-the-life-of-the-rt-hon-sir-charles-:
Sir Charles Dilke was a leading radical Liberal in Victorian Britain, and this first volume of his life draws mainly on his own papers. Stephen Gwynn began the biography, and Gertrude Tuckwell completed and edited it from Dilke's memoirs, private diaries, and correspondence, including letters supplied by friends. The method lets Dilke speak often in his own words.

Volume one follows his rise in politics and his work on the great questions of the age, with notes touching Ireland, Egypt, and South Africa. Readers get a view of Parliament, cabinets, and reform campaigns from inside the room, rather than from later legend. As a Victorian political life built from documents, it is a solid source for Dilke's career before the scandal that later overshadowed it.
7475-from-the-easy-chair-volume-1:
George William Curtis took his motto from The Tatler: from time to time he would report and consider all matters whatsoever that occurred to him. The Easy Chair essays in Harper's Magazine did exactly that, and this first volume gathers them. Edward Everett in 1862, At the Opera in 1864, Emerson Lecturing, and Dickens Reading in 1867 anchor the book in the public life of its age.

Other essays turn to shops and shopping, Mrs. Grundy and the cosmopolitan, Thoreau, and the pianists of the day, with holiday sauntering and Wendell Phillips at Harvard in 1881. Curtis writes as a cultivated New Yorker thinking aloud, civilized, curious, and humane. The volume is a window onto American culture from the Civil War to the Gilded Age, kept by a man who knew its leading figures.
7531-a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-1:
Beverley Nichols selected this first volume of old ballads with an introduction that prescribes them as a tonic. The post-war poetry of his day, he argues, is the thinnest and most watery England has ever produced, but here are great draughts of poetry, strong and strange. The acknowledgments show the range: a music-hall song like Tipperary beside Kipling's Mandalay and Wilde's Ballad of Reading Gaol.

The ballads themselves reach back to the old story-songs: the Earl of Mar's daughter, the Wife of Usher's Well, and the Three Ravens among them. Nichols presents them as living poetry, not museum pieces, with color plates to match. The volume opens a set that lets modern readers drink from the deep well of English balladry.
7750-godolphin-volume-1:
A letter to Count Alfred d'Orsay opens the first volume of Lytton's Godolphin, asking the count to take the hero under his wing. The author jokes that his long-disowned offspring now wants to borrow d'Orsay's name and parade his debt to the most polished gentleman of the age.

Prefaces on self-criticism follow, in the French manner, before the tale itself begins. Through London and Rome, Godolphin will learn how charm, rank, and feeling pull a gifted man apart. This volume sets up a novel of love, ambition, and the world.
7757-falkland-book-1:
Lytton's Falkland, his earliest prose fiction, returns in Book One after long withdrawal. Written in his boyhood before Pelham, the author later judged its morals harshly and kept it out of English reprints through his life, though a Tauchnitz edition spread it abroad.

With his son's consent, this collected edition restores it, with a note explaining why a work once hidden can no longer be withheld. The first book sets up Emily, Falkland, and a love that defies marriage, in a tale its author both owned and disowned. It is a curiosity of literary history.
7850-memoirs-of-aaron-burr-volume-1:
Matthew L. Davis's Memoirs of Aaron Burr, volume one, draws on forty years of close acquaintance and Burr's entire confidence. After Burr's return from Europe in 1812, he asked Davis to note his political life, and Jefferson's memoirs on the 1801 contest in Congress spurred him to open all his papers.

Davis promises explanations for doubtful points and dictation where needed, with Burr's letters to guide him. With a frontispiece of Burr and a motto of burying Caesar, not praising him, the volume opens a frank, partisan, and intimate life of a founder later tried for treason.
7876-passages-from-the-english-notebooks:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Passages from the English Note-Books, volume one, is dedicated to Francis Bennoch, whose generous hospitality made Hawthorne's English stay homelike. An editor's preface explains why private journals, meant only for reference, reach the public at all, despite the author's reserve.

Readers had long demanded a life of Hawthorne, yet he hoped no biography would be attempted, and his reserve barred outsiders from the task. These notes answer that wish partway, offering his own daily record instead. Through dinners, streets, and travel, volume one opens an author's England with shy candor.
7879-passages-from-the-french-and-italia:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Passages from the French and Italian Note-Books, volume one, opens January 6, 1858, at the Hotel de Louvre. A dozen trunks and half a dozen bags stand packed for France and Italy. Cabs wait at half past six, and at seven the family leaves in dark, bitter cold for London Bridge station.

Market carts crowd Newgate Street near deadlock. Fellow travelers sit round a waiting-room fire, and through tickets carry them via Folkestone and Boulogne to Paris, with a long tin foot-warmer for the ride. The notebooks that follow record art, streets, and daily life abroad.
8088-passages-from-the-american-notebook:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's first volume of American notebook passages begins at Salem on June 15, 1835, with a walk to the Juniper. The shore lies strewn with seaweed driven in by recent winds, eel-grass bundled and tangled, great olive-coloured marine plants with snake-like stalks. Shoals of fish, painted wood, bark, and round pieces of brick worn by the waves. Hawthorne records each detail with the patience that would mark his fiction.

The notebooks are a writer's field book, full of observed faces, places, and odd facts waiting for a story. They show Hawthorne before fame, walking New England and storing impressions. For readers of his novels, the volume is a pleasure in itself and a key to how his imagination worked, turning a heap of seaweed into a scene.
8166-gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrate:
Book one of Rabelais's Gargantua and Pantagruel tells of the giant Gargantua himself. It covers his strange birth, his school years, his wars, and the founding of the Abbey of Thélème, whose rule was do what thou wilt. The English text reprints Sir Thomas Urquhart of Cromarty's 1653 version, with notes from the Maitland Club edition of 1838. Urquhart's later books and Motteux's completions are described up front, with passages restored from the 1738 edition edited by Ozell.

Rabelais's first book is a riot of learning, hunger, and satire, mocking school learning and monkish life while praising free thought. Gargantua's huge appetites and his son's future deeds begin here. For readers new to Rabelais, this is the starting point, in a version that is itself a classic of English prose.
8210-biographia-epistolaris-volume-1:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge's Biographia Epistolaris, edited by A. Turnbull in this first volume, gathers thirty-three letters as the biographical supplement to Coleridge's Biographia Literaria, with additional letters. Turnbull's introduction calls Coleridge the mightiest genius since Milton, a poet without like when he rose to full power, a philosopher whose mind cannot be gauged by what he left. And a critic, the subtlest and most profound of his time, whose powers flowed away in talk like a receding ocean.

The letters show Coleridge thinking aloud about poetry, philosophy, and friendship, in the intimate form he handled best. They supplement the Biographia's theory with a life. For Coleridge students, this volume is indispensable, offering the poet-critic in his own voice, brilliant, digressive, and endlessly suggestive.
8458-marse-henry-an-autobiography-volume:
Henry Watterson, called Marse Henry, tells his life in this first volume, dedicated to his friend Alexander Konta from Mansfield in 1919. The Louisville editor and Confederate veteran looks back on a career in newspapers and politics, and the volume's contents open his story, with a frontispiece picturing Watterson about 1908. His famous verse on fame, a mound of earth and a dab of printer's ink, sets the tone.

Watterson founded the Louisville Courier-Journal and shaped Kentucky politics for decades. Volume 1 covers his early life and rise, in the voice of a man who knew presidents and editors alike. Readers of newspaper history get a firsthand account, witty and partisan, from one of America's great editors.
8471-life-on-the-mississippi-part-1:
Mark Twain opens Life on the Mississippi by calling the river's basin the body of the nation, with all other parts as members. Part 1 measures that body: about 1,250,000 square miles, second among the world's great valleys only to the Amazon. It is larger than Europe without Russia, Norway, and Sweden, able to contain France six times and the British Isles ten times.

The part sets the stage for Twain's river book, part history, part memoir, part tall tale. Readers get the Mississippi as geography first, vast and defining, before pilots, steamboats, and stories take over. It is Twain at his most expansive, using numbers and comparisons to make a river feel like a continent.
8488-the-literary-remains-of-samuel-tayl:
Henry Nelson Coleridge collected and edited the literary remains of his uncle, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, in this first volume, inscribed to Joseph Henry Green, the approved friend of Coleridge. The preface notes that Coleridge, by his will of September 1829, authorized his executor to publish his remains, and the volume gathers fragments, notes, and unpublished writings.

Readers meet Coleridge beyond the famous poems: as thinker, critic, and talker, in pieces his nephew judged worth preserving. The remains show a mind ranging over poetry, philosophy, and theology. For Coleridge students, the volume is a primary source, and for general readers, a glimpse of a genius in draft.
8511-the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-vo:
Émile Zola's Lourdes, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, opens the Three Cities trilogy with the first day of a pilgrimage. Pilgrims and patients, packed on hard third-class seats, finish chanting the Ave maris Stella as they leave the Orleans terminus. The chapters follow Pierre and Marie, Poitiers, miracles, and Bernadette, the girl of the grotto.

Zola studies Lourdes as a naturalist: trains, hospitals, priests, and crowds, with faith and suffering at the center. Volume 1 sets the pilgrimage in motion, introducing the sick who hope for cure and the priest who doubts. Readers get a novel that is also a social study, skeptical, detailed, and compassionate toward its pilgrims.
8526-eve-s-diary-part-1:
Mark Twain's Eve's Diary, illustrated by Lester Ralph and presented as translated from the original, opens on Saturday, when Eve is almost a whole day old. She arrived yesterday, as it seems to her, and reasons that if there was a day before yesterday, she was not there when it happened, or she should remember it. She resolves to be very watchful now.

Part 1 gives Eve's first days in Eden, discovering the world, naming things, and meeting Adam, in Twain's comic, tender voice. Readers get Genesis retold as a woman's diary, curious and delighted. The book's humor lies in Eve's logic, and its warmth in her wonder at a world made new each morning.
8551-the-seaboard-parish-volume-1:
George MacDonald opens The Seaboard Parish in volume 1. Its contents include Homiletic, Constance's Birthday, The Sick Chamber, A Sunday Evening, and My Dream. The New Baby, Another Sunday Evening, Theodora's Doom, A Spring Chapter, An Important Letter, Connie's Dream, and The Journey follow.

MacDonald, the Scottish minister whose fantasies influenced C. S. Lewis, writes a parish novel in sermons, family scenes, and seaside reflections. The narrator, a minister, tells of his children, his people, and his faith, by the shore. Readers get Victorian religious fiction at its most personal, where theology grows from daily life. Volume 1 sets the parish and its people in place.
8577-charles-o-malley-the-irish-dragoon-:
Charles Lever wrote Charles O'Malley, the Irish Dragoon, with illustrations by Phiz, in two volumes, and volume 1 opens the tale. The dedication, to the Marquess of Douro, calls the book an imperfect attempt to picture scenes of the most brilliant period of the author's country's history. It suggests the dedication to the son of him who gave that history its glory.

O'Malley, a young Irishman turned dragoon, rides through the Peninsular War and Irish society, in Lever's rollicking style. Readers get a classic military adventure, full of horses, battles, and humor. Volume 1 sets the hero on his road, and the illustrations by Phiz, Dickens's illustrator, add period charm.
8582-roughing-it-part-1:
Mark Twain opens Roughing It as a personal narrative, not a formal history, of several years of wandering in the Far West. This first part covers the long stagecoach journey westward, with Twain presenting himself as a greenhorn learning the road, its stations, and its rough company. He warns readers that his aim is to entertain an idle hour, not to lecture on science or philosophy.

Humour carries the travel detail: bad food, worse beds, strange fellow passengers, and a landscape that keeps surprising him. Yet real information slips in about the West just as settlement, mining, and stage lines were remaking it. The book's easy, talking voice made it a lasting American classic, and this opening stretch is the funniest and freshest way into Twain's West.
8593-normandy-the-scenery-romance-of-its:
Gordon Home pictured and wrote about Normandy for travellers in 1905, and this first part follows the Seine country and its old towns. From Rouen, the ancient capital, the route runs through Evreux, Bernay, Lisieux, and Falaise, with side notes on castles, churches, farms, and poplar-lined roads. Home pairs his own drawings with short notes on what each place looks like.

Later chapters in this part reach Argentan, Avranches, Mont St Michel, Coutances, St Lo, Bayeux, and Caen, before closing with notes on Norman history. The writing mixes plain travel detail with stories about kings, builders, and battles tied to each town. Readers get a slow, picture-filled walk through a region where medieval walls and farm life still sit side by side.
8685-memoirs-of-henry-hunt-esq-volume-1:
Henry Hunt, the radical orator, writes his own memoirs in this first volume, introduced by a portrait engraved from a drawing made in the King's Bench Prison the morning after judgment. Hunt, known as Orator Hunt, led the campaign for parliamentary reform that ended in the Peterloo Massacre of 1819. His memoirs, written in prison and after, mix personal narrative with political argument, in the voice of a man who loved a crowd and a fight.

Volume one covers his early life, his entry into radical politics, and his clashes with authority, with spelling of names left inconsistent as in the original. The transcriber's note on quotation marks warns readers that Hunt's punctuation does not follow modern usage. Historians of British radicalism value the book as a firsthand, combative source, while general readers meet a vivid, vain, and brave agitator telling his own story.
8701-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-1:
Gustave Dore's first Bible volume opens the gallery with Genesis and the patriarchs, in the pairing of engraving title and Bible passage that made the collection famous. The preface notes that the original grand work met warm recognition but cost too much for most admirers, so this cheaper gallery was made for a wider circle. Creation of Eve, expulsion from the garden, the murder of Abel, the Deluge, Noah cursing Ham, and the Tower of Babel begin the sequence.

Abraham entertaining strangers, the destruction of Sodom, Hagar in the wilderness, and the trial of Abraham's faith follow, with Joseph's story and Moses in the bulrushes further on. Dore's dramatic art gave these scenes a visual life that shaped how generations pictured the Bible. Readers can follow Genesis in short, vivid episodes, and sense why Dore's Bible became a household treasure.
8721-the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volum:
Emile Zola's Rome opens, in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, with Abbe Pierre Froment arriving in the Eternal City, author of a book called New Rome that hopes for a rejuvenation of Christianity. Part one follows his first impressions, then the Boccaneras, their mansion, ancestors, history, and friends, under the heading black mouth, red soul. Romans of the Church complete the opening movement: Cardinals Boccanera and Sanguinetti, Abbes Paparelli and Santobono, Don Vigilio, and Monsignor Nani.

Part two, begun in this volume, turns to the Romans of new Italy, the Pradas and Saccos, the Corso and the Pincio. The blood of Augustus in palaces, forums, and St Peter's. Zola sets Pierre's idealism against two Romes, papal and secular, both ancient and both stubborn. The first volume lays the novel's groundwork with extraordinary fullness of street, church, and character.
8774-poems-in-two-volumes-volume-1:
William Wordsworth's Poems in Two Volumes, volume one, gathers the lyrics that followed Lyrical Ballads. A Latin motto promising the Muse will speak later in a graver tone, when times give secure fruit. Contents include To the Daisy, Louisa, Fidelity, She was a phantom of delight, The Redbreast and the Butterfly, The Sailor's Mother, and poems to the small celandine. The Character of the Happy Warrior, The Horn of Egremont Castle, The Affliction of Margaret, The Kitten and the Falling Leaves, and The Seven Sisters follow.

Ode to Duty and poems to a child of six show Wordsworth's maturing voice: nature, memory, and moral reflection in plain, musical diction. The volume captures the poet at Grasmere, writing short lyrics of great concentration. Readers who know only the famous longer poems will find here the intimate Wordsworth. A book that repays reading poem by poem, slowly, rather than in a rush.
8790-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Cary's Purgatory opens in this first part, cantos one through four, as Dante's light bark lifts sail over better waves, glad to leave so cruel a sea behind. He will sing of the second region, where the human spirit is purged of sinful blot and prepared for ascent to Heaven. Calling on the holy Nine Muses and on Calliope for a higher song, he lands on a shore of sweet sapphire light.

Cato guards the mountain's foot, the souls arrive by angel boat, and Dante meets friends and musicians among the excommunicated and the late repentant waiting on the lower slopes. The mood, after Hell, is dawn, music, and delay borne with hope. This opening part sets Purgatory's distinctive temper: discipline as mercy, time as healing, and a mountain climbed step by step toward Paradise.
8796-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
Cary's Paradise begins in this first part, cantos one through fourteen. Dante's glory, by whose might all things are moved, pierces the universe, shedding more light in one part and less elsewhere. In Heaven, which partakes most largely of that light, Dante was a witness of things surpassing power to retell. Beatrice lifts him beyond the moon, and the spheres of Mercury, Venus, and the Sun unfold.

Just and active souls, lovers, and great theologians appear as lights, answering Dante's questions about fate, free will, and the Church. The part's difficulty is real, but so is its beauty: light, music, and geometry carry theology that prose would flatten. Readers starting Paradise here should read slowly, letting Beatrice's explanations and Dante's wonder set the pace for the ascent that parts two and three complete.
8825-the-life-and-letters-of-maria-edgew:
Augustus J. C. Hare edits this first volume of the life and letters of Maria Edgeworth, opening at Edgeworthstown in the flat, featureless county of Longford. The large, handsome, unpretentious house stands amid scenery with few natural attractions, beautified by generations of loving care. Valued as the centre of a large family circle gathered in unusual sympathy and love. Hare draws on family memoirs telling how the Edgeworths, who gave their name to Edgeware near London, settled in Ireland more than three hundred years earlier.

Letters and narrative then follow Edgeworth's youth, her father's influence, and her emergence as a novelist. The volume suits readers who know Edgeworth's tales and want the woman behind them: witty, practical, and deeply Irish in her attachments. Hare's Victorian life, with its wealth of correspondence, remains a foundation for Edgeworth studies, even where modern biographers revise its picture.
8892-adela-cathcart-volume-1:
George MacDonald's Adela Cathcart, volume one, originally published in 1864, opens at Christmas Eve, with church, Christmas dinner, the new doctor, the Light Princess, the bell, and the schoolmaster's story. MacDonald dedicates the book affectionately to John Rutherfurd Russell, and quotes Chaucer on telling of corn rather than chaff. The volume's frame introduces Adela, a young woman ill in body and spirit, whose friends gather to tell her stories through the winter.

The Light Princess, MacDonald's famous fairy tale of a princess without gravity, appears early, alongside other tales and parables meant to wake Adela's imagination. Volume one sets the pattern volume two continues: story as medicine, told by a circle who believe wonder can heal. Readers new to MacDonald can start here, with Christmas, fairy tale, and sickroom, and find the author's theology of imagination in its most charming form.
890-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Gibbon begins here, in the age of the Antonines, when Rome's power stretched from Britain to Syria and its armies seemed unbeatable. He measures the empire's extent and wealth. He then shows the rot setting in under Commodus, whose cruelty and folly end in murder, and under the buyers and sellers of the throne who follow.

Septimius Severus wins the civil wars and restores order at a price, and Gibbon weighs that price with irony and learning. Milman's notes support the text. This opening volume sets the whole history in motion, and it is the place where readers first meet Gibbon's grand style and stern judgement.
8901-the-works-of-lord-byron-letters-and:
Rowland E. Prothero edits this 1898 first volume of Lord Byron's letters and journals, in a new, revised, and enlarged edition with illustrations. The list of letters begins in 1798 with a letter to Mrs Parker, continues in 1799 to his mother and to John Hanson. Runs through 1803 and 1804 with letters to his mother, to his half-sister Augusta Byron, and to Elizabeth Bridget Pigot. Byron's youth, schooling, and early fame unfold in his own words.

The letters show Byron witty, restless, and already myth-making, writing to family, friends, and publishers with a candour his poems sometimes hide. Prothero's scholarly edition, with notes and dating, made the correspondence accessible as a continuous life. Readers who know Byron only through Don Juan will find the man himself here, in prose as brilliant as his verse. A foundation for any serious Byron biography.
8905-lyrical-ballads-with-other-poems-18:
William Wordsworth's Lyrical Ballads, with Other Poems, volume one, second edition 1800, opens a book that changed English poetry. Contents include Expostulation and Reply, The Tables Turned, Animal Tranquillity and Decay, The Complaint of a Forsaken Indian Woman, The Last of the Flock. Lines left upon a seat in a yew-tree near Esthwaite. The Foster-Mother's Tale, Goody Blake and Harry Gill, The Thorn, We Are Seven, Anecdote for Fathers, and Lines written in early spring follow.

The Female Vagrant, The Dungeon, Simon Lee the old huntsman, and The Nightingale complete the volume's range, from rustic tales to meditations on nature and suffering. Wordsworth's preface, in the full edition, defended plain language and humble subjects against Augustan polish. This first volume lets readers meet the experiment at its source, and understand why Lyrical Ballads marks the beginning of English Romantic poetry.
8937-tales-and-novels-volume-07-patronag:
Maria Edgeworth wrote Patronage, the first part of which fills this seventh volume of her Tales and Novels. Her father, Richard Lovell Edgeworth, signs the preface, urging young readers to trust their own work rather than the favor of the great. The novel follows families who seek posts, places, and patrons in early nineteenth-century Britain.

Through brothers, sisters, and scheming patrons, Edgeworth shows how dependence on powerful friends corrupts judgment and wastes talent. Merit, good manners, and steady conduct, she argues, win truer friends. The book still reads as a lively satire on influence, ambition, and the price of getting ahead by favor.
9164-the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volu:
Émile Zola wrote Paris as the third book of his Three Cities trilogy, translated by Ernest Vizetelly. This volume holds Book One, with Vizetelly's preface. Pierre Froment, the doubting priest, failed to find faith at Lourdes and hope in Rome. Now his story reaches what Zola calls its logical close.

Vizetelly explains the symbol at work: Pierre stands for Man, torn between the Church and Reason and Life. The preface warns that no other end was possible from Zola's views. The volume opens a vast novel of Paris, faith, and the modern soul.
919-ethics-part-1:
Baruch Spinoza set out his philosophy in geometric order in the Ethics, translated here by R. H. M. Elwes. Part One concerns God, opening with definitions. That which is self-caused means that whose essence involves existence. A thing is called finite after its kind when it can be limited by another of the same nature.

Spinoza argues, proposition by proposition, that God is the one substance, and that all things follow from God's nature with necessity. His method is austere, like Euclid, and his conclusions startled his age. Part One is the foundation of the whole work, and essential reading for anyone who wants Spinoza's system from its first stone.
9296-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-:
Samuel Richardson's Clarissa Harlowe, in nine volumes, opens here with volume one, on the most important concerns of private life. Its subtitle promises the distresses that attend misconduct of parents and children in relation to marriage. Clarissa, a young lady of great beauty and merit, faces her admirer Lovelace, her father James, and her brother and sister.

Roger Solmes, favored by her friends, presses a hated match, while Miss Howe, her intimate friend, and Mrs. Norton, her pious guide, counsel her. Told in letters, the novel builds slowly toward tragedy. It remains one of the greatest English novels, vast, moral, and heartbreaking.
9315-a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-1:
Ian Maclaren opened his Doctor of the Old School with Book One, A General Practitioner, set in Drumtochty. The glen folk break every law of health except wholesome food and fresh air, yet live to the Psalmist's farthest limit. Men wear the same clothes summer and winter, save a topcoat on Sabbath, and stand longest at funerals in the north wind.

Dr. MacLure moves among them, plain and tireless, in a community of dour humor and deep kindness. Maclaren's Scots dialogue flavors every page. The volume introduces a world readers would love, and a doctor they would trust with their lives.
9413-the-poetical-works-of-alexander-pop:
George Gilfillan edited this first volume of Alexander Pope's poetical works in 1856, with memoir, critical dissertation, and notes. Pope was born in Lombard Street, London, on May 21, 1688, the year of the Revolution. His father, a thriving linen merchant, claimed noble blood, and his mother Edith Turner came from York.

Carruthers' life notes a namesake clergyman from Caithness who rode to Twickenham for a copy of Pope's Odyssey. Pope's father made a fortune, and the son made verse his trade. The volume opens a standard Victorian edition, learned and warm toward its poet.
9443-samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen's Wife, opened Samantha Among the Brethren in 1890 with this first part. Samantha, a plain-spoken farm wife, takes up her pen for what she calls the cause of eternal justice. Her chief target is the meeting house, which she holds to be in the wrong. The book is dedicated to women who work to bring hope to dark lives.

In Holley's broad dialect humor, Samantha spars with her husband Josiah, who fears what his wife will tackle next. Church folk, fairs, and home trials fill the early chapters. Beneath the jokes runs a firm plea: women deserve a voice in church life. A reader gets warm, funny reform fiction, told in a voice both homely and sharp.
9750-night-and-morning-volume-1:
Volume one of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning opens with the author's plea for sound learning over cheap knowledge. Lytton warns that popular treats and quick books cannot fit men for life's strife, nor lift hopes in healthful trust. Toil must wed knowledge, and trial must wed experience, for rich and poor alike. Book one then opens the novel's tale.

The volume sets the novel's moral frame: education must be earned, not handed out like a patent cure. Lytton's prose favors grave, polished argument. A reader gets the first book of a Victorian novel of ambition and fate, with its author's creed stated up front.
9820-a-writer-s-recollections-volume-1:
Mrs. Humphry Ward, the Victorian novelist, published her memoirs in November 1918, and this first volume covers her early life. She recalls Fox How, the Westmorland home of her grandfather Dr. Thomas Arnold of Rugby, and the family circle around it.

Later chapters move to Oxford, to Balliol and Lincoln colleges, to early married life, and to the beginnings of her famous novel Robert Elsmere. Readers meet Matthew Arnold, John Henry Newman, and other figures of her youth. It is a warm, detailed record of a literary childhood and young womanhood.
9823-lives-of-the-poets-volume-1:
Volume one of Samuel Johnson's Lives of the Poets, in the 1825 edition of his works, gathers lives from Cowley to Sheffield. Cowley, Denham, Milton, Butler, Rochester, and Roscommon lead, with Otway, Waller, Dryden, and Addison beside. Johnson's prefatory notice calls the Lives a new style of biography, plain and unpretending in aim. Critics called it dogmatic, yet readers prized its taste.

Johnson judges each poet's life and verse with familiar knowledge and blunt sense. His lives shaped English criticism for ages. A reader gets the first volume of a classic, where a great critic meets great poets face to face.
989-theologico-political-treatise-part-1:
Baruch Spinoza wrote this treatise on theology and politics, here in Part One, covering chapters one to five, with sentence numbers added by a volunteer. His preface traces the origin and consequences of superstition, the causes that led him to write, and the course of his inquiry, with a note on his intended readers.

Spinoza argues that prophecy, miracles, and scripture must be read by reason and history, not by fear, and that a free state needs freedom of thought. His claims shocked his age and cost him safety. Part One opens his boldest work, and it remains essential for readers of philosophy, religion, and politics.
9910-canadian-notabilities-volume-1:
John Charles Dent's first volume of Canadian Notabilities opens with Joseph Brant, the Mohawk leader known as Thayendanegea. Dent argues that most readers learned the Indian character from Cooper's romances, and that those notions are widely at variance with facts.

Brant's life gives Dent his test case: a leader who moved between two worlds, fought in wars, and negotiated for his people. The volume promises a series of Canadian lives told with documents rather than romance. Readers interested in early Canada get biography that corrects legend with evidence, beginning with its most famous Indigenous statesman.
a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-1:
Beverley Nichols selected and introduced A Book of Old Ballads, and volume 1 opens the set with a foreword and a mixed company of old and newer songs. The acknowledgments trace most pieces to Percy's Reliques and to the Child and Kittredge collection of English and Scottish ballads, with Kipling's 'Mandalay' included by permission of the poet and his publishers.

The volume's ballads run from 'The Frolicksome Duke' and 'King Estmere' to 'Barbara Allen's Cruelty,' 'Fair Rosamond,' and 'Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne.' Kings, shepherds' daughters, outlaws, and faithless lovers act out short dramas in verse, many of them in old spelling. Colour plates face selected ballads, and an appendix at the end names the source of each piece.
a-catechism-of-christian-doctrine-no-1: Januarius De Concilio presents the first Baltimore catechism for first communion classes. Approved by the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore, it sets out Christian doctrine in short questions and answers. Children learn the prayers, beliefs, and duties of the Catholic faith in a form made for memory. The little book served generations of pupils preparing for their first communion.
a-collection-of-old-english-plays-volume: Arthur Henry Bullen edits the first volume of a collection of old English plays. Its plays include The Tragedy of Nero, The Mayde's Metamorphosis, The Martyred Soldier, and The Noble Soldier. Most of the pieces had not been reprinted, and some had never been printed at all. Bullen's edition recovers rare drama for students of the English stage.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Mark Twain's A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court begins when Hank Morgan, a smart mechanic at a Hartford arms factory. Is knocked on the head in a fight and wakes under an oak in sixth-century England. A knight rides him to Camelot as a prisoner, and the court takes him for a monster in strange clothes, bound for the dungeon.

Chapters carry him through King Arthur's court, the knights of the Table Round, and Sir Dinadan's humour to a scaffold and a death sentence. Hank remembers that an eclipse is due, threatens to blot out the sun, and times his miracle to the darkness. The eclipse makes him the king's chief minister, called the Boss, and sets up everything that follows.
a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-1: The first volume of Ian Maclaren's Doctor of the Old School opens in Drumtochty. Its folk break health laws except for wholesome food and fresh air, yet live long lives. Men keep their blacks at funerals and wear a topcoat on Sabbath only as a mark of position. Maclaren paints a Scottish glen and its doctor with humor and affection.
a-far-country-volume-1:
Winston Churchill's narrator introduces himself in the first lines: Hugh Paret, a corporation lawyer, though by no means a typical one. He calls the book he is about to write the autobiography of a romanticist, and a biography of the inner life. In this first volume he looks back at the making of that life in modern America.

Book one follows Paret's boyhood, schooling, and start in the law in a growing midwestern city, under the eye of older men who run its railroads and courts. Ambition, friendship, and a first love shape him before success hardens him. Churchill writes the volume as confession, promising the passions and evils of the life to come.
a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-1:
William Dean Howells tells in a bibliographical opening how this novel was the first fruit of his New York life, after twenty-five years in Cambridge and Boston ending in 1889. He borrowed his own move for his hero, Basil March, a literary man who brings his wife Isabel to New York to edit a new magazine. The Dryfoos fortune, made in natural gas, pays for the venture.

This first volume settles the Marches in the city and gathers the magazine's odd company: the promoter Fulkerson, the artist Beaton, and the old German socialist Lindau. Howells builds his New York from boarding houses, elevated trains, and editorial rooms. The volume opens his largest and most serious novel.
a-history-of-indian-philosophy-volume-1: Surendranath Dasgupta writes the first volume of his history of Indian philosophy. Opening with an introduction, it treats the Vedas, Brahmanas, and their philosophy. Dasgupta dedicates a lifetime's work to the great sages of India. The volume lays the foundation for his survey of Eastern thought. Later volumes build on this base with care and depth.
a-history-of-science-volume-1:
Henry Smith Williams, assisted by his brother Edward H. Williams, opens his five-volume history of science with the beginnings of the subject. The contents run from prehistoric science through Egypt, Babylon, and Assyria, then to the Greek thinkers. A chapter on the development of the alphabet sits among them, treating writing itself as a tool of knowledge.

Later chapters follow Greek science in Italy and Athens, the age after Socrates, and the great Alexandrian schools, ending with the Roman period and a backward glance. Williams writes for general readers, in clear prose, and treats ideas as part of human growth. The volume gives the whole ancient foundation in one readable sweep.
a-lover-s-diary-volume-1: Gilbert Parker's A Lover's Diary, volume one, traces a love affair in short poems from a vision above the din through love's courage and language to a meeting, a nest and Pisgah. The shrine, the torch, armour and a woman's hand mark stages of devotion, while denial, testament and captivity test it. The volume ends with a sealing, a pledge and love's tributaries, still ascending.
a-political-and-social-history-of-modern:
Carlton J. H. Hayes wrote his textbook, by his preface, to give college courses in modern European history secure foundations, and he made it long on purpose, refusing to feed collegians scanty pabulum. This first volume covers 1500 to 1815. Part one lays the foundations: the countries of Europe in 1500, the commercial revolution, and sixteenth-century politics.

The Protestant revolt and Catholic Reformation get a chapter, as does the century's culture: printing, humanism, art, and the beginnings of modern science. Part two follows absolutism in France, Parliament's triumph in England, the world conflict of France and Britain, and the rise of Russia. Hayes writes political and social history together, in clear order.
a-popular-history-of-france-from-the-ear: François Guizot begins his popular history of France with Gaul, from its earliest peoples through conquest by Julius Caesar to life under Roman dominion. He treats history as a vast drama in which events follow defined laws, yet men remain free agents responsible for their own influence. Natural causes and human will together, he argues, make up the truth of a people's story, and this volume lays that pattern down in Gaul.
a-romance-of-youth-volume-1:
Francois Coppee, a French poet of humble life, opens A Romance of Youth with a Paris boyhood. Volume 1 presents little Amedee, son of a widow in narrow rooms. Primrose sellers push carts along the sidewalks below his window. A kind neighbor offers to take the child to play with her own little girls.

The Gerard family, engravers and artists, become Amedee's second home. Their rooms overflow with old furniture, casts, and children's noise. Amedee grows fond of the girls and of the warm kitchen order Madame Gerard keeps. Coppee builds the tale from mercies: shared dinners and afternoons of play. Poverty stays visible in every room, yet shame never enters with it. Readers starting the volumes meet the pattern of the work: a memory of youth among the Paris poor, told by a poet who trusted kindnesses to carry a novel's weight.
a-voyage-towards-the-south-pole-and-roun: James Cook voyages towards the South Pole and round the world in this first volume, performed in the Resolution and Adventure in the years 1772 through 1775. The volume includes Captain Furneaux's narrative of the Adventure during the separation of the ships, with maps, charts, and portraits drawn by Hodges. Book one runs from Deptford to the Cape of Good Hope, in search of a southern continent, through Dusky Bay and Queen Charlotte Sound to Otaheite.
a-woodland-queen-reine-des-bois-volume-1:
André Theuriet opens his French pastoral novel in this first volume, the first book of three, whose opening chapters include The Unfinished Will and The Heir to Vivey. An old man's will, left incomplete, hangs over a woodland estate in the east of France. The heir who comes to Vivey finds tenants, foresters, and a household shaped by the dead man's wishes.

Theuriet, crowned by the French Academy for this novel, writes the woods of Lorraine in every season and the slow manners of country life. A young woman of the forest country stands at the tale's heart. This volume sets the inheritance, the place, and the people in position for the loves and secrets of the books that follow.
a-writer-s-recollections-volume-1: Mrs. Humphry Ward writes a writer's recollections in this first volume, published in November 1918. The contents run from early days and Fox How, its family, friends, and other children, through young days at Oxford, Balliol and Lincoln. Early married life and the beginnings of Robert Elsmere complete the volume, with illustrations of Thomas Arnold of Rugby, Matthew Arnold, John Henry Newman, and Benjamin Jowett.
a-year-s-journey-through-france-and-part: Philip Thicknesse makes a year's tour of France and part of Spain in this first volume, printed at Dublin in 1777. The first letter, from Calais in June 1775, opens a second correspondence with a friend who found the author's earlier letters useful on a little French tour.
