Manners and customs of the French nation, gathered nine or ten years before, now return in fuller form for readers unacquainted with the kingdom.

Philip Thicknesse continues a year's tour of France and part of Spain in this second volume, printed at Dublin in 1777. The thirty-fourth letter, from Nismes, praises the mistress of the house where he lodges near the city. She is a woman of such beauty, elegance, and breeding that a man might cross Spain twice and half of France before seeing her equal. Directed and recommended to the house as a lodger, he finds both house and lady superior to all he has seen.
abigail-adams-letters-vol-1:
Abigail Adams wrote the letters in this first volume to her husband John during the American Revolution. The 1840 edition, prepared by her grandson, made them public. Abigail was at home in Massachusetts while John served in Congress and abroad.

She reports on war news, prices, smallpox, and farm life, all in a sharp, lively style. Her most famous letter asks John to 'remember the ladies' when making new laws. The correspondence shows the founding era through a wife's eyes. Historians rank these letters among the best records of the Revolution at home. Her spelling is her own, but her mind is among the sharpest of the era.
account-of-a-tour-in-normandy-volume-1: Dawson Turner gives an account of a tour in Normandy in this first volume of letters to the Reverend James Layton of Catfield, Norfolk. His purpose is investigating the architectural antiquities, history, country, and inhabitants of the duchy, with engravings. The observations come from three summer tours in 1815, 1818, and 1819, chiefly the second. Authorities are quoted where they supply facts, while journals of his companions, his nearest connections, and of a friend named Cohen go unquoted.
adela-cathcart-volume-1: George MacDonald writes the first volume of Adela Cathcart, originally published in 1864 and dedicated to John Rutherfurd Russell. Under a Chaucer epigraph on the chaff and the corn, the contents run from Christmas Eve and Church through the Christmas dinner and the new doctor. The Light Princess, The Bell, and The Schoolmaster's Story complete the volume. The opening Christmas Eve shows wintry light diluted with fog, the dying day smothered between mist and darkness, and a window full of dim space.
alfred-russel-wallace-letters-and-remini: Alfred Russel Wallace appears in this first volume of letters and reminiscences through his early years and his famous parallel path with Darwin. Family papers and correspondence trace the naturalist's youth, travels, and the growth of his ideas on evolution. The volume gives an intimate, first-hand view of a scientist whose work shaped biology, told largely in his own and his friends' words.
amelia-volume-1: Henry Fielding's Amelia, volume one of the Saintsbury edition, opens in a prison, where Captain Booth meets Miss Matthews and begins to relate his history. Examinations before a justice of the peace, the inside of the prison-house and table-talk among prisoners frame a story of marriage, debt and reputation. The dedication to Ralph Allen and an introduction head a novel Fielding left as his last.
amundsen-south-pole-vol-1:
Roald Amundsen, the Norwegian explorer, reached the South Pole on December 14, 1911, the first man ever to stand there. His account, The South Pole, came out in 1912 in A. G. Chater's English translation. This first volume covers the plan and the road to the starting line.

Amundsen tells how he secretly switched his goal from the North Pole to the South. He lays out his base in the Bay of Whales, his dog teams, and his depots of food laid southward. The volume ends ready for the dash. His calm, workmanlike tone hides how bold the plan was.
an-account-of-sa-go-ye-wat-ha-or-red-jac:
John Niles Hubbard wrote An Account of Sa-Go-Ye-Wat-Ha, or Red Jacket, and His People, 1750-1830, and dated his preface at Tracy, California, in April 1885. His subject is the great Seneca orator Red Jacket, whose speeches defended his people's land and ways through the years after American independence, when councils decided the fate of nations.

Hubbard builds openly on Colonel William L. Stone's earlier life of Red Jacket, while promising a more charitable reading than Stone gave him. Chapters trace Red Jacket's origins, the councils and eloquence of the Seneca, and his dealings with chiefs, missionaries, and American officials. The result is a nineteenth-century memorial of a speaker whose fame rested entirely on the spoken word.
an-account-of-the-english-colony-in-new-: David Collins gives an account of the English colony in New South Wales in volume one, with remarks on the dispositions, customs, and manners of the native inhabitants. Added particulars of New Zealand, compiled from Lieutenant-Governor King's manuscripts, widen the view. Illustrated with engravings, the work is a first-hand record of Australia's founding colony.
an-attic-philosopher-in-paris-volume-1:
A life of the author opens An Attic Philosopher in Paris, Volume 1, the first English portion of Emile Souvestre's garret journal. The essay recalls Souvestre of Morlaix in Brittany, a lawyer turned teacher and novelist who wrote for working readers. His Un Philosophe sous les Toits of 1850, crowned by the Academy, made the attic philosopher famous. The journal then begins above the roofs of Paris.

Inside, the poor scholar keeps his diary of neighbors, errands, and small mercies in the streets below. A bandbox maker, a bookbinder, and clerks pass through his days and reflections. Souvestre writes poverty without self-pity: the garret is cold, but the view, in every sense, is wide. The philosopher measures men by how they treat the weak around them. Readers starting the journal meet French domestic realism at its kindest, a book once given as a school prize.
ancient-records-egypt-breasted-1906-vol-:
James Henry Breasted published Ancient Records of Egypt in 1906, the foundational English corpus of Egyptian historical inscriptions in translation. Volume one covers the first through the seventeenth dynasties. Temple walls, tombs, stelae, and papyri supply the texts, from Egypt's earliest kings toward the rise of its empire.

Breasted, founder of the Oriental Institute's work in Chicago, ordered the records by reign and theme. Royal annals, expedition reports, and tomb biographies let Egypt speak in its own formal voice. His notes date and place each inscription for the reader. Before this corpus, English readers met ancient Egypt mostly through Greek and biblical echoes. Volume one runs from shadowy beginnings to the Hyksos age.
andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-military-:
John McElroy's Andersonville, published in 1879 and dedicated to Justice Noah Swayne, is a private soldier's account of fifteen months as a guest of the Confederacy. McElroy, late of Company L, 16th Illinois Cavalry, announces his route in the subtitle: Richmond, Andersonville, Savannah, Millen, Blackshear, and Florence. His introduction warns the schoolboys of 1879 that the young men of the prison years are already passing. He writes to fix the record before it fades: capture, Libby and Belle Isle, and the cars south to Georgia.

Volume 1 carries him through enlistment, the East Tennessee campaigns, and capture into the Richmond prisons. The stockade at Andersonville waits at the volume's end like a name spoken too often to be believed. Readers get the war's most famous prison memoir from its gate: an enlisted man's memory, bitter, funny, and exact, written while the graves were still being counted.
ante-nicene-fathers-vol-1:
The Ante-Nicene Fathers set out to give English readers the Christian writers of the first centuries, before the Council of Nicaea. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson edited the series, and the first volume appeared in 1885. It opens with the Apostolic Fathers, men who stood close to the apostles in time.

Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Polycarp, Barnabas, and Papias speak here in letters and scraps. Then come the works of Justin Martyr, the first great defender of the faith in Greek. The volume ends with Irenaeus, the bishop who mapped the heresies of his age. It is the ground floor of the whole patristic library in English.
appian-roman-history-white-vol-1:
Appian of Alexandria wrote his Roman History in Greek around 160 CE, sorting the wars of Rome by the peoples Rome fought. Horace White translated the work into English in 1899. The first volume covers the foreign wars, from Spain and Carthage to the wars of the east.

Inside are the wars with Hannibal, the Punic wars, and the long fights in Illyria and Syria and against Mithridates. Appian also kept fragments of books now lost. His history gives a connected account of how Rome took the Mediterranean world, war by war. It often preserves details found in no other ancient source.
arabian-nights-lane-1838-vol-1:
Edward William Lane published Volume 1 of The Thousand and One Nights in 1838, beginning his landmark scholarly translation of the Arabian Nights. Lane, an Arabic scholar who had lived in Cairo, aimed for accuracy where earlier versions had been loose. His edition ran from 1838 to 1840.

Scheherazade's frame tale opens the volume: a king, betrayed, marries a new wife each night and kills her at dawn, until Scheherazade's stories stall the sentence. Tales of merchants, genies, and sailors follow, with Lane's notes on Arab customs woven in. His was the first complete scholarly English version, and its notes made it a guide to Arab life as well.
arabian-nights-payne-1882-vol-1:
John Payne gave England its first complete Thousand Nights and One Night in 1882, and Volume I opens the nine-volume set. His rendering follows the Calcutta Arabic edition of 1814 to 1818, unexpurgated where earlier versions trimmed. Shahrazad's frame tale begins the long nights of stories within stories.

Sindbad, Aladdin, and Ali Baba belong to the later volumes, but the spell is cast from the first night. Payne's Victorian prose keeps the tales' strangeness and heat in full. His version stood as Burton's great rival, plainer in style and complete in scope, and Volume I starts the whole vast design.
aristophanes-eleven-comedies-vol-1:
Aristophanes wrote biting comic plays for Athens during the Peloponnesian War. Volume one gathers the first five of his eleven surviving comedies. An anonymous English translation presents them in this edition.

The Acharnians mocks war fever, while the Knights attacks a leading politician. The Clouds ridicules Socrates and new-style education with lasting effect. Wasps satirizes jury mania, and Peace celebrates a fantasy end to war. Aristophanes mixes slapstick, obscenity, and sharp politics freely. No other ancient writer shows ordinary Athenian life so vividly or so rudely. Athenian audiences voted on these comedies at public festivals each year.
aristophanes-plays-rogers-loeb-1924-vol-:
Benjamin Bickley Rogers translated Aristophanes into English verse for the Loeb series, and volume one appeared in 1924. It holds The Acharnians, The Knights, The Clouds, and The Wasps. Aristophanes, the great comic poet of Athens, mocked generals, thinkers, and juries while his city fought Sparta.

The Clouds sends a worried father to Socrates' thinking shop, with wild results. The Wasps laughs at Athens' addiction to jury duty through one old juror's cure. Rogers kept the jokes in rhymed, singing English rather than flat prose. His version became the classic verse Aristophanes. The library also holds a prose set of eleven comedies for comparison.
arnold-history-rome-vol-1:
Thomas Arnold, the famed headmaster of Rugby, wrote a History of Rome whose first volume appeared in 1843. Rome's murky origins and the early Republic fill its pages. Arnold sifted legend from fact with the new critical care of his age.

Kings fall, consuls rise, and a small city learns to rule itself. Arnold writes with moral seriousness and a teacher's clear hand. His Rome is a school for citizens as much as a tale of wars. The volume began a work that Victorians took as their standard Roman history, praised for rigor joined to humane judgment.
athenaeus-deipnosophists-yonge-vol-1:
Athenaeus of Naucratis composed the Deipnosophists, the Banquet of the Learned, around 200 CE. C. D. Yonge translated the work into English, and volume one opens it. Learned guests at a Roman-era banquet talk through course after course.

The diners quote poetry, argue grammar, and display endless learning. Their talk preserves fragments of some seven hundred lost Greek authors. Food, music, customs, and scandal all surface between the quotations. Without Athenaeus, whole shelves of Greek letters would be bare names. Yonge's translation opened the feast to English readers in the Bohn library. Gossipy and vast, the banquet doubles as antiquity's oddest library.
ausonius-evelynwhite-loeb-vol-1:
Decimus Magnus Ausonius, a schoolmaster from Bordeaux, rose to tutor the emperor Gratian and to hold the consulship. Hugh G. Evelyn White translated his poems for the Loeb series. This first volume shows the most versatile Latin voice of the fourth century at work.

The jewel here is the Mosella, a long poem in praise of the Moselle river, its fish, its vines, and its villas. Around it stand verses on daily things: teachers, kin, prayers, and the counts of the days. Ausonius could turn any small theme into neat, humane verse. His poems give late Roman Gaul a warm, learned face.
autobiography-of-andrew-dickson-white-vo:
Andrew Dickson White begins his autobiography with a boyhood in central New York from 1832 to 1850, in a new settlement on the headwaters of the Susquehanna. Volume one follows him through Cortland Academy and Syracuse schools to Geneva College, then Yale. White recalls dull lectures, strong teachers like James Hadley, and the influence of Emerson, Carlyle, and Ruskin on his reading.

Politics pressed in as slavery divided the country, and White trained himself in essay writing and debate. The volume carries him toward the career that made him a university president and Cornell's cofounder. His memory is orderly and generous, interested less in scandal than in how schools and books form a public man.
b09-zwingli-latin-works-1:
Volume one of the Latin Works and Correspondence of Huldreich Zwingli covers the years 1510 to 1522. Zwingli led the Reformation at Zurich, in the Swiss lands, apart from Luther's path in Germany. Samuel Macauley Jackson edited this English rendering, issued in 1912, with full notes and introductions.

The writings run from Zwingli's early humanist years to the first open moves of reform at Zurich. Letters stand beside treatises, so readers can watch his mind change in his own words. Henry Preble, Walter Lichtenstein, and Lawrence A McLouth shared the translation work. The volume opens the fullest English record of the Swiss Reformation's founder.
babylonian-talmud-rodkinson-vol-1:
Michael L. Rodkinson's English Babylonian Talmud was the first full translation of that vast rabbinic work. This first volume, in the 1918 edition, holds part one of Tract Sabbath. The Babylonian Talmud, finished around 500 AD, records centuries of rabbis debating the Mishnah's laws.

Tract Sabbath works through the 39 kinds of work banned on the day of rest. The rabbis test each rule against hard cases: carrying between house and street, lighting lamps, and handling tools. Rodkinson renders the give-and-take in plain English with notes. The volume opens a twenty-volume path into the Talmud's legal mind.
back-to-back-night-watches-part-1:
Back to Back opens W. W. Jacobs's Night Watches, his late set of tales about a night watchman and his circle. Mrs. Scutts watches from behind a curtain as a cab delivers her husband Bill in daylight, carried between two men with his arms round their necks. Down she flies to the door, gasping his name, while a deep groan confirms he is, as his helpers insist, all right.

Bedridden, Mr. Scutts wearies of his mouldy bed and talks of an offer: if that chap comes round tomorrow and offers five hundred, he might take it. A week of waiting follows with no knock at the door. Jacobs builds the comedy on injury, compensation hopes, and a wife's vigilance, in the flat, funny dialogue of his waterside world.
badauni-muntakhab-vol-1:
Abd al-Qadir Badauni chronicled Mughal India under Akbar, and George Ranking's 1898 English version opens the tale in this first volume. Badauni served at a splendid court whose splendor he only half admired. He frowned on the emperor's bold new ideas on faith.

Court gossip, campaigns, and debates fill his frank and sharp-tongued pages. Where official histories flatter, Badauni grumbles, doubts, and tells tales. His dry asides give the reign a human, gossipy pulse. Readers gain a view from inside one of the richest courts on earth, written by a learned man who refused to clap on cue.
beauchamp-s-career-volume-1:
The first volume of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career introduces Nevil Beauchamp in chapters one to ten. Young Nevil throws off his midshipman's jacket as French officers threaten England across the Channel. His uncle, Everard Romfrey, heads a race of fighting earls. Baronial views of the present time set the family creed.

Nevil is glimpsed in action during the Crimean fighting. A morning at sea under the Alps takes him toward Italy and first love. A singular council gathers the Romfreys to judge the heir's wild opinions. Meredith launches his hero between two worlds: the navy's honour and Dr. Shrapnel's radical gospel. This opening volume establishes the election at Bevisham, the loves, and the family war that drive the seven-volume whole.
beethoven-s-letters-1790-1826-volume-1:
Ludwig van Beethoven's letters fill this first volume, drawn from Dr. Ludwig Nohl's collection and translated by Lady Wallace for the Ditson houses of Boston and New York. Letters to his pupil the Archduke Rudolph, from Dr. von Köchel's collection, are inserted in their dates and marked with a K. A portrait and facsimile front the volume. Only a few bare notes of apology were left out.

Youth, Bonn, Vienna, patrons, publishers, and the first deafness pass in Beethoven's own abrupt voice. One editorial note handles the famous Goethe meeting at Teplitz in 1812: neither master seems to have pleased the other much. Beethoven dedicated Meeresstille to the immortal Goethe, yet wrote only once, in 1823, begging a subscription for the Grand Mass — and got no answer. Pride and need fight in every line.
bernal-diaz-vol-1:
Bernal Diaz del Castillo, a foot soldier under Cortes, wrote his memoirs of the conquest of Mexico in old age, finishing them around 1568. John Lockhart's translation gives Volume One. Diaz wrote because official histories praised the captains and forgot the men in the ranks.

He tells of the first landings, the march inland, and the wonders and terrors of Tenochtitlan. Battles, hunger, and gold fill his plain soldier's prose. Diaz claims he was present at 119 fights, and his memory for detail is famous. No account of the conquest feels closer to the ground it crossed.
biographia-epistolaris-volume-1:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge's letters form this first volume of the Biographia Epistolaris, edited by A. Turnbull as the biographical supplement to the Biographia Literaria. Thirty-three letters stand here, under an Academy verdict quoted at the front: surely the mightiest genius since Milton, whose vast powers flowed away in the shifting sands of talk. The preface sets out to recover the man from the correspondence he left behind.

Early letters fight early battles. One asks an editor not to exhibit Coleridge's name in future months, and to keep a letter private — unless Crito and the Alphabet-men continue their attacks. His poems, he notes, are Mr. Cottle's property, and a school exercise among them stayed in print at Cottle's request. Youth, Bristol booksellers, and the first reviews pass in letters that already argue like the Biographia itself.
blackstone-commentaries-sharswood-vol-1:
Sir William Blackstone published his Commentaries on the Laws of England between 1765 and 1769, the first full map of English law ever drawn. This first volume, in George Sharswood's 1893 edition, holds the introduction and the first two books. Book one treats the rights of persons; book two, the rights of things.

Blackstone writes law as a clear, ordered story a lay reader can follow. He explains Parliament, the courts, and the rights of husbands, parents, masters, and corporations. Book two then lays out property: land, inheritance, and title. The Commentaries trained lawyers on both sides of the Atlantic and shaped American law at its birth.
brant-ship-of-fools-barclay-vol-1:
Sebastian Brant loaded a ship with a hundred kinds of fools and sailed it into literary history in 1494. The Ship of Fools appears here in Alexander Barclay's English verse translation, in the 1874 Jamieson edition, Volume One. Misers, quacks, gamblers, and corrupt priests crowd the decks.

Each fool gets a woodcut and a moralizing poem aimed at his particular folly. The satire was the bestselling book of the German Renaissance, read across Europe for generations. Its ship became literature's favorite image of a society steering itself toward ruin. Illustrated and very funny, the first volume already shows why. Renaissance readers saw themselves in the crew, and modern ones may too.
bryce-american-commonwealth-vol-1:
James Bryce surveyed American democracy in The American Commonwealth, whose first volume appeared in 1888. The British scholar traveled widely and read deeply in American life. Here he examines the Constitution, the presidency, and Congress from an outsider's keen view.

Bryce explains how the federal machine is built and how it moves. He compares American ways with British ones at every turn. His fairness and range won praise on both sides of the Atlantic. Often ranked just behind Tocqueville, the book remains a searching foreign study of the republic, and this volume lays its legal and political groundwork in full.
burton-pilgrimage-medinah-meccah-vol-1:
Richard Francis Burton, soldier, linguist, and explorer, made the pilgrimage to Medina and Mecca in 1853 disguised as a Muslim pilgrim. His Personal Narrative of a Pilgrimage, first published in 1855, is the founding text of Victorian travel writing. This first volume, in the Memorial edition, covers the road to Medina.

Burton passes as a wandering dervish and doctor, riding with the pilgrim caravans from Egypt across the Red Sea. Every custom, coin, prayer, and danger is noted in his sharp, learned prose. Few Europeans had entered the holy cities and lived to write; Burton's disguise had to be perfect. The volume made his name for daring and scholarship alike.
byron-letters-vol-1:
Rowland Prothero edited Byron's Letters and Journals in 1898, and Volume One covers the poet's youth. Lord Byron was the most famous poet in Europe, and his letters are as prized as his verse. The young lord writes with speed and sparkle.

The letters run from school and Cambridge days to the Grand Tour through Portugal, Greece, and the Levant. Swimming the Hellespont and the first fame of Childe Harold appear here. Byron jokes, complains of debt, and charms everyone in sight. Prothero's notes tie the letters to the life, making this the standard Byron for generations of readers.
canadian-notabilities-volume-1:
John Charles Dent wrote lives of famed Canadians, in a first volume made from scans lent by a Canadian store of old prints. Joseph Brant — Thayendanegea — opens the book at length. Hard work of mind change fronts his tale. Youth views, grown firm with age, fight hard against fact, Dent holds.

False views of the Indian fill the start. Cooper's tales and their kin taught them, he charges. Red men as born trait'rous and fell, whose joy is to slay the weak — that is the school view he sets out to break. Brant's life gives the test case in full. Fact by fact, the sketch works to set a true face in the false one's place. More lives fill the rest of the book past the part in view.
captains-all-captains-all-part-1:
W. W. Jacobs's tale Captains All stands here as part one of its book, told by a night-watchman. Each sailor grouses at the sea, the watchman grants. Man's bent is to grouse, and sea men stick to the sea for lack of shore work they fit. Watch work is one such berth, and it wants a clean name few can show.

One man took up butcher work and did well till the law took him. One wed a washer wife, lost her in six months, and went back to sea. Old Sam Small groused worst of all. Hear him when four or five months' pay had gone in two weeks: heartbreak, the watchman owns. Sam's tales form the stock of Jacobs's line, and this part opens his file in the watchman's own slow voice.
carlyle-cromwell-letters-vol-1:
Oliver Cromwell speaks for himself in the first volume of Carlyle's edition of his letters and speeches, in the 1904 Lomas printing. Carlyle rescued the Lord Protector from two centuries of contempt. Cromwell's own words, blunt and biblical, make the case.

Carlyle's fierce notes frame each letter like a advocate's plea. The young Cromwell rises from farmer to soldier of God in these pages. Faith and force blend in a voice like no other in English prose. The edition founded modern study of Cromwell, and its first volume shows why: a great editor championing a hero he believed England had wronged.
carlyle-friedrich-vol-1:
Thomas Carlyle opens his vast life of Frederick the Great in this first volume, in the 1888 printing. The young prince suffers under a brutal father who mocks his love of books and music. His seizure of Silesia announces a new power in Europe.

Carlyle's hero-worship runs at full stretch across six planned volumes. Prussia's rise becomes, in his hands, a tale of will against chaos. He digs through archives yet writes like a prophet, not a clerk. The result is among the strangest and most personal works of Victorian history, and this volume lays its epic foundation stone.
carnac-s-folly-volume-1:
Carnac's Folly, Volume 1, by Gilbert Parker, is Book I of a three book Montreal novel. Parker opens in the days of childhood. Eleven years pass in the second chapter. Then Carnac returns, and the house on the hill receives him. Carnac as manager follows, inside his father John Grier's lumber business. Luke Tarboe has an offer, and Grier makes another. At Our Price is the firm's fighting motto.

Denzil tells his story before Carnac talks with his mother and says goodbye. The folly of the title waits in that goodbye. Carnac Grier, painter by gift and lumber heir by birth, has tangled himself in a French Canadian marriage he cannot avow. Parker builds his Canada from mills, elections, and mixed marriages. Book I sets the two worlds turning. Book II will make them collide, and Book III will send Carnac into politics to pay for both.
castren-nordische-reisen-1:
Matthias Alexander Castrén's Northern Travels appeared in German in 1857, after his death. Volumes One and Two follow the Finn among Siberia's far peoples. The founder of Uralic language study did his science on the march.

Samoyed camps, tundra treks, and word lists crowd his brave record. Castrén froze, starved, and kept writing through years of hard travel. He sought the roots of his own Finnish tongue in the north. Travel and language study fuse in his notebook-driven narrative here. The heroic age of northern research speaks in his own brave voice here. His early death at thirty-nine cut short a vast, bold plan.
cecilia-or-memoirs-of-an-heiress-volume-:
Cecilia, or Memoirs of an Heiress, Volume 1, by Frances Burney, opens her second great novel in a three volume edition. The preface quotes her sister Charlotte, writing in January 1783. Fanny's Cecilia, Charlotte says, is as much liked and read as any book ever was. The publishers paid two hundred fifty pounds for it. Most people thought she ought to have had a thousand. The first edition printed two thousand copies, when five hundred was common for a novel.

Cecilia Beverley is an heiress with a condition on her fortune. Her husband, if she marries, must take her name, or she loses the estate. Guardians of three different tempers divide her care in London. Burney submitted the manuscript to her father and to Mr Crisp as she wrote. The preface judges it less fresh than Evelina, and more mature.
celt-and-saxon-volume-1:
George Meredith's Celt and Saxon begins in this first volume, chapters one to eleven. Patrick O'Donnell, a young Irish gentleman, drives up to the gates of Earlsfont. Mr. Adister, the stern Saxon squire, receives him in a library that breathes of Caroline. Caroline Adister, the daughter of the house, is the still centre of the story.

An excursion in a Celtic mind opens the book, contrasting Irish feeling with English reserve. A princess visits, brothers gather, and a new character enters late. Meredith planned a tale of two races learning to understand each other. The Celt brings warmth, music, and impulse; the Saxon brings order and pride. This first portion, all that many readers meet, is rich in talk and landscape, though the novel was left unfinished.
chambers-cyclopaedia-1728-vol-1:
Ephraim Chambers published the first volume of his Cyclopaedia in 1728, a universal dictionary of arts and sciences. Chambers, a London compiler, arranged the knowledge of his age from A to Z for any reader with curiosity. The work opened the age of the encyclopedia in English and made its maker's name a household word.

Volume 1 carries the alphabet through its first great stretch, with articles on trades, sciences, and arts, linked by a web of cross-references. Chambers designed those links so a reader could follow a subject across the whole work, an early paper version of the hyperlink. Diderot's mighty French Encyclopédie began as a plan to translate Chambers. Knowledge thrown open to the public was the eighteenth century's information revolution, and this volume is where it started.
charles-o-malley-the-irish-dragoon-volum:
Charles Lever published the first volume of his Irish dragoon novel in 1841, illustrated by Phiz. A dedication to the Marquess of Douro recalls the son of the man who gave the age its glory. A comic preface follows, in which Harry Lorrequer claims a bashful young Irishman forced him to edit the tale.

Charles O'Malley tells his own story from Daly's club-house onward. An escape, a hunt, a drawing-room, and a dinner fill the early chapters. Flight and a duel follow. An election brings Irish politics into the sport. O'Malley boasts that his countrymen drink, sing, court, and fight better than any John Bull. The volume runs on talk, horses, and high spirits toward the army life ahead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100070004-1:
Memorandum DD/P-6-9015, dated 19 November 1959 and sent to the DD/P Training Officer, is headed Requirements for Junior Officers for the Clandestine Services. It answers a review sent up three days earlier under the same subject. The writer calls that review an excellent addition to a growing body of work on training programs.

He agrees with all of its stated conclusions, he says, with one partial exception and one more complete one. On numbers, he questions an implied assumption behind the estimates. That was that outside recruitment beyond the junior officer channel would stay limited to scientific specialists for TSS. Promoting from within was sound, he allows, given a bulge in the middle grades. But too rigid a bar was a mistake, he argues. A large organization needs at least a trickle of outsiders into its middle and senior ranks. Annual intake of 100 to 120 trainees is also discussed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100080012-1:
Memorandum of March 1972, subject Research and Development, goes to all deputy directors and several office heads. Research and development is an inherent element of every part of the agency's mission, it opens. Collection, analysis, and production of intelligence must stay a dynamic process, it states, to overcome hostile defenses and meet changing needs.

The agency had been responsible for a number of research breakthroughs, and that momentum had to continue, the memo argues. Such work could support running operations directly, through new equipment and techniques tied to live needs. Work begun for one need often served others as well, it notes. Beyond clear-cut requirements, exploratory work probing new areas had to be pursued continuously and with vigour. Later pages assign a senior official to flag serious technical gaps and program overlaps to the Director. He would also spot where technology on hand could be better used.
cia-crest-cia-rdp00-01458r000100130007-1:
Memorandum of 20 July 1979 from John H. Waller, Inspector General, to the Director of Medical Services is headed Critique of the Professional Test Battery. It is sent for information only. Attached are the names and career summaries of people under consideration to carry out the critique, Waller writes, plus a draft statement of work.

That statement seeks an expert, independent critique of how the agency used its Professional Test Battery. The work formed part of a wider Inspector General survey of recruitment, the text states. At issue was whether the testing program was valid, relevant, and up to the current state of the art, or in need of repair. Developing a replacement system was expressly not the contractor's job, it says. Tasks run from judging the battery's content and reliability to probing possible bias. They also cover how staff interpreted scores in narrative reports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100020009-1:
Memorandum for the record, dated 28 May 1981, describes History Staff holding MISC 21. It concerns material on the agency's contribution to presidential libraries, mainly the LBJ Library. The holding runs to about four inches of folders, the memo states. References also reach the Hoover, Roosevelt, Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Nixon libraries.

One older memo in the set states flatly that no CIA contributions were made to either the Truman or Eisenhower libraries, the memo notes. Staff were adding a folder pointing to where CIA reference material might be found for six presidents. Material already sent to the LBJ Library was catalogued on index cards held by the DCI History Staff, it states. A twin set of cards sat at the Records Center for the library itself. An attachment describes folder contents, starting with the instruments of gift that transferred presidents' personal papers to the government.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100030008-1:
Ken McDonald, the CIA Chief Historian, reported on a conference trip in a memorandum dated 21 September 1981 to Tom Cormack, the Executive Secretary. He had attended the 23rd annual conference of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, held over three days that month. Its theme was America's security in the 1980s, and attendance was limited to Institute members.

About 150 members came from the United States and about 100 from some 28 other countries, with large groups from Britain, Germany, and France. The sessions met at the Williamsburg Hilton and stayed off the record. Discussion papers went to members, and Barbara Tuchman, Caspar Weinberger, and Henry Kissinger gave addresses. A program and a long list of those attending close the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100040025-1:
Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald wrote to Colonel Robert N. Waggoner at the Army Center of Military History on 29 October 1982. His letter answers a request passed on from Dr. Marc Pincemin in France. The request sought facts about OSS Mission BEGGAR in France in 1944 for a Professor Lepretre.

McDonald sends four reports, newly cleared for release by the keepers of the OSS Archives, for Waggoner to pass along. The list gives the final activity report of Maurice Basset, a diary of activity tied to the BEGGAR circuit, and final reports by Raphael Beugnon and Sergeant Maurice Martin. Page counts for each item are printed in the letter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100040052-1:
Four CIA papers on the air war against North Vietnam are sent out for a release ruling in a memorandum dated 9 August 1982. McDonald, the Chief Historian, addresses Walter Elder at the National Foreign Intelligence Board. The papers were wanted by the Office of Air Force History for an official Air Force history then in research.

The request began with a November 1980 letter about access at the Lyndon Baines Johnson Library. Historian Wayne Thompson would use the papers there under the Agency access policy for presidential libraries. That policy requires CIA review before released material can be downgraded or published. The memo asks that the papers come back with a ruling on each one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100040098-1:
Eleven questions about wartime civilian service with the OSS are answered in a file sent on 10 May 1982. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald writes to Roderick Engert at the Army Center of Military History. He encloses the reply he had just received from the Agency custodian of OSS records, and notes the long wait since the questions arrived the previous August.

The attached study is headed OSS Civilian Service in World War II. Its questions cover how civilians were recruited, whether they swore an oath, and what contracts they served under. Later questions ask about set terms of service, the right to resign, uniforms and insignia, and assimilated military ranks. The answers form the bulk of the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100050060-1:
Release of six CIA papers to Army historians is requested through a routing sheet and memorandum dated 5 April 1983. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald writes to the Executive Officer of the National Intelligence Council, through its top secret control officer. The papers came from the Lyndon B. Johnson Library.

Army historian Vincent Demma wanted the papers for a volume of the Army official history of the Vietnam conflict covering 1961 to 1965. The memo lists five top secret items by control numbers and one secret item. It asks the council office to review them and rule on release. The routing sheet at the front records the paper's path through the Agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01-00569r000100080058-1:
Whether the Director should meet a museum promoter is left open in a memorandum dated 29 February 1984. Chief Historian J. Kenneth McDonald writes to the Director of Central Intelligence about Martin Cramer and his long campaign for a National Historical Intelligence Museum. Cramer had written to the Director asking for a meeting.

McDonald makes no call on the meeting itself, but he warns against Agency involvement. He backs the line held since 1967, that direct involvement is not in the CIA interest. A museum and linked television series, he argues, would draw their standing from being free of official control. The promoter's own letter is attached to the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp01m00147r000100050001-1:
Presidential approval of a directive on arms and technology sales to China is transmitted in a White House memorandum dated 2 October 1981. National Security Affairs aide Richard Allen writes for the President to the Vice President and the heads of State, Defense, and the CIA, among others. The subject line names munitions and technology transfer to the People's Republic of China.

Attached is National Security Decision Directive Number 11, dated 22 September 1981, which the President had formally approved for action. The covering note is marked secret with a secret attachment, and copies go to Commerce and the budget office. The file holds the transmittal and the opening of the directive itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp02t06251r000900310022-1:
Reorganization of the intelligence community is weighed in a paper headed Team B Submission, with no date printed in the text shown. Three questions open the argument. Should change alter the basic shape of the Director's post, the CIA, and the wider community? Should it stay inside that shape? And when should any change come?

On timing, the paper argues against basic change early in President Reagan's term. Deep reorganization, it says, brings disruption and confusion. Performance drops for a time. After the shocks of recent years, the Agency needs steady leadership first. It needs a healing hand, not surgery. Deep change should wait until things settle.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00184r000400010001-1:
Early years of the National Photographic Interpretation Center are told in a secret internal history, Volume I, covering Project HTAUTOMAT from 1956 to 1958. The volume is marked NPIC 3, dated December 1974, and flagged as a permanent historical document. Access was controlled by the CIA History Staff and the science and technology directorate.

The narrative closes with the end of Project HTAUTOMAT and the setting up of a permanent office, the CIA Photographic Intelligence Center. It was to carry on reading high-resolution photography from the U-2 and from newer overhead systems then in development. Monthly reports, memorandums, and meeting minutes supply much of the source base, and test work on winter photography at high latitudes appears in the text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000301710001-1:
Japan's prime minister turns toward economic issues in a secret memorandum dated 14 June 1984. The Japan Branch of the Northeast Asia Division prepared the paper, using information available that day. It looks ahead to the November Liberal Democratic Party presidential election.

Prime Minister Nakasone will be forced to deal with the economy, described as his weakest suit. Growth is recovering and should top 4 percent, near the official target of 4.1 percent for the fiscal year. Trouble spots remain: a Diet session running into summer must handle bills such as health care costs. A stubborn central government deficit leaves Nakasone little room to move if growth slows, the paper says.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00367r000301990001-1:
South Korea's opening to foreign investment is described in a memorandum dated 5 September 1984. The Korea Branch prepared the paper, using information available as of 21 August. Seoul's aim, the summary says, is to draw in advanced technology and cut reliance on foreign borrowing.

Revised rules that took effect on 1 July open many new areas to foreign investors and trim approval red tape. The paper expects the best openings in electronics, machinery, and transport equipment, where friction with Washington had been sharpest. Changes to the Foreign Capital Inducement Law of 1962 scrap a list system that had barred all unlisted fields. Actual inflows, the paper warns, will hinge on working-level officials.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100020001-1:
South American views of Central America's turmoil fill a secret intelligence assessment dated January 1985, ALA 85-10001. The Office of African and Latin American Analysis prepared it. The operations directorate coordinated the work. It rests on information available as of 27 November 1984.

Key judgments say most South American leaders watch the long unrest in Central America with mild, detached concern. Outside involvement draws their attention more than the local fights. The risk of wider war also weighs on them. Country sections follow the theme. One passage reports that Argentina's president grew doubtful about his country's means to shape events. He also turned toward better ties in the region, after El Salvador's new president took office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000100110001-1:
Events touching Cuba through 1984 are listed in a confidential reference aid dated May 1985, ALA 85-10048. Titled Cuban Chronology 1984, the aid follows the same form as the prior year's volume. A long key to abbreviations opens the book, expanding the names of Cuban bodies, foreign parties, and world agencies.

Entries then run country by country in date order. A Guinea section, for example, records three days of official mourning in March for President Ahmed Sekou Toure. Cuban leaders signed the condolence book at the Guinean embassy in Havana, with Fidel Castro signing on 30 March. The aid is built for quick lookup of who did what, where, and when during the year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000200830001-1:
China's timber imports and the outlook for American sales are studied in a secret research paper dated July 1985, EA 85-10125. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it, using information available as of 24 June 1985. Logs are the core of the trade.

China has become a major buyer of American logs since entering the market in 1979, the paper reports. Sales rose nearly sevenfold in four years to nearly 300 million dollars. Port work supports the flow: most Chinese ports have a timber berth for a 20,000-ton ship, and larger berths are planned by 1990. American shippers load carriers to an agreed draft under a working deal with China's log buyers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000201370001-1:
Japan's car exports once American limits lapse are weighed in a memorandum dated 13 March 1985. The Japan Branch prepared the paper, using information available that day. The voluntary restraint agreement on car exports to the United States expires on 31 March.

Fearing that an export surge would provoke American payback, Tokyo will likely set up a semiformal watch system to hold exports down, the paper judges. Pure self-policing by makers could draw antitrust suits from American dealers. An increase of 10 to 20 percent above the current 1.85 million units is seen as the level Tokyo would view as proper. Officials state firmly that Japan will not flood the American market.
cia-crest-cia-rdp04t00447r000302350001-1:
Chinese countertrade is weighed in a memorandum dated 30 December 1985, EA M-85-10230. The State Department asked for the paper, and East Asian analysts prepared it, using information available that day. Countertrade means paying for goods and technology with goods rather than cash.

China has pushed countertrade harder over the past year, the summary reports. Its aims are to save foreign exchange, to tighten ties with Third World nations, and to press rich countries to shrink their trade surpluses with China. A trade ministry move in October to set up machinery for the practice is noted in the body. Still, the paper judges that Beijing will not demand countertrade in all deals with American firms, but will bargain case by case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000100040114-1:
Executive Seminars of the Aspen Institute are promoted in a brochure for 1980-81. The seminars are called the core of the Institute for thirty years. Senior corporate executives commit to two weeks of intensive study and discussion with peers from business and leaders from other parts of society.

The stated purpose is to give decision makers insights and tools unlike those of management training. Value questions, stated or not, form the base concept of the program. A front testimonial from Gaylord Freeman, former chairman of the First National Bank of Chicago, calls his first seminar the single most significant experience of his past twenty-five years. A new seminar on energy is described, centered on business, government, and private citizens.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000100160003-1:
Management of the Agency under its Director is reflected on in a secret memorandum dated 14 October 1980. A staff officer in the Director's office writes as the Director ponders his tenure and the future. The writer avoids single issues and aims at the macro problems of running an intelligence organization.

Uniqueness is the first target. Talk of the CIA being unique because of secrecy is called balderdash: many agencies in town do clandestine work. Later sections judge that the institution has bowed before the Director's pressure but not broken. Deputy directors, the memo claims, kept watching for a chance to resume business as usual. Leadership and control in the directorates are faulted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000100320014-1:
An Intelligence University is proposed in a memorandum dated 27 March 1980, marked eyes only for the Director. The writer answers the Director's long-standing request for new ideas sent straight to him. He credits a former deputy director of research and development with most of the thinking behind the concept.

That officer's early death last year had stalled the idea, the memo explains. The time has come, the writer argues, for the intelligence community as a whole, not the CIA alone, to weigh a university on the model of the National War College. The work of intelligence, from collection through delivery to policymakers, is ripe for study at the highest levels of academic rigor, he holds.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200440001-1:
A Charlottesville trip for the Director on 2 and 3 December 1977 is planned in a memorandum dated 1 December 1977. The party is the Director, Herb Hetu, and security staff. A short Gulfstream flight and a club dinner open the schedule.

Dinner at the Greencroft Club brings together members of the Student Legal Forum, the Navy League, and the Chamber of Commerce, with the Director's parents attending. An address to the same groups follows at the University of Virginia chemistry auditorium. The next morning is set aside for a visit to the Army Foreign Scientific and Technology Center. Lists of local dignitaries fill part of the file, and a job description for the center's work appears later in the folder.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200470062-1:
Program guidelines for the Rockefeller Foundation's work in international relations are set out in a booklet dated July 1977. The foundation's New York address is printed on the title page. The program rests on three premises about the world it faces.

Cooperation is needed to manage world problems and meet the basic needs of a growing population, the booklet states. Large-scale war carries catastrophic risk. And institutions able to foresee and settle the economic and political conflicts of rapid change are lacking. Three problem areas follow: world energy, world food and agriculture, and regional conflicts and security arrangements. Within each, the aims are to name the core problems and to test courses of action from a global view.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200480007-1:
Vincent Davis writes to Stansfield Turner in a long letter dated 20 May 1977. Davis directs the Patterson School of Diplomacy at the University of Kentucky. He opens with a joke about two old mules meeting at the same plow, then thanks Turner for a good letter of 12 May.

Two of Turner's stated goals win his praise. One is setting a new tone of care for ethical issues, to which Davis would add constitutional and legal ones. The other is turning the intelligence apparatus from separate fiefdoms into a coordinated effort, which Davis calls desperately needed. He faults the academic community for a decade of weak leadership, calling its leaders sheep who would follow a few who stood up.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000200490015-1:
Senate debate over a United States Foreign Service Corps is reproduced in Congressional Record pages dated Wednesday 26 June 1968. Senator Dominick introduces S. 3700, a bill to amend the Higher Education Act of 1965. His speech opens the file and runs at length.

More than 75,000 federal civilians serve in foreign countries, Dominick states. The nation has military academies for its soldiers and a Peace Corps for volunteers, yet lacks any real program of professional education for its people abroad. Twenty-five years have passed since the first Foreign Service Academy bill, he notes, and ground keeps being lost. His corps would join the purpose of many fine American schools to the task.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300730008-1:
Outside criticism of CIA strategic analysis is recorded in a confidential memorandum for the record dated 10 June 1980. Dissatisfaction had been voiced at a recent convention of the Military Operations Research Society. The writer sets down what was said and gives his own view of its weight.

At a Strategic Forces session on 3 June, four big studies of the strategic balance were reviewed. The speaker, Tom Brown of the defense planning office, rated three as sophisticated work using the best data available. The fourth, the national estimate NIE 11-3/8, he called simplistic and superficial, a mere toting up of beans. Only the estimate reached the President, Brown noted, because its presentation was clear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300830016-1:
A third hearing on charter legislation is reported in a memorandum dated 19 April 1978, OLC 78-0399/66. Senator Biden chaired the Senate Select Committee session on S. 2525. Senators Mathias, Garn, and Chafee also sat. The single witness was McGeorge Bundy.

Bundy brought no prepared statement. After short opening remarks he said he was glad to discuss the uses of intelligence and what policymakers need from it. He backed many views given earlier by Clark Clifford, William Colby, George Bush, and Henry Knoche. Among them: the Director of National Intelligence should remain head of the Central Intelligence Agency. Senators then questioned him at length, and the memorandum follows the exchange.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000300830034-1:
How authority is delegated inside the Agency is analyzed in a memorandum dated 9 March 1979 for the Director of Central Intelligence. The writer is a special assistant to the Deputy Director. The scan is rough in places, but the structure of the study is clear.

An attached matrix, Tab A, maps where decisions now sit, with a listing of how choices are spread inside the Agency and references to law and executive orders. Respondents in Tab B take different cuts at the question. Science officers split decisions into operational, programmatic, and administrative kinds. Operations officers sort by money at stake, sensitivity, and whether a matter stays within one directorate. The paper builds toward guidance for a fuller analysis.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401040002-1:
DCI Schedules, August 1977 opens with a topic index of the Director's actions for the month. The headings are academic relations, analysis, and Congress. Executive Order 12036, the Middle East, and MKULTRA appear too. So do the President and security. Each heading lists what was produced. It may be a memo, a letter, or a record of a talk. Each entry gives its addressee and its date. The items run from naming ties with university administrators to two Senate letters. The letters went to Senators Inouye and Kennedy. They dealt with telling universities about MKULTRA.

Day-by-day appointment pages follow the index. They log staff meetings and briefings on the warning estimate for Europe. They also log meetings with the President and Dr. Brzezinski. Calls on security matters appear as well. Many names and subjects stay redacted in the released copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000401140001-1:
Business Council, 13-15 October 1977 papers gather around one fall meeting. Director of Central Intelligence Stansfield Turner attended the meeting. The Council met at the Homestead in Hot Springs, Virginia. The file holds the Council's letterhead. It holds rosters of its officers, and of its active and graduate members. Those members were the chairmen and chief executives of major American corporations. They came from AT&T and Sears, and from DuPont and IBM.

Letters between Turner and his hosts follow. J. E. Corette of Butte, Montana, thanks Turner in one letter. He thanks him for reports on Soviet and Chinese oil production. He also accepts an invitation to visit the Agency. Turner's letter of 18 October thanks the Corettes for their hospitality. He does so despite his on-again, off-again travel arrangements. More letters and guest arrangements complete the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000501310001-1:
Late 1978 press clippings, from November and December, make up this Central Intelligence Agency file. An early piece is dated 20 June 1978. It asks what proof backs claims of Cuban help in Zaire. The proof went to Congress in secret, it notes. The public got little of it.

Arms talks fill much of the rest. Writers weigh SALT and human rights. Some warn against breaking off talks with Moscow. Life is the first right, one piece argues. Arms talks guard that right. The file shows the press testing spy claims in public. It asks how much trust secret proof should earn.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601400037-1:
Staff across the agency got a promotion plan on 7 June 1978. The note is numbered 25 in the director's series. Turner sets out a uniform system for the whole CIA. Staff care had been strong for 31 years, he writes. It had been highly personal too. A grown agency now needs rules that fit all staff alike.

No sweeping change is in view, he says. Each new hire should know the path ahead. The hire should know what chances a full career brings. Rights that come with service should be plain too. The note pledges a system that is simple and fair. It pledges that the rules will be well shared.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601460013-1:
Owensboro, Kentucky supplies the setting for this visit file. The papers give background for the Director of Central Intelligence's trip to the Academy of Achievement Golden Plate awards. A routing slip sits at the front of the file. The body of the file deals with safety and crowds.

Plans call for a fence around the whole inn area and its parking lots. Only cars with stickers could pass inside. City police and the county sheriff would handle crowds outside the fence. State police stood by. Guest sketches and a town festival timetable fill later pages. The file is the working brief for a public trip with tight control.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601470021-1:
Foreign and Military Intelligence, Book I, is the final report of a Senate probe. The panel studied state operations with respect to spy work. Its report is dated April 26, 1976. A long opening part sets the inquiry in its times. Thirty years since the war's end frame the tale.

Those years saw wide change in what the United States did abroad. Cold war fears, wars of liberation and then talks fill the arc. Later parts judge how spy work was run and used. Top users of spy facts often found their key queries unanswered, the report finds. Some queries were not even taken up. The book, kept in Central Intelligence Agency files, is a base text of the reform era.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601480020-1:
Vincent Davis of the University of Kentucky wrote to Turner with a full program pack. The file opens with agency office forms and a routing slip. Davis ran the Patterson program in international studies at Lexington. His material covers the WORLDVIEW '78 institute, set for mid-March.

Program notes run to social hours and local drink rules, warning that the nearest wet county lay about 100 miles away. Plans for the school's year fill more pages: a full-scale fall meeting at Lake Cumberland Resort, and a spring meeting on a like pattern. A newsletter reports on student interns. The file is a campus host's working pack for a visit by the spy chief.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05s00620r000601540005-1:
Guidelines urged for recruiters is the theme of this Stanford clipping dated 21 April 1978. The piece reports claims made by Morton Halperin about Central Intelligence Agency recruiting on campus. A student who refuses to join the CIA faces a risk, Halperin said. His file might be passed to SAVAK, the Iranian service.

Such a file would interest SAVAK, the piece argues. It would hint that the student had some reason to be disloyal to the Shah. The pitch might even be made at SAVAK's request, to test loyalty. The clipping shows the campus fight over spy recruiting at its sharpest that spring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00280r000100060001-1:
Views on emerging areas of science and technology fill this committee report. The Scientific and Technical Intelligence Committee issued it in December 1975. Its mark is STIC 75-4, graded confidential. Copy number 477 is printed on the cover. The theme is which new fields might matter to national security.

The committee speaks for many agencies at once. The CIA, the Defense Intelligence Agency and the National Security Agency sit on it. Energy, treasury and defense research arms sit there too. The report is a joint look ahead: where science might shift the balance, and where watch should be kept, as the member agencies saw it in 1975.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00280r000100230002-1:
Proposed intelligence activities in support of United States energy policy fill this panel report. The Director of Central Intelligence's Science and Technology Advisory Panel wrote it in June 1978. Its mark is STIC 78-005, graded confidential. The panel is a group of outside scientists and engineers. The DCI chartered it to advise on science and technology.

The report sets out what spy work could do for energy policy and planning. It weighs needs, gaps and the shape of a program. Energy stood high on the national agenda in 1978. The file shows outside experts telling the spy chief how his craft could serve that agenda, and where its limits lay.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100020001-1:
Annual Report to Congress anchors this memo dated 8 January 1980. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, writes to the deputy director and to the chiefs of the DIA, the NSA and the State Department's research bureau. He thanks them for their parts in the report. The report would go to Congress on 24 January.

His overview goes with the memo as an attachment. He asks each chief to review it with care. Community goals for 1980 get special stress in his ask. The memo is short and formal. It shows the yearly rite by which the spy world's chiefs present one joint account of their work and aims.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100040009-1:
Report on the CIA fills this broadcast transcript from July 24, 1977. The program is Sixty Minutes on CBS. A radio and TV reports firm typed the transcript for the public affairs staff. Dan Rather fronts the report. Turner speaks at the head of it in his own defense of the trade.

Some things in spy work are not fully decent, Turner says. His job is to do the indecent things as decently as possible. A floor of decency must hold, he adds. Rather then traces the closed world of the agency for viewers. The file shows the CIA making its case on prime-time television in a hard year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000100170005-1:
Reorganizing the Central Intelligence Agency is the theme of this journal exchange in Foreign Policy. Peter Szanton and Graham Allison wrote the lead piece. The time had come, they argued, to seize the chance and restructure the American intelligence community. The editors print comments and a reply.

William E Colby and Walter F Mondale comment on the plan. Colby grants that a chance to rethink the system stands open. A year of probes by a presidential panel and two Congress panels frames his view. World concern over tales of CIA deeds adds weight, he notes. Szanton and Allison reply at the end. The file holds a full print debate on reform.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200510033-1:
Wilfrid Knapp wrote on November 11, 1977 from the Wilson Center in Washington. He was a fellow there, on leave at the Smithsonian building. Murat Williams had written first, he notes. Their task at Oxford is a memorial to Alastair Buchan. Knapp now follows with his own letter and an appeal brochure.

Great importance is attached to the appeal, he writes. The brochure goes with the letter for Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, to read. The file is part of a fund-raising approach to a public man. Scholars at Oxford sought a lasting memorial to a defense thinker, and sought the spy chief's support in the venture.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200650001-1:
Agenda dated 24 May 1978 lists five problems for a management group. More reporting and analysis work competes for limited means, the first item says. No uniform planning for automated data processing comes second. New methods of analysis need building, third. A uniform promotion system is fourth.

Views on choosing managers close the list. A problem statement fills the body of the file. Information volume grows, some of it in real time. Demands on the community grow with it. Shifting means to meet the load cuts quality, the paper warns. The agenda shows the Central Intelligence Agency wrestling with a flood of facts and a fixed purse, in one page of plain items.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200650010-1:
NFAC MAG meeting of 1 March 1978 gets its minutes in this file. Members present are listed by name in the released text as initials and marks. A meeting with the Director of Central Intelligence was set, in pencil, for the week of 13 March. A staff representative would meet the group first, in the week of 6 to 10 March.

The whole of the 1 March sitting went to editing draft papers. The papers were meant for the meeting with Admiral Turner. The first hour firmed up a paper on slots for analysts. A few top-grade slots would go to analysts who do not seek to manage. The file shows staff drafting their case for the top.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660019-1:
Status of women in CIA is the subject of a memo dated 7 November 1977. Edith M Schneider writes it to the Director of Central Intelligence. She was deputy director of equal employment opportunity for programs. She also coordinated the Federal Women's Program. An attached report goes with the memo.

The report holds the latest statistics on women in the agency. The figures may help in talks with the Federal Women's Program Board, she writes. That meeting was set for 9 November. She offers her help in any way on women in the agency. The file is the briefing pack for a first meeting on a standing theme.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200660028-1:
Agenda for a meeting with the Director of Central Intelligence opens with attitudes, then moves to access. The order of discussion is set out at the head. Management and employee attitudes come first. Sign language interpreters come second. Access to buildings and safety procedures come third. Work transport comes fourth.

An addendum lists special problems with no clear fix. An introduction cites the laws behind the effort. The Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and a veterans act of 1974 require fair action, it notes. Handicapped persons and disabled veterans must be employed, placed and advanced. The file is the discussion pack for a meeting on access and fair treatment in the house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680008-1:
Routing and record sheet heads this file, with an agenda folded into it. The agenda returns to points discussed on 28 April. A review of major points, prepared for the operations arm, is attached. Item one seeks the DCI's comments on that April session.

A second part of the file treats review points on personnel management. Assignments depend on who you know, one point charges. The proposal is a more central assignment process. Profiles of open posts should go to field and headquarters alike. Promotions run slower in the operations arm, another point says. The file is the follow-up record of an April talk, with fixes drafted in plain terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200680017-1:
Agenda heads for a talk with the Director of Central Intelligence open this second issues file. Polygraph use as a clearance requirement leads again. A national intelligence operations center follows. Personnel evaluation, position classification authority and personnel management fill the rest of the list.

The body starts, as its twin file does, on the polygraph. Base rules for access are cited: an executive order and a community directive. Grades of secret are sorted under those rules. The file is a companion pack to the issues agenda, kept as its own record. It shows the same hard questions carried in more than one briefing book that season.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000200730002-1:
Secretary of Defense's memorandum of 17 November 1980 gets a reply dated 3 December 1980. Turner, then Director of Central Intelligence, writes to members of the Special Coordination Committee. His subject is basic strategy issues. Harold Brown's paper urged the building of a basic national strategy. A super idea, Turner calls it.

Two premises sit under the strategy urged, he notes. The United States lacks the military power to handle three theaters at once. Europe, Asia and the Persian Gulf are the theaters named. The memo works from that hard fact. The file is a short, top-level exchange on how a superpower with finite force should order its aims.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000301090001-1:
Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) schedule book for Amherst, Tarrytown and Manchester fills this file. The trip ran from 31 May to 3 June 1980. Tabs sort the pack by letter. Schedule and points of contact come first. Amherst 35th reunion information follows. Amherst correspondence and Pace University correspondence come next.

A copy of the Pace University address closes the tab list. The run mixed duty with old ties. Amherst was Turner's own college, and 35 years had passed since his class. Pace gave him a commencement stage in the same days. The book is the staff pack for a four-day swing through three towns, built tab by tab.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401180019-1: Director of Central Intelligence (DCI) invitation form 80-292 logs a joint Christmas party for Thursday 4 December 1980. A flyer brought the invitation, received on 24 November. The Amherst Alumni Association of Washington hosted the party. Hours were 1930 to 2230. The place was the Potomac Boat Club on Water Street in Washington. Turner was an Amherst man, and the party was his college club's yearly night in the capital.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000401260001-1:
Accepted social engagements through 16 July 1977 fill this memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence and Mrs Turner. A staff member compiled it for the couple. Each entry gives a date, a time, a function and a host. Saturday 2 July opens the list: dinner out with the Watsons, then a performance at Wolf Trap. Dress is noted for the night.

A reception follows on Wednesday 13 July. The list runs on through the season in the same form. The memo is a social diary in office dress. It shows the round that came with the job in a first summer: dinners, receptions and hosts, all accepted and all set down for the pair to plan by.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501340001-1:
Press clippings fill this file under a miscellaneous head, from the turn of 1980. A Time article of 14 January 1980 leads the sampled pages. Its theme is standards: to Americans, the world's judgment seems rigged by a perverse measure, the essay argues. News and opinion from many papers fill the run.

The file has no single month on its cover in the catalog. Its pages gather the stray and the saved: essays, reports and comment the agency kept as the decade turned. Read as a bundle, it shows the press mood as the hostage crisis ran on: judgment of America, and of its spy service, weighed in print day by day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp05t00644r000501430001-1:
Loose newspaper pages clipped for the autumn of 1980 form a bulky Agency file released in 2009. A Washington Post column dated 30 October 1980 opens the set held here. It warns that sending AWACS planes to Saudi Arabia left gaps in warning cover at home.

Other pages turn to the Senate probe of Billy Carter and his Libya ties. News reports from early October 1980 sum up the panel's findings and note loose ends it left open. The column on radar gaps cites a secret Pentagon review of low flight attack routes. Together the pages keep a slice of late campaign season news as staff filed it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp06t00412r000200070001-1:
Pakistan under President Zia is assessed in a report dated February 1981, numbered PA 81-10045. The National Foreign Assessment Center issued it with facts current to 15 December 1980. Key judgments open the report and state that Zia had tightened his grip on power.

Pages trace how hopes for a swift return to elected rule faded after 1979. Local poll results showed the Pakistan People's Party could still win, the report states. The army then put off national polls, banned parties, and curbed the press and courts. Zia is portrayed as a reformer set on shaping society along Islamic lines. Findings are framed as the centre's assessed view.
cia-crest-cia-rdp07-00617r000200180001-1:
Dated August 1972 and marked ER H 71-1, the 1972 handbook was prepared by the Office of Economic Research. The Directorate of Intelligence issued it under a no foreign spread marking. An opening map sorts lands by gross product per head in 1971.

Top band on that map holds lands above 4,000 dollars per head, Canada and the United States among them. Charts then show energy use shares for the United States and West Europe. One table tracks primary energy output in coal terms from 1960 to 1971. United States output there peaks at 2,145.1 million metric tons in 1970.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10m00666r000301060001-1:
Economic steps against Libya are ordered in National Security Decision Directive Number 27, dated 9 March 1982. A White House memo of the same date sends it to a long list of top officials. William P. Clark signs the covering memo for the President.

Steps aim to cut the threat posed by Libyan policies, the directive states. New export controls bar set goods for Libya, with carve-outs for old contracts and small parts in goods made abroad. Old controls on Libya are not to be weakened by the change. Defense, the Director, and the Joint Chiefs must watch for Libyan and Soviet replies. A Libya task force led by State and the security adviser carries the work forward.
cia-crest-cia-rdp10t01930r000100090009-1:
Records held by the Office of Communications are counted in a memo dated 11 October 1983. The Chief of the Information Management Center sent the count to the DDA records officer. It serves as the office's annual records inventory for fiscal year 1983.

Forms list each kind of holding in linear feet and cubic feet side by side. Office files run to 2,320 linear feet on the form as printed. Reference books, catalogs, and manuals run to 2,627 in the same count. Magnetic stock is large too, with 1,142 computer tapes and 2,186 video tapes listed. Card files are shown as nil for this office in the year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp11s00229r000202220001-1:
Foreign technology in China's phone and message systems is weighed in a paper dated 9 May 1986. The Office of East Asian Analysis prepared it with facts current to that date. Japan had been China's chief supplier in recent years, the summary states.

Goals for the Seventh Five-Year Plan span 1986 to 1990 and are called bold. Plans cover wider phone service, a better network, and a satellite system of China's own. Foreign sellers put the market at 3 to 5 billion dollars over five years, the paper reports. Faults in buying and taking in foreign gear will slow the work, the paper judges. Findings are framed as assessed views, not settled fact.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100080005-1:
Mixed wartime papers of the Coordinator of Information make up a file catalogued under three heads for 1941. Heads listed are an economic defence setup, a joint security order, and a work agreement with the Department of Agriculture. Minutes of a staff meeting dated 8 December 1941 appear in the file.

Colonel Donovan chairs that meeting in the minutes as printed. Names listed as present include Richards, Kimbel, Wiley, Phillips, Langer, and Bruce. Talk turns to steps made urgent by the emergency of that week. Later pages hold a letter on shared film laboratory use and photo staff working side by side. The scan is uneven, with some pages far clearer than others.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100150007-1: OSS files with reports on Liberia and Bulgaria, a life sketch of Czech leader Benes, notes on Japanese-American relocation, and reporter Theresa Bonney's quiet Finland trip. This CREST bundle is a world-wide war scrapbook, full of odd corners of history.
cia-crest-cia-rdp13x00001r000100360004-1:
Friction with the FBI heads the catalogue line for a large 1942 file of OSS letters. Other heads listed name use of foreign groups for guerrilla war, a request from Mrs. Roosevelt, and staff letters. A letter dated 17 December opens the readable text.

Donovan writes to the Secretary of State for help on two Spain-bound trips. Enrique Godoy and his brother Raoul, both of Cuba, are named for one such trip. Stewart S. Hoppe and F. Wiley Clark are named for a trip to Turkey in the same letter. A later memo treats Albert Grzesinski, past Prussian Minister of the Interior and a 1933 refugee. His data on German figures fed Foreign Nationalities studies until the deal ended on 15 November, the memo states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100390006-1:
More U-2 aircraft are sought in a memo dated June 1963 to the Deputy Director. The writer reports months spent in a tug of war over added planes. Both the Air Force and the Agency state they are short of the craft.

A Joint Chiefs paper is said to show a net Air Force deficit of seven aircraft. The Agency grants it is two and perhaps three planes short of its own needs. Together the two could use about ten more U-2s with profit, the memo argues. Kelly Johnson at Lockheed was sounded out the past Friday on cost and timing. First delivery could come within eight months, he is reported to have said.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100390024-1:
Rest and rehabilitation for overseas staff is set as policy in a memo dated 13 December 1960. Richard M. Bissell, Jr. signs for the Deputy Director (Plans) area. The program had been approved in September 1957, the memo recalls.

Fifty-six stations and bases now take part, with nineteen rest points approved. Three years of use make it time to merge the patchwork plans into one policy, the memo argues. Part one grants rest leave to any overseas employee under set terms. Part two grants leave at set points for staff at hardship posts. One rest period per two year tour is the norm in the attached policy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000100390033-1:
Detachment G support needs fill a trip report memo dated 6 June 1961, DPD-3511-61. The report goes to the Acting Chief, DPD after a full tour of the site. Allowances briefing for staff bound for the post is still in draft, it states.

No added guards should go out before August 1961, the report advises. A personnel technician is wanted at once, while a medical technician can wait. Supply and warehouse clerks may be sent at any time, it adds. Two security posts stand empty, with men due on board in June and ready by July. One man's house lease ends 13 June, and leave that day was approved on the spot.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200010015-1:
Pressure to end United States flights over Cuba is plotted in a paper cast in a Soviet voice. The text speaks to Comrade Nikita and weighs the harm the flights do to ties with Fidel. It asks if the time has come to force the flights to stop.

Later pages set two phases for a campaign against the flights. Phase one builds a public case that the flights break the law of nations. Phase two then steps up pressure, with Berlin held in reserve as a threat. British ears would be told in private that their Cuban stake serves United States aims only. Gains at the UN and on the test ban are named as linked aims.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200180017-1:
A Honolulu trip on Pacific support is reported in a memo dated 28 September 1958. The memo goes to the Special Assistant to the Director for Planning and Development. Talks at Pacific Command on CHALICE material handling form its core, in garbled scan text.
