Admiral-level briefing at PACOM is urged as a courtesy, the memo states. A TALENT exhibit briefing would be led by a named staff officer with service help. Security and support plans are treated in attached papers, kept apart for clarity. Detachment C airlift and base support needs close the file's last paper. The scan is rough throughout, though heads and key lines stay legible.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000200270053-1:
Support at the Detachment A training site is graded in Supervisory Visit Report number 1. The visit was made on 15 November 1956 by the SAC Liaison Unit at March Air Force Base. Beds on site total 232 against a base strength near 200, the report states.

Housing and messing pass with no major fault found. Vehicle counts are listed, from two carryalls to five jeeps and two ambulances. No clear plan says who supplies test gear parts to the detachment, the report warns. The base flight section is called a missed area, with two men for many aircraft. A new storehouse 100 by 40 feet is going up for supply use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300150028-1:
May 1962 brought a long bad weather sit in a commander's report dated 6 June 1962, IDEA-0502. Ten weeks of poor flying weather faced the unit from the month's start. One operational sortie was flown in the whole month, the report states.

Aircraft 358 and 378 flew 30 hours in all, mostly training work. Fuel stocks now suffice to keep pilot skill from fading, it adds. Two sound engines are fitted, with spares in place on site. Hostel building added two bedrooms to ease crowding for guests. The unit stands ready for a long run once the weather breaks, the commander writes.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000300160009-1:
Far East flight counts are tabled in an attachment of approvals and missions by month. September 1963 opens the run, with daily weather watch kept through the autumn. China flights lead the counts month by month in the table.

Four China missions flew in September 1963, with Sino-Indian and Vietnam Laos work beside them. COMOR advised no flights in December 1963 pending a review, the table notes. One flight on 25 December 1963 went ahead by higher authority. Fuel control faults left the aircraft non-operational in mid-January 1964. A weather annex then logs Vietnam sky grades day by day for January and February.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050028-1:
Air Force memorandum dated 23 July 1962, sent to the NRO Program Directors and the Director of the NRO Staff, sets out the organisation and functions of the National Reconnaissance Office. It rests on the June 1962 defence and CIA agreements and on a defence directive of 14 June 1962. The stated aim is a basic structure that holds until formal NRO rules replace it.

Core concepts stress concealment: the Office is an operating agency hidden inside other agencies, using their staff and resources full or part time. It is to stay as small as possible, run by a Director, a staff, and Program Directors who control far larger groups through overt added duties. Program A, the satellite effort run through the Air Force side, is named as one of the two program lines.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050037-1:
Agreement dated 2 May 1962 between the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence fixes responsibilities for the National Reconnaissance Office. Opening definitions set the National Reconnaissance Program as all overt and covert satellite and overflight projects for intelligence, geodesy, mapping photography, and electronic signal collection. The Director of the NRO, named jointly by the two principals, answers directly to them for the program.

The Office is to respond only to collection needs and priorities set by the United States Intelligence Board. CIA acts as executive agent for covert projects already under its management, plus any later assigned. Staff from the Army, Navy, Air Force, and CIA fill NRO posts full time, and a firm liaison channel links the Office to the National Security Agency on signal work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050046-1:
Agreement dated 20 March 1962 between the Department of Defense and the Central Intelligence Agency establishes a National Reconnaissance Program. It deals with management and operation of that program, and with handling of its product, all on a covert basis. The program takes in all satellite and overflight reconnaissance, whether overt or covert, including photography for intelligence, geodesy, and mapping, plus electronic signal collection.

A National Reconnaissance Office is set up in secret to manage the program, led by a Director and a Deputy drawn one each from Defense and CIA. The Under Secretary of the Air Force serves on the Defense side and the Deputy Director for Research on the Agency side. A uniform security system covers the whole program, with CIA defining policy, and products go to users named by the United States Intelligence Board.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400050055-1:
Letter dated 6 September 1961, on Department of Defense letterhead and addressed to the Honorable Allen W. Dulles, confirms an agreement on management of the National Reconnaissance Program. It sets the program's scope as all satellite and overflight reconnaissance, overt or covert, including photographic work for intelligence, geodesy, and mapping, and electronic signal collection. Handling of the product is to stay on a covert basis.

A National Reconnaissance Office is established in secret to run the program, under the Under Secretary of the Air Force and the CIA Deputy Director for Plans acting jointly. A small special staff is drawn from both organisations, and the Office holds direct control over all parts of the program. The Under Secretary is also named Special Assistant for Reconnaissance to the Secretary of Defense, with full authority in the field.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400060045-1:
Agreement text between the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence, surviving here from a middle section onward, lists the functions of the National Reconnaissance Office in lettered items. Visible items cover presenting the program to the Special Group and the President's Foreign Intelligence Advisory Board. They also cover keeping one uniform system of security procedures. Policy for that system is set by the Director of Central Intelligence.

Budget work is assigned in detail. The Office prepares requests for all its programs. It defends them before the two principals, the Bureau of the Budget, and congressional committees. Funds handed to CIA under Public Law 110 are administered and accounted for by the Agency. An authorities section then empowers the Director to organise, staff, and supervise the Office and to establish and manage its projects.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000400300002-1:
Attachment chart set headed IDEALIST Mission History, filed with a 1970 headquarters paper, counts U-2 missions by region and year in a wide table. Regions listed run from the USSR and the Mid East to Cuba, South America, and the China and Tibet borderlands. A satellite column and an ELINT row sit beside the regional counts, with yearly totals along the foot of the table.

A short history page gives the program in dates: presidential approval in December 1954, first flight in August 1955, and first overflight in June 1956. Detachments at Adana in Turkey and Atsugi in Japan are dated to their spans, and Edwards Air Force Base follows from October 1960. Later pages list personnel and aircraft authorised at two detachments, naming U-2C and U-2G aircraft among the types held.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500070016-1:
Memorandum commenting on the charter agreement between the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence, document BYE-6647-63, gives the CIA view of the draft. The proposed agreement is judged, in general, a logical and workable charter for managing the National Reconnaissance Program. It sets out what the program and the Office will do, the memo notes, without specifying how, and the rest of the paper offers changes for the final form.

The lead change puts the Deputy Director squarely in the chain of command, between the Director and the NRO staff and program directors. He would act with the Director's powers in his absence and stay informed on all activity at all times. Further edits strike an ambiguous paragraph, drop the word managing from one clause, and tighten the wording of the Office's collection functions over denied territory.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500120029-1:
Evaluation report on mission GT 67-466 uses a flight of 29 November 1967 to test BIMAT processing against standard field methods. Mobile resolution targets, of the T bar type, were displayed at Tucson and Phoenix, and passes were flown toward and away from the sun over both. Forward and aft cameras thus gained negatives under matched light angles, and the target areas were cloud free.

Forward camera material was processed with BIMAT transfer film, while aft material went through conventional Versamat field processing. Extra copies of the forward negative were also run through a standard system and a second transfer method, and all products went forward for scoring. Five evaluators read the resolution targets frame by frame, and the report tabulates their readings by camera, heading, and sun angle.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000500120038-1:
Questions and answers paper TA-47-100169-2, dated 13 November 1967, works through practical points on a proposed diffusion transfer processing system. Early questions cover stop-and-go processing that lets staff inspect film mid-run, and how much of it is done now on the more advanced materials. Inspection, the answer notes, must happen on the fly in the dark, using infrared scanners or snooperscopes.

A staffing comparison gives the sharpest figures. A typical mission load of film now keeps twenty-eight men in a photo laboratory, counting supervisors and maintenance staff. The same load, the paper states, could be finished by three people in five hours inside a diffusion transfer shelter. The answer is candid that the small crew takes shortcuts, such as hand marking leaders rather than titling frame by frame.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600040117-1:
Ordering and issuing supplies at Detachment H follows SOP H-45-33, dated 10 August 1970. The Logistics Officer watches over the use of these rules. Section heads must learn them, and they apply to all staff who order or receive property for the unit. The aim is a single clear path from request to issue, with each step recorded.

Stock items are drawn at the warehouse counter by stock number and logged on a daily issue sheet. For a returnable item, the person drawing it must hand back a like item for repair or sign a hand receipt, AF Form 1297. Shipping papers, DD Form 1149, then go to stock records staff for posting. An annex from September 1970 closes the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070024-1:
Flight control in clear weather for aircraft flying to and from a test area is described in standing operating procedure 50-3060-1, dated 22 October 1965. It applies to all pilots using the area. Flights other than set missions with prior approval need notice in advance, arranged by collect phone call to named extensions at the base, during or after duty hours.

Aircraft from Nellis Air Force Base may arrange notice through its dispatcher and switchboard. Any shift of more than one hour in arrival or departure times needs fresh notice. Clearance is filed on DD Form 1080. Night rules close the text: aircraft stay high enough to clear the hills around the station until their position over the aid is certain.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000600070051-1:
Per diem and mileage payments are set on a single footing in standing operating procedure 22-3177-1, dated 1 August 1968. It covers military staff, Air Force civilian staff, and contract staff assigned or attached to the unit. Civilian claims follow the Standard Government Travel Regulations. Military claims follow the Joint Travel Regulations, as the text names them both in its opening pages.

The unit's duty point for travel claims is stated, and changes to travel plans need approval from the base commander or his deputies. One paid compensatory trip a month may be granted to deserving staff. Other pages treat proficiency and cross-country flights, official flights, and a master ledger kept by the Finance Officer recording each payment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700010010-1:
Attachment titled Format and Sample Report shows how a detachment's periodic report should be built, using a filled-in sample as the model. Part I, Activities, opens with a summary. The sample detachment reports a healthy readiness state, with two proven aircraft and six highly proficient mission pilots. A third aircraft is due to be ready by mid June.

Operations matter follows. It includes ferry support for Articles 383 and 385 to an operating location. It also covers a deployment of twenty-five people. The sample also notes strain from upkeep work, two poor engines from a repair shop, and a study seeking more shop space. Later parts set pilot recurrency rules, tying ready status to a set share of quarterly flying.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050016-1:
Project Headquarters directive 50-10-28, dated 20 June 1966, gives standard camera procedures for all headquarters directed IDEALIST missions. It replaces a March 1964 directive. The aim is the best photo quality and gear reliability that can be had. Headquarters will try to warn detachments of changes for local or seasonal conditions. Detachment commanders may still vary the rules when time runs short.

All photo gear must be bench checked before a mission. Set settings follow for each camera: exposure, aperture, overlap, and filter. The Bravo camera on 3400 film is listed first. Then come the Delta III on 3404 film, and the Mark II Tracker at a thirty-two second interval. A second paper in the file covers report formats.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000700050034-1:
OSA headquarters directive 300-51, dated 31 March 1964 by the printed heading, covers staff going on annual leave. Each person must leave an address and a phone number where they can be reached. Supervisors must keep track of where their people are during an absence. Key staff must tell both their own office and the Assistant Director's office where they will be while away.

Bound with it is Project Headquarters directive 300-5-1, dated 24 March 1966. That directive covers weekend duty officers for the Office of Special Activities. Later papers in the file turn to unsolicited proposals. They show how proposals reach OSA from firms, other agencies, or its own staff. They also show how proposals are screened, and who is named Proposal Control Officer to track them.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800250004-1:
Research and development quarterly report for April, May, and June 1968 is sent 2 July 1968 to the Director of Operations, OSA. Its OXCART section opens with sensors: nineteen photographic missions were flown from 1 April to 28 May 1968, the date of the last camera configuration flight in the quarter. Mission counts by camera type follow in the attached text.

Engine oil system work is covered in detail. A boost pump change to hold steady inlet pressure needs careful hand adjustment on the ground, which may cause field problems. Pratt and Whitney was studying whether design changes could remove the flaw. Life support notes add S-1010 suit fittings for three pilots, and filter tests that showed less gain than hoped with black and white film.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800310007-1:
Quarterly property report dated 18 February 1969, to a contracting officer, proposes a format for an informal report on all headquarters programs and contracts. The next issue, in early April, would cover the first quarter of calendar year 1969. Industrial plant equipment comes first: General Services Administration appraisal work tied to a Lockheed offer to buy government facilities, including Building 199, is complete, with talks expected in March.

Flight test equipment inventory holds about 2,500 line items, with about 235 items turned in since the prior October. Later sections cover OXCART property lists, tooling and government property disposition under an October 1968 memorandum of understanding, and contract status for government furnished equipment across OSA contracts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340004-1:
Attachment to DDS&T-2679-68, dated 9 July 1968, reports the state of the historical program for the Deputy Director for Science and Technology as of 1 July 1968. A routing slip from the Historical Board chairman sends the report to the Director of Special Activities and the Historical Officer. Each office's history is graded as done, submitted, or still in draft.

The Office of Special Projects history is done and submitted, in sixty-nine pages in five parts, from the office's start in September 1965 through December 1967. The Office of Research and Development history runs 141 pages, with twenty-nine monographs of 300 to 400 pages. The ELINT history is done but not yet approved, at sixty-four pages plus seventeen appendices. Other offices, including Special Activities and the missile analysis center, remain unfinished.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340013-1:
Memorandum OXC-0003/68, dated 25 April 1968, from the Intelligence Division, OSA, answers a division-wide call for OSA history material. The division's outline begins in 1958, when its staff helped draw up requirements for Project GUSTO. Inputs came from naval, air force, and other intelligence offices, plus target forecasts and system performance data.

From 1962 onward the outline covers OXCART planning. It lists vulnerability work, intelligence support staff and materials, cable control, and briefing formats. Targeting and resistance-to-interrogation training are also named. BLACK SHIELD and other mission operations close the first page, with command post and SKYLARK items named. The file is short, a draft outline rather than a finished history.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030053-1:
Bundle of blank agency forms opens with a request for overseas shipment of cargo, Form No. 36-4, dated September 1946. Its instructions tell the shipper to phone the cargo officer first, so a cargo number can be assigned and marked on each unit of the shipment. Fields cover units shipped, contents for customs and censorship, packing or crating needs, the consignee's name and destination in the clear, and where goods will be gathered for pickup.

Further forms in the bundle include a government transportation request certificate, a travel order form with routine and secret routing boxes, and a movement request for families and household goods. Weight for household effects is estimated by a printed rule: one thousand pounds per room. Signatures of authorizing and approving officials close each form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030116-1:
Administrative Services regulation gathers the housekeeping duties of that office in numbered sections. Space comes first: the Chief, Administrative Services, holds responsibility for agency space planning, acquisition, assignment, and disposition. Operating offices must not negotiate for space on their own without notice to and approval from that chief. Requests for space by permit, lease, purchase, or construction go to him in writing from office heads.

Building services follow. Requests for work carry full details of what is required, with drawings or sketches where practical, and name the person to contact. Jobs touching the physical security of an area go to the inspection and security staff first. Reproduction rules close the file: finished work is receipted on the original of Form 36-2 and returned to the Reproduction Division.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050006-1:
Executive Order 10483, signed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower on 2 September 1953, establishes the Operations Coordinating Board. The board is set up to secure integrated carrying out of national security policies by the several agencies. It reports to the National Security Council. Members are the Under Secretary of State as chairman, the Deputy Secretary of Defense, the Director of the Foreign Operations Administration, the Director of Central Intelligence, and a presidential representative.

Each agency named may provide an alternate member. The alternate serves when the regular member cannot attend a meeting. The board's work is to advise agencies on their detailed planning duties for each policy. It also coordinates the interdepartmental parts of agency plans, and watches over timely and coordinated execution. The order closes by stating the board gains no internal security function, and no legal function of any agency is cut back.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000100020024-1:
Memorandum dated 25 January 1949 resubmits a proposal to reorganize the Training Staff, TRS. A first version went forward on 1 October 1948, but action was held at Col. Galloway's request until his successor arrived. Training commitments are now hard to meet for lack of staff, the memo states, and no recruits can be taken on without vacant posts. Some new posts are therefore asked as ceiling positions, to be filled later when clearly needed, marked in red on the final table.

Covert training posts draw the higher grades, since only mature, field seasoned men should give that tutorial teaching. A Deputy for Special Projects would carry both instructional and services duties. A records, tests, and evaluations section is also proposed, to supply facts for placement, reclassification, and advancement decisions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00252a000200040021-1:
Memorandum dated 4 August 1950, to the Chief, TRD, answers the final report of the Training Review Committee point by point. Each item was discussed with the section chiefs and chief instructors of the Staff Training Branch. A two week seminar refresher course, mornings only, is backed as an excellent idea. Such courses ran well in 1948 and 1949 and stopped only for lack of students in 1949, the memo says. A draft outline is in preparation.

A one week administrative course for clerical staff is also recommended, beside the regular administrative training course. On classified material, chief instructors agreed the clarity the committee wants can be reached inside a Confidential limit, and steps are being taken to stress principles common to operational and information reporting. Requests for statements on specialized courses have gone to OPC, and plans are in discussion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00337a000100030001-1:
Navy papers of Underwater Demolition Team Two open with a letter on sneak attacks, from the Submersible Operations Officer. Italy, Japan, Finland, and Germany showed the most active interest in sneak attack as a naval weapon, the letter states. Only Italy and England scored notable success with such attacks in World War II. Russian effort is unknown, but captured German craft and their builders are in Russian hands, and the letter presumes the gift was not left idle.

United States interest has been slight, and exercise practice is criticized. Defenses that succeed in exercises may breed contempt for a real attack. Ill defined rules have also produced a cops and robber spirit. Closing pages urge a standing unit, its nucleus drawn from submersible operations platoons of the teams, the best qualified men in the Navy for sneak craft work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00355a000100020039-1:
Course outline for Section V, Intelligence Methods and Techniques, treats the intelligence processes as professional skills and shows how they are used in the intelligence cycle. Scope covers collection and source exploitation, production and presentation, dissemination, planning and coordination, and counter intelligence. Lectures run through the 1951 season in morning and afternoon slots, each followed by discussion.

Early lectures follow the policy planning cycle from problem to reappraisal of effects, given by the State Department's policy planning staff. Collection lectures draw on mass communications media, aerial photography, foreign language documents, and foreign nationals as sources. The evaluation, collation, and analytical processes each get a lecture from O/RR. A closing lecture covers planning the scope and terms of reference of the intelligence product, and how firm such decisions can be.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00001a000100050037-1:
Shorter statement of the area specialists project, dated 19 January 1951, gives the plan's numbers. Federal funds would train 1,000 specialists at university area centers. The first thousand are split by region. The USSR takes 250, the Far East 200, and Central and Western Europe 150. South Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Middle East take 100 each. Latin America takes 60, and Africa 40. Sub-area choices follow, as with Burma, Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines inside Southeast Asia.

Costs are itemized to a total of 15,500,000 dollars. Student upkeep for two years, at 200 dollars a month, comes to 4,800,000 dollars. Travel and field work for a year, at 5,000 dollars a head, adds 5,000,000 dollars. Books and teaching materials are put at 400,000 dollars. Stronger course offerings take 1,000,000 dollars, and running the program for three years 300,000 dollars.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100020002-1:
Official report on the Eleventh Agency Orientation Course covers a four day program held 4 to 7 August 1953 in the Department of Agriculture Auditorium. Contents run from format through evaluation and recommendations to appreciation. The four days carry set themes: Background, Support and Coordination, the Production Function, and the Agency in the present day. This was the seventh course held under the regulation calling for one every three months.

Speaker judgments fill the evaluation. One colonel's collection talk is faulted for shallowness in the question period, despite a deeper story being available. Sherman Kent's coordination talk is called a good academic performance that made a foggy impression, short on examples. His method is judged less successful than Mr. Amory's at the last course. Thanks close the report, for a staff member whose calls held the program together.
cia-crest-cia-rdp55-00110a000100020011-1:
Official report on the Fifth Agency Orientation Course covers the first program held under the regulation calling for a course every three months. It ran four days in the Department of Agriculture Auditorium, whose 550-plus seats are still not enough to clear the backlog of staff waiting, the report states. The hall is already booked for the sixth course, set for 8 to 11 April 1952. The program follows the four part pattern used across this run of courses.

Registration figures close the body. Total attendance is tabled at 526. Twenty-three mismatches were found between the first and final registration slips: twenty-three people appear on one and not the other. The office will hold all slips from the five courses so far until a machine system can take the data, its filing space being very limited. Thanks to the small team, for long hours gladly given, end the report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100030031-1:
Reference sheet on standard government allowances and differentials, explaining each payment in plain terms and giving the steps for starting it. The payments named are quarters allowances, cost-of-living allowances, and post differentials, run by the Agency under Department of State and Civil Service Commission rules. A quarters payment applies when government housing is not on hand.

Two kinds of living quarters payment are set out: temporary lodging on first arrival at a new post, and the standing quarters allowance. Cost-of-living payments come in four kinds: post, special post, transfer, and separation. For most, the field unit tells the Finance Division that the person has arrived, and no forms are asked of the person. Foreign and territorial post differentials, paid as a share of basic pay, close the sheet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00071a000100040003-1:
File on mileage and parking fee claims, opened by a routing slip. A memorandum dated 30 March 1951 sits inside. It went to the Comptroller through the Deputy Comptroller. The Audit Division chief signed it. The Finance Division chief added comments. The Training Division had asked for such payments. Its instructors used private cars on official business.

Claims had grown sharply since June 1950. Many parts of the Agency were filing them. A staff meeting took up the question. Finance was told to stop most claims. Clear need and travel orders could save a claim. Regular trips to covert training sites qualified. City trips were treated in a stricter way. Public transport or the motor pool should serve them. Later pages weigh taxi rules as well. Government travel rules are quoted and compared.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020042-1:
File built around a cardex card system. A card was filled out for each strong candidate. The Junior Officer Training Division chief interviewed first. The card held a short personal history. It also held a statement of qualifications. Training and current status went on the back. Fields covered tests, clearance, and language skill.

A program account fills most of the file. The Agency Junior Officer Trainee and OCS program is explained. General Smith first proposed the program. He wanted a junior officer corps built with care. College success alone did not satisfy him. Discipline and character were needed as well. He held that military service built those traits. Entry steps are set out in order. A candidate could gain a draft deferment. Unclassified training filled the wait for clearance. Full clearance led to the Basic Intelligence Course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100020079-1:
Status paper on Office of Training (Special) activities. Its mission serves the Clandestine Services. Courses run inside the United States. A draft catalog forms an appendix. Course aims and data are stated there. The catalog supplements a handbook dated 27 March 1953. Training began with OSO personnel only. Courses later spread across the plans directorate.

New Agency staff training became mandatory for professionals. The Career Service Program required that step. The Director approved that program himself. Basic intelligence grounding was the aim. Minimum standards for clandestine staff followed. Those standards date from 21 January 1953. Changes at training sites are reported too. One phase was set to move in January 1954. A headquarters refresher was planned for returnees. Ground training courses were revived and reshaped. Shorter courses gained weight over longer ones.
cia-crest-cia-rdp56-00403a000100040013-1:
Office of Training Regulation number 5-2, dated 14 April 1952. Its subject is preparing Agency OTR regulations. A set format guides all such drafting. Order of parts is fixed by the guide. Drafts go to the Chief, Support Staff. That chief checks them in final form. Issuance numbers are assigned there. Reproduction and spread happen there too.

Paragraph style is set out with care. Headings are used where matter suits outline form. Letter and number symbols mark each level. Double spacing is required between parts. The first rule in each series sets policy. Duties for carrying out policy sit there too. Detailed steps go in separate rules. That split avoids frequent rewriting of base rules. A second regulation follows in the file. It covers a historical file for Training (General). Support sections and their services fill later pages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000010121-1: Short memorandum dated 10 September 1955 from the Project Security Officer, reporting inquiries made at the Shuttle Terminal in Burbank. A captain had sought information about a shuttle flight and its passengers from a West Coast security officer, and no specific information was given. The matter was reported to the Agency Deputy Project Director, and headquarters handling through Air Force officials was expected to prevent further inquiries of this kind.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000070053-1:
Memorandum dated 14 March 1956 to the Agency Project Director. Justification of an operations table of organization is its subject. The jobs listed man the Operations Control Center. That center runs around the clock each day. An administrative supervisor post is justified first. Code 70370 marks that post in the table. A statistical post follows in the list.

An operations staff officer post comes next. That officer works in the Control Center itself. Air navigator posts are justified after that. Navigators give mission coverage for the aircraft. Peak traffic hours shape their numbers. Air operations posts follow in the justification. A supervisor and a specialist are both listed. Status boards and charts fall to those posts. Full twenty-four-hour coverage is the stated aim. Commissioned officers supply that coverage in shifts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000080151-1:
Summary dated 26 March 1956 of a visit to Watertown Strip. The visit ran from 21 to 23 March. Problems of a detachment fill the opening summary. Tests set for 9 to 13 April raised a concern. Some detachment personnel would not be available then. They could not fill their primary jobs for the tests. A review of the table of organization followed.

Four positions were judged critical for the tests. A physiological training officer was one of them. An aeromedical technician held position 714. A warehousing supervisor held position 790. A warehousing specialist held position 351. Supply help could come from an outside unit. One or two men might serve sixty-five days overseas. That time would let Agency project supply staff finish processing. Pilot billets get separate treatment in the summary. Detachment A pilots would be billeted overseas. They would be treated as integral detachment members.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000110111-1:
Report of an Agency visit to the Eastman Kodak processing plant. The visitor's name is sanitized out of the title. Much of the scan reads very poorly. Legible parts name processing equipment items. Items A-4012 and A-4015 are discussed together. Partial time figures appear beside those items. A-4019 received only prior development, one passage states. A-4012 received intermediate development instead.

Printers get attention in the legible fragments. One printer is called one of the latest types. A finishing problem with coupled film is noted. Film and paper tearing is the problem named. That fault was to be remedied shortly. A register device needing a part is mentioned. The role of the processing plant is discussed as well. Whether development should stay there is weighed. Because so much text is garbled, fine detail cannot be read with confidence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00011a001000150009-1:
Memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence. Amendment number eight to contract A-101 is its subject. The Ramo-Wooldridge Corporation is the contractor. Project AQUATONE is named in parentheses in the head. A recommendation is submitted for the Director's approval. That recommendation is set out in paragraph seven. The base contract and amendments one to seven are surveyed.

Those papers cover research on systems one to three. Deployment equipment for those systems is covered. Production of system one is included as well. Limited production covers systems two and three. System four sits in study phase only. Government-furnished tooling is also provided for. Amendment six swapped in a new schedule. Its points are listed one by one. System two production needs are final for AQUATONE. System four sees partial production requirements set. Ground exploitation gear purchases are final too. Cost tables close the memorandum.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00012a000100060005-1:
Paper on the value of audio-visual aids in modern education. Most knowledge comes through the eye, it argues. Aids clarify information for the student. They increase retention of new information. They fix impressions in the mind more firmly. They also shorten the learning period. The motion picture is treated as the chief such aid.

Training films suit clandestine instruction in a special way. Students identify with figures on the screen. Set attitudes can be reshaped by that means. Wrong information can be corrected through film. A practical approach to field problems can be taught. Survey results on a film fill the later pages. Viewers judged its area background for Agency use. Most found that background satisfactory for the purpose. More area detail was the chief complaint raised. Some wanted an Iron Curtain setting instead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100020006-1:
Memorandum for the Director of Central Intelligence, untitled in the catalog. A reference memo dates from 3 September 1954. Its subject was withdrawal of twenty-seven positions. Those positions came from the Director's Reserve. The problem here matches that earlier paper. A reservoir of civilian ceiling positions is needed. The Director's Reserve supplying it is diminishing.

Four methods now meet requests for ceiling increases. Agency increases without the reserve form one method. Withdrawals from the Director's Reserve form another. Intra-Agency transfers and other reserves follow. No uniform criteria govern the four methods. Record keeping is split between two offices. The Comptroller keeps the Director's Reserve records. The Office of Personnel keeps all other allocations. The reserve is not budgeted for specifically. Confusion results from that split, the memo states. A contingency cushion is urged in closing. It would sit inside the total ceiling. The Administration deputy would administer that cushion.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100060011-1:
Memorandum dated 3 January 1950 to the Agency Executive. Management recommendations on the Liaison Division are its subject. The Assistant Director for Collection and Dissemination wrote it. The paper under review dates from 8 September 1949. It is called a good paper in the opening. Most recommendations were concise and already acted on. Some had come from the division itself.

Requirements form the one broad problem left. That problem is called damnably knotty in the text. More memoranda had grown from it than any other. A proposed panel draws the writer's dissent. Such a panel would eat highly paid time. It would delay action on pending requirements. It would add formalized paper work as well. A separate OCD memorandum was being written instead. Speed in reproduction gets a defense later. A multigraph could be used without forms or requisitions.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100070001-1:
Agency memorandum dated 18 October 1949 on the Industrial Register. A management survey of that register is its subject. The Management Officer sent it through the Executive. Five months had passed since the last survey. Substantial improvements were found in that span. A master index tab card now exists per extract. A sizeable indexing backlog was eliminated by it.

No product cards had yet been prepared, though. A typing backlog on ICF cards was shrinking. Three to four months would clear it fully. Serious problems still impaired the register, however. Dissemination of the Industrial Card File weighed heavily. Much of that work was duplicate and unnecessary. Only Army and Air had asked to continue it. Materials in the register were not evaluated. Their form blocked ready use by consumers. An evaluated file was planned for coding and punching.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100140021-1:
Cover memorandum with attachments on the Foreign Documents Branch. The branch sits in the Office of Operations. A revised statement of functions is attached first. It rescinds all earlier statements in conflict. A management survey report is attached second. The Chief, Management Branch, wrote that survey. The pair went to the Agency Assistant Director for Operations.

The survey serves use and guidance for development. Coordination with other activities is part of that use. Coordination with other agencies is included as well. Implementing action had already been taken on one part. Paragraph E of section three is the part named. The survey text weighs how exploitation should run. Significant information should reach analysts in report form. Time-consuming steps before that point are questioned. Intelligence Catalog Cards list German document contents. The Foreign Documents Division prepares those cards. Another body disseminates them under the system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100150002-1:
Management study of the Map Division in the reports office. The Office of Reports and Estimates is its parent. Mission opens the study in formal terms. The chief runs an interdepartmental geographic service. Map intelligence is part of that service. Foreign map procurement requirements are coordinated there. Reports and evaluations of geographic intelligence are produced.

New map compilations are made for intelligence purposes. A working reference collection is maintained as well. It holds maps and related material on foreign areas. The chief may delegate parts of his duties. Overall responsibility for results cannot be delegated. Functions are listed under his authority. Concurrence practice gets close treatment later. Signing CIA papers implies partial co-authorship. Concurrence can clash with an agency's own conclusions. That tension is set out as a problem. National intelligence directive problems close the passage.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000100310004-1:
Summary tables of outgoing personnel communications for a division. June, July, and August 1953 are the months covered. Cables and memorandums are counted by subject. Leave matters head the visible subject list. Table and personnel report matters follow. Military personnel, promotions, and travel are listed. Position classification and conversions appear as subjects too.

Resignations and personnel evaluations are counted in the table. Security, training, and procurement matters close it. Averages per month are computed at the foot. Chronological files began only in the periods shown. Records kept by the section are described next. Personnel files use divided folders per person. Pseudonym slots combine with true name slots there. Four document groups fill each folder. Personnel actions, travel, fiscal matters, and general papers appear. Functions of the Agency personnel section close the file. Current status of the table must be maintained.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200040003-1:
Memorandum dated 10 February to the Agency Comptroller. Transfer of activities from General Services is its subject. The Office of the Comptroller would receive them. Transfer would take effect on 15 February. The General Services Office makeup is described first. A machine records branch forms part of it. A special branch and distribution branch are named. Mail control sits inside that office as well.

Those activities are the ones moving to the Comptroller. Logistics Office would take a different named activity. Attached lists sort the positions involved. Positions in the framework of the moving activities are listed. Four employees form one part of the transfer. Their names and present positions are given there. Positions that cannot be filled are noted too. Existing personnel ceilings block those fillings. Fiscal year budgets for the records division follow. Mail control budgets appear beside them in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200080027-1:
Report of survey on the Personnel Procurement Division. The Personnel Office, Central Intelligence Agency, is its setting. Personnel Studies and Procedures Staff conducted it. Three sections structure the long report. General findings open the survey treatment. Review of work forms the second section. The closing section gives the survey's advice.

Added parts follow that advice in the volume. Working quality of hiring is the survey theme. Staffing plans were reviewed fully in it. Current and put-forward steps were examined too. Ties with other staff work were studied. Ties to other Agency offices were included. Relations with the general public were covered. A plan of structure is urged at the end. Administrative changes are put alongside that plan. Applicant files receive close treatment in the text. Control records govern access to those files. Partial files and referral forms are discussed. Location of each file must be easy to find.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00042a000200200023-1:
Memo sending on a staff study on three programs. Testing, assessment, and psychiatric programs are studied. The Agency Organization and Methods Service prepared the study. It went to the deputy chief for Administration. The problem is to analyze three missions. The Psychiatric Program of the Medical Office is first. The Assessment Program of the Training Office follows. The Testing Program of the Personnel Office is third.

No widely agreed meanings open the assumptions. Psychology and psychiatry lack agreed senses. Three units in the chart perform the key roles. Persons on board are counted against sixty-seven slots. Unknown numbers do related work too. Their slots are not labeled as psychologist slots. Yet their duties touch the three programs. Calm under strain receives attention later. Traits must be weighed against that calm. Psychiatric rulings may be duplicated thereby. Psychologists cannot treat emotional troubles here. Psychiatrists are allowed to treat them instead.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000200010006-1:
Agency office memo dated 30 March 1954 on a course study. The Basic Training unit chief wrote to the Training chief. Revised Phase III Course number one is studied. Content and conduct both receive general study. Matter made for the course is judged fitting. Stated course aims are the measure used. Coverage appears enough overall. Gaps are commented on in part two.

Conduct proceeded as scheduled throughout. No real trouble arose during its run. Transfer from Washington had threatened that smoothness. Guest lecturers appeared on time regardless. One exception to that punctuality is noted. Minor schedule adjustments were made without trouble. Headquarters coordination with Washington proved effective. Records integration site gets a critique later. A lecture there centers on a site tour. Without the tour it runs dry and weak. Name checks draw a steady complaint onward. Guest speakers limit that lecture's use repeatedly.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00259a000200040012-1:
Summary report copy on a Human Resources Program. Senior officials of the Agency are its participants. The memorandum is dated March 1954 in the text. A ninety minute initial phase was conducted. Six groups of senior officials took that phase. The period ran 1 December 1953 to 12 March 1954. Three groups drew officials across the Agency.

Two groups were exclusively administration personnel in makeup. One group held plans division chiefs and equivalents. A roster of participants is attached as an appendix. Earlier participants are noted there too. Objectives in conducting the program are stated plainly. Basic supervisory training reached top operating personnel. Their reactions and suggestions were secured by it. Cooperative action at senior level was stimulated. Improvement of management in CIA is the end. Decentralization emerges in the later discussion. Management improvement must decentralize to be effective. Directorate level is the minimum depth suggested.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100150079-1:
Agency memorandum dated 23 October 1951 calling for progress reports. The Assistant to the Director addressed many officials. Deputies, assistant directors, and the Training Director appear. The General Counsel is also an addressee. A comprehensive progress report is due 1 January 1952. The President and National Security Council receive it. Its period runs October 1950 to December 1951.

A critical self-analysis of operations is intended. The President should be accurately updated by it. Health of the national intelligence system is the measure. Temper, character, and range are prescribed carefully. Objectivity and honesty in appraisal are insisted upon. Over-emphasis on internal organization must be avoided. Analytical examination of guiding concepts matters more. An outline structure appears in the later pages. Place and role within the system come first. Coordination, collection, and processing responsibilities follow it. Covert operations responsibility completes the outline given.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000100220008-1:
Tenure, job security and cuts in staff size form the subject of a task force memorandum dated 1 October 1953, sent to the Director of Central Intelligence. The paper asks whether new law is needed to fix the standing of career employees and to run any forced cuts fairly. It sets out the Agency aim: a picked, trained group who want intelligence work as a lasting career. Career staff, it argues, should face cuts only after other groups are cut first.

Attached tabs weigh the Director's special powers, veteran preference in staff cuts, and the risk that outside review could expose sources and methods. The paper treats job safety as part of building a stable career service, not as a bare perk. It leaves open how far law, rather than Agency rule, should carry that promise.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400050004-1:
House Report Number 2698, sent to the full House on 20 July 1950, backs a bill to set a hiring path for the competitive civil service. The Committee on Post Office and Civil Service reported the bill, H.R. 8925, in favour with changes. Its stated aim is choice of staff by open contest and merit. The listed changes adjust wording on the Commission's role and on help from each department.

The report then walks through the bill part by part, setting out what each clause would do. Open testing, public notice, and merit sit at the centre of the case made to the House. Kept among Agency papers, the report marks the hiring rules debate that shaped how most federal staff, CIA's included in part, entered service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400050031-1:
PPD Memorandum Number 15-52, dated 31 March 1952, gives working instructions for a Requisition Inventory covering open hiring requests. The stated purpose is a better system for giving procurement, placement, and operating officers sound, ordered data. Better data, in turn, should yield more well-qualified candidates. The inventory runs on a flexible set of Requisition Cards that carry the facts on each open request.

Card faces record unit, grade range, priority, age range, schooling, and the traits wanted in a candidate. Parts of the inventory go out from the requesting unit to personnel officers in the field. Later sections cover how cards are made, sent, filed, and kept current. The memorandum is a small window on the paper machinery behind Agency hiring.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400050040-1:
Two short memoranda dated 7 January 1952, from the Office of General Counsel to the Assistant Director for Personnel, name sources of specialised manpower. Each sheet lists one kind of lawyer the office needs. The first calls for an attorney in corporate law, the second for one in contracting and procurement. Law firms and bar groups are put forward as good sources to develop for both needs.

Each sheet is signed by the branch or division chief and routed through the administration office. Together they show hiring at its most concrete: a law office naming the exact skills it lacked and where such people might be found. The sheets are brief, signed forms rather than a study, and they carry no names of candidates.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400060003-1:
Circular Number A-42 from the Bureau of the Budget, dated 22 November 1950, sends out a ruling on which agency programs count as tied straight to national defense. The ruling rests on Executive Order 10181 of 20 November 1950. It is issued only for the purposes of section 1302(b) of the Supplemental Appropriation Act of 1951. The circular warns that many programs left off the list may still bear on defense.

Agencies are told not to treat the attached list as a general sorting of defense agencies. That caution matters: the label carried money and staffing effects under the act named. The document is a budget office ruling with a narrow legal use, kept because the label could decide how programs were treated in a mobilising government.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400090082-1:
From the Strategic Services Unit of the War Department, a memorandum dated 25 July 1946 briefs the Director on the Foreign Service Act of 1946. The bills, H.R. 6967 in the House and S. 2451 in the Senate, were much the same in content. Both had cleared their foreign affairs committees, and State Department officials expected passage that session. The act, as described, wipes away all older statutes and rules covering the Foreign Service.

In their place it sets a full reordering meant to modernise the service and answer charges about its staff and results. The writer flags the parts that matter most to intelligence bodies, which would work beside the Foreign Service and fill gaps in it. The memorandum is a watcher's brief on a law about to reshape overseas staffing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400110214-1:
Whether the head of the wartime intelligence service could pass his hiring power to others is the question in a General Counsel memorandum dated 1 September 1943. It adds to an opinion from the same office of 29 July 1943. Counsel holds that the Director of OSS could not hand the power to employ departmental staff to subordinates at large. That bar, though, does not stop him from letting his top deputies act.

Letting the Assistant Director or Deputy Directors perform such duties is judged lawful. It also fits what Congress meant in July 1943 when it created those senior posts. The opinion leans on the old idea of a deputy as the chief's other self. Fine lines about who may sign a hiring paper fill the rest of the text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400160084-1:
Travel allowances for prospective employees are the subject of a short memorandum whose scan is partly legible. Legible passages deal with a round trip made by a person being considered for a post, and with per diem for the days of travel. One passage ties payment to the time the person spends travelling to the place named in the invitation. Another looks at when such a trip ends the claim, if the person does not go on to employment.

Qualification for the job during the period named is also touched on in the readable lines. Because whole lines are garbled, fine terms cannot be recovered with confidence from the scan. What stands clear is the narrow question: when the Agency brings a candidate in, which of his travel costs may public funds bear?
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400170001-1:
Filed under a transmittal slip, the text is a memorandum dated 11 April 1951 to each office head on emergency plans. It states Agency policy for keeping the work going through attack or other grave disruption. An Agency Relocation Center would serve as the alternate seat. Provision is made for a ninety-day minimum span of emergency operations. That span would let the Agency rebuild itself and, if fitting, move again.

Only a limited number of senior officials and vital staff would go to the center if a real emergency struck. The center would not be marked as tied to CIA, and knowledge of it stays narrow. Dependents cannot be housed there. Office heads must send the Emergency Planning Officer, by 24 April, lists naming who they want inside their totals.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000400180091-1:
A transmittal letter of 22 August 1950 sends out Section 165, on emergency storage, for Volume I of the Department of State Foreign Service Manual. The new section gathers and clarifies the standing rules and instructions on storing goods in an emergency. One change ties the weight or volume allowed in storage to the same limits used for shipment. Another spells out what counts as a housing emergency.

Start and end dates for the right to storage costs are also made clearer. The rules took effect on 1 July 1950 and replace a part of the Foreign Service Regulations dated 14 January 1949. Filing instructions name the exact pages to insert and remove. Agency staff abroad lived under this manual, which is why the update sits in the file.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500020079-1:
Claims for flying dependents home for medical reasons are examined in a memorandum of 15 May 1953 to the Deputy Director for Administration. The claims cover return flights of dependent wives who had been sent out for childbirth care. Outward flights had gone on Air Force planes at no cost, on a space-available basis. Return the same way was barred by a fresh Air Force ruling against infants travelling on its planes.

Attached claims set out their grounds one by one, with earlier papers of 4 May and 3 April 1953 in the file. Those papers dealt with refunds for dependent transport and with medical costs for staff at foreign stations. The memorandum asks whether the Agency should meet return fares that its families had no cheap way to avoid.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500050094-1:
Writing to General Bradley at the Veterans Administration on 17 January 1947, the Comptroller General takes up a pay question about retired officers. The Administrator's letter of 19 December 1946 had described former officers retired for disability. Their disability did not come from combat, explosion of a war instrument, or like causes. Such men, it was said, were well fitted to help as consultants in the Department of Medicine and Surgery.

The question asked is whether the Veterans Administration may pay such consultants above a three thousand dollar limit. That limit comes from section 212 of an act of 30 June 1932, as amended. The decision that follows weighs retired pay against consulting pay. The case shows how dual-pay law reached even part-time expert help.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500070010-1:
A regulation on hiring consultants and experts lays down policy, duties, and steps in eight numbered parts. It rests on section 15 of the Act of 2 August 1946, Public Law 600. A consultant is defined as a person with special skill, knowledge, or experience whose advice is supplied from time to time. Such a person may confer with working officials and propose answers to hard technical problems.

Experts are treated beside consultants, with their own terms of engagement. Prior approvals and contact clearances come before any hiring. Later parts cover how requests are made, how terms are set, and how each engagement is reviewed. Lists at the head name the older rules this one replaced. The regulation turns outside advice into a governed, checkable process.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140003-1:
The Final Act of the United Nations Conference on Declaration of Death of Missing Persons, signed at Lake Success, New York, on 6 April 1950, is printed with the convention it produced. A United Nations sales publication of 1950 carries both texts. The General Assembly, by resolution 369 (IV) of 3 December 1949, had called the conference. Government delegates met to settle a shared treaty on declaring missing persons dead.

War had left families across many countries unable to prove a death or settle an estate. The convention sets terms under which a court may declare death after a set absence. Signatures and the closing acts of the conference follow the articles. The pamphlet priced at ten cents in the United States made the treaty easy to consult.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140012-1:
Some Interesting Angles of the Federal Retirement System, Civil Service Commission Pamphlet 13 of October 1946, opens with a worker's hard choice. Part One deals with what the Commission calls the separation-annuity. A typical question runs through the first pages: a worker with almost five years of service faces a cut in force. Should he take his five per cent retirement contributions back as a refund, or transfer and finish five years?

Many such staff had come for war work and never meant to stay. The pamphlet weighs refund against annuity in plain terms, with figures for common cases. Later parts take up other corners of the system that puzzled staff. It is advice writing of a high order, aimed at people deciding under pressure.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r000500140067-1:
A Legal Staff memorandum dated 6 November 1950 answers a request on how the Social Security Amendments of 1950, Public Law 734, bear on Agency staff. Under the law then standing, federal employees sat outside old-age and survivors insurance. The new law changes that picture from 1 January 1951. Coverage is extended to a listed set of workers, group by group.

Temporary staff head the list, whether awaiting permanent appointment or in posts not meant to last. Staff of wholly owned government companies and of federal credit unions follow. Civilian workers in the Army and Air Force exchange services are also named. The memorandum sorts CIA's own mixed workforce against each new class, so personnel officers could tell who gained coverage and who stayed out.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040008-1:
S. 1809 itself, printed with Report Number 338, was reported by Mr. McClellan on 9 May 1949 and placed on the Senate calendar. The short title in section 1 names the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. A contents list runs from the declaration of policy into Title I on organisation. That title creates a General Services Agency in this draft's wording.

The Bureau of Federal Supply passes over with its contract settlement work. Federal Works Agency affairs are transferred. The National Archives move under the new body, and the War Assets Administration is wound up through the same title. Later titles handle procurement, surplus property, and records. Read as a bill, the text shows the exact clauses the Senate weighed in the spring of 1949.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000040017-1:
Public Law 152 of the 81st Congress, Chapter 288 from H.R. 4754, prints the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949 as enacted law. Its short title comes first, then a full contents list. Title I creates the General Services Administration and moves the Bureau of Federal Supply, the Federal Works Agency, and the National Archives into it. Liquidation of the War Assets Administration follows in section 105.

Redistribution of functions, transfer of funds, and the standing of transferred staff fill the title's later sections. A general supply fund is set up in section 109. Title II then turns to property management, starting with procurement and warehousing. Unlike the bill prints in this file, this copy carries the act in its final, approved form.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001000060006-1:
General Accounting Office Salary Table Number 23, dated 20 November 1945, fixes executive branch pay on and after 1 January 1946. It replaces the tables in force through 31 December 1945. The audience is the set of officers who prepare, certify, and pay civilian payrolls for staff on yearly rates. A forty-hour week is printed at the head of the table.

Two-week period amounts are given for every salary rate, under the Federal Employees Pay Act of 1945. Hourly and daily unit rates are also listed. Tax deduction figures follow the Revenue Act of 1945. Certification and audit needs shape the notes that follow the tables. This set marks the first full pay table of the post-war year, as war agencies shrank and peacetime rates took hold.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001100020036-1: Two Central Intelligence Agency document receipt forms, on Form 38-16, record top secret paper moving through the General Counsel's office in October 1951. One receipt, dated 13 October 1951, acknowledges a log sheet of 12 October from the General Counsel's Office at 317 South Building, classed top secret. The second, dated 2 October 1951, covers a top secret item in two of three copies with no attachments. Each form orders the receiver to sign at once and return the receipt as the reverse side directs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200030007-1:
An analysis of United States government supplies of Lloyd's publications is set out in tables of weekly copies. Columns sort the titles by short marks such as S.I. and L.L., with a further column for foreign supply. Figures split copies sent from London against copies sent from New York. Weekly totals of seventy-six and eighty-nine appear in the visible rows, beside a daily copy count.

A second table lists government subscriptions distributed from Lloyd's, naming the United States Naval Attaché in London first. Annual subscription prices in pounds, expiry dates, and pro rata refund figures run beside each entry. Tangier and other overseas posts appear in the list. The sheet is an accountant's view of how shipping intelligence reached American offices, copy by paid copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp57-00384r001200110125-1:
Establishment of an FBIB Mediterranean monitoring station on Cyprus is directed in instructions dated 8 January 1948. They rest on a memorandum of 28 December 1947 about transferring the Mediterranean station, and on travel orders effective 26 January 1948. The CIA group will leave Washington on 26 January at 8:00 p.m. by air. Athens, Greece, is the first stop, reached on 28 January.

There the group is to contact the chief of the engineers' district office, under a cable of 7 January 1948 from Brigadier General J. S. Brandon of the Army engineers. Once arrangements in Athens are settled, the party goes on to Cairo. Mr. Ben Ball, chief of the FBIB monitoring station in Cairo, is the named contact. Names of travellers are redacted in this sanitised copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00039a000200010108-1:
Weekly Activity Report number 32, for 1 to 5 August 1955, was sent on 8 August 1955 to the Chief of the Operations School and marked secret in the original. Its main item records a visit on 5 August by the Director of Training. He took up the Field Training Staff, an action unit, and an evaluation program for an operational support course. Tours for senior visitors and training of field supervisors were also covered.

Later entries cover course and office business in brief. A revised plan for the Operations Course was finished and sent for approval, and its deputy took on the chief instructor role as well. Reports on junior officer trainees were forwarded, and interim reports were sent on. Guest lectures were given, and instructors prepared lesson plans. Staff held a series of meetings on course evaluations and a communications examination.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100300001-1:
Senate Foreign Relations Committee report deals with the Japanese peace treaty and other Pacific security treaties. It sets out the purposes of the treaties and the setting in which they were made. The report is held in a Central Intelligence Agency legal file. Its contents list covers the background, the talks that produced the treaties, committee action, and United States aid to Japan.

Long sections work through the peace treaty itself: its terms and when it takes effect. They also cover land, security, trade, reparations, debts, and damage suffered by United States citizens. Other parts take up the security treaty between the United States and Japan, Japan and Korea, Japan's ties to Nationalist and Communist China, and Japan's trade with the Soviet bloc. A letter in the report gives Japan's view that it had no plan to make a separate treaty with the Communist regime in China.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000100300010-1:
Department of State Bulletin, volume XXIX, number 736, dated 3 August 1953, is a weekly issue of the Department's public journal, held in a Central Intelligence Agency legal file. Its cover leads with the armistice in Korea. The listed items include a message from the President to the nation, a statement by Secretary Dulles, and the text of the armistice agreement, with a supplementary agreement on prisoners of war.

Other listed items include a talk on aid in a healthy free world and a statement on administering the Pacific trust territory. Inside pages explain the Bulletin's role: it carries press releases, statements by the President and the Secretary of State, and special articles on foreign relations. A long article in the issue weighs exchange of goods and services in the Soviet system against a competitive private enterprise system, in the writer's own terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000200200001-1:
Pamphlet titled Federal Firearms Laws prints the texts of the two main federal laws on firearms, taken directly from the United States Code for ease of reference. A note states that both laws are enforced by the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax Division of the Internal Revenue Service, Department of the Treasury. The pamphlet is an NRA legislative publication from the National Rifle Association in Washington.

The Federal Firearms Act, Public Law 785 of the 75th Congress, approved 30 June 1938, controls interstate and foreign commerce in firearms and pistol or revolver ammunition. The National Firearms Act, Public Law 474 of the 73rd Congress, approved 26 June 1934, is a tax law. It carries a transfer tax of up to two hundred dollars on certain firearms and a duty to register them. It does not apply to pistols, ordinary sporting rifles and shotguns, or old muzzle loading weapons.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130044-1:
Memorandum dated 28 June 1956, for the General Counsel, titled Implications of Cole v. Young and the Director's Termination Authority under Section 102(c) of the National Security Act of 1947. The memo quotes that section, under which the Director may, in his discretion, end the employment of any Agency officer or employee. He may do so when he deems it necessary in the interests of the United States.

Set beside that power is the Act of August 1912. Under it, a person in the classified civil service may be removed only for cause that will promote the efficiency of the service, with reasons in writing. The memo then takes up the Supreme Court ruling in Cole v. Young, where an employee was let go on loyalty grounds under a summary suspension law, and weighs how broad the Director's power is.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130053-1: A declassified CIA-held paper on bonding of agency personnel. This CREST record covers the staff surety bonds, the employees, bonded, the employees, bonded, in the files, surety bonds, covered. Kept for the record. Covered and filed away, kept, saved.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130125-1:
Booklet copyrighted in 1956 by the Government Employees Insurance Company answers a question its writers say they heard often. The question is what follows if a government employee, driving a government owned vehicle, is responsible for an accident. The opening asks whether the United States accepts full blame for damage caused, and whether the driver's own automobile insurance policy protects him.

The company, formed in 1936 to provide automobile insurance for government employees, prepared the booklet to clear up wide misunderstanding on the subject. It states that plain language will be used as far as possible. The subject rests on two technical documents, the Federal Tort Claims Act of 1946 and the Standard Automobile Liability Insurance Policy. Later pages take up limits on cover for other automobiles. They include the rule on a vehicle furnished for regular use, where the right to use a car matters more than how often it is driven.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00453r000300130152-1:
Note dated 21 March 1956 is titled Building: Operation and Maintenance. It returns to a legal dispute treated at greater length in an office opinion dated 26 August 1955, a copy of which is attached. The dispute is whether the Agency or the General Services Administration holds the chief authority for construction of the Agency building.

The summary states that the General Services Administration relied on fairly broad provisions of 40 U.S.C. 361, while the Agency argued that the section was not so broad as to bar Congress from granting construction authority to the Agency. An agreement signed between the two sides is read as accepting the Agency view that work was done at its request. The note quotes section 210(c), codified at 40 U.S.C. 490(c), on acquiring land and making surveys, test borings, plans, and drawings at the request of a federal agency.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100030009-1:
Memorandum for the files dated 20 October 1950, titled Subpoena of CIA Records by Subversive Activities Control Board, weighs whether the Director could refuse to produce Agency records to the new Board. Section 13 of the Internal Security Act of 1950 is quoted, giving the Board power to require testimony and production of books, papers, and memoranda, with court orders and contempt for refusal.

Cases where the Board itself or the Attorney General wants the records are said to raise no difficulty, since production would be handled by consultation. The hard case is a demand by another party in a Board proceeding. The memo argues the Director may safely refuse a court order where disclosure would harm the public interest, and notes no attempt had been made to hold a department head in contempt. State secrets and the President's conduct of foreign relations are also invoked.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070113-1:
Public Law 215 of the 83rd Congress, chapter 348, first session, 67 Stat. 472, is the enacted form of H.R. 5495, an act to extend the President's authority to enter into trade agreements under section 350 of the Tariff Act of 1930. Its short title is the Trade Agreements Extension Act of 1953.

Section 101 extends the period for entering foreign trade agreements for a further year from 12 June 1953. Section 102 shortens the time for certain Tariff Commission reports from one year to nine months. Later titles set up a commission on foreign economic policy, with sections on its staff, appointment of personnel without regard to civil service laws, and pay under the Classification Act of 1949.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100070131-1:
Memorandum for the record dated 15 January 1952 is titled Legislative Problems of the Psychological Strategy Board. It follows a meeting on 14 January 1952 between Agency officers and the Board's deputy director and staff. A reference memorandum of 5 January 1952 from the Board's Office of Coordination, on liaison with congressmen, is cited.

The Board's legislative problems are divided into three classes: budget, personnel, and substantive. On budget, the Board is financed by equal contributions from State, Defense, and the Agency. Its administrative officer preferred one appearance before each Appropriations Committee rather than defending its budget three times to each House. Ideally the appearance would be before the subcommittee that hears the Agency. The memo notes he probed how the Agency was financed and before whom it appeared. Later passages warn that congressional questions could draw out operational information on Agency activities.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100090021-1:
Paper titled Documents Branch describes the mission and work of the Documents Branch of the Office of Operations in the Central Intelligence Group. The branch exploits important intelligence information on other countries found in foreign language publications and documents, processing thousands received from the Far East and from the War, State, and Navy Departments.

Documents of intelligence value are translated, summarized, or abstracted for consumers. The consumers include branches of the Group and the White House, the Library of Congress, and the War, State, Navy, and Commerce Departments. The branch was examining some 650,000 documents captured from the Japanese, including 150,000 volumes of the South Manchurian Railway and 50,000 volumes of the East Asia Research Institute. Later sections list project work, card files of industrial information, a scientific project, and a publications section that edits translations and reports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100150033-1:
Printed bill introduced in the House on 16 June 1954 by Mr. Graham and sent to the Committee on the Judiciary, in the 83rd Congress, second session. Its title is to revise and extend the laws relating to espionage and sabotage, and for other purposes, and its short title is the Espionage and Sabotage Act of 1954.

Title I covers war and defense materials, premises, and utilities. Section 101 rewrites section 2151 of Title 18. It defines war material to include arms, ammunition, livestock, forage, forest products, timber, clothing, air, water, food, and fuel. It also covers all articles intended for, adapted to, or suitable for use by the United States or an associate nation in war or defense. A contents list in the text names later sections on destruction and on production of defective war and national defense material, premises, and utilities.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100160005-1:
Proposed reply to the questions submitted by the Chairman of the Commission on Government Security concerning Executive Order 10501 gives numbered answers in the same order as the questions. Answer one states that no distinction is made between the term security information, used before 15 December 1953, and defense information, used after that date, since the two are considered the same.

Answer three estimates that at least a stated share of documents originating in the Agency are classified, with no other authority for classifying defense or security information. Answers four and five state that, because of compartmentation, even rough percentages by level for documents originated or received would be costly and slow to produce. The confidential class should be retained, answer seven states, for information not sensitive enough for secret that would still harm intelligence activities if revealed. Later answers cover notice to recipients when documents are regraded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000100160032-1:
House Report number 1407, 84th Congress, first session, dated 26 July and ordered to be printed, is a conference report submitted by Mr. Celler from the committee of conference, to accompany H.J. Res. 157, a joint resolution establishing a Commission on Government Security. The committee met on the disagreeing votes of the two Houses on the Senate amendment.

The report recommends that the House recede from its disagreement to the Senate amendment and agree to it with an amendment, the agreed text being inserted in place of the Senate wording. That text opens with a declaration of policy on protection of national security and defense secrets against espionage, sabotage, disloyalty, subversive activities, and unauthorized disclosures. It then states a congressional policy of a sound government program. The program includes procedures for security investigation, evaluation, and adjudication of government employees, and a study of how existing laws and orders are administered.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020018-1:
Joint resolution S.J. Res. 96, Report number 1049, Union Calendar number 396, reached the House on 24 July 1953 and was ordered printed on 30 July 1953, in the 83rd Congress, first session. In this version the title is to strengthen the foreign relations of the United States by establishing a Commission on Governmental Use of International Telecommunications.

Recitals cite the growing importance of the overseas information program and the President's message of 2 February 1953. Section 1 establishes the Commission on Governmental Use of International Telecommunications.
