Section 2 fixes membership at nine: five appointed by the President, of whom at least one must come from the telecommunications industry and at least one from another stated field. Later sections provide for a secretary general and an assistant at not over twelve thousand five hundred dollars a year, other staff, and experts at up to seventy five dollars per day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020027-1:
Printed bill H.R. 6819 was introduced in the House on 3 August 1953 by Mr. Wolverton and sent to the Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce, in the 83rd Congress, first session. Its title is to establish a Telecommunications Policy Committee, a body distinct from the commission proposed in Senate measures of the same season.

Section 1 creates the Committee to coordinate development of telecommunications policies and standards. It is also to frame plans for the best use of the radio spectrum and communications media in the interest of the United States. Membership is one representative of each participating agency, at first State, Defense, Commerce, and the Federal Communications Commission. The President may add other agencies and name the Chairman and Vice Chairman from among the members. Section 3 provides an Executive Secretary appointed without regard to civil service laws, plus experts and assistants as the Committee judges necessary.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200020045-1:
Copy labelled Tab C holds Senate Report number 602, dated 18 July 1953, from the Committee on Foreign Relations, to accompany S.J. Res. 96. The committee states it had the resolution under consideration, reports it with amendments, and recommends passage, under Calendar number 601 of the 83rd Congress, first session.

The report's summary gives a nine member Commission on International Telecommunications. Five members are named by the President, two by the President of the Senate, and two by the Speaker of the House. The Commission is charged to study the subject and recommend agreements, policies, and measures to the President and Congress. Two hundred fifty thousand dollars is authorised and a final report is due not later than 31 December 1954. A background section lists regions to be linked in instant television communication: North Atlantic countries, Latin America, the western Pacific, southern and southeast Asia, and the Mediterranean.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200060014-1:
Untitled paper dated January 1956 argues that covert operations must be judged against a background of what the opposition is doing. Clandestine activities are described as an essential and major part of the Communist effort worldwide. They cover espionage, political action, propaganda, and psychological warfare on an immense scale, as well as armed warfare in some areas.

Examples given are Communist party work and semi-overt papers such as the Daily Worker and covert leaflets. They also include the Stockholm Peace Petition and Ban the Bomb campaign, guerrilla support in Malaya and Laos, and riots in Singapore and India. Support for front organizations in labor, youth, women's, and other fields is estimated in the paper at as much as two billion dollars a year. Subversive effort is said to have grown, not shrunk, since Geneva. United States answers include aid to free trade unions and help to private groups abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp58-00597a000200100019-1:
International Cooperation Administration cablegram, marked official use only, forwards a questionnaire directed by Senator Ellender to the United States Operations Missions, titled Summary of Operations of ICA. The Senator's office supplied a copy of the questionnaire, which he had sent directly to the missions, and asked for its completion before his impending visit.

Analysis in the cable warns that much of the data requested is not available in precise figures in the missions or in the Agency at all. Fiscal 1957 data in particular was not final until approval of that program. The request for information by mission is so comprehensive, the cable adds, as to require staff time that might endanger some missions' primary work. That work is carrying out the Mutual Security Program in their countries. Later lines give reporting rules, directing missions to insert counterpart fund figures as of 30 June 1956 from stated functional reports.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100010003-1:
Senate Report number 2265, Calendar number 2286, 84th Congress, second session, ordered to be printed 19 June, accompanies S. 3897, a bill to improve governmental budgeting and accounting methods and procedures. Mr. Kennedy, from the Committee on Government Operations, reports the bill favorably without amendment and recommends that it pass.

The purpose stated is to amend the Budget and Accounting Act of 1921 and the Budget and Accounting Procedures Act of 1950. The changes follow recommendations of the Commission on Organization of the Executive Branch of the Government. Changes listed would permit program costs in the annual budget and budget requests on an accrued expenditure basis. They also cover lapsing of excess appropriations, agency budgets on a cost basis, and consistency between accounting and budget classifications. A section by section analysis follows, tying section 1(a) to numbered recommendations of the Hoover Commission budgeting and accounting report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100010012-1:
Printed bill S. 3199 was introduced in the Senate on 14 February 1956 by Mr. Payne for himself and twenty one other senators and sent to the Committee on Government Operations. Its title matches the later budgeting bills in the file: to improve governmental budgeting and accounting methods and procedures, and for other purposes.

Section 1(a) amends section 213 of the Budget and Accounting Act, 1921. It directs the Director to use information obtained under that section to prepare full reports, other than purely fiscal reports. The reports show the financial results of the activities of departments and establishments. Later matter requires an accounting system with adequate monetary property accounting records as an integral part of the system. New sections added after section 119 include a staff office of accounting, beginning at section 120 in the portion shown.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100080006-1:
Printed bill S. 2470 was introduced in the Senate on 11 July 1955 by Mr. McCarthy, by request, and sent to the Committee on Government Operations, in the 84th Congress, first session. Its title is to add a new title on real property management to the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949.

The inserted Title IIA opens at section 220 with a declaration that the provisions are necessary for more effective and efficient management of real property owned or leased by the United States. Section 221 makes the Administrator responsible for management of all real property after the title takes effect, except as the title provides. A middle page lists aims: improvement of office space quality, consistent with economy, to improve morale, reduce turnover, and raise efficiency, and relocation of offices to cheaper areas.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100130019-1:
Printed bill H.R. 5096 was introduced in the House on 21 March 1955 by Mr. Keating and sent to the Committee on the Judiciary, in the 84th Congress, first session. Its title is to authorize the admission into evidence in certain criminal proceedings of information intercepted in national security investigations, and for other purposes.

Information covered is that obtained before the act's effective date by the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Army G-2, Air Force intelligence, and Naval intelligence. It was obtained through interception of wire or radio communications, on the written approval of the Attorney General, in an investigation of threats to national security. A later clause deems such information admissible, despite section 605 of the Communications Act of 1934, in criminal cases involving the listed violations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100560003-1:
House Report number 1803, dated 22 February 1956, from the Committee on Armed Services, submits a report by Mr. Kilday to accompany H.R. 9429, the dependents' medical care bill. The committee reports it favorably with an amendment, which strikes the word unlawful on page 2 and inserts lawful, and recommends passage as amended.

Purpose is a uniform and improved program of medical care for dependents of members of the uniformed services. A history notes that dependents have long been cared for in service facilities: the Army has had statutory authority since 1884, and its Medical Department gave such care from 1818. Covered charges listed in the middle include hospital bed and board in semiprivate rooms for up to 365 days per disability. The first twenty five dollars is paid by the patient. Surgeons' fees in or out of hospital, and in-hospital physicians' calls, are also listed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100560012-1:
Printed bill H.R. 7806 was introduced in the House on 1 August 1955 by Mr. Price, by request, and sent to the Committee on Armed Services. Section 1 gives the act a name: the Armed Forces Dependents Health Care Act of 1955.

A declaration of purpose finds that high quality hospital and medical care for the families of members of the Armed Forces is an important factor in morale. Such care should be available to all on as nearly equal terms as possible, and should not depend on the accidental nearness of military or civilian facilities or staff. Military facilities should, so far as consistent, be relieved of dependent care. A middle passage provides that on a member's separation, maternity care, including hospital care of the newborn, continues without cost for a pregnancy that had begun by his separation.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100670056-1:
Congressional Record, Senate, pages print a floor debate on oversight of the Central Intelligence Agency, in an exchange between Mr. Russell and Mr. Hickenlooper. Russell defends the closed supervision then in place, noting the National Security Council's direct supervision, and praises Allen W. Dulles for answering searching questions forthrightly about activities he calls chilling to hear.

Both speakers stress the danger of disclosure: naming agents operating abroad could mean their death by hanging or execution within days, and exposed agents would be liquidated at once. Russell says he will not dwell on the many differences between the Agency and the Atomic Energy Commission. A passage deeper in the debate argues that a joint committee could keep fully and currently informed only by placing a staff watchdog at every National Security Council meeting. It heads into the objection that the legislative branch cannot take over an executive function.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100690018-1:
Allowances and Differentials, dated 14 June 1955, is a study paper behind the overseas allowances bill. It opens with the President's message to Congress of 11 January 1955 on personnel matters, which listed allowances among the subjects needing attention for United States citizens employed overseas.

Three major systems then applied to American citizen civilian staff outside the continental United States. They were foreign area allowances, territorial allowances for the Territories and possessions, and a maximum twenty five percent salary differential for the Canal Zone. Practices varied among the systems, among agencies, and among pay groups, some differences warranted and some not. The paper argues far greater uniformity is possible for foreign areas and for Territories. A later section treats education help, noting the Panama Canal Government's schools, kept under annual appropriation acts, and reimbursements for dependents of other agencies' staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000100690036-1:
Copy of the Analysis of the Proposed Overseas Allowances Act of 1955 dated 14 June 1955, held with the bill file. Its Title I notes match the analysis copy elsewhere in the file. Section 101 states objectives, and section 111 defines continental United States as the existing states and the District of Columbia. The Trust Territory sits under the foreign areas definition.

A passage in the middle of this copy treats missions to international organizations, such as the United States Delegation to the United Nations. Only a very few agencies are expected to need the authority, and regulations will set the conditions and control its use. Part D then covers storage expenses at section 241, which would extend to all agencies an authority for paying storage costs like that already held by agencies authorised under stated laws. Employee coverage is civilian only, set by presidential regulations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200110001-1:
Memorandum for the Legislative Counsel comments on S. 688, a bill to authorize the Civil Service Commission to make a study of the classification of, and rates of compensation for, technical, scientific, and engineering positions in the classified civil service.

In view of the Agency's exemption from the Classification Act of 1949, the memorandum finds the proposal would have no direct bearing on Agency personnel activities. Because the Agency follows a policy of compliance with the Classification Act, it will be interested in the proposal's progress, and asks for any further material issued on it. The attached notice of pending legislation is dated 2 February 1955 and addressed to the Assistant Director for Scientific Intelligence. The bill print lists study factors, including pay for comparable work in private employment and the factors that set it, and the supply of persons with technical and scientific training.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200480001-1:
A CIA file on S. 2286, a Senate bill about shipping privately owned automobiles for Defense personnel, pairs a short Agency memorandum with a Senate committee report. The bill would amend the Merchant Marine Act of 1936. It would let military personnel ship their cars on American commercial vessels as well as Military Sea Transport Service ships, and would newly let Defense civilians ship a car at government expense.

The Director of Logistics advises that the change would alter Agency practice very little. Public Law 110 already lets CIA civilian employees move a car at government expense on an overseas change of station, and detailed military staff ship under the Joint Travel Regulations. The memorandum therefore recommends no further action. The Senate report, dated 27 July 1955, recommends the bill pass without amendment.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00224a000200510016-1:
A CIA letter of June 1954 goes to the Director of the Bureau of the Budget. Legislative Counsel Walter Pforzheimer signed it. The Bureau had asked about H.R. 4723. That bill would simplify the laws on pay from dual federal employment. It also asked whether CIA objected to repealing Public Law 53 of the 82nd Congress inside the bill.

Public Law 53 let CIA employ up to fifteen retired officers. Their service was otherwise barred by law. The Agency raises no objection to the repeal, if the bill passes as drafted. An attached memo gives the bill's main rule. No one could draw two federal salaries once combined pay passed $6,250. The person could choose the larger salary instead. The older dual-employment laws would be replaced.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100040012-1:
A printed Senate report of 24 May 1956 presents findings on the episode of the Russian seamen. It comes from the Internal Security Subcommittee of the 84th Congress. It was printed for the Committee on the Judiciary. Five seamen had sought asylum in the United States. They then redefected to the Soviet Union. The subcommittee held a fifteen-day inquiry. It looked for Soviet activity behind the returns.

The facts section starts with the tanker Tuapse. Chinese forces seized it on 23 June 1954. Its crew of 49 was taken to Formosa. Then 29 men went back to the Soviet Union. Twenty stayed, and nine entered the United States in October 1955 on parole. The report also prints testimony on the parole terms. Those terms covered security screening and a government sponsor. The State Department also had to find that entry served the national interest.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100250028-1:
A small CIA file of 15 March 1955 forwards a settled case for filing. A letter of 19 January 1955 reported the settlement. The United States Attorney for the District of Columbia was closing his file. A caption names a Central Intelligence Agency claim. It was brought for the use of the American Fire Insurance Company. Names in the body are redacted. One original page is marked missing.

A second memorandum in the file takes up proxy voting. The question concerned GEHA members stationed overseas. Reading GEHA's constitution and by-laws, the memo finds no duty to mail proxies abroad. Members overseas attend no annual meeting in person. Still, the memo urges a real chance to take part. Stations could be sent the names of members likely to be in Washington. Those members could then hold the proxies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000100370034-1:
A transcript records a hearing before a Board of Special Inquiry. The applicant was Ellen Raphael Knauff, also known as Ellen Bonhomova. The hearing sat in Washington on 26 March 1951. The heading describes her as married, stateless, and white. She sought admission to the United States. Inspectors Clark, Danielson, and Joseph sat on the board. A government representative appeared, and so did her counsel, Alfred Feingold.

The record opens with her exclusion. She had applied for admission at New York on 11 August 1948. On 6 October 1948 the Attorney General ordered her excluded without a hearing. The ground was that her admission would harm the interests of the United States. Long testimony follows on her wartime work. Witnesses were asked about civilian censorship work. They were also asked whether enemy aliens monitored switchboards. One witness declined to answer.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200020004-1:
A CIA file gathers papers on a draft presidential proclamation. Its title is 'Control of Persons Departing or Entering the United States'. The Bureau of the Budget sent the draft to Director Allen W. Dulles. The Office of Defense Mobilization and the Department of State had prepared it. It was to be brought to readiness and kept on file at the White House.

One review came from the Acting Director of Security. He judged that the proclamation would not harm the travel of aliens of interest to the Agency. He expected the Secretary of State and the Attorney General to keep cooperating. They had done so under the earlier proclamation of 17 January 1953. The draft gives the Secretary power to issue rules on travel. It gives the Attorney General temporary power to stop an alien's departure.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030102-1:
A draft bill of 23 February 1948 would provide for the administration of the Central Intelligence Agency. The Agency was created under section 102 of the National Security Act of 1947. A table of contents heads the draft. It lists nine sections. They cover definitions and a seal of office. They also cover procurement, education and training, and travel costs. General authorities, appropriations, and separability follow.

The text defines the Agency, the Director, and a government agency. It also defines the continental United States. It then gives the Agency procurement powers from the Armed Services Procurement Act of 1947. The travel section covers expenses, leave, and shipment of cars. It also covers hospital care and cost of living allowances. The general authorities include moving appropriations and exchanging funds. They include arming couriers, leasing property, and employing retired service staff.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200030120-1:
A bill draft would establish a Central Intelligence Agency. It opens with a declaration of policy drawn from two world wars. Separate departments gathered and analysed foreign intelligence on their own. That could not properly inform the American people or their representatives. Events, trends, and plans abroad might, if known, avert armed conflict. So procurement must be coordinated, and analysis centralised.

The bill sets four programs to carry out that policy. The first coordinates the procurement facilities of existing intelligence work. The second covers research and analysis of all intelligence received. The third covers accurate dissemination to the proper officials. The fourth covers procurement of all available foreign intelligence. Intelligence is defined as facts on the activities, trends, capabilities, and plans of foreign powers. The Director would serve a term of not more than seven years, at $12,000 a year.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200180025-1:
A CIA legal memorandum of 13 July comments on a draft dispatch to the field. It went to the Director of Personnel. The dispatch would explain how the 1955 legislative pay increase applies to contract personnel. The office finds the draft unclear. Paragraph 3 seems to invite raises for all contract staff. It speaks of increases substantially equal to the legislative rise. That covers employees and independent contractors alike.

Yet approval is also said to turn on the legal relationship of the person. The memo asks that this relationship be defined up front. It points to Agency Notice 31-52, which announced the increase. It also points to Notice 31-53, on applying the October 1951 increase to contract staff. That notice set the basic test. Some contract personnel, called contract agents, count as employees in fact. Those who truly work under Agency control should receive the increase. Others should not.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000200240028-1:
A short CIA memo lists the Comptroller General decisions behind the rules on invitational travel. Much of the scan is garbled, so only the main points can be read. The memo says its conclusions rest on all decisions issued to date on the subject. It cites volume 3, page 590 of the Comptroller General decisions among them. Decisions in volumes 15, 31, and 34 are also cited.

The rule stated concerns travel for a set purpose. Travel from a person's home to a post is not repaid when the trip serves only to test his fitness for a named post. The memo adds rulings on contracts of Coast and Geodetic Survey staff. It also answers a question on the Classification Act of 1949. Where a post falls under that Act, the schedule rate of pay is not changed by earlier law.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300270015-1:
A statement records damage to one family's household effects in shipment. The writer's name is redacted. The effects were packed, the statement says, in a careless and negligent fashion. Delicate kitchen equipment went into boxes with no padding. Items were separated by no more than a single sheet of paper. They were packed loosely and crushed one another. A Mesco roaster and a Sunbeam waffle iron sat on smaller items. Both were ruined.

The faults run through the whole shipment. Large items went on the bottom or the top, with small items thrown into the gaps. There was no regard for weight, value, or fragility. A portable sewing machine was crated loose with many other items. Its parts flew around and wrecked its case. An unprotected alarm clock was packed against six plastic dishes, and all seven broke. Nails driven through the boxes dented a coffee maker and a pitcher.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300280014-1:
A CIA letter to the Comptroller General, Joseph Campbell, argues two travel vouchers. The vouchers are for $211.86 and $101.00. They cover travel expenses of employees' dependents. The sums had been cut from the expense accounts before payment. The dependents, travelling under home leave orders, chose to travel in the 'on' season. Fares were higher than in the 'off' season.

The facts are set out for two employees, with names and posts redacted. One order of 31 August 1953 sent a man to Washington for temporary duty. Off-season rates, saving $211.86, took effect on 1 November. The letter quotes Public Law 110. It pays family travel for staff at permanent posts outside the continental United States. The argument turns on advance travel of dependents. If such travel is authorised as in the Agency's best interests, the added cost is a valid claim. The finding must rest on facts, fully supported.
cia-crest-cia-rdp59-00882r000300330072-1:
A motor vehicle accident report form, filled in by hand, records a crash in the national capital parks. The form comes from the Department of the Interior, National Park Service. It is a U.S. Park Police report. Handwriting fills the fields for three vehicles. The entries are partly hard to read. They give driver details, directions, points of impact, and estimated speeds.

The form also asks for the date each car was last inspected, and whether it was insured. A section at the back asks for a brief description of the accident. It asks for distances to landmarks and measurements from the point of impact. A part for the official investigator covers charges and disposition. It asks whether photographs were taken, and whether the investigator visited the scene or a hospital. Names in the form are redacted or illegible in the scan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100030038-1:
A CIA memo of 5 December 1955 answers manpower questions for the Office of Training. It went to the Deputy Director (Support). It responds to the Inspector General's ad hoc Manpower Committee. Figures for positions are redacted. Before 15 August, OTR's ceiling stood higher. On that date it fell by 17 percent, counting 60 Junior Officer Trainees. The DD/S has now promised 19 more positions.

OTR had analysed all its functions. It could not keep discharging its duties on the lower ceiling. A further ten percent cut would force more eliminations. One option studied is ending internal language and area instruction. The Language and External Training School holds 18 positions. Ending internal training would save 8 of them. The memo weighs that saving against the cost of sending staff outside.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000100040019-1:
A CIA memo of 25 November 1955 reports manpower use for an intelligence office. It went to the Deputy Director (Intelligence). Two years earlier the office had its divisions list activities in priority order. That exercise showed which positions could go with least disruption. Four weeks ago the divisions updated those papers. The present answers were due in under a week.

The writer warns that clear-cut answers need more thought than the time allowed. A hard question runs through the paper. If each division takes a ten percent cut, spread across all activities, might every activity end up too weak to run well? Cutting one activity whole might be better. The three division chiefs prorated their cuts. The writer, after brief scrutiny, believes they were correct. He asked each chief to deepen the cut slightly, for flexibility in reapportioning.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00213a000200020001-1:
A CIA staff study of 9 September 1953 addresses preparation of materiel estimates. The scan is heavily garbled, but the subject and findings can be read. The study went to the Chief of Logistics. Its task was twofold. It was to consolidate staff requirements for area division use of estimates in fiscal 1954. It was to develop a system for future estimates tied to operational plans and budget justifications.

Under present practice, area divisions hold long-range estimates they barely use. Headquarters senior representatives overseas lack the factual data to turn estimates into line items. Requirements pass through several numbering systems, causing confusion. The product often failed to reflect the real money value of division submissions. Much manual effort followed. Discussions with a colonel of the Requirements Staff are recorded. The study aims at a single workable system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100010081-1:
A progress report covers the Geographic Area, ORR, for April 1957. Published output rose sharply. Reference service in the Map Library stayed at a very high level. Coordination pressed ahead on collection requirements, economic-geographic studies, and Soviet geodesy and gravimetry. Mapping, photography, and IGY Antarctica also figure. The Cartography Division completed 59 maps and charts, 56 for CIA and 3 for State.

The Map Library Division received 3,547 maps and 1,174 related publications from foreign sources. It sent out 29,134 map sheets in answer to 1,423 requests. Outgoing communications totalled 266, most tied to procurement abroad. A new identification system for D/GP reports was approved. Its first report covers stream control and utilization in Southeastern Fukien Province, China. Photo intelligence work included studies of Moscow airframe plants.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410005-1:
A status table lists Geography Division projects as of 3 June 1957. MR-52 went to reproduction on 29 March. MR-53, begun 17 April 1957, is due in the third quarter. Far East entries lead with geographies of Ningsia, Suiyuan, Chahar, and Shensi. Research there covers mineral and agricultural resources. A geography of Sinkiang also advances, with a text in final review.

A geography of Tibet, open since October 1954, waits on another project. A Northeast Thailand regional analysis has been edited and is in post-editing review. Maps and a photo-mosaic overlay were due in June. Other entries cover town plans, with Burgas and Bucharest chosen for Plan A work after talks with the DD/P. One project was deferred indefinitely. Analyst and requester names are largely redacted.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100410014-1:
A Cartography Division project status list is dated 1 March 1957. The USSR-Satellites Branch leads. A set of Sino-Soviet Bloc trade and credit charts is complete for February. Twenty production charts comparing the Soviet Bloc and the West are also listed. Other entries cover USSR railroads in first revision, Hungary's iron and steel plants, and economic maps of the Volga and Ural regions.

Poland's administrative divisions for 1956 appear, as do USSR civil airline routes, waterways, and roads. A general survey map of the USSR is listed. Soviet aircraft capability charts run to twenty maps. Yugoslavia and Albania administrative divisions follow. Rumania entries cover the food processing and chemical industries. Copper, lead-zinc, aluminum, and magnesium sheets round out the mining coverage.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000100490007-1:
Minutes record NIS Committee Meeting No. 241 of 2 April 1957. The committee reviewed Chapter I on NIS 19, Hungary. The draft was approved with certain changes. The Task Group was asked to review agency comments. The chapter was controlled in its entirety, since several sections were controlled by contributors. The chairman praised the thoroughness of the reviews.

Hungary's chapter was hard to prepare, he noted, because of the recent revolt. It may need earlier revision than normal as the new situation develops. The committee tentatively renamed Supplement 3. It changes from Air Facilities to Coasts and Landing Beaches. The change awaits final approval of the revised guides. Other items cover Middle East studies that might support an ONI requirement. A State research list is cited.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00346r000200100017-1:
A monthly report covers the Map Library Division for October 1957. Reference Branch services rose over September. Staff filled 1,264 map requests, an increase of 189. Yet the maps needed were the fewest of any month in 1957. Added requests covered publications, place-name information, and miscellaneous reference questions. Seventy-four new CIA and NIS maps entered the reference file.

Maps on Europe and Africa went to the Assistant Secretary of State for Congressional Relations. They were bound into books for a House subcommittee traveling abroad in November. The Air Target Unit sent out 1,067 sheets in answer to 60 requests. An AFOIN visitor praised its organization as the finest of five similar Washington units. Cataloging of the USSR map backlog is complete. A statistical table closes the report.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100150061-1:
An opinion of the Agency's Office of General Counsel dated September 29, 1949, answers questions about quarters allowances for staff posted overseas. The questions were raised in a memorandum of June 27, 1949. They concern the use of Confidential Funds for repairs and renovations to rented quarters abroad. They also concern the rental of furniture for those quarters.

The opinion works through the legal authorities. They include Section 901(1) of the Foreign Service Act of 1946 and the Act of June 26, 1930, as amended. It notes the large sums at stake and the lack of precedent. On furniture, it holds one point clearly. An employee who estimated costs for unfurnished quarters, then found only furnished quarters on arrival, could fairly amend the estimate. The extra rental cost could be included.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00442r000100160015-1:
A sanitized copy of legal comments on a draft Agency travel regulation is dated May 20, 1955. Names and regulation numbers are blanked out. The comments respond to a December 1954 draft and its transmittal letter. That letter described a planned set of ten travel regulations. Because the general regulation in the set is not yet final, the reviewers warn that their comments on this draft can only be tentative.

The body works through the draft paragraph by paragraph. Points raised include the length and complexity of the regulation, which runs to twenty pages. They include the rules for train berths for children under five. They also include doubt about making staff use upper berths when no lower berth is free. Several passages propose plainer replacement wording for clauses the reviewers found hard to apply.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00538a000100010003-1:
A Management Staff study examines the Agency's Cable Secretariat. It asks how the secretariat should be organized and where it should sit. The study argues that its functions require a location next to the Signal Center. Speed, coordination, and ready access to cable files and references all point that way. It recalls that the secretariat was created in 1952. It was a central office to handle all classified cable traffic.

In practice, the study finds, the central role leaks. Cable traffic on seventeen special operational projects bypasses the secretariat. It is handled directly elsewhere. The study counts the positions needed to carry the mission. It proposes merging some duties with the work of the duty officers. The merged duties include cable brief preparation and special handling for the Director's officers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00538a000100070007-1:
An office memorandum dated December 17, 1952, from the Chief of the Organization and Methods Service reports on the present distribution and use of Travel Order Form No. 33-27. Sent to the Assistant Deputy Director (Administration) through the Comptroller, it answers a request with an attached chart showing how the form moves for every type of Agency travel.

Copy counts vary by trip: foreign travel that is vouchered needs ten copies, the most the current system requires, while domestic travel without vouchers needs six. The form was first ordered as a twelve-part carbon insert form; over two thousand copies remain in Agency stock, and an order for 15,000 more, about a year's supply, is outstanding. The memorandum also notes steps taken to cut needless personal copies.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100060009-1:
Point-by-point comments answer a Weekly Activity Report item about the content and distribution of the Agency's OTR Bulletin, ahead of a meeting set for Monday, October 22, 1956. The first point records a request from the acting chairman of the CSTC: that each issue of the Bulletin, or parts of it, be coordinated with his committee before publication each month.

The counter-point is blunt: coordination here means censorship, and censorship is called both unnecessary and unwise. Training policy, it notes, already has a staff officer with DD/P experience and the security officer consulted while each issue is prepared. A later point defends printing the list of National War College lectures, with the editor directed to add a line reminding readers about supervisors' permission.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000100070008-1:
A memorandum dated April 25, 1956, goes from the Chief of the Plans and Policy Staff to the Director of Training. It proposes an Office of Training planning conference built around the free creation of ideas. Attached as Tab A is a paper dated November 30, 1955, titled An Idea Creating Group. The writer had been handed that paper on returning from a training assignment.

The argument is two-sided. A plans staff fails if it claims a monopoly on ideas. It also fails if it plans at a distance from the work. Its best service is to build settings where senior staff and school chiefs develop ideas freely. The attached paper urges one trial. Group idea-creating methods, proven in business, industry, and scientific research, should be tried on the Agency's own problems.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030019-1:
Weekly Activities Report number 25, dated June 25, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Language and Area School. It reports the school completing the first phase of a management program. The program covers its contract personnel. Announced six months earlier, it aims to regularize the employment of contract staff. It also aims at their use, development, and advancement. Its principles resemble those for staff employees. The first phase chiefly evaluated staff qualifications and responsibilities. Those were tied to the school's activities.

Other items look outward. A Far East division project would train one person full-time in Japanese outside the Agency. An application to Yale University was recommended. A new instructor in Chinese arrived to take up her duties. A division man returned from five months of outside training in Chinese.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300030028-1:
Weekly Activities Report number 16, dated April 24, 1958, comes from the Chief of the Language and Area School. It reports the panels that sort people into language training. The Qualifications Review and Placement Panels met on April 21. They considered candidates for Indonesian, Persian, German, Spanish, and Russian. The candidates were nominated by components across the Agency. Two members of the full-time Chinese course also came in. They discussed how they might continue their study once the course ended.

A course loss is recorded on April 4. One of the original six members of the full-time French course withdrew. The course was the French Intermediate Integrated Language and Area Course. The man, from the NEA division, left after three weeks of the ten-week course. Pressure of office duties caused the withdrawal. The report notes it as a hardship for the five who remained.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300050026-1:
Weekly Activity Report number 17, from the Registrar's office, covers April 23 to 29, 1958. One item passes on a report from OSI. It concerns a training device shown at a London exhibition. Its makers claim it can train a punch-card operator in eighteen hours. The present method of instruction normally takes fifty hours. Machine records people in the Office of Personnel were interested in the device.

Language business follows. Interest had been expressed in sending a student to the full-time Persian course. The CI Staff raised no objection. The Language and Area School chief was authorized to extend the offer. The report notes one new rule. This was the first step in carrying it out. The Registrar was personally to keep Mr. Karamessines advised of outside personnel in Agency Office of Training courses.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110001-1:
Weekly Report number 1 comes from the Agency's Assessment and Evaluation Staff. It covers December 25, 1957, to January 7, 1958, and opens with no significant items. The chief's first recorded business is a consultation. A representative of the operations side met with the Chief, A&E. They discussed building a fitness report form for use with contract agents. The talk re-oriented the concepts behind the form. It settled what should and should not go into such a report. The staff agreed to keep giving consultative help as the form was developed.

The rest of the report is the staff's working tally, set out in tables. Assessments are sorted as standard, special, and intensive. Interpretive conferences are counted as well. They were held with the individual tested, or with the personnel officer and supervisor concerned.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000300110010-1:
Weekly Report number 10 comes from the Agency's Assessment and Evaluation Staff. It covers March 5 to 11, 1958. The chief had been summoned to the Director's office at 12:15 on Wednesday, March 12. The reason was unknown. The report then prints, at length, a consultant's letter. The letter resigns his connection with the staff. Over-commitment to outside work, he writes, is damaging his main work and his health. First things must come first. The staff records its deep regret at losing him.

Other business concerns the evaluation reports themselves. It covers how expense controls press for punctuality without harming quality. It covers who bears responsibility when evaluations are delayed. It covers who has the final say on what makes a good evaluation report. It also covers who may change evaluation practice and policy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400040050-1:
Weekly Activities Report number 36 of the Orientation and Briefing Officer covers September 3 to 9, 1958. Its centerpiece is the National War College briefing of September 5: a two-hour session in the R&S Auditorium for the college's 150 staff, faculty, and students. General Cabell spoke for twenty minutes on the Agency, followed by Mr. Amory and Mr. Karamessines on their own areas, with a coffee break and a fifteen-minute question period in which all three took part.

The officer grades the performances without mercy: Amory's speech was brilliant and the highlight, Cabell was at his best, and Karamessines was good. An attached note complains that a colleague's perfectionism had made another report sound worse than the facts warranted, over a chart that was in fact adequate.
cia-crest-cia-rdp60-00594a000400060030-1:
Weekly Activity Report number 2 comes from the Agency's Instructional Services Branch. It covers January 8 to 14, 1958. The Audio Aids Section counts a busy week. It received sixty-seven requests for service. It procured fifty-three films and projected forty-eight films. The projections ran a total of twenty-eight hours. Equipment failed once at a bad moment. The amplifier for the booth projectors died on January 3 and 4. A screening for the Operations Support Course was under way. The last quarter of the film had to be projected from the auditorium floor.

A forward-looking item proposes a new use for the Film Unit. It would record, on movie film, the significant changes at a construction site as work proceeds. The footage would keep the Director and other top officials advised of progress. They would not have to visit the site.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000100100055-1:
A weekly summary report from January 1953 mixes a course census with two items of training news. The first concerns a program then being shaped. Its theme was Soviet imperialism, its anatomy and its impact on the world. The interest of the various offices in the program was being sounded out. Registration of Agency personnel would be limited. Tentative nominations were to reach the Office of Training by January 16.

The second item is an outside honor. The dean of a graduate school of business administration had made a choice. He chose among the recommended candidates for its Advanced Management Course. Of the two men nominated by the Agency, one was accepted. He was Mr. Lawrence Houston. He would begin his studies at Harvard in February 1953.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000300100010-1:
An agenda packet for the fifteenth meeting of the CIA Career Service Board gathers the papers the board would weigh. Prominent among them is a paper from the DD/A Career Service Board. It concerns responsibility for the assignment and career development of general administrative personnel. The packet also carries material on administrative personnel. It carries a definition of the career service. It carries points arising from discussion at the board's thirteenth meeting.

The personnel machinery in the papers turns on a first judgment. An Initial Evaluation Report would be completed by each employee's immediate supervisor. It would recommend one of two outcomes. The employee would be retained in Agency employment for eventual consideration for the permanent Career Service. Or he would not. The packet thus shows the board building the gate through which a career service would be staffed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400120008-1:
A memorandum dated November 4, 1954, goes to the Director of Central Intelligence. It answers two papers. One is a committee memorandum of October 19, 1954. The other is a Director of Training staff study titled CIA Overseas Training, dated September 22, 1954. The office writing concurs in principle with the committee's findings. It excepts one paragraph, which it names. The Director of Training's role, it reports, had been clarified. It was defined to embrace staff responsibility for the technical supervision of Agency training activities.

An enclosure spells those staff responsibilities out. They include technical supervision of all training not conducted by the Director himself. They include staff coordination with the offices doing that training. They include technical assistance to them. The memorandum thus fixes where the training chief's authority runs. It runs over standards and supervision everywhere. It runs over conduct only in his own house.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00017a000400140015-1:
Notes of the Agency Director of Training's trip, prepared for the Operations School, survey the extent and effectiveness of training done overseas. The regions covered run from Europe and Southern Europe through the Near East and Southeast Asia to the Far East. Training found abroad falls into three kinds: security training, work with liaison services in foreign intelligence and political action activities, and case officer agent training conducted in safehouses. The notes judge the general effectiveness of the effort and the competency of current instructors.

Shortfalls are named. Singleton training of high-level types is called unsatisfactory, with better screening, interpreters, and qualified case officers sent out with groups as the remedies. A maritime item closes the Far East section: the need for adequately trained maritime personnel.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100090007-1:
A memorandum dated March 28, 1958, reports a study of the Administration Building printing plant. The study covered the plant's staffing and operating costs. The plant is known as the Main Plant. The study was made at the Deputy Director (Support)'s request. The question was what savings, if any, the Agency had won. The savings would date from its takeover of operating control of the plant. The Government Printing Office had run it before. The takeover date used throughout is January 12, 1957. On that date the work in process was valued and billed by the GPO.

The study works through the plant's disbursements. They include payments to the GPO for work completed or in process. The study sets a figure of 125,050 dollars. That was the cost of the Agency's printing in the Main Plant across the period reviewed. Paragraphs on recruitment for the plant's positions are flagged for the deputy's particular attention.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100120003-1:
An analysis of overtime usage and costs under the Director of Training's allotment goes unit by unit through the Agency training office. Each entry names the causes of the overtime: after-hours work on files, after-hours training of a new secretary, emergency requirements. Then come the measures taken. Workloads were redistributed, after-hours filing was ended, and overtime was authorized only for top priorities, emergencies, or inflexible deadlines, with savings estimated for fiscal 1958 and 1959.

Some savings are structural. The Visual Aids unit was transferred to the Intelligence School, and one entry calculates that closing one of the language laboratories would save an estimated 1,815 dollars, or 550 hours. Small sums recur throughout, in tens and hundreds of dollars, each tied to a named corner of the office.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100200004-1:
A memorandum dated October 18, 1954, asks three officials to concur in a staff study on personnel paperwork. They are the Comptroller, the Director of Security, and the Chief of the Management Staff. The study was proposed for approval by the Agency's Assistant Director for Personnel. It would adopt a modified Standard Form 50, the Notification of Personnel Action. That form would authenticate and notify official personnel actions. The employees covered are paid from confidential funds. Standard Form 52 would no longer serve for notification. It would still be used to request actions.

The case against the present practice is legibility. Corrections on the distributed Form 52 copies could be extensive. The typing could be poor. The form sometimes had to be retyped. The Machine Records and Finance Divisions were asked to accept barely legible documents. Those documents were much altered, yet counted as official.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000100220011-1:
A staff paper on the Transportation Division of the Agency's Logistics Office proposes no significant change. The division's organization stays as it is. Its business is numbers. The staffing put forward rests on three things. They are past, current, and anticipated workload. They include the count of people presently assigned. The case is supported by workload data. It is expressed as a proposed table of organization, measured against the approved one then in force.

The paper also carries the office-wide ceiling arithmetic. Eliminating six positions brings the Logistics Office to a set ceiling. That ceiling would hold until January 1, 1955. Sixteen more positions were then to go, and the ceiling would drop again. If circumstances changed, the office could ask a question before December 15, 1954. It could ask that certain positions be spared.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200010004-1:
A Department of State guide, Performance Rating Plan: A Guide to Supervisors, opens with the supervisor's duty to see that work is done as efficiently as possible. Supervisors have long known, it says, that they must reach a full understanding with employees about their duties and the standards expected. Congress now formally requires that employees be completely informed of their duties and of those standards before their performance is rated. The department's plan, approved by the Civil Service Commission, spells the system out.

One section gives the supervisor room to act on what a rating shows, suggesting how performance weaknesses can be strengthened or an employee used to better advantage. The rating form is signed by the employee as evidence the rating was discussed with him; the signature does not imply agreement, and it does not bar an appeal. The copy survives in the Agency's declassified files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200100022-1:
Annex II sets out how a CIA Reading Panel then worked, routing incoming documents, cables, and publications to analysts in the Office of Research and Reports. Panel members used guide requirements supplied by divisions, branches, and the Requirements Branch, plus direct contact with analysts. The annex notes that guidance arrived in mixed forms, from formal memos to verbal notes, and that panels were not always told when a need had ended.

Later sections cover control cards sent with material from the Office of Collection and Dissemination, missing enclosures, and the handling of requirements. Cards often needed correction, which doubled mail clerk work, and card copies varied widely. Readers gain a close view of the daily sorting work behind finished reports, and of the small faults that slowed it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00274a000200130001-1:
Proposed changes in the table of organization for the Office of Scientific Intelligence are set out in a staff paper whose scan is heavily garbled in places. Legible parts deal with the office's divisions and staffs, the roles of division chiefs, and the duties of a Deputy Assistant Director linked to the Scientific Staff. Changes to production and coordination posts are also discussed, though many lines cannot be read with confidence.

Because the OCR is poor, fine detail in this record should be treated with care. What can be grounded is the subject itself: a planned reshaping of the scientific office's structure, its staff lines, and the place of its chiefs. The paper belongs with other early Agency efforts to fix reporting lines as scientific work grew in weight and scope within the office system.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300040001-1:
A large set of 1958 Senate Congressional Record pages is cataloged under the Inter-Parliamentary Union conference at Rio de Janeiro. Much of the visible debate, though, concerns an education bill. One senator argues that nothing in the bill bars spending on pursuits such as flower arrangement or tap dancing, and attacks the stress on mathematics and science as a sales device. Title VIII aid for foreign language training draws special fire for its wide list of fields.

Toward the middle, Union business appears in the form of amendments offered at the conference. One French amendment, offered by de Maupeou, would add a call for a study group inside the Union to plan toward an international force. The vote shown is nine in favor, ten against, with two abstentions. Senator Case of South Dakota presents parts of the record. The set joins floor debate and conference papers.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300040029-1:
A State Department foreign service despatch reports a visit to Dublin by members of the United States delegation to the Inter-Parliamentary Union conference in London. The sightseeing trip took place on 8 September 1957. The despatch, numbered in the 460s and dated later that month, sends Washington a list of the party, a program, and press clippings. The party numbered some twenty-eight persons.

The group landed at Dublin airport at half past noon and was met by the Ambassador, the Counselor, the Military Attache, and other Embassy staff. A modern sightseeing program followed, run by an Embassy control officer. Later pages note the group's general interest in Ireland. The despatch is a routine diplomatic report, valued for its names, timing, and press coverage rather than for any policy argument.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300180006-1:
A magazine article from The Reporter, headed The Growing Missile Gap, asks whether a time is coming when the Soviet Union could attack without fearing retaliation. The author is Thomas R. Phillips, a retired United States Army brigadier general. The article opens with two boasts by Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev. He told military academy graduates in Moscow on 14 November that one button press could blow cities sky-high and destroy whole countries.

Phillips writes that such statements were made for home consumption, not foreign propaganda, and that intelligence agencies take them seriously. He then weighs missile counts and warhead weight in hard figures. One passage works out how many Soviet missiles would be needed to destroy a set share of a thousand American launching pads. It also works out how many American missiles the reverse task would take. The piece is a period statement of missile-gap fears.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300190005-1:
A memorandum for the record dated 26 January 1959 notes a CIA briefing of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee lasting about three hours. The Director attended with Mr. Amory and Mr. Warner. Ten senators are listed, led by Chairman Theodore Francis Green of Rhode Island, with J. W. Fulbright, Mike Mansfield, Albert Gore, and others from both parties. Four committee staff members are also named.

Since a transcript was taken, the memo gives no detail of the briefing itself. It records that Senators Green, Capehart, and Aiken praised the Director's presentation, a point also carried on the news ticker that day. Follow-up items are listed. Several senators wanted comparative pay rates for Soviet and American military staff. Others wanted figures on Hungarian refugees who left in 1956, split by country of refuge, and on how many had returned.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00357r000300200003-1:
Briefing notes prepared for the House Foreign Affairs Committee give an outline view of the Soviet Union, updating a briefing last given on 22 October, after the Taiwan Straits events. New tendencies are listed first. Abroad, lines of conflict with the West had tightened and talk of easing tensions was no longer a major Soviet theme. At home, the line was steadier control, a return to rigor in policy and belief, but no return to a police state.

Khrushchev is described as firmly in control, with maneuvering for succession perhaps under way and Suslov, Kirichenko, and Kozlov named as men to watch. Foreign policy shows a harder tone, with Berlin, Iraq, and support of China at Quemoy as examples. Economic notes compare Soviet consumer supply and investment with American levels, and defense spending is expected to grow as the economy expands.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020007-1:
A draft position evaluation chart dated December 1956 sets grade level distinctions for the Geographer series, GS-0150. The page shown covers the GS-13 level in detail. Duties at that level match deputy branch chief and section chief posts. The holder serves as technical expert on all phases of geographic production and on the world region his branch or section covers.

Work at this grade includes helping a branch chief set project aims, scope, outlines, work schedules, and assignments. A section chief also takes direct charge of the functions tied to his section. Research procedures and the use of outside contacts and services fall within the role. The chart closes on personal demands: steady initiative, resourcefulness, original thinking, and good judgment while several projects run at once.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020016-1:
Minutes and an action table record a Geographic Research Area staff meeting held on 18 November 1958 under the Chief of the area. The action list assigns follow-up work. An area list was to go to the Office of Security, and invitations to divisions for the next staff meeting. Names were to be sent for a training briefing, and a check made on inviting outside units to briefings. Divisions were also told to add a paragraph on expected key developments to future monthly reports.

Notes from the meeting cover a Ready-Reserve list reviewed and sent to Security, and new fitness report forms to be explained at a branch chiefs meeting. A training briefing for division and branch chiefs is also noted. A possible outside research project on the population of North Korea was discussed, with stress on strictly geographic factors tied to the area mission.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000100020133-1:
A monthly report for the Photo Intelligence Division covers June 1958 and opens by noting a high work level. Most effort went on top priority projects for the Director and the intelligence and plans directorates. Reports issued came to twenty-two, split evenly between written and informal reports. Nineteen reports sat in editing, seven in reproduction, and nineteen projects were cancelled during the month.

Requirements received are listed by source, led by self-initiated work, with others from research, scientific, and plans offices and from the Army and Navy. Projects in process are counted by branch, across geographic, special projects, industrial, technical, central, and support units. Branch notes add that four informal reports were finished in one branch, and much time went to area studies for the plans directorate. City plan work continued in planning and production.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200110006-1:
Minutes of a Chapter IX Subcommittee meeting held at two in the afternoon on 14 February 1958 were sent to members in a memorandum dated 28 February 1958. Attendees are named from air, army, and navy charting and oceanography offices and from CIA, which supplied the chairman and several members. The first business was the Chapter I Annuals. The chairman reported that the Section 19 portion of the Annual for Poland had been very well received by the Chapter I Coordinator and by the chairman of the survey committee. Members were praised for the quality and speed of their contributions.

Later discussion turns to a planned three-part division of material. Contributors saw snags. An arbitrary line at seventy-five or eighty percent coverage for the first part might leave some contributors with material only in the later parts and none in the first.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00391r000200220013-1:
A survey of Soviet activity and capability in the Arctic answers a Department of Defense request for information, with maps attached. For two requested items, firm data were lacking, and the survey says material under the other items partly fills the gap and suggests the scale of the whole Soviet Arctic effort. Logistics for the drifting stations and research sites come first.

Supply ran by combined sea and air work. In the years described, material moved from inland points to coastal bases and was then airlifted to the drifting stations by aircraft under Polar Aviation, probably about one hundred in number. Later, most supply moved by ship over the Northern Sea Route. Long tables in the middle list Arctic towns and populations by region, including Arkhangelsk, Severodvinsk, Onega, and Nar'yan Mar, and towns across the Karelian and Komi republics.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100060003-1:
Weekly Activities Report No. 21 from the Chief of Field Training, dated 2 June 1959, covers 25 to 29 May 1959 and goes to the Director of Training through the Chief of the Operations School. Monday and Tuesday of the week went to a visit by a named guest, which the report says was covered in a separate memorandum. The rest of the week is called rather quiet, marked by visitors.

One visitor came to discuss a forthcoming briefing course set to begin on 6 June, and another spoke on operations in a named area. A deputy chief from a logistics planning staff also called. On guest lecturers, the report notes that one instructor covered a four-hour period alone, by small schedule changes, instead of the normal three-person complement. Later pages weigh how well a student would fit a small station against a large one.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100060012-1:
Weekly Activities Report No. 20, dated 21 May 1959, covers 13 to 19 May and reports no significant items. Its other activities open with a complaint passed by phone on 18 May. A deputy chief relayed anger over a remark by an unidentified instructor in a recently finished course, called sniping at training instructors. The remark, as quoted, said one office had to do things outside its role because another was not doing its own work.

The chief writes that he at once directed an inquiry to the instructor concerned. A student angle follows: a woman had told him a trainee was enrolled in the course ahead of an assignment as a representative of the scientific office. Later talk, on 20 May, held that statements in the lecture outline were factual but that the whole story was not told. An offer was made to bring the instructor to headquarters for a talk.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00442a000100060030-1:
Weekly Activity Report No. 17 from the Chief, Overseas, Operations School, dated 29 April 1959, reports no significant items. Its first other item chases desert survival training materials. The training office had asked the Air Force Subsidiary Plans Division for such materials, as an earlier weekly report recorded. After a talk with a colonel the week before, the chief tried to pin down who had first made the request. He wanted to be sure the Agency had not already sent the Air Force a memorandum.

On Monday, 27 April, an Air Force captain on duty at the Pentagon called from that colonel's office. On the captain's suggestion, a draft memorandum had been prepared for the Air Force setting out the Agency's exact needs, and a copy had been passed along. Later pages turn to background reading drawn from resistance movements and Agency papers, and to a planned trip to the field training base.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100110011-1:
A Fourth Annual Progress Report of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee covers 1 July 1955 to 30 June 1956, a year earlier than the fifth report in this band. Its program section is fuller. It lists general work, support for commodity controls, and support for analysis of Soviet Bloc trade tactics. It also lists support for analysis of trade in decontrolled goods and exception shipments, and efforts to improve collection. Tabs list completed reports and cases and documents sent to members.

One passage notes new instructions issued as a confidential supplement to the Foreign Service Manual, tied to the State Department side of the work. Looking ahead, the report expects the committee to keep contributing to the economic defense program as a pending government review leads toward revision of economic defense policies and programs. The report is marked Secret, with State review and Commerce release notes on the cover.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100190031-1:
A Sixth Annual Progress Report of the Scientific Estimates Committee, dated 18 August 1958, covers fiscal year 1958. The committee was established on 14 August 1952 by a Director of Central Intelligence directive, under a National Security Council directive and a survey committee's recommendation. Its permanent members come from the CIA, the Joint Staff, State, Army, Navy, Air Force, and the Atomic Energy Commission. It uses ad hoc subcommittees as needed rather than a standing structure. The year is summed up as one of significant advance in almost every field the committee covers.

Gains listed include stronger work on new types of agents, above all those drawn from natural products. Much stronger reporting on Soviet electronics in nearly all aspects is also listed. Stress falls on present and long-range capability, air defense, and telecommunications. Other advances are listed in the same summary passage.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000100230009-1:
A long survey report examines the intelligence needs and assets of the United States Information Agency. Its index shows four main parts. They cover identification of the agency's intelligence needs, related needs of other agencies, and organizational arrangements. The agency's own assets form the fourth part, followed by an account of how the survey was conducted. Eight tabs follow, from a list of intelligence publications and recommended distribution to functions of a proposed agency intelligence organization.

Other tabs hold letters exchanged between the Director of Central Intelligence and the agency's director, and terms of reference for the survey. They also hold the earlier survey paper IAC-D-82, a list of persons consulted, and basic documents considered. A terms-of-reference passage records that the Director agreed, at the agency's request and with State Department support, to appoint an officer to conduct the survey of essential intelligence needs.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200030019-1:
A memorandum dated 10 June 1959 examines the character and prospects of the Somoza regime in Nicaragua. The regime, it states, has held the country for twenty-five years through firm control of the armed forces and the set political process. Opposition had so far been weak, divided, and manageable. Now exile revolutionary movements and a bolder internal opposition threaten it.

The danger is judged mainly one of belief: less the strength of any one opposition group than a fast-spreading view that the Somozas' time has run out. The memo judges it unlikely that President Luis Somoza can stay in office to the end of his term in 1963. A separate exile movement gathered in Cuba after Fidel Castro's call to overthrow the regime. The memo says Castro gave Che Guevara the task of helping organize and prepare those exiles.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200030028-1:
Director of Central Intelligence Directive 3/5, issued as USIB-D-34.2/1 on 31 December 1958, sets policies and practices for producing and coordinating scientific and technical intelligence across the government. It supersedes Directive 3/4 of 14 August 1952, while separate directives govern atomic energy and guided missile and astronautics work. Two opening principles govern all that follows.

No complete separation of fields of interest is desirable or possible, the directive says. Full, free interchange of information among departments and agencies is essential where it serves national security. That covers raw information, finished products, and news of internal and outside research programs. Tables later in the directive assign duties by member: setting scientific aims and judging progress toward them, and producing coordinated drafts of national estimates and other joint products. The Joint Staff and Navy are among those listed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00549r000200050026-1:
A budget analysis on overt intelligence collection survives in a scan so rough that its structure can only just be made out. It covers joint arrangements beyond the Council directives for a coordinated overt collection program, beginning with publications procurement. A directive had set up an advisory committee on foreign language publications. Geographic reporting appears early in this copy, through a guide for geographic attaches.

Basic geographic reports there include a monthly activity report, and reports on mapping and research organizations abroad. They also include reports on key personnel of foreign mapping bodies. Country reports giving a current assessment of mapping activity complete the set. A radio passage agrees that broadcast monitoring rests on careful selection rather than directed collection. Because of the poor scan, fine wording in this copy should not be relied on.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000100080203-1:
A further copy of general provisions opens with the same index pattern, in rougher OCR. First articles are definitions, changes, inspection, payments, and assignment of claims. Excusable delays and disputes follow, then notice and assistance regarding patent infringement and the Buy American Act. Convict labor and the Eight-Hour Law of 1912 appear in sequence, with the Walsh-Healey Act after them. The body text sampled in the middle deals with termination pay.

On termination, labor hours spent up to the effective date are paid at the hourly rates set in the schedule, less hourly payments already made. Reimbursable material costs not yet paid are also counted in. Several provisions sets in this band repeat the same stock articles with small changes. This copy is best used to check the exact wording of a given article in its own contract.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000200010182-1:
A negotiated contract numbered CT-701 names a Pasadena, California manufacturing company as contractor, incorporated in Delaware; the firm name is garbled in the scan. The amount is left to Part VII of the contract, and the performance period is stated on the face: 1 July 1959 through 30 June 1960. The contractor agrees to furnish the necessary personnel and perform all services set out in the attached schedule.

The schedule and general provisions govern the parties' rights and duties. Part V, on period of performance, repeats the year's span and grants the government the right and option of renewing or extending the contract for additional periods. The file is a services contract for a single fiscal year, with the commercial detail held in parts and schedules rather than on the signature page itself.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300020054-1: An allotment transcript print lists balances brought forward and voucher entries for an account in the 6-100410000 group. Column heads name voucher, obligation, allotment, and balance forward fields, and the rows repeat the same account code with small entries in the ninety-nine series. A second section in the middle shifts to summary figures in dollars and cents, many marked CR. The sheet is a raw accounting print for that project account, with no narrative text and heavy OCR garbling of its digits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300020063-1: A machine ledger print sorts project account entries under column heads for date, allotment, general ledger, current 1956, prior year 1955, prior years, and cumulative total. Accounts shown sit in the 10043 and 10045 series, with balance forward rows and small entries such as nine dollars and 280 dollars beside larger coded sums. The sheet is a raw accounting print with no narrative text, and many digits are garbled in the scan.

The sheet is a raw payroll-linked account print with no narrative text and partly garbled digits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300050042-1: A long machine listing of voucher entries runs past thirty pages in print terms, with description, requisition, obligation, and allotment columns. cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080003-1: An allotment ledger headed Aquatone lists accounts in the 7-1004 series under expenditure issue, unliquidated obligation, total obligation, allotment authority, and unobligated balance columns. The 7-1004-10-001 account carries the largest figures, closing near five million dollars, and a 7-1004-10-004 account shows 676,479.97 dollars in one column. The sheet is a raw ledger print with no narrative text, and some digits are garbled in the scan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080012-1: A November reconciliation worksheet for fiscal 1957 survives as handwriting and figure columns that the scan renders almost wholly illegible. A few amount shapes can be seen, including five-figure sums, but no account heading or remark can be read with confidence. The sheet can be grounded only as the November entry in the monthly reconciliation series for the project accounts; its workings cannot be recovered from this copy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080030-1: A voucher register pairs dates with voucher numbers in an 811 and 813 series and names the payees in abbreviated form. Names that recur include Galbraith, Hycon Manufacturing, and a General Precision laboratory entry, beside other short payee codes. The register is a plain payment listing for the project accounts, with no narrative text. Several payee names are clipped or garbled in the scan, but the voucher sequence and the main vendors are clear.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080049-1: An allotment ledger headed June 1957 covers Aquatone accounts for fiscal 1957 in the 7-1004 series. The 7-1004-10-001 account shows rows of 823,226.20 dollars and a combined 354,513.55 dollars, a 30-010 account closes at 919,076.89 dollars, and a 50-011 account passes nine hundred thousand dollars. Column heads cover expenditure issue, obligation requests, allotment authority, and unobligated balance. The file is a raw ledger print with no narrative text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080058-1: An allotment ledger headed February 1957 lists Aquatone accounts across the full 7-1004 series, each in full and partial rows. The lead 7-1004-10-001 account shows an expenditure figure of 383,162.00 dollars and a combined 405,634.09 dollars, and a 30-010 account shows 368,311.72 dollars. Column heads cover expenditure issue, obligations, allotment authority, and unobligated balance. The file is a raw ledger print with no narrative text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080067-1: An allotment ledger sheet for Aquatone gives account rows in the 7-1004 series with closing totals. The 7-1004-10-001 account shows 172,231.18 dollars in its full row, a 30-010 account closes at 50,749.80 dollars, and a 50-011 account totals 500,172.10 dollars. Small accounts sit beside them, down to a 226 dollar row. The sheet is a raw ledger print with no narrative text, and several totals are partly garbled in the scan.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00763a000300080076-1:
Agency allotment ledger pages for fiscal year 1957, marked Secret, list accounts in the 5-1004-50 series, running from 5-1004-50-002 through 5-1004-50-010. Columns give amounts issued, unliquidated obligations, total obligations, allotment authority, and unobligated balance. One account shows an allotment of 22,500,000 dollars, and the page totals run into tens of millions.

Following pages dated 31 August 1956 break the accounts down by individual voucher. Payroll entries appear as main roll and staff agents, each tied to an allotment number and a small payment amount. Together the pages show both the scale of the funding and the small daily charges that were posted against it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100060021-1:
Office memo dated 14 September 1949 proposes a records program for the Agency. It comes from the Management Officer. It goes through the Assistant Director for Collection and Dissemination. Space, gear, and manpower needs for Agency records were growing fast at the time. A partial count in August 1948 had found over 6,100 pieces of filing gear in office use. That gear was worth 560,000 dollars.

The same count found 5,363 letter and cap size cabinets and safes. It found over 62,000 square feet of office space, at a cost of 125,000 dollars a year. Nearly 42,000 cubic feet of papers were on file across the Agency. About 18,000 cubic feet of that stock was judged to be of lasting value. The memo sets out how one central program would control the making, keeping, and disposal of records.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61-00910a000100070002-1:
Staff study addressed to the Acting Deputy Director for Administration asks whether the Agency Records Center should be assigned to the Management Improvement Staff. A permanent centre at a redacted site, replacing the interim facility at Rosslyn, Virginia, had been approved by the Project Review Committee and the Director. Some services, such as limited storage and distribution of published intelligence reports, would stay in the capital area.

The study, resting on an administrative staff study of 22 December 1953, argues against the move. Centre work is repeated routine: accessioning, storage, servicing, processing, and disposal of records. That operational character, and the small place of the centre in the whole Agency mission, point away from a managerial staff home.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100050022-1:
Survey of the Agency's Electrical Equipment Branch reviews how the branch works and how it is set up. It also puts forward changes. Three questions frame the study. First, what problems are likely in the current plan of work? Next, what changes to branch research would help support papers in the rest of fiscal year 1958? Last, what longer term changes in method would not badly disturb current duties? The survey finds the branch mission and its tasks clear to all staff.
