Branch strength is given as seven professional and two clerical staff. The survey makes no firm comment on the table of organisation. Work was split among groups of analysts under three heads. Electronic parts were handled on their own. The reason is that their output serves as an index of total output in that sector.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100090028-1:
Attachment in the Agency's files reconciles Chinese Communist cotton crop figures with other estimates of the cotton position in China. Several different production figures were in circulation, and the paper works through why they differ. References in the legible parts point to crop years in the mid-1950s and to a reported crop on the order of tens of millions of units, set against lower outside estimates.

Much of the scan is garbled, so many of the figures cannot be read with confidence. What can be grounded is the task itself: checking a claimed crop against acreage, yield, and trade figures, and showing where a large gap between the figures comes from. The paper is an analyst's working note, not a finished estimate.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00137a000100140040-1:
Project Action Memo dated 29 October 1956 sets the terms for a study of the Soviet nuclear energy program. The study is Project No. 30.1646. It runs through the Joint Atomic Energy Intelligence Committee. A reference memo of 15 October 1956 had asked the Agency's ORR office for studies of set goods and trades of the USSR. The studies were due by December 1956. They were to support the 1957 estimate on the Soviet atomic energy program.

Subjects are assigned branch by branch in the memo. They include hydrofluoric acid, nickel powder, mercury, and graphite. They include compressors, converters, electric motors, and power-factor capacitors. Concrete and structural materials close the list. A later page adds more branches that would take part. It gives estimated man-hours for each branch's share of the work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100020059-1:
Editing note dated 31 October 1956 suggests retentions, revisions, and additions for the Agency's OCI reading requirements covering 1 December 1956 to 31 March 1957. Latin American countries take up most of the pages. For Argentina, one new item asks whether Bloc countries had tried to join the Paris Club or set up a separate multilateral arrangement with the Bloc.

Other Argentine items ask about the standing of Czech and East German offers to aid industrial development and any use of Czech and Soviet credits granted under trade agreements. Bolivia and Brazil items are mostly marked retain, with one Brazil item rewritten to ask about the status of new trade agreements with Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary after the old ones expired.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100110031-1:
Memorandum dated 1 November 1955 reports a recruiting trip to the West Coast, 3 to 21 October 1955, made for the Agency's Assistant Director for Research and Reports. Once dates, universities, and route were fixed, letters went to friends on each campus, or to department heads or other leads where no friend was known. All lead people were cleared by the Security and Personnel Offices before contact.

Letters set out the visitors' interests and the departments where likely graduate students, or standout undergraduates, might be found. Economics came first, with related social science fields and area or language study as added possibilities. Later lessons include pooling impressions of large universities by questionnaire, rating each as good, fair, poor, or unknown, and being more specific with faculty contacts about campus procedures.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180025-1:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-227, record an Executive Committee meeting on 5 March 1957. The meeting sat at 2:00 p.m. in Room 1213, Maiatico. Mr. Hale was in the chair. Members came from MDAC, Defense, ICA, Agriculture, State, Commerce, and Treasury. The agenda lists the Polish talks. It lists a report by the Ad Hoc Group chairman. It lists an Agriculture request that touches the Battle Act. It lists draft outlines for a change to the work program.

The Polish note reports talks with Polish delegations in progress at the Department of State. The Battle Act item turns on the Treasury view. The Treasury member could not yet give his agency's view that day. His reading that morning showed the change sought was much narrower than Treasury had supposed. It was too late for a settled position at that meeting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180034-1:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-245, record a meeting at 2:30 p.m. on 17 June 1957. The meeting sat in Room 1213, Maiatico. The minutes were issued on 24 June 1957. Agenda notes open with a letter of commendation for Mr. William Cargo. They add a letter on Polish trade, EDAC D-132 of 14 June. Numbered items cover a fresh look at an objection. They cover List II quota talks. They cover Defense and State proposals on policy.

Commerce, State, and MDAC men had drafted two letters for Cargo, for the EDAC chairman's signature. The objection item took most of the rest of the notes. Members agreed the United States could tell a partner it had looked again and, the amount being small, would withdraw its objection to a shipment. The statement was to be qualified, as in an earlier West German case. State was to check that case.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180052-1:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-267, record a meeting at 10:30 a.m. on 30 August 1957. The meeting sat in Room 1213, Maiatico. The minutes were issued on 9 September 1957. Notes cover a COCOM exception for aircraft landing systems. They cover fitness for aid. They cover Commerce reporting of requests for export to Poland. They cover how far the Treasury rules on deals reach. The numbered item is a work program for paragraph 9 of economic defense policy.

The landing systems problem was due for talks at a higher level that afternoon. State and Defense were to hold those talks. Other talk touched a live trade question. An American oil company had asked State a question of its own. Was there any objection to supplying aviation gas to Russian planes in Greece? The gas was not United States gas. Commerce noted that COCOM countries did not report their own such sales.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180070-1:
Minutes in the Agency's files, ED/EC M-285, record a meeting at 10:00 a.m. on 18 December 1957. The meeting sat in Room 814 of the District National Building. The minutes were issued on 20 December 1957. Notes cover draft Presidential Determination letters and talks on rolling mills. The numbered item is a plan for work to get ready for the Consultative Group meeting. That meeting would take up paragraph 9 of economic defense policy, and a long string of EDAC and ED/EC papers is cited.

Members were to review the draft Determination letters before any decisions were taken. Agencies were told to study the Ad Hoc Subcommittee on List Review reports in detail. Each agency was to tell the chairman of anything it objected to in them. A meeting was planned on parts of a September draft, on exceptions to security controls, not yet taken up.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000100180089-1:
Department of State letter dated 19 February 1958, addressed to Mr. Walter C. Sauer, Executive Vice President of the Export-Import Bank of Washington, answers a question raised in his letter of 19 November 1957 to Mr. Staats of the Operations Coordinating Board. The copy sits in the Agency's files. The question was whether loans under section 104(e) of Public Law 480 would be barred to Finland by the Mutual Defense Assistance Control Act, the Battle Act.

The reply, written after consulting the State Department's Office of the Legal Adviser, draws a line between loan types. Certain types of loans would not count as assistance within the meaning of the Battle Act, while others might well fall within its ban. A memorandum by Mr. Metzger explaining the differences in detail is enclosed with the letter for the Bank's use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200010068-1:
Agency Current Support Memorandum dated 2 September 1954 is an all-branch project on flood conditions in Communist China. Heavy, steady rain had set record crests on the Yangtze and Hwai Rivers. Floods were reported from Tibet to the Sungari, Liao, and Yalu Rivers of the northeast. As yet, the paper says, there was no evidence the floods were worse than in 1931.

The 1931 comparison is given in figures here. In that year 34,000 square miles were badly flooded. Between 25 and 50 million people were driven from their homes. Works built since 1951 had plainly lessened the force of the floods. Damage to transport is detailed in later pages. Rail lines between Shanghai and Suchow were believed cut or washed out along long stretches. The Hankow to Chenghsien line was cut at bridges over Hwai tributaries.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200100004-1:
Table set in the Agency's files gives China's exports and imports by goods type for 1956. Values are in millions of United States dollars. They are split by source or buyer: the Free World, the USSR, the European Satellites, and the Far Eastern Satellites. Export rows run from grains and oilseeds through fruits, eggs, fish, meat, tea, silk, and tobacco, on through tung oil to coal, cement, salt, and minerals. Rice is shown at 64.3 million. Soybeans lead the oilseeds group.

An imports table reverses the flow. Metals and machinery dominate the import side. Machinery less vehicles, power plant, machine tools, and petroleum gear are listed apart. Complete plants, farm machinery, and vehicles are listed apart as well. Petroleum and products, ferrous metals, cable and wire, and chemicals also appear. Fertilisers, paper, nonferrous metals, and cotton close the list. Cotton is given by tonnage as well as value.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120011-1:
Agency Current Support Memorandum dated 9 October 1958 examines Communist China's economic policy toward Poland. Peiping had first set a goal for total 1958 trade far below the levels of recent years. That stance probably followed Poland's past record on deliveries. Poland had failed to deliver on time. It had failed to ship goods that matched the agreed terms. Early in 1958, the paper says, Peiping reversed its position.

In April an agreement was concluded for the year. It envisaged deals worth 87,500,000 dollars. Further contracts, raising the 1958 goal again, would let Poland expand its imports of core goods. That growth would come without draining its reserves. The short paper is a case study in trade used as a policy lever inside the Bloc. Pressure was applied through a lower trade target. It was eased once a new agreement was signed on better terms.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200120020-1:
Agency Current Support Memorandum No. 585, dated 4 June 1958, reports a sharp change in rail freight balance. The balance is that of tonnage shipments between the USSR and the European Satellites. Reliable reports showed the ratio of westbound rail movements shifting markedly. The shift ran against the earlier pattern of those movements. The paper explains how the railway systems on both sides took the new flow. They took it without breaking down.

Heavy spending on transloading sites from 1951 through 1957 had built the needed capacity. The sites stood on both sides of the Polish and Soviet border. They stood at Chop, the Soviet border link with Czechoslovakia and Hungary. Soviet and Satellite railways could handle the rearranged traffic. Large daily and seasonal swings in tonnage did not stop them. Changing needs for car types did not stop them either. Getting cars for transit traffic stayed the chief difficulty.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130047-1:
Agency paper on recent trends in Turkish foreign trade describes an economy pressed toward the Bloc. Excessive home demand, very high price levels, and poor grain exports had plagued Turkey for years. With credit nearly exhausted and most products priced too high to compete in Western markets, Turkey had turned more and more to barter deals with the Bloc. Imports from the Soviet Bloc rose from 7.9 percent of the total in 1950 to 18.3 percent in 1955, and exports to the Bloc from 6.9 percent to 21.8 percent in the same years.

The Turkish government, aware of the drawback of heavy Bloc dealings, had taken steps to reverse the trend and reorient trade toward dollar and EPU areas. Pressure from exporters, though, worked against full realisation of that aim. Bloc imports listed include Soviet iron products, timber, glass, and machinery, and Czechoslovak trucks, paper, and textiles.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00527a000200130056-1:
Agency paper dated 20 August 1956 sets out the air raid shelter program in the Soviet Bloc. The USSR has an extensive civil defence system that has steadily grown since 1948 and is now being reorganised for atomic weapon defence. Permanent staff officers of Local Air Defense, a branch of the MVD, serve at all levels of government down to city districts. Urban crews rest on medical, police, firefighting, utility, and service organisations, and home and factory teams are organised by DOSAAF, which also trains the general population.

Reports show a shelter building program under way for several years at factories, railway stations, and river ports. New apartment construction includes basement shelters, and shelters are being added to suitable standing buildings. Static water tanks, reservoirs, and swimming pools for emergency firefighting, and underground storage depots and fuel tanks, are also reported.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200030004-1:
Memo dated 29 March 1955 to Agency offices circulates thinking on coordination of requirements. A meeting with the offices had been held on 18 February 1955. A discussion with the IAC agencies followed on 25 February. Informal talks with IAC representatives followed. On that basis, the writer would send the Director a report along the lines of an attached draft. Written reactions from the offices were requested. The key question was whether their views were properly reflected in the draft.

The draft scheme in later pages divides the work between two bodies. One subcommittee would frame intelligence requirements. It would be drawn from those concerned with production. Its frame would be the critical deficiencies named in the governing paper. A second subcommittee would turn those requirements into information requirements. It would be drawn from those who run the government's collection systems. It would allocate the collection tasks among the systems.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000200030077-1:
Procedures paper on coordination of external research survives in part in the scan. Its first page is badly garbled. The numbered steps on later pages are legible. One step concerns Agency external research projects above one size. It covers projects involving more than 5,000 dollars. The projects are in support of economic intelligence production. For them, staff will arrange with the Assistant Director for Research and Reports to submit the project's scope to the Economic Intelligence Committee for review. If possible, an EIC recommendation is won before final approval.

Other steps require guidance from the Security Office on the security aspects of a proposal, and exploratory meetings with prospective performers before a project is fixed. A further step covers change to a project after review. Where review turns up objections, the project may be reshaped. A sound project can then go forward rather than be dropped outright.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400050019-1:
Memo dated 14 June 1957 goes to the Assistant Director for Scientific Intelligence, through the Deputy Director for Intelligence. Its subject is a review of how Agency responsibilities under the Technological Capabilities Panel were carried out. It cites a National Security Council memorandum of 2 January 1957. The memo quotes an action approved by the President: departments and agencies will make periodic reviews of the panel report areas in their charge. The reviews spot problems for special study where new intelligence or new technology alters vulnerability to surprise attack.

Such a review was under way, and a report on it was requested by 5 July 1957, covering the period through 30 June 1957, on Specific Recommendation C.3. The memo is marked TS X64568, copy 1 of 5. The file also carries the Top Secret control cover form, limiting access to Top Secret Control personnel and those whose duties relate to the matter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000400070017-1:
Memorandum IAC-D-55/11, dated 22 June 1956, goes to the Intelligence Advisory Committee and its subcommittee chairmen. Its subject is the status of national security programs on 30 June 1956. It refers to IAC-D-55/10 of 20 June 1956, and to the final IAC-D-55/9 of 16 August 1955. It refers to a memorandum of 4 June 1956 from the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council, attached as Tab A.

Tab A makes one request of the Director of Central Intelligence. He is to submit an annual report on the status of the foreign intelligence program to the President and the Council, due no later than 15 August. IAC agencies and subcommittees are asked to prepare contributions for it. The form and content of the contributions follow what Tab A requires. Primary responsibility for the annex is assigned in Tab A as well. The rest of the file is the standard Top Secret control form text.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600010002-1:
A long run of RDD Diary entries fills this file, opening with the week of 16 to 20 August 1954. Entries record day to day coordination in short numbered notes. One early item concerns terms for a national estimate on resistance potential. Another weighs a plan for an Intelligence Advisory Committee panel on photographic intelligence, a plan the writer opposed. Service coordination in that field already seemed workable without a new committee.

Other entries follow papers and clearances across agencies. The writer asks a Joint Intelligence Committee team for copies of a photographic intelligence paper, a presidential memo on overflight questions, and a directive on Southeast Asia needs. Later entries handle support for psychological warfare and a dispute over what a U.S. officials only marking meant for release abroad.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600070006-1:
A secret study dated 26 January 1955 surveys collection programs and how their needs get coordinated. Part I works through the collectors, starting with the Foreign Service. Reporting instructions rest in the end with State Department bureau heads. The Foreign Service also speaks for the United States abroad and guards its interests, so reporting is one duty among several. Desk officers lean on the Department's intelligence staff to frame reporting needs.

Details follow on fields such as farm reporting, then handled by State under a temporary deal while talks with the Agriculture Department went on. Political reporting drew in CIA's current intelligence office to help draft instructions. Later sections cover service intelligence work and support to the Joint Chiefs. A closing note ties overt collection abroad to the split set out in NSCID-2.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600090068-1:
A draft summary pulls together the war plans of offices under the deputy directorate for intelligence. It works office by office in short entries. The estimates office plan calls for fewer broad country papers and more special, fast estimates on narrow areas. It floats a regular global review and more military input to estimates. It also flags a wartime problem: weak communications could hamper the whole estimates process, so shorter estimates sent by wire may be needed.

The science office plan stresses work on war-making power. It offers staff abroad to inspect captured equipment and question captured staff, and backs new collection methods fit for combat. The current intelligence office plan keeps its daily role and its briefing duty for the Council. It adds a current intelligence centre and a situation room for the President, and its staff would grow from one shift to three in war.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600130018-1:
A global war plan for the Office of Operations survives here as a partial text, opening at its fifth paragraph. Present facilities could move onto a wartime footing at once, the plan states. Even so, fresh demands in war would call for more staff and more kit across its divisions. A 1951 agreement shapes one key duty. Under it, CIA speaks for State and the Atomic Energy Commission in exploiting material won by military forces in war theaters.

That duty sits with the Office of Operations. Its foreign documents division and a Soviet materials staff hold the work. The plan then sets out how the office would run if headquarters escaped the first attack and stayed in Washington. Its three divisions would keep a semi-free hand, with tweaks. A planning and coordinating staff would grow to five professionals and three clerks.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000600140008-1:
A proposed first spread of Talent-Keyhole billets for the Navy fills the file, marked for Keyhole channels only. A basic table gives totals by area and command. The Washington area takes 171 billets. Operating forces take 50, the Pacific Fleet area 22, and naval forces in Europe 14. Unified commands take nine.

Detailed pages then break the Washington share down by office. The Secretary of the Navy's staff takes two billets, Marine Corps headquarters six. Naval operations offices follow by code: plans and policy, air, development, and strike warfare among them. Named posts appear beside each code, from deputy chiefs down to branch heads. Intelligence sections list target, vulnerability, and Soviet bloc analysts. Fleet intelligence centres and fleet staffs abroad fill the later pages, post by post.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700050034-1:
Part I of a project book lists work the coordination office is actively chasing. First item: requirements for all offices. The office now owns the task of joining up general guidance for collection units, inside CIA and beyond. It also helps settle clashes over spot requests. A new Agency requirements committee backs that work.

That committee has held its first meeting. It picked ten high priority countries for guide requirements, written to one agreed pattern. Offices owe their parts by 27 June, after which clashes between items and offices will be weighed. Later items turn elsewhere. A science committee problem asks whether its subcommittee layers should be dropped for a more direct setup. One entry records that State will try a regular report on Communist activity for the current intelligence office. Another seeks better ways to draw economic facts from photographic material.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700060015-1:
A fuller statement on coordinating collection requirements fills the file, marked as cleared by a Security Council review. Its first test asks whether a need can be met from Washington shelves. Requirements officers press researchers on that point before any field task is set. Machinery built in recent years backs the check. An advisory committee under NSCID 16 works on reference tools for foreign writings.

That committee also guards three linked aims: better recovery of facts already gathered, fuller buying of foreign language works, and best use of language skills across agencies. Even so, leaks will occur, the paper concedes. Later parts weigh whether a like need has been tasked before, and how field links run both ways. Chance plays a part beside planning, it admits. Secret collection, costly and risky, should wait in the main until open sources fail or plainly will fail on a matter that counts.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700060033-1:
A memorandum for the record, dated 26 February 1955, captures an interagency talk on coordinating requirements. State staff Buford and Trezise sat at the table. Colonel Montgomery and Mr Guenther came from G-2. Colonel Berry came from the Air Force. The chair summed up how national priority objectives arose, then sought views on a Tab B plan for two new committees.

Tab B, the group was told, was not an Agency stance. CIA views aired in the room were blunt: collection looked chaotic to some. No system ranked collection tasks by priority. Worry centred less on overlap than on missing machinery to fit top needs and hand each task to the ablest collector. Colonel Montgomery pushed back later. Field machinery already sat under the senior United States official abroad, he noted. He doubted any committee could steer all of it.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070032-1:
An Intelligence Advisory Committee paper dated 23 December 1952 sends round a draft NSCID 16. The topic is foreign language publications. Talk of such a directive had run on and off for five years. A recent Economic Intelligence Committee report pushed CIA to draft one, with terms for an advisory committee. Agencies were asked to send staff to a meeting on 8 January 1953 in Room 1128, M Building.

The draft directive itself follows. It makes the Director answerable for joining up the buying of foreign language works for intelligence use. As a core duty, he must supply member agencies with English excerpts, summaries, and abstracts. An annex weighs how the draft would change each agency's current work. Pages on buying note that CIA would guide the State Department and other collectors. Emergency buying plans also fall to the new committee to frame.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070041-1:
A memorandum dated 23 December 1953 answers a Budget Bureau request on sorting intelligence spending. It goes to Mr Robert Macy at the Bureau. On 17 November he had asked the committee for help in building a fuller budget picture of United States intelligence programs. He also wanted a set of classes for that study. An initial list is attached.

Internal security programs are left out, by agreement reached when Macy sat with the committee. Early soundings suggest the Bureau finds the classes fit for first use. The Bureau may call for more help as the survey runs, and its findings should in turn reach the committee. The attached paper, marked IAC-D-77/1, opens with a simple rule. Head classes should follow the old three-way split of intelligence work: collection, production, and dissemination. Collection then splits into open and secret work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp61s00750a000700070050-1:
A second yearly report of the Economic Intelligence Committee, dated 15 August 1953, covers July 1952 to June 1953. It opens with legal roots. Under NSCID 15 of June 1951, the Director set the committee up that same month. Its terms won committee backing. The chair is CIA's Assistant Director for Research and Reports.

Members sit in two grades. Staff from member agencies hold full seats. About twenty outside agencies hold associate seats, called in where their skills fit. Nine standing subcommittees cover the main foreign economic fields, with three more due within a month. A further subcommittee handles collection needs and sorting facilities. When a sharp problem needs focus, ad hoc working groups form. Later parts list the committee's duties one by one, with progress notes. One duty is to review, and report on, how well the data and studies in hand fit the questions posed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100110021-1:
An intelligence summary dated April 1957 tracks current trends in Sino-Soviet bloc building and buying of merchant and fishing vessels. An ad hoc subcommittee of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee prepared it. The work was done at the call of the Economic Defense Advisory Committee's executive arm. Six parts structure the study.

Early parts retell COCOM and CHINCOM shipping talks and the controls now in force. The present makeup of bloc merchant fleets follows. Bloc yard strength for building merchant ships is then weighed, as is free world building done for bloc buyers. Six tables back the text. They give fleet makeup at 1 January 1957, world comparisons by type, age, and speed, and naval auxiliaries fit for cargo work. One finding stands out: satellite yard output should reach only fifteen percent of planned goals. Part of any new tonnage must also replace worn-out ships.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470013-1:
Minutes of the fourteenth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee cover a session held on 9 February 1956. They are dated 20 February. First, the November minutes won approval. Next came a State paper on trade in goods freed from control. The chairman praised it as careful work. It would help judge what the 1954 easing of trade controls had done.

State's member gave the gist: since the strategic lists were eased in August 1954, bloc imports had not jumped in bulk. Their makeup, though, seemed to have shifted. A paper on bloc gold sales in free markets was set to pass unless views arrived by 16 February. None came, so it stands approved. Later talk turned to new reporting rules on economic ties with the bloc. Commerce stressed that steady review of such work guards the trade control program.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100470022-1:
Minutes of the fifth meeting of the Economic Defense Intelligence Committee are dated 24 January 1955. The group met on 18 January. First business was a report back from the Executive Committee. It had weighed a paper on the Soviet bloc's external financial operations, coded IWG/R-16. Members were told to study that paper and grade its problems by weight and range.

Working groups under the parent body must also review their own work against those financial operations. Two listed functions would be cut, since their ground fits inside two others. The Executive Committee further urged that the Director look at the whole field, above all where it touches enforcement work. Later, a research office reply to an admiral drew careful handling. The acting chairman set out CIA's view against building one new single office for the field.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490002-1:
A status note on pending committee projects survives in part, opening at its third item. That item covers a request numbered twelve: diversion of strategic material from South to North Korea. A June request went to G-2, with a copy to the defence staff. One office states it cannot supply the facts sought.

Other matters follow in short notes. A subgroup on the committee's own functions met on 31 May and reached no firm view. Two agencies want talks held till the aid agency's place clears in the new fiscal year. Work on research programming was aired on 28 April, then held for moves elsewhere. Action on Soviet external financial operations waits on a packaged set of views from above, tied to report IWG/R-16. A stock list of all economic defence projects across the community, first urged in October 1954, is also in hand. Once done, it will go round the committee.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000100490048-1:
A reference desk report for March 1955 is dated 1 April. It opens with the committee's 17 March meeting. All but one subgroup were dissolved there, and three pending cases were cancelled. The acting chairman also reported on several live economic defence problems. Staff work for the month is then logged in detail.

One officer pushed the COCOM downgrading project and readied committee papers for vital records storage. Another indexed every item in the reference desk files. Defence staff were briefed on committee work. Staff also joined State and research colleagues on added facts for a revised paper on oil. Clearance status for all committee members was listed for the security office. A new cable plan stalled: no deal on its use was reached by month's end. From 1 April, cables would file by date and class, and the subject file would end. A stock list of the desk's files went round the division.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200010175-1:
A memorandum dated 18 January 1954 guards the spread of economic defence material. It goes to the chief of the security control staff. The working group secretariat works hard, it states, to see group papers reach only cleared hands. With the memo goes a long list of names. All are people now in, or once in, some part of the economic defence program.

The list is explained in care. Some names sit on the field's many bodies: the parent advisory committee, its executive arm and working groups, the joint operating body, and the export policy committee. Others simply work for agencies with a stake in the field. Names run in letter order, not by body. Two marks sort them. A double star flags current group members. A single star flags those whose clearance papers the secretariat holds from an agency other than CIA.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200050054-1:
A Battelle Memorial Institute letter dated 6 June 1956 lists four staff who plan to attend a propellants seminar. The seminar runs in Washington on 13 and 14 June. For each man the letter gives a job title and clearance standing. One is a consultant chemist, one a division chief, and one an assistant division chief. Clearances run at secret and top secret level.

Verification is directed to a security office channel at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, naming a chief and a phone line. Personal birth details printed in the letter are not repeated here. A second sheet in the file logs more names expected at the seminar. Defence, aid, and other offices appear, with ticks and notes in hand. One pair of names carries a warning that they will not be able to attend after all. The file thus works as a clearance and attendance record for a closed technical meeting.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00328a000200080015-1:
A Commerce Department study dated November 1951 maps the Office of International Trade. Julian Lowe wrote it. A contents page shows the plan: first the office as a whole, then its five great branches one by one. Charts show where the office sits inside the Department, and how each branch is wired.

Part I covers the office's birth, its broad duties, and its shape. Part II opens with the staff offices: the director's own office, foreign needs and claims work, aid work under Point IV, legal counsel, and public information. An intelligence and services branch follows, with trade growth, commercial intelligence, and travel arms. Economic affairs holds area desks split by world region, plus a study division. The export branch runs goods divisions, a strategic controls division, and the Foreign Service operations arm. Training and review branches close the pack.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200010018-1:
A Bureau of the Budget letter of June 1958 stalls a draft executive order. The order would name CIA a defence agency under the patent secrecy law, chapter 17 of Title 35. The Director had sent the draft on 13 December 1957. Two enclosed letters shape the reply. One comes from the Atomic Energy Commission's general manager, dated 12 February 1958. The other comes from the Defense Department's general counsel, dated 4 June.

The atomic body backs a narrower form: the naming should skip bids that involve restricted data. The defence counsel will not agree as the draft stands. He asks for a joint talk with CIA and the Commissioner of Patents first. His side needs a fuller briefing before it takes a stance. The Budget office will hold the order, the letter states, till the Director advises how to proceed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200010045-1:
Army legal papers in the file pass a patent disclosure to CIA for action. A letter dated 24 August 1955 comes from Major John Neary, acting chief of the Patents Division in the Judge Advocate General's office. It goes to the chief of CIA's physical security arm. A phone talk with Agency counsel set the path: the enclosed file on a patent disclosure goes to CIA for declassification action, then back to the Army.

A November memo names the device at stake. It is a modification of a deadbolt re-locking device for combination locks. An Agency employee designed and built it. Papers, the device itself, and two working models were to go before the Army Patents Division. A later note insists the idea grew from the man's own study of locks in for repair, not from any secret tie to the lock's maker.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200070003-1:
Legal correspondence in the file handles a Court of Claims suit, John Zavodny against the United States. A letter from John Warner, Deputy General Counsel, goes to the Justice Department's civil chief. It answers a letter of 26 June 1956. The Agency, Warner writes, has no means of disputing the commissioner's finding on one item. It hopes that sum might shrink in a compromise settlement.

Negatives sit at the heart of the deal. Copies may be handed to the plaintiff if giving them up is a term of final settlement. Warner is unsure whether Justice or CIA now holds them; if CIA does, a search will start at once. Court findings filed on 24 May 1956 open with the plaintiff's roots in Czechoslovakia. Later findings admit a hard fact: material taken out for work in the field was lost, destroyed, or misplaced.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000200100027-1:
A short paper sets out a clearance plea in the atomic field. It opens with a plain fact: CIA runs some work that touches atomic energy. For that work, a number of its staff need access to restricted data. The Agency has asked the Atomic Energy Commission to grant those clearances on the strength of CIA's own clearances. A letter from the Acting Director is attached as proof.

Scale is given in round terms. About two hundred staff in all are caught up in such work. Fresh requests run at about two a month. The paper then quotes section 145 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. That section bars any access to restricted data till the Civil Service Commission has probed the person and reported. The commission must also find that access will not endanger common defence and security.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300030015-1:
A memo for the record dated 13 August 1958 sorts legal help for task force staff. A staff arm is building teams of mixed skills, ready to fly to the field at short notice. Some chosen men asked how they could get legal counsel to settle their own affairs first. Their support office asked the general counsel for a list of lawyers it could hand out.

Counsel chose a different path. Rather than pass a bare list, it would see each man alone. That way it can judge whose case truly needs a lawyer. The support office agreed to that plan. A wider memo of 12 June 1958 rides in the file. It tells all area divisions why task forces are being built: cold war crises can flare fast. Teams must be rounded and versatile, and the roster must be deep. Depth keeps sudden calls from gutting other vital work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300080010-1:
A legal memo answers whether the Agency may back employee groups with rooms and help. The ask came from the personnel side. It sought the law behind giving space and other support to employee organisations. It also sought a digest of Comptroller General rulings on three forms of help: space and gear, staff services in duty hours, and payroll deductions.

The base rule is hard. Appropriated sums may be spent only on the objects they were voted for, under Title 31, section 628. Bar express leave in an act, that rule binds. On its strength, the Comptroller has barred funds for buying or renting recreation grounds. Pay for recreation supervision has been barred too. Lack of such facilities at a base, and harm to morale, did not move him. Four rulings are listed, two of them unpublished, from 1943 and 1945. None has been overturned since, the memo states.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300180028-1:
A memo sets the ground rules for a contract program under a secret project. The project head is blanked in this copy. The plan rests on talks between the two offices, and goes up for review and a green light.

Men hired under it will work largely on their own drive. Their task: work a body of material toward set goals. No count of hours or days binds the pace. In law, then, each man stands as an independent contractor, not a staff hand. The work runs on an open footing. Pay for service comes by government check. All of it takes place inside the continental United States. First steps are fixed. The field man sends in a Form 57, in first copy and one more, with a top fee he proposes. That fee and the broad shape of the work go to the Special Contracting Officer for his say.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000300210006-1:
A memo dated 11 February 1957 pitches a handbook for Agency counsel. A draft list of chapters rides with it. Built out, the book would hold most of the base legal ground the Agency stands on. The writer calls it a store of first rules, both for the work bench and for the thought behind the work.

New hands gain most, he argues. Men fresh to the Agency lack its lore. The book would also force plain thought on the Agency's place under the constitution. Past chiefs won good rulings at short call, he grants. Fresh counsel, left with no guide if the old hands were gone at once, could not be counted on to match that feat. One chapter is done and rides along: on holding back facts. Its CIA part weighs past fixes, the case for each, and the tight spots sure to come.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400020006-1:
A thin file tracks the Agency's reply to a big security review. The Wright Commission, set up to study government security, sent its report in 1957. Its chair, Loyd Wright, wrote to Mr Dulles on 21 August. A note of 12 September tells the acting general counsel what to keep from that mail.

One piece is worth filing with care, the note says. A mid-August letter gives a clear, full take on a sore point: how secret work is bought. That text should be kept close, in case the point is raised again. A draft reply to the Justice side rides in the file too. The commission meant to leave the Agency out of its scheme, counsel notes. So no deep, point-by-point views should go to Justice. A short, signed note to a Mr Tompkins is the wiser course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400030014-1:
A kept court text prints a 1956 appeal ruling, Mallory v. United States. The District of Columbia appeals court heard it; Judge Prettyman wrote. Andrew Mallory stood found guilty of rape, with death added by the jury. The first, and the one dwelt on here, is a sworn tale he gave the police.

The facts are set out cold. An attack took place in a basement furnace room on the night of 1 April 1954. Mallory lodged in the same basement, in the janitor's rooms. Police seized him the next day and held him with two kin at headquarters. A wait while the test man was found, a meal, and no more questions fill the gap in the time line. The legal head-notes name the stakes: the McNabb rule on swift charge, and what a jury may know of fixed terms when it weighs death.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050003-1:
A file from October 1957 gathers views on a plan to amend Order 10501. That order, of 5 November 1953, sets the rules for guarding state facts in the name of defense. The Budget Bureau sent a draft change round for Agency word. With it came a draft note to all shop heads, and an Attorney General letter of 11 October.

John S. Warner, the legislative counsel, drives the in-house round. His memo of 10 October goes to both deputy directors, the General Counsel, and the security chief. Views must reach him by 14 November so one Agency stance can be built. A long staff reply rides in the file. It takes the Attorney General's points in his own order. The first change in line would hand a power back: shops that once held stamp rights, then lost them, could win back a say in clearing their own old files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00631r000400050021-1:
A memo dated 22 August 1957 reworks one clause of a draft shield rule. Counsel writes to Warner, and backs a change first raised by Colonel White. The point: what a served man should say when the Director holds facts back in the state's good. The new text is given in full, with fresh words in brackets.

The served man will still turn up, as the writ demands. He will state, with respect, that he acts on the Director's own firm word in his refusal. Counsel gives two grounds for the soft form. It is unfair to the man himself to leave him looking stiff and shut-mouthed. And it guards the Agency's gain less well than a calm, voiced ground. A gap is flagged too. What if the man cannot turn up at all? Then counsel, or his named stand-in, should go and put the case in words.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100080034-1:
A 13 October 1959 office memorandum to the Director of Training, sent by the Plans and Policy Staff, takes up a study of the CIA Introduction briefing given to new employees. The study proposed ending the shared briefing because new staff groups were too mixed. Separate briefings would instead serve clerical staff, professional staff, communications technicians, and service workers such as chauffeurs and printers.

Replies gathered from Agency offices follow, along with notes on when new employees tend to arrive during the year. The closing conclusions pull back part of the plan. Dropping the briefing for professional staff met enough opposition to warrant retraction, while keeping the introduction for clerical staff was judged to have merit worth trying to meet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00634a000100130047-1:
Emergency planning for the Intelligence Advisory Committee is reported in a 3 April 1956 memorandum marked IAC-D-96/2. An ad hoc working group had been formed after concern grew over how war or a wartime emergency would affect the committee's work. Operation Alert 1955 served as a testing ground, exposing problems the group was asked to name and help solve.

Pages that follow weigh how the committee could keep meeting if offices had to relocate. Military intelligence would form the main flow of news about the enemy in the early phase of a war, giving service intelligence chiefs and the Director of Central Intelligence central roles. The group recommends that, under relocation, committee meetings be held at or near the alternate site.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000100160004-1:
Annexes to a Coordinating Committee document numbered 3700.8 list export-control items sent for technical discussion and record where agreement had been reached. Long columns of item numbers fill the first annex. Items marked with a star show that partial agreement had been reached, with detail promised in a second annex.

That second annex works item by item through settled changes. One item was agreed for deletion, parts of another were dropped, and a third was redefined to cover spin-forming machines above a set motor size. Further entries treat machinery for making aircraft, rockets, and missiles. The dry lists capture allied governments in 1959 quietly redrawing the lines around goods kept from the Soviet bloc.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200020062-1:
Budget and finances of the Coordinating Committee occupy a record of discussion dated 28 March 1960, issued as document 3958 on 5 April 1960. Eleven delegations sat for the meeting. The chairman drew attention to a report from the Budget Sub-Committee and to a French memorandum, sent that same day, about France's contribution to the committee's budget.

Money pressure came from a coming change of premises, which forced the funding question open. Annexes to the budget report set out 1959 spending, counting both cash outlays and contributions in kind such as rent, office gear, and staff paid by single countries. French officials argued that total costs should instead be shared by an agreed scale across member governments, a fairer method than the patchwork then in use.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00647a000200110008-1:
Bilateral talks between the United States and Japan on export control levels are documented in a September 1953 paper for the Economic Defense Advisory Committee. The negotiations ran from 23 July to 2 August and were finalised on 5 September, alongside five-power talks on organising Far Eastern economic security measures. Background, detail, and results are all included for committee members.

Four parts structure the record. The first reports the joint working group on levels of Japanese controls over trade with Communist China, with five attachments setting out the understandings reached. The second covers talks between the two delegation heads, with ten further attachments. Long item lists in the later pages name controlled goods in fine detail, down to optical lenses, prisms, and X-ray darkroom outfits.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200160063-1:
Industrial growth in Slovakia is the subject of a project initiation memorandum from the Geography Division, dated 10 March 1959. The study would prepare a subject report from an attached outline and survey transport and mineral resources. Its aim was to measure how far industrialisation had gone and what it had done to transport and power networks and to the use of natural resources.

A second aim was to judge where the new industries pointed: toward raw material sources inside or outside Czechoslovakia, and what that meant for Slovakia's future direction. The project was self-initiated inside the division. Three hundred man-hours were estimated, one or two maps were wanted, and completion was planned for 30 June 1959 in two phases.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-00680r000200210003-1:
East Germany's military mapmaking service is described in a geographic memorandum dated 14 December 1959, numbered CIA/RR G/S 59-31, from the Office of Research and Reports. The Cartographic Service of the National People's Army had its headquarters at Barbarastrasse 2 in Halle. A survey unit elsewhere was reported to work as a branch office of the service.

Sections inside the headquarters are taken one by one, with staff numbers, shifts, and duties for each. One section is reported working two shifts on most days, including Sundays, for about a week each month. The bindery alone is put at an estimated forty-five to fifty men and women under a single officer. The detail gives a ground-level picture of how a Warsaw Pact army produced its maps.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62-01094r000500040027-1:
Assignment of military personnel to the Central Intelligence Agency is governed by a Department of Defense directive dated 5 December 1957, numbered 1316.3. The directive cancels and replaces an earlier one from 9 December 1952. Its stated purpose is to announce the governing policies to everyone concerned, across the armed services and the Agency.

General policy begins with representation and liaison. Some military staff should serve in the Agency to give the armed forces a proper part and voice at the right levels. Those chosen should be the best qualified and most experienced available. Later rules cover services and facilities the military could furnish. Warn that the services should not be asked to staff remote or undesirable posts for the Agency as a matter of course.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200010083-1:
Decisions on the future of Project AQUATONE are pressed in a 25 September 1956 memorandum to the Acting Director of Central Intelligence. The writer urges that, at the next meeting with higher authority, full guidance be sought on every course open to the project. Only then could a steady course be charted for some months ahead instead of lurching from one delay to the next.

Continued uncertainty, the memo argues, was already hurting the morale of project staff. Recommendations follow on the stance to take with political authorities. One passage reconsiders flying tempo in light of a national estimate on enemy reactions to overflights. Quite rare operations, perhaps three missions a month spread over a long period, are floated as a pattern worth weighing.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200040026-1:
Recommendations for the next phase of the AQUATONE program fill a planning group report from 1957. Overflight operations would continue for another two years, or until the fall of 1959, using United States bases in Europe and the Near East or staging through them. The project would keep its present command character, directed through a direct channel from the Director of Central Intelligence.

Priority inside the Agency and in logistics would be retained, and the U-2 would stay the project's primary aircraft, kept operationally ready at all times. Planning factors listed for choosing detachment sites include present occupancy, facilities, and security, with special attention to the Far East. The report reads as an effort to lock in a further full season of operations before the aircraft's edge faded.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200080040-1:
A field letter to Mr. Bissell dated 19 April 1958 reports progress at an overseas detachment working with Hycon camera gear. The new equipment had arrived in March, which was set aside as a shakedown month. A visiting party led by Dr. Scott is praised warmly: small operating faults were cleared up and advice on daily handling proved very helpful.

Reliability is the letter's main theme. The writer judges the 'B' configuration ready, with at least two successful flights on each unit and nine missions flown in all, six of them successful. Three losses traced back to one faulty shutter, which was being returned. New trackers had also troubled the unit until a binding film-reel latch was found. Staging ideas using a C-124 as a mobile shop close the letter.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62b00844r000200160041-1:
Status of the OXCART program is reported in a paper on a covert follow-on aircraft for photographic reconnaissance. The system grew out of a feasibility study devoted to a successor aircraft, and it is carried on under the joint auspices of the Central Intelligence Agency and the Air Force. A specially developed Lockheed airframe sits at the centre of the design.

Twelve aircraft were being procured for the operational program, and development and flight test work are described as under way. Aerial cameras for the system were in development alongside the aircraft. Much of the supporting detail in the released copy is blacked out or garbled in the scan, so the paper's firm facts are its subject, its sponsors, its maker. The size of the planned fleet.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100040072-1: This declassified CIA document is marked Country USSR. The Soviet file. The file holds the marking. The record stays. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add detail to the Cold War story.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120046-1:
Project 30.1535, a study of plant capacity growth in the non-food consumer goods industries of Communist China from 1953 to 1962, is reviewed in notes dated 9 September 1959. The reviewer calls the project essentially sound. It judged Chinese plans for a major sector and so should aid understanding of the whole Chinese economy, and its estimates, though critical of Chinese plans, appear reasonable.

The paper even anticipated a recent Chinese admission that the official estimate of 1958 cotton production had been too exuberant. Faults to fix are still listed. Investment for the sector is developed for the first five-year plan but not followed into the second plan's comparable plans. Cotton spindle figures draw a query: one table accounts for only part of the additions to capacity shown earlier. A note is needed on whether the unreported remainder was allocated the same way.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100120073-1:
Comments on a draft of ORR Project 20.1776, on long-term trends in supplies and costs of metals, fuels. Electric power in the Soviet Union, are sent in reply to a memorandum of 30 July 1959. Much of the draft lies outside the Industrial Division's power to coordinate, the comments note. Statements on power and metallurgical equipment were checked with the analysts responsible for those items, who in general concurred with the draft on past and probable future availability of such equipment.

Judgment on the future rested more on past performance than on detailed data about production planned under the Seven Year Plan. Specific queries follow: whether petroleum industry investment for petrochemical capacity shows in a stated investment measure, a sentence that mentions efficient equipment twice. Two percentage figures for the electrotechnical industry and machine building that appear non-comparable.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100160024-1: This declassified CIA requirement covers Hungarian refugees. The displaced, aided. The file holds the requirement. The record stays. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00231a000100190030-1:
A note on Soviet submarine building at Komsomolsk is sent in with this covering memo. A new transporter dock on the river was finished in October. It is read as a sign that the yard plans to build very large submarines. A new submarine was finished at the same time. A large nuclear dock was also being built. The new submarine is larger than any built before in the Soviet Union. It is only a few feet shorter than the American nuclear submarine Triton.

Before the new dock, ships built at Komsomolsk were moved by pontoons. They included W-class submarines and Kotlin and Kildin class destroyers, with drafts of fourteen feet. Depths in the Amur River and the Tartar Strait run as shallow as ten and a half feet. Komsomolsk sits one hundred fifteen miles up from the river's mouth. It is a safe but awkward site for shipbuilding.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00346a000100050010-1:
Minutes of a committee on exchanges are dated 17 September 1957. The body was an ad hoc group of the Intelligence Advisory Committee. Debate turned on a Soviet plan for exchanges of specialists. The State Department had aired the plan with an American factory owner. He said United States trade might go along with it. But it would not want to send its first-rank men for so long a span.

Major Mickelson raised a sharp thought. The Soviets might aim above all at building spy rings. Others noted that other parts of the government already own that risk. The chairman agreed on one point. The spy judgment itself would not be the committee's work. It would more likely reach the Operations Coordinating Board as a spoken briefing. The National Security Council might hear it the same way. The group also sought set bounds to guide its subgroups.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100020067-1:
Further cuts in the authorised strength of the Economic Research Area are costed in a 7 October 1958 memorandum. Since 1 July 1956 the area's activities kept expanding, largely in answer to sharply increased demand from priority consumers, even while authorised strength shrank. New duties were met only by abandoning or cutting back work and reshuffling staff, ending in a large 1958 reorganisation of three of the four divisions.

The paper warns that this economy drive has used up the area's flexibility. A two percent cut in authorised strength would mean losing eight positions out of four hundred eleven; a five percent cut would cost twenty. A table then walks through programs one by one, from basic studies of bloc communications to the publications staff, stating what each lost position would do to the work.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100020120-1:
A net evaluation of the Soviet economy, quoted from a confidential paper by a company's economist, is forwarded on 8 July 1958. On the production front, the excerpt reports near-unanimity among experts: Soviet industrial production in the late 1950s was about forty percent as large as that of the United States. Soviet investment in heavy industry was proportionately larger, and output of specific industries had approached the American level.

Machine tool output is said to be overtaking American output, coal output in 1958 about equal, and steel capacity now half that of the United States. The excerpt also looks at Soviet oil: domestic consumption is put near five hundred million barrels. Director Allen Dulles is quoted to the effect that by 1972 the Soviets could export about two million barrels a day.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090015-1:
A newsletter supplement on the Soviet economy is passed round inside the Agency, with a routing note from Sherman Kent. The supplement, 'Popular Delusions About Russia,' comes from the Whaley-Eaton American Letter service. It is dated 15 August 1959. It argues that American business needs a better grasp of the Soviet economy. It aims to give a balanced picture of Russian progress and problems.

The Russian world is vast in area and population, the supplement begins. But therein lie weaknesses as well as strengths. Russia has lagged for two centuries behind Western Europe and North America. By all standards it remains a backward country. Yet it pours its total energies into catching up. American ideas of Russia are shaped by fears and false beliefs. Farming draws the sharpest verdict: wheat land is worked with modern machines, yet the mean farm worker grows food for only two or three other people.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090024-1:
Concluding remarks to the National Strategy Seminar at the National War College are delivered by Allen W. Dulles on 24 July 1959. The reserve officers present had covered Soviet strategy and tactics. They had covered the nature of the Communist threat. They had covered the relative military strength of East and West, and the face of war in the nuclear age.

Analyses of the Soviet threat tend to go to extremes, Dulles warns. One class of experts magnifies every aspect of Soviet power. They become prophets of gloom. Others discount Soviet accomplishments and magnify internal difficulties, risking unhealthy complacency. He notes recent magazine articles that try, on flimsy evidence, to discredit recognised Soviet accomplishments. The Communist program itself is called an insidious interference in the internal affairs of free countries. Were it advanced by open, peaceful competition, he says, the challenge could be accepted. The peoples could be left to choose.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090051-1:
Soviet Capabilities for Future Trade and Aid is a declassified Agency briefing text on what the Soviet Union could do in trade and aid over the next seven years. It frames the years 1959 to 1965, the span of the next Soviet plan period. Enough plan goals had been made public, the speaker argues, to judge the plan's broad shape.

Trade and aid are treated as one claim on Soviet output among several. Living standards, housing, and farm output press on one side. High investment and rising military costs press on the other. The text expects producer goods output to near three quarters of the United States level by 1965, and it stresses Soviet offers of engineers and technical help to poorer nations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090088-1:
The Soviet Economy is a declassified Agency briefing text that compares the Soviet and United States economies sector by sector. Soviet output is converted into United States prices with ruble-dollar ratios. The contrast in shape is the point: the Soviet side is strongest in military goods and producer goods.

It is weakest, the text says, in farming and consumer goods. Industry sections note rich mineral resources but past shortfalls in metals output. Plans for a third metals base in Siberia and Kazakhstan are mentioned. Farm sections cover new stress on output per person and the January 1958 plan to end the machine tractor stations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100090114-1:
The Sino-Soviet Bloc Economic Offensive: Hazards for the Underdeveloped Countries is a declassified Agency report dated 3 April 1958. It dates the Bloc's economic push from 1953. Credits, technical help, and trade offers went chiefly to new nations in Asia and Africa.

The report frames those offers as political tools. Their stated aims were to cut United States influence, strain free world alliances, and raise Bloc prestige. A quote from President Eisenhower's mutual security message opens the case. Later sections stress that Bloc trade was highly selective. It targeted nations that lived on one or two crops, such as rice or cotton, and could be hurt by price swings.
cia-crest-cia-rdp62s00545a000100100022-1:
Sino-Soviet Bloc Economic Offensive is a declassified Agency talk given in a Brookings Institution series on 27 April 1959. It takes up Soviet trade with the West, the drive into poorer areas, and estimates of future Soviet growth. Soviet exports are put at a rate of 4.5 billion dollars a year.

In set prices, Soviet exports in 1957 stood six times their 1938 level. The Soviet Union had climbed from sixteenth to sixth place among trading nations. Yet three fourths of its trade stayed inside the Bloc. Bloc credits and grants over the four years ending in 1958 came to about 2.5 billion dollars, centered on a few key nations.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100020003-1:
Ruble Dollar Ratios is Appendix B of a declassified Agency study, giving 1950 price ratios between Soviet rubles and United States dollars. A short essay warns readers how to use the table. Swings among single ratios do not by themselves prove swings in real costs, and all figures are called preliminary and tentative.

The table gives group averages first: total output at 8 rubles per dollar, farm production at 11, and so on. Ratios rest on ruble prices with the turnover tax removed where it applied. No change was made for cost items left out of Soviet prices. Depletion and interest charges are named as the chief gaps of that kind.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100160008-1:
Redraft, CFEP Staff Study No. 16 is a marked-up revision of a draft dated 7 June 1955 on enforcement of controls. A head note explains the marks: underlined words are new text urged for insertion, while words in parentheses are text urged for deletion. The section handled is the study's analysis of enforcement problems.

One kept passage records how joint enforcement grew only through delay and hard bargaining. Transactions controls were traded against the August 1954 list reduction, then took five months to start. A further point blames technical descriptions of controlled goods. Fine technical gaps between banned and allowed items, it notes, defeat officials not trained to spot them. The redraft survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100170007-1:
East-West Trade in Embargoed Commodities is a declassified Agency study of banned goods moving to the Sino-Soviet Bloc. Because joint agreement bars these goods, their movement is typically missing from trade statistics. Intelligence sources must supply the evidence instead, and the study builds its picture case by case.

Changing lists complicate that picture. After the 1954 revision, the Soviet Bloc list ran much shorter than the China list. Goods cleared for Soviet ports were passed on in breach of the China embargo. Volume estimates center on copper: about 100,000 tons in 1953, and about 80,000 tons in 1954, are estimated to have moved to the Soviet Bloc.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100190005-1:
Note on the Balance of Payments of the European Soviet Bloc with the Free World is Staff Study No. 19 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 15, 1955. The six page note exists to explain a seemingly opposed feature of East-West trade. It sets Bloc payments with the free world into a single account.

One large gap in that account is unrecorded trade. The note is careful with words here: trade can be missing from, or wrong in, official figures for many reasons. Unrecorded trade is thus not the same thing as clandestine or illegal trade. Still, the Bloc is known to have gained substantial illegal imports in those years, and that fact helps close the gap. The Agency's CREST files preserve the study.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000100210002-1:
Economic Structure of the Communist Bloc is Staff Study No. 21 of the CFEP Drafting Group, draft of June 17, 1955, contributed by the Defense Department. Its summary opens with a measured claim. The Soviet economy had kept growing at a high rate since World War II, but that rate was now slackening.

Free gains that once fed Soviet growth had ended, the summary notes. Later pages map trade inside the Bloc itself. Satellite imports from China matched the Soviet pattern in kind, with iron ore and pig iron added in quantity. Signs of Soviet concern over sending a large share of Chinese goods onward to the European satellites are also recorded. The study survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00084a000200060008-1:
1950 Ugine Cobalt Diversion is a declassified Agency case account of a strategic metal that slipped past controls. In the summer of 1950, a London firm, Industrial Specialty Company, ordered 5,080 kilos of electrolytic cobalt from the French firm Ugine in Paris. The order looked like a large but honest British market need.

Ugine had to buy ore in Morocco to fill it, and charged a premium for the extra refining that ore needed. The cobalt still moved on to the Bloc through transshipment, the account shows. Named figures in the chain include a French agent who profited from Armco process rights. A British general served as the London firm's titular head until about 1950.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020011-1:
Information Sheet is a declassified Agency notice that explains a revision of the Language Development Program rules. Material is rearranged so the overall program stands out more clearly. The subsidiary Awards Program, once the louder part, is set in its proper place behind it.

Award concepts shift toward use. Stress moves from a broad interest in language study to the value of the language studied to the Agency. Award requests now need backing from career service heads or operating officials. Certain awards are cut from 1 July 1960, and the list of languages that earn awards is changed. Test rules and limits on repeated Maintenance Awards are also reset.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020020-1:
Employment of Language Tutors by LAS is an office memorandum dated 1 June 1960, sent to the DDTR from PPS. Its author is frank about its base: a hasty survey made that same day. The notes cover only the points judged most significant, not every detail of tutor hiring.

Spotting of tutor candidates fell to members of the language school itself. Contact clearance came through the training security officer, and the Director's approval was needed before any talk of a job. Tutors were then hired by contract. Student enrollment ran on formal training requests that estimated hours. Those estimates later served as a cross-check on the hours tutors reported, and tests bracketed each course of study. The memo survives in the Agency's CREST files.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200020084-1:
OTR Comments on SR Division Training Requirement for Calendar Years 1960 and 1961 form a memorandum dated 8 September 1960 to the DD/P Training Officer. Thanks open it: estimates of this kind from all components would be of great value for Agency wide planning. The SR statement is praised for its views on course content and teaching methods.

One gap is named at once. The SR needs are stated in terms of current courses run by the training office and TSD. Future needs that no current course can meet should also be stated, so new courses or revisions can be weighed. A balanced program, the memo adds, needs estimates from the bulk of DD/P components, and mixed language and job training for one student needs close joint planning.
cia-crest-cia-rdp63-00309a000200060017-1:
General Recommendations for Agency Mid-Career Course is an office memorandum dated 20 January 1960 from the Chief, Intelligence School. The writer offers personal ideas, drawn in part from recent service as a student in the State Department Mid-Career Course. He adapts that model to Agency needs and adds thoughts of his own.

The need is framed as a gap. Junior Officer Trainees now got one to two years of thorough training, while mid-career staff had no like path. One stress of the State course is urged for adoption: knowledge of peoples, cultures, and social frames. Agency work, whether running agents or writing current intelligence reports, turns on people shaped by just those forces.
cicero-letters-shuckburgh-vol-1:
Cicero's letters begin in the first volume of Evelyn Shuckburgh's version, in the 1908 printing. Rome's greatest speaker writes to Atticus, to Caesar, and to dear friends. Politics, gossip, wit, and fear flow from his pen in turn.

No letters from the ancient world feel so alive or so frank. Cicero schemes, jokes, grieves, and boasts as the Republic totters. He never meant these pages for the public eye. That candor makes them a rare window on Rome's fall. The set stands as a source that historians mine like no other from the age. New readers will find no better first guide to his world.
cinq-mars-volume-1:
Alfred de Vigny, a French romantic poet turned novelist, built Cinq-Mars on a real conspiracy against Cardinal Richelieu. Volume 1 opens the English edition with critical essays on De Vigny, by French Academy writers. The novel turns to 1639, as Henri de Cinq-Mars leaves home for the court of Louis XIII. Ambition and love launch him toward glory and ruin.

Cinq-Mars rises fast as the king's favorite at a fearful court. He loves Marie de Gonzague, a princess whose rank sits far above his reach. Richelieu, the cardinal who rules France, watches the favorite climb with patience. War with Spain, sieges, and festivals fill the background of the man's ascent. De Thou, his friend and a counsellor's son, walks beside him toward the plot. Readers starting the English set get the setup: a favorite's charm, a minister's power, and a love that ambition will poison by degrees.
clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of-a-you:
Clarissa Harlowe; or, The History of a Young Lady — Volume 1 opens Samuel Richardson's novel in letters. A list of persons sets the stage. Clarissa stands between two admirers: Robert Lovelace, and Roger Solmes, the suitor favored by her family. Her father, mother, brother James, and sister Arabella head the Harlowe side.

Her intimate friend and correspondent, Miss Howe, anchors the letter exchange. The volume builds the family quarrel that drives the whole work. Letters from her father press obedience in hard terms, down to orders given to the servant Betty Barnes. Every path Clarissa might take, marriage, defiance, or flight, is argued out in writing.
conscience-volume-1:
Hector Malot's crime novel begins in Conscience, Volume 1, the first English portion of the French Immortals edition. A life of Malot opens the file: the Norman novelist of Sans Famille, dead in 1907, praised for honest work over fashion. Conscience itself appeared in 1893. The story opens at Crozat's Wednesday reunion of old school comrades, where fortunes made and missed are quietly compared over dinner.

Inside, Saniel steps forward: a poor young doctor from Auvergne, brilliant, starved, and proud. He has begged three thousand francs from Glady, a comrade grown rich, and felt the humiliation to the bone. The moneylender Caffie holds the papers that could crush his start in medicine. Malot sets poverty, pride, and ambition in one room and lets them argue. Readers starting Conscience meet the murderer before the crime, as a man whose conscience is still loud enough to make his fall a tragedy rather than a puzzle.
correspondence-of-wagner-and-liszt-volum:
Richard Wagner and Franz Liszt, the two giants of romantic music, exchanged the letters gathered in Correspondence of Wagner and Liszt, Volume 1. Francis Hueffer translated the German letters into English. Wagner's own preface tells how Liszt rescued his art when success had failed and exile loomed. At Weimar, Liszt took the conductor's baton and gave the homeless composer a stage.

Letters from the 1840s onward track premieres, money troubles, and plans between the two men. Liszt conducts Tannhauser at Weimar while Wagner watches, hearing his music as if from a second self. Lohengrin, forgotten on paper during Wagner's despair in Paris, sounds at last through Liszt's loyalty. Requests, thanks, creeds, and family news fill the pages between the events. The friendship becomes the plot: one man composing, the other fighting the world's stages open. Readers use the volume as a record of how opera survived its hardest decade.
cosmopolis-volume-1:
Paul Bourget, a French novelist of society and belief, sets Cosmopolis in Rome, where Europe's aristocracies mix in one salon world. Volume 1 introduces the Marquis de Montfanon, a scarred French legitimist turned collector. Montfanon gathers documents for a history of the French nobility and the Church. Rome itself is a museum that everyone raids for relics.

An old socialist bookseller named Ribalta trades epigrams with the marquis across the counter of ideas. Catholic faith and free thought spar politely while sharing old hatreds. Princes, artists, diplomats, and beautiful visitors of many nations crowd the drawing rooms. Love affairs begin under the cover of art talk and antiquarian hunts. Bourget studies each soul like a case: pride, faith, and desire pulling in different tongues. Readers starting Cosmopolis should expect psychology over plot, with Rome's ruins and churches judging the modern chatter around them.
critical-and-historical-essays-volume-1:
Thomas Babington Macaulay made his fame with the Edinburgh Review essays gathered here in volume one of his Critical and Historical Essays. Macaulay's editor lists the pieces with their dates, beginning with Milton in 1825. This volume includes his essays on Hallam's Constitutional History, on Burleigh and his times, on Horace Walpole, and on Warren Hastings, the governor of India later impeached.

Each essay starts from a book under review and gallops off into a full retelling of an age, confident, quotable, and partisan for progress. Macaulay writes history like a speech to a jury, with scenery. Later scholars corrected his details, as his editor admits, but his bird's-eye surveys still give readers a first map of English politics and letters.
curtius-history-greece-vol-1:
Ernst Curtius begins his History of Greece in this first volume, in A. W. Ward's 1867 English version. Land and sea come first, then legend and the Dorian migrations. Curtius, a German scholar who dug at Olympia, grounds myth in soil and coast.

He explains Greece through its harbors, hills, and scattered islands. Tribes move, shrines rise, and the first cities take shape in his telling. Learning and landscape walk hand in hand throughout. The volume opened a history that married the spade to the scroll, and Victorian readers took it as the fullest Greek story of its day.
darwin-descent-of-man-vol-1:
Charles Darwin published The Descent of Man in 1871, twelve years after his Origin of Species. In the first volume he at last applies his theory of evolution to human beings directly. The first edition text is used here, in the first of two volumes.

Darwin compares the bodies and minds of humans and animals, trait by trait. He argues that the likeness is too deep for separate creation, and that humans descend from earlier forms of life. He also sets out his second great idea, selection in relation to sex, which volume two then takes up in full.
darwin-life-and-letters-vol-1:
Francis Darwin edited his father's Life and Letters in 1887, five years after Charles Darwin's death. Volume One covers the making of the naturalist. It includes Darwin's own short autobiography, written for his family.
