This first volume, in the 1899 Newnes edition, covers the start: Zanzibar, the inland march, and the lakes. Stanley had found Livingstone in 1871; now he aimed to settle the map's last great questions.

He circumnavigates Lake Victoria and Lake Tanganyika, proving their shapes and outlets by boat. Then he commits his party to the Lualaba river, gambling that it is the Congo. The volume ends with the expedition poised above the unknown river. Stanley's driven style, and the expedition's heavy death toll, hang over every page.
statius-mozley-loeb-vol-1:
Publius Papinius Statius, a Neapolitan poet at the court of Domitian, wrote the Thebaid, an epic in twelve books on the war of the Seven against Thebes. J. H. Mozley's Loeb translation opens the poem in this volume, with books one through seven. The Latin text faces his English.

Two brothers, Eteocles and Polynices, agree to share the throne of Thebes by turns, then fall out and raise armies. Statius fills the road to war with omens, feasts, a night raid, and the deaths of young heroes. His verse is rich, swift, and steeped in Virgil. The Thebaid was the great Silver Latin epic, read all through the Middle Ages.
stories-by-american-authors-volume-1:
Volume I of Stories by American Authors, in its 1903 printing, gathers five tales: Who Was She by Bayard Taylor, The Documents in the Case by Brander Matthews and H. C. Bunner, One of the Thirty Pieces by William Henry Bishop, Balacchi Brothers by Rebecca Harding Davis, and An Operation in Money by Albert Webster.

Taylor's opening tale is told by a man pressed by a friend to confess a strange, unhappy love that left him shamed yet glad he can feel shame. The set shows the range of American short fiction of its day, from mystery and money matters to street musicians and secrets kept too long.
stories-by-foreign-authors-german-volume:
German, Volume 1 of Stories by Foreign Authors, presents six tales in English dress. It holds Heyse's The Fury and Lindau's Philosopher's Pendulum. It also holds tales by Sacher-Masoch, Baumbach, and Hoffmann. Zschokke's Adventures of a New-Year's Eve closes the set.

Heyse's Fury, also called L'Arrabbiata, opens at dawn under Vesuvius, where fishing folk along the Sorrento cliffs haul in nets cast the night before and rig their boats for the day. Passion by the sea, music, magic, and strange bargains carry the volume's mix of German story craft.
strabo-geography-hamilton-falconer-vol-1:
Greek geographer Strabo mapped the known world in his Geography, written near the start of the Roman Empire. Hamilton and Falconer translated it for English readers. Volume One holds Books One through Seven.

Strabo covers Spain, Gaul, Britain, Italy, and the northern lands. He mixes maps in words with history, myth, and trade notes. His learning is vast, drawn from many lost writers. Errors sit beside sharp, firsthand-grade reports. The set is the largest geography to survive from the ancient world. This volume opens that atlas for readers who love old places.
strange-stories-chinese-studio-giles-188:
Herbert A. Giles translated Pu Songling's Liaozhai zhiyi as Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio in 1880. Volume one gathers the first half of his pioneering selection. Pu Songling, a Qing dynasty scholar, collected tales of fox spirits, ghosts, dreams, and judges of the dead over a long life of teaching.

In these brief tales the dead visit lovers, foxes take wives, and scholars bargain with spirits. Giles, a British consular officer and sinologist, made Chinese supernatural fiction known in the West. His notes explain customs, beliefs, and wordplay for English readers. The tales mix horror, humor, and tenderness in a few pages each. Volume two completes Giles's selection.
sunny-memories-of-foreign-lands-volume-1:
Mrs. Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, published Sunny Memories of Foreign Lands at Boston in 1854, in two volumes illustrated from designs by Hammatt Billings. Volume I opens the record of her tour through Britain and Europe, made in the first flush of her fame.

Her preface owns the charge before critics make it: everything here is given couleur de rose, rose-colored. Why not, she asks; the book holds the impressions, as they arose, of a most agreeable visit, and could not honestly be otherwise. The letters home report the people, houses, and scenery that delighted her, and the warm welcome that antislavery readers abroad gave the author of Uncle Tom's Cabin.
sylvia-s-lovers-volume-1:
Volume I of Elizabeth Gaskell's Sylvia's Lovers, printed at London in M.DCCC.LXIII, or 1863, opens the three-volume novel. Chapter I introduces Monkshaven, a town on the north-eastern shores of England holding about fifteen thousand people at the time Gaskell wrote.

The contents run from a ship home from Greenland and buying a new cloak to the story of the press-gang and a sailor's funeral. Philip Hepburn is named in the fourth chapter, and later heads promise attraction and repulsion, the specksioneer of the Greenland fleet, a refractory pupil, and visions of the future. The volume ends with perplexities and partnership, having set Sylvia between the whaler who courts her and the cousin who keeps his love quiet.
symonds-renaissance-italy-vol-1:
John Addington Symonds opened his Renaissance in Italy in 1875 with the despots. Volume 1 paints the tyrants whose courts made the age possible. Visconti and Sforza rule Milan in his vivid, crowded opening book.

Power becomes an art form in the Italian city-states he describes. Courts shine with poets and painters while daggers wait in halls. Symonds writes with a poet's eye for splendor and for blood. He neither hides the cruelty nor dims the era's bright genius. Readers feel why strongmen and great art grew side by side. The volume sets the stage for the whole vast work.
tabqat-i-nasiri-raverty-vol-1:
Minhaj-i Siraj Juzjani wrote the Tabakat-i Nasiri in Persian in the thirteenth century. H. G. Raverty put Volume 1 into English in 1881 for modern readers. The chronicle covers the Muslim dynasties of Central Asia and India.

Ghurid kings, early Delhi sultans, and court wars fill the narrative. The Mongol storm gathers at the edge of his world as he writes. Minhaj served at court and saw much of what he records. His voice carries the weight of a witness, not a mere copyist. Scholars treat the work as a prime source for medieval India.
tales-and-novels-volume-07-patronage-par:
Volume VII of Maria Edgeworth's Tales and Novels, in ten volumes with engravings on steel, holds the first part of Patronage, her long novel of professional life. The pages at hand give the title and a contents list of numbered chapters without heads, so the shape must be taken from the volume itself.

Patronage follows the Percy family, whose sons must make their way in law, medicine, the church, and the army, against rivals lifted by interest and connection. Edgeworth's theme, stated across the novel, is the contest between merit left to itself and careers carried by patrons. This first part sets the family, the suitors, and the great man's promised favor in motion, leaving the reckoning to the volume that concludes the tale.
tales-from-the-arabic-payne-1884-vol-1:
John Payne followed his Nights with Tales from the Arabic, and Volume I appeared in 1884 as the companion set. These stories come from the Breslau and Calcutta Arabic editions, tales the main cycle lacked room for. Payne Englished them in the same full, unexpurgated manner that marked his Thousand Nights.

The companion volumes catch the overflow of a story-world too big for one frame. Kings, lovers, and tricksters appear in fresh combinations, with the same narrative relish. Volume I opens a three-volume supplement that completists prize, since it widens the map of Arabic tale-telling beyond the famous nights.
talleyrand-memoirs-vol-1:
Charles Maurice de Talleyrand served France under kings, a revolution, and an emperor. The first volume of his memoirs, in Beaufort's translation, covers his youth and rise. Talleyrand wrote late in life, defending his own record.

Volume One moves from his birth and church career into the Revolution and the Directory. It ends amid Napoleon's climb to power, with Talleyrand at his side as foreign minister. The tone is cool, witty, and self-assured throughout. Readers meet the supreme survivor of French politics explaining, in his own words, how he stayed standing. Readers should note he writes to justify choices that many condemned.
targums-etheridge-vol-1:
The Targums are the old Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible, read aloud in synagogues when Hebrew faded from daily speech. J. W. Etheridge's 1862 volume gives the first English rendering of two of them: Onkelos on the Torah, and Jonathan ben Uzziel on the same books. This volume covers Genesis and Exodus.

A targum is more than a translation: it smooths hard verses, adds bits of story, and softens bold pictures of God. Etheridge prints the two versions so readers can follow where each expands the plain text. The result shows how ancient Jews heard and taught their scripture. Scholars still use Etheridge as a first path into the targums.
terence-comedies-sargeaunt-loeb-1912-vol:
John Sargeaunt translated Terence for the Loeb series in 1912, with the Latin text facing his English. Volume one holds The Lady of Andros, The Self-Tormentor, and The Eunuch. Terence, a former slave from Carthage, became Rome's most polished comic playwright, famed for humane plots and clean Latin.

The Self-Tormentor punishes himself for exiling his son over a love match. The Eunuch, his boldest play, threads disguise and mistaken identity through a soldier's rivalry. Sargeaunt's edition was long the standard English Terence for schools and general readers. The facing Latin lets students test the translation line by line. Volume two completes Terence's six surviving plays.
the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-volume-: No page of George Meredith's novel stands here for volume one. The book is The Adventures of Harry Richmond. A Project Gutenberg wrapper stands in its place. The wrapper names the book and author. It marks the part as number 50 in a Meredith set. It gives file number 4444. A release date of September 2003 is given. The file's maker is named as David Widger.
the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-1:
Mark Twain, whose real name was Samuel Langhorne Clemens, wrote The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, and this first part carries his preface, signed at Hartford in 1876. Twain says most of the feats in the book really occurred, one or two from his own boyhood.

Huck Finn, he says, is drawn from life, while Tom blends the traits of three boys he knew. The odd beliefs he touches on were common among children and slaves in the West thirty or forty years back. He aims the book at boys and girls, yet hopes adults will read it to recall how they once felt and talked. Readers meet Tom, Aunt Polly, and the whitewashed fence in St. Petersburg.
the-amazing-marriage-volume-1: Contents pages alone open the first volume of George Meredith's The Amazing Marriage, dated 1895. Dame Gossip enters as a chorus and tells of the Countess of Cressett running off with an old buccaneer, helped by postillion Charles Dump. Book One moves through a mountain walk, a natural philosopher, and the lady's letter. Book Two lists Small Causes, The Prisoner of His Word, and Opening Stage of the Honeymoon. Book Three promises fog, gout, and an old seaman. It also promises a kidnapping that does no great harm.
the-armourer-s-prentices-1:
Charlotte M. Yonge aimed this 1889 Macmillan novel, pictured by W. J. Hennessy, at citizen life in early Tudor days, as her preface explains. She drew on Stowe's Survey of London, Loftie's history, and Burton's work on English merchants. Stowe, she says, fully describes how apprentices stood toward their masters.

Yonge confesses one doubt: whether her Edmund Burgess could rightly become a citizen of York after serving his time in London. Evil May Day, she notes, follows Hall's Chronicle closely, though a ballad ascribed to Churchill differs in places. A story-teller, she claims, may follow whichever source suits the tale. Hall also supplies her sermon, the king's sports, and the Field of the Cloth of Gold.
the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-of-tw:
Gilbert Parker's first volume carries the same introduction as the complete romance, in which he refuses to write only of Canada. He had spent seven years on northern tales and feared ending by imitating himself. A trip to Jersey in 1897 gave him a fresh field.

Contents list an invasion, then scenes eleven years after, in France, and in Jersey five years later. That spread of time and place sets up a long romance rather than a single episode. Volume one therefore holds Parker's statement of purpose and the opening movements of a story he planned to range widely, in line with his own conscience and impulse.
the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-1: Volume three of a New England magazine of history, biography, literature, and state progress was published in Boston in 1885 by the Bay State Monthly Company at 43 Milk Street. Its opening pages list the contents of the whole volume. Entries include Samuel Adams the Patriot, the home of Whittier at Amesbury, John Albion Andrew, and pieces on assessment insurance. Page numbers and illustration counts are given for many items. No article text itself appears in these opening pages.
the-boy-slaves-1:
Captain Mayne Reid opens The Boy Slaves, dated 1865, with a grand address to Africa, which he calls the land of Ethiope. He hails it as the home of the lion, the panther, the elephant, and the great crocodile. Then his tone turns: last and most sad, it is the land of the slave.

Reid warns his readers that doom may sit closer to their own homes than they think. White men by the hundreds, he claims, toil in the far inner lands as slaves of slaves. Two wastes meet there, the desert of sand and the Atlantic, with no line but in thought between them. The shore from Susa to Senegal is dreaded by sailors above all shores. Thousands of ships' men have found a watery grave there, or a fate he calls worse than death.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-percy-bys:
Volume 1 of Percy Bysshe Shelley's complete poetical works, in the Oxford Edition of 1914, carries the same front matter as the companion record of the same volume. Thomas Hutchinson, M.A., edited the text with notes, and the title page promises materials never before printed in any edition. Two records thus present one volume, not two different books.

Hutchinson's preface states the edition's scope and method. It gathers all Shelley's ascertained poems and verse fragments that had appeared in print. His rule was to treat the earliest printing as the chief authority and to make a fresh collation of the early editions. He would not merely reprint Mrs. Shelley's recension of 1839, nor any later editor's version. Material departures from an original's wording are flagged, with the rejected reading set in a footnote.
the-complete-works-of-james-whitcomb-ril: Volume 1 of the complete works of James Whitcomb Riley was issued as a Project Gutenberg text in October 1996, etext number 691. Only the Gutenberg header is present here, with its standard notes on copyright, donations, and release dates a month ahead of the official date.Past that front matter, the record is silent.
the-complete-writings-of-charles-dudley-: Volume 1 of Charles Dudley Warner's complete writings reached Project Gutenberg in June 2001 as etext number 2671. Nothing beyond the Gutenberg header is present: the usual copyright warnings, the note that the header must legally be seen first on opening the book, and the donation appeal.Only the frame of the book is present, not its pages.
the-confession-of-a-child-of-the-century: Volume 1 of Alfred de Musset's Confession of a Child of the Century, in the French Immortals series crowned by the French Academy, reached Project Gutenberg as etext 3939. The header alone is present, noting a release date of April 2003 and a first posting in September 2001, with David Widger as producer.The story, if any, begins beyond what is present.
the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-volum:
Volume 1 of Charles James Lever's Confessions of Harry Lorrequer covers chapters I to X, printed at Dublin in 1839. A note explains that the title page bears no author's name, though the work is generally attributed to Lever, whose life dates are given as 1806 to 1872. The same barracks verse about pipe-clay and mortars stands at its head.

A dedication letter to Sir George Hamilton Seymour opens the volume. Lever jokes that if a feather shows how the wind blows, dedicating even light matter like these confessions may prove his gratitude. He thanks Seymour for many kindnesses received in the course of their acquaintance. The volume thus starts the episodic tale of a young Irish officer with a formal, witty bow to a patron.
the-coquette-s-victim-everyday-life-libr:
Charlotte M. Braeme wrote The Coquette's Victim, issued in Chicago as No. 1 of the Everyday Life Library. Chapter I, called The Trial, opens in a police court on the morning of May 14. Mr. Kent, the magistrate, is a man of long service, great legal skill, and a rare gift for reading faces.

That morning's cases run from drunken men fined and scolded to a small boy who stole sixpence sent with him on an errand and spent it on cakes. Kent speaks kindly to the sobbing child and urges him toward better ways. Then a new prisoner puzzles him: a tall, handsome young man of not more than twenty, with a clear-cut, noble face and dark gray eyes, plainly a gentleman by birth.
the-culture-of-vegetables-and-flowers-fr: Sutton and Sons of Reading issued The Culture of Vegetables and Flowers from Seeds and Roots in a sixteenth edition of 1921. Its contents lay out a year's work in the vegetable garden month by month. They then turn to the rotation of crops, the chemistry of garden crops, and manures made by art and their use. Later sections treat the culture of flowers from seeds, flowering bulbs, flowers all year round, and the pests and fungus pests of garden plants. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-day-s-work-part-1: Only a Project Gutenberg header stands at the head of this record for The Day's Work, Part I, by Rudyard Kipling. The header dates the electronic text to April 2000, numbers it Etext 2138. It names Bill Stoddard as its preparer, with the usual notes urging readers to keep the file and pass it on. No title page, contents, or story text follows in what is present here.
the-days-of-bruce-a-story-from-scottish-: Grace Aguilar's The Days of Bruce, a story from Scottish history in two volumes, appears here in volume I of the edition from D. Appleton and Company, dated 1871. Aguilar is named on the title page as author of Home Influence, The Mother's Recompense, Woman's Friendship, and The Vale of Cedars. A preface begins with mingled pain and pleasure, regretting that she whose work of love the book was cannot share in its passage through the press. Only the title pages and the preface's opening lines are present here.
the-diary-and-letters-of-madame-d-arblay: Volume 1 of The Diary and Letters of Madame d'Arblay, by Frances Burney, runs from 1778 to 1787, with notes by W. C. Ward and Macaulay's essay at the front. A billing line calls her the cream of diarists. The contents open with Miss Burney publishing Evelina, under a mystery, finding herself famous, visiting Mrs. Thrale, and meeting Dr. Johnson, then follow the author of Evelina into society at Brighton and Tunbridge Wells in 1779. Only the title page and this contents synopsis are present here.
the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustrated-p: Part one of Paradise in Dante's Vision of Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise names Dante Alighieri as author and the Rev. H. F. Cary as translator. A list of cantos follows, running from canto one through canto twenty-nine. No verse text appears in these pages. Only the title matter and the canto list are present, tracing the ascent through the lower and middle heavens.

Part one of Purgatory in Dante's Vision of Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise holds cantos one through four, in the verse rendering by the Rev. H. F. Cary. Dante leaves the cruel sea of Hell behind and sings of the second realm, where the human spirit is cleansed of sin and made fit to rise. Dawn spreads a sweet blue hue over the pure air.

Four stars, seen before only by the first people, shine at the other pole. A stern old keeper guards the shore and questions the travellers. Hope, shut out of Hell, rules this island mountain.
the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-1: Volume one of The Doré Gallery of Bible Illustrations carries a preface shared with the complete set. It tells how Doré's grand Bible folio won warm praise but cost too much for most buyers. This series answers that want with picked plates of famed Scripture scenes. A page of narrative text stands before each cut. Only the title matter and preface are present in these pages.
the-dwelling-place-of-light-volume-1:
Volume one of Winston Churchill's The Dwelling-Place of Light, dated 1917, opens as the complete novel does: with Edward Bumpus at the Chippering Mill gate. At fifty-five, this Yankee gate-keeper feels rolled from firm granite into loose shale, ringed by folk from lands he never saw. Hampton's mills sprawl along an old river, rich and bewildering.

His faith has worn away church by church, and his daughter Janet now faces the new world he fears. This first volume sets the town, the mill, and the family before strife breaks out.
the-early-short-fiction-of-edith-wharton:
Volume one of The Early Short Fiction of Edith Wharton holds five tales, each tagged with its first magazine date. Mrs. Manstey's View dates to July 1891, The Dilettante to December 1903, The Bolted Door to March 1909, and Kerfol to March 1916. A list of her early verse, not printed here, runs from 1880 to 1889.

Kerfol opens the volume: a host urges his guest to buy the most romantic house in Brittany, cheap from broke owners. Wharton's tales mix ghost lore, sharp manners, and trapped lives. A full Wharton bibliography closes the set. The tales reward slow, close reading.
the-forsyte-saga-volume-1: John Galsworthy wrote this volume of The Forsyte Saga, titled The Man of Property. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. The first heads name an at home at Old Jolyon's. They name Old Jolyon at the opera and dinner at Swithin's. They name plans of the house, a Forsyte household, and James at large. The death of Aunt Ann closes the part that can be read. No page of the novel itself is present. So its scenes cannot be described from the front matter alone.
the-french-revolution-volume-1:
Hippolyte A. Taine wrote this first volume on the French Revolution for his Origins of Contemporary France, and its theme is anarchy. Three books trace the spread of revolt and the work of the Constituent Assembly.

Taine's preface says revolts and the assembly's laws joined to wreck all rule in France. Chapters move from the first sparks to Paris up to July 14, then through the months of mob sway that followed. He judges the Assembly's work as damage first, then as a flawed new frame in the Constitution of 1791. The last book shows that frame at work in a land ruled by raw passion.
the-gilded-age-part-1:
Part 1 of The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today is dated 1873. Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner wrote the novel. Its preface speaks straight to the reader. The authors joke that no excuse is needed for the book. It was not written for friends, for rest, or to pass an idle hour.

The preface then turns wry. It claims the tale shows an ideal land. That land has no wild hunt for quick wealth, no graft, and pure public life. The pose is the joke. Such a land left the authors short of real cases to copy. Heads set at the top of each chapter, they add, are there to stir interest. They are not there to give the story away.
the-golden-bowl-volume-1: Henry James wrote The Golden Bowl. This record is Volume I of the novel. Only front matter is present here. It is a Project Gutenberg header. The header gives a long notice on copyright laws. It tells readers to keep the file as it is. It honors the volunteers who made the text. It gives the title and author, a release date of July 2003, and Edition 10. No page of the novel itself is present. Nothing about this volume's own chapters can be told from what is here.
the-great-conspiracy-volume-1:
John Logan wrote The Great Conspiracy: Its Origin and History. This record is Part 1 of that work. Its preface is the same preface that stands at the head of the complete work. Logan sets his aim there. He will present authentic facts with historical accuracy. He will be fair in grouping them, and just in the conclusions drawn. He will not mince words, and he seeks favor in no quarter.

In that preface Logan traces the conspiracy from its obscure birth. It began in the earliest days of the Republic. It ran through nullification to the bloody period of armed rebellion. It reaches a more sinister development of his own day. He worked from the records open at the seat of government. He lets the chief actors speak for themselves where he can. The part itself is not present beyond that preface.
the-great-english-short-story-writers-vo: William J. Dawson and Coningsby W. Dawson wrote the introductory essays for The Great English Short-Story Writers. This record is Volume I. It was printed in The Readers's Library in 1910. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. An opening essay traces the evolution of the short story. The stories run from Defoe and Hogg to Irving, Hawthorne, and Poe. They name Dickens, Twain, Bret Harte, Hardy, and Henry James. A Stevenson tale closes the list.
the-heart-of-mid-lothian-volume-1:
Walter Scott wrote The Heart of Mid-Lothian, Volume 1. The tale belongs to Tales of My Landlord, second series. The title page credits Jedediah Cleishbotham as collector and arranger. An editor's introduction opens the volume. It reports that Scott began the tale almost before he had finished Rob Roy. The introduction quotes a letter of November 10, 1817, to Archibald Constable.

Scott promises the best volumes yet in that letter. He says he prides himself on the first tale. The same title page stands in the complete record. The same introduction stands in the sibling volume records. That shared front matter is stated here plainly.
the-history-of-the-united-states-from-14: Julian Hawthorne wrote The History of the United States from 1492 to 1910. The record shows Volume I. It runs from the discovery of America on October 12, 1492. It ends at the Battle of Lexington on April 19, 1775. The contents list fourteen chapters. Early titles include Columbus, Raleigh, and Smith. Later titles include The Freight of the Mayflower. The list ends with The Shot Heard Round the World. A picture by Frederic Remington is noted. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-home-book-of-verse-volume-1: Burton Egbert Stevenson edited The Home Book of Verse, Volume 1. The poems are by various hands. A contents note explains the shape of the set. The volume holds the contents of Volumes 1 through 4 of the etext editions. Part I is called Poems of Youth and Age. It opens with The Human Seasons by John Keats. A section called The Baby follows. Its poets include Matthias Barr, William Blake, and George MacDonald. Only the title page and contents are present here.
the-ink-stain-tache-d-encre-volume-1: René Bazin's novel The Ink-Stain is split across three records in this set. This first volume shows only an old etext header here. None of the novel itself appears. The header names the file as etext 3972. Release came in April 2003. The volume stands fifty-ninth in one series. That series honors French works crowned by the Academy. It stands first among Bazin's works in the set. Nothing of the story can be read here. Its scholarly hero and its ink-stain incident stay out of reach.
the-land-of-midian-revisited-volume-1:
Richard F. Burton led a second expedition through Midian in northwest Arabia, and volume one appeared in London in 1879. His preface credits support from Ismail, Khedive of Egypt. Between December 1877 and April 1878 his officers covered about twenty-five hundred miles by sea and land.

Burton says six hundred miles were mapped and planned on the march. He also answers reviewers of his earlier Gold Mines of Midian volume. Readers get a survey report, a travel narrative, and an argument that a forgotten biblical land still held mines and ruins worth study.
the-landlord-at-lion-s-head-volume-1:
William Dean Howells opens volume one with the same bibliographical note found in the complete record of his summer hotel novel. He recalls seeing a lion shaped Vermont peak across Lake Champlain in 1891. That view supplied the title before the story itself was planned in detail.

Volume one presents part one of the novel, first serialized and then published as a book in 1896. The setting centers on a hotel at Lion Head and the landlord whose drive shapes the place. Readers should note this record and the complete record share identical opening pages.
the-lane-that-had-no-turning-volume-1: Gilbert Parker labeled this record volume one of his Pontiac tales, and its opening pages match the complete set record. Only the full contents and the start of a dedication to Sir Wilfrid Laurier are present here, naming the title tale as the sole piece in volume one and listing later volumes. The title tale itself does not appear in this record, so the dedication and table stand in place of the story.
the-legends-of-the-jews-volume-1: Louis Ginzberg gathered Jewish legend from many sources, and Henrietta Szold translated volume one from his German manuscript. Only the title page and contents are present here, covering Bible times from the Creation to Jacob. Sections list the first things created, the alphabet, each day of creation, Adam and Eve in Paradise, the Fall, and the death of Adam. The legends themselves, retold in full prose, cannot be seen in this record beyond those headings.
the-letter-bag-of-lady-elizabeth-spencer:
A. M. W. Stirling compiled family letters from the Cannon Hall papers, covering 1806 to 1873 in two volumes. Her preface calls this set a sequel to earlier works on Coke of Norfolk and on a Yorkshire house. The narrative resumes in 1805 and 1806 where the earlier Annals volume stopped.

Most letters here go to or from John Spencer-Stanhope, who lived from 1787 to 1873. His father Walter, a member of Parliament, centered the earlier series. Volume one gives gentry family news, politics, and travel across nearly seventy years of British life, preserved by Lady Elizabeth at the old Yorkshire house.
the-letters-of-horace-walpole-earl-of-or: Horace Walpole letters, many first published from original manuscripts, fill four volumes, and volume one covers 1735 to 1748. Only the title page and detailed contents are present here, listing a preface, a life sketch by Lord Dover, and reminiscences of the courts of George the First and George the Second. Early entries promise court intrigue, the South Sea scheme, and royal family quarrels. The letters themselves cannot be read in this record.
the-letters-of-robert-louis-stevenson-vo: Sidney Colvin selected and edited Robert Louis Stevenson letters to family and friends, first published in November 1899. Only the title page and Colvin short note for the 1906 seventh edition are present here, recording three added letters to Austin Dobson, Rudyard Kipling, and George Meredith. Two of the new letters replace pieces judged less interesting. The letters of volume one themselves, from Stevenson youth and early travel, stay beyond the pages held in this record.
the-life-and-adventures-of-baron-trenck-:
Thomas Holcroft translated Baron Trenck memoirs, and Cassell issued volume one in London in 1892. An introduction sorts out two cousins who shared the Trenck name. Franz, the elder, served Austria with a band of Pandours and took poison in prison at Gratz.

Frederick, the Prussian cousin, tells his own story in these memoirs. His adventures show the age of Frederick the Great from inside courts, armies, and prisons. The introduction warns that both men told their tales with admiration for themselves, so readers should expect daring deeds told large. His fame rests on daring escapes from Prussian prisons.
the-life-and-letters-of-maria-edgeworth-:
Augustus J. C. Hare edited the life and letters of Maria Edgeworth, and volume one opens with the family seat at Edgeworthstown in County Longford. Generations of loving care, Hare says, beautified a plain landscape around the large house. The family reached Ireland more than three hundred years earlier.

Pages trace the line from Roger Edgeworth through a bishop of Down and Connor to Richard Lovell Edgeworth, born in 1744. His high spirits and scrapes fill the early story. Maria own letters will carry the second half of a life spent writing novels and tales for the young.
the-life-of-the-rt-hon-sir-charles-w-dil:
Stephen Gwynn began the life of Sir Charles W. Dilke, and Gertrude M. Tuckwell completed and edited it. Volume one preface explains that the book rests mainly on Dilke own memoirs and letters. Dilke built those memoirs from private daily diaries between 1888 and his return to Parliament in 1892.

He called his notes bald and refused to write them up, so editors condensed them into narrative. Later chapters by other hands cover work his notes skipped. Readers get a radical politician career, a famous scandal, and an imperial thinker life told largely in his own record.
the-literary-remains-of-samuel-taylor-co:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge left notebooks, letters, notes in margins, and work he never printed. After his death these were gathered as The Literary Remains. Henry Nelson Coleridge edited the volumes, acting under the will Coleridge made in September 1829. The first volume is inscribed to Joseph Henry Green, the friend Coleridge trusted to oversee the whole plan.

In his preface the editor warns that the pieces were fragments in the extreme, like loose leaves of old prophecy. His own share was the criticism and the general writing. He asks readers' patience with a book its author never finished. The preface gives a frank account of how the set was put together, gaps and all.
the-love-affairs-of-great-musicians-volu:
Rupert Hughes published The Love Affairs of Great Musicians in 1903, and his note to volume one boasts of fresh material. The identity of Beethoven's "Immortal Beloved" had just been revealed, along with Liszt's letters to his princess and Chopin letters long supposed burned. A vast amount of Wagner material was new. So were a full life of Tschaikovski by his brother and a biography of Clara Schumann tracing her love story to the marriage day.

Hughes says the book is, so far as he knows, the first on its subject, and that the new sources give it especial novelty. The volume opens under an epigraph from the Romaunt of the Rose. It calls love a tangle of contradictions: a hateful peace, a heavy burden light to bear, and a sorrowful paradise.
the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1620-m: Only the Project Gutenberg header is present for this record, so no page of the book itself appears here. The header names the work as The Mayflower and Her Log, volume 1, by Azel Ames. It gives the release date as June 2003, etext number 4101, and credits the file's production to David Widger. The rest of the header is standard Gutenberg material about copyright checking, redistribution, and keeping the electronic path open for later readers.
the-modern-regime-volume-1:
Hippolyte A. Taine's The Modern Regime, Volume 1, forms volume 5 of his Origins of Contemporary France. Its contents divide the study into four books. Book First treats Napoleon Bonaparte, his character, genius, ideas, and passions. Book Second covers the formation of the new state, its government institutions, and their use and abuse.

Book Third weighs the system's object and merits, including the recovery of social order, taxation, and conscription. Book Fourth turns to defects and effects, especially local society before and after 1830. A preface begins by explaining that this third and last part of the Origins was planned in two volumes. Napoleon and the state he built are therefore the whole subject here.
the-money-box-odd-craft-part-1:
W. W. Jacobs's Odd Craft, dated 1909, opens with its story The Money-Box, told by a night-watchman. Sailormen, he begins, are poor hands at saving money, whatever they promise themselves at sea, a thousand miles from a public house. Trying is not the problem, he insists; keeping the money is.

Ginger Dick and Peter Russet, two sailors the watchman has described before, sickened of spending a whole pay-off within a week or ten days ashore. Homeward bound from Melbourne, they took advice from Isaac Lunn, the steamer's oldest fireman and a steady teetotaller. Lunn offered to share a room ashore and hold their wages, paying out a moderate daily amount. The pair signed a paper agreeing, a step the narrator calls foolish.
the-money-master-volume-1:
Gilbert Parker's The Money Master appears in a record labelled Volume 1, yet its contents list runs through all five epochs and the epilogue, chapters I to XXV. In that respect its opening pages match the record labelled Complete exactly, contents and introduction alike. The duplication is plain in both records and is not resolved by either title.

Jean Jacques Barbille's grand tour opens Epoch the First, followed by a tale called To-Morrow. Epoch the Second jumps thirteen years ahead to a clerk of the court's story. Parker begins his introduction by placing the novel apart from his other books and answering critics who called it a return to Canada, the scene of his first success in fiction. Only that introduction opening follows the contents here.
the-nests-and-eggs-of-indian-birds-volum:
Allan O. Hume's The Nests and Eggs of Indian Birds, in a second edition published in London in 1889, opens with the author's own preface. Hume had spent years accumulating material for a revised edition after his first rough draft appeared. Circumstances stopped him, and his friend Mr. Eugene Gates took the work up; the title page credits Eugene William Gates as editor of the volume, with four portraits promised.

Hume then explains a loss no editor could repair. During his absence from Simla, a servant broke into his museum and stole several hundredweight of manuscript, sold as waste paper. The theft took life-histories, more or less complete, covering some 700 bird species, written on full sheets, while small notes on slips survived. Months passed before the loss was even discovered.
the-new-york-times-current-history-of-th:
The New York Times Current History of the European War dated January 23, 1915, forms part of its volume 1. It prints Sir John French's own story. Those are the famous dispatches of the British commander in chief. He sent them to Lord Kitchener, Secretary of State for War. Portraits of French and of General Sir Horace Smith-Dorrien, from paintings by John St. Helier Lander, head the number.

The first report from the front is dated September 7, 1914. French reports that troops crossed from England by sea and rail without a hitch and in the best order, every unit arriving within its scheduled time. By the evening of Friday, August 21, the concentration was practically complete, and dispositions followed for the advance General Joffre had requested.
the-north-american-indian-vol-1: Edward S. Curtis wrote, illustrated, and published the first volume of The North American Indian in 1907, edited by Frederick Webb Hodge, with field research funded by J. Pierpont Morgan. Only the front matter is present here, so the chapters do not appear. The opening pages carry a 1906 Curtis photograph, The Pool - Apache, plus a guide to the alphabet used for recording Indian terms. The volume was the first of twenty planned.
the-notebooks-of-leonardo-da-vinci-volum:
Volume 1 of Leonardo da Vinci's notebooks appeared in 1888 in Jean Paul Richter's translation. The same preface also opens the record called the complete notebooks, word for word. Richter begins with the fate of Leonardo's famous works: the Sforza monument and the Battle of Anghiari were never finished, and the Last Supper suffered decay and clumsy repairs.

The preface then asks why such prized manuscripts stayed unpublished for so long. Leonardo wrote backwards with his left hand, and few readers could work through the script. Richter describes the labor of reading the notes, which cover painting and much else in the artist's wide-ranging mind.
the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volume-1:
Volume 1 of George Meredith's novel The Ordeal of Richard Feverel appeared in a 1905 printing. Its contents cover Book 1 only, eleven chapters from The Inmates of Raynham Abbey to a letter that closes the Bakewell comedy. A complete record of the novel lists the same opening titles among its forty-two chapters.

Chapter One begins with a book of aphorisms, The Pilgrim's Scrip, by an anonymous gentleman with a bruised heart. One saying, that woman will be the last thing civilized by man, stirs excitement among ladies. A reader traces the crest on the title page, a griffin between two wheatsheaves, to Sir Austin Absworthy, linking the sayings to Richard's father and his system.
the-phantom-ship-1: Captain Frederick Marryat's The Phantom Ship is headed with the date 1839 in this record. Yet its title page is the same London printing, dated in roman numerals 1896, found in a sister record. The clash is stated rather than smoothed over. Only that title page and a contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. This list stops at chapter thirty-one. The sister record's list runs to thirty-seven.
the-physiology-of-marriage-part-1:
Honoré de Balzac's The Physiology of Marriage opens with a dedication teasing the man of distinction to whom the volume is addressed. Its full title presents the work as the musings of an eclectic philosopher on the happiness and unhappiness of married life. A warning at the front tells women readers they may as well not open the volume at all.

Balzac's introduction traces the idea to words Napoleon spoke before the Council of State while the civil code was under discussion. Studying French law as a young man, Balzac kept meeting the word adultery in the code. That word left a deep mark on him. Marriage, the quoted passage argues, is no institution of nature, since families differ between east and west. Laws must change with manners. That claim sets the ground for the meditations that follow.
the-poems-of-emma-lazarus-volume-1: Volume I of The Poems of Emma Lazarus gathers narrative, lyric, and dramatic verse. Here only the title page, notes, and contents appear, so the poems themselves are absent. A biographical sketch of Lazarus heads the contents. Her sequence Epochs runs from Youth and Longing through Storm and Grief to Work, Victory, and Peace. Poems listed include How Long!, Heroes, Admetus, and Tannhauser. The notes add that Sunrise elegises President Garfield, dead on September 19, 1881. They also note that The New Colossus is engraved on the Statue of Liberty's pedestal.
the-poems-of-jonathan-swift-d-d-volume-1: Volume I of The Poems of Jonathan Swift, D.D., was edited by William Ernst Browning, a barrister of the Inner Temple. G. Bell and Sons published it at London in 1910. Here only the title page and contents appear; the poems themselves are absent. An introduction comes first. Odes to Sancroft, Sir William Temple, King William, and the Athenian Society follow, plus a poem to Mr. Congreve. Later entries include Mrs. Frances Harris's Petition and Baucis and Philemon. Descriptions of the morning and a city shower close the list.
the-poetical-works-of-alexander-pope-vol:
Volume I of The Poetical Works of Alexander Pope, issued in 1856 with memoir, critical dissertation, and notes by the Reverend George Gilfillan, opens with a life of the poet. Pope was born on May 21, 1688, in London's Lombard Street; the memoir notes it was the Revolution year. His father, a linen merchant in thriving circumstances, retired from business at forty-six. Being a Roman Catholic with a taste for country life, he settled near Windsor Forest.

The life stresses Pope's frail body and quick mind. He was an only child, delicate in health, short and humped in figure. His sweet voice earned him a nickname, the Little Nightingale. An aunt gave him his first lessons in reading, and he taught himself to write by copying printed characters. At eight he learned Latin and Greek grammar from the family priest, Bannister. Then he moved to a Catholic seminary at Twyford.
the-pomp-of-the-lavilettes-volume-1:
Volume 1 of Gilbert Parker's The Pomp of the Lavilettes opens with the author's introduction. That is the same introduction that heads the complete record in the sibling file. Parker explains that the book is the only one he ever sold outright. In 1896 Mr. Lamson of the Boston firm Lamson and Wolffe bought its English, American, and colonial rights at Atlantic City. Parker never expected a phenomenal sale from it, though he felt the story had to be written.

Set in 1837, the novel brings a ne'er-do-well of the overseas aristocracy into a little secluded French-Canadian society. The moment is one of collision between French interests and the prejudices of the British executive in Quebec. Parker presents it as a short forerunner to The Right of Way. He stands by its pictures of French life in Canada. A second volume record continues the story at a later chapter.
the-portrait-of-a-lady-volume-1:
Volume I of Henry James's The Portrait of a Lady opens with the author's preface on the making of the novel. James recalls starting it in Florence, where he spent three months in the spring of 1879. It was designed for The Atlantic Monthly, which began serialising it in 1880. Macmillan's Magazine ran it month by month as well, a near-final case of a novel appearing on both sides of the Atlantic at once.

He was long in writing it and took it up again the following year in Venice. His rooms stood on the Riva Schiavoni, near the passage to San Zaccaria, with the lagoon before him. James describes the fidget of composition that drove him to the windows. He watched for the ship of some right suggestion in the blue channel. Rich historic places, he warns, offer an artist questionable help when not themselves the subject.
the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-1:
Part 1 of Mark Twain's The Prince and the Pauper opens before the tale itself, with a letter from Hugh Latimer, Bishop of Worcester, to Lord Cromwell. The letter, dated October 19 and written in old spelling, rejoices at the birth of the Prince of Wales, afterward Edward VI. Latimer calls God the God of England for the gift. He prays for the child's preservation and for governors of right judgment to guide him.

A dedication follows, inscribing the book to Susie and Clara Clemens by their father. Then Twain's framing paragraph begins. The tale was told to him by one who had it from his father, and so back for three hundred years. It may be history, or only a legend that could have happened. The part file thus sets the documents and the frame in place before the story proper.
the-purcell-papers-volume-1:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu, author of Uncle Silas, left the tales gathered here, introduced by a memoir from Alfred Perceval Graves. Volume one opens with that memoir, tracing the Le Fanu family from Normandy through exile after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes into service under William the Third.

Four tales follow the memoir in this volume. Their titles promise a ghost and a bone-setter, the fortunes of Sir Robert Ardagh, the last heir of Castle Connor, and a drunkard's dream. Readers meet both the biographical frame and the Irish Gothic storytelling for which Le Fanu became known.
the-seaboard-parish-volume-1:
George MacDonald, LL.D., wrote The Seaboard Parish, and this record holds volume one. Its contents list Constance's birthday, a sick chamber, and two Sunday evenings. Theodora's doom, Connie's dream, and a journey follow. The list ends with the narrator's first sermon in the parish. A record labeled complete opens with these same volume-one pages. One heading differs between them: this list calls chapter six The New Baby, while the other calls it The Kew Baby.

Chapter one, Homiletic, opens as a letter to dear friends. The narrator admits he begins a new book like an old sermon. A lifetime of preaching shapes whatever he writes, he says. He thought he had bidden his readers farewell. Now he sits again at his writing-table for them. He imagines his whispered words heard aloud by multitudes he cannot see.
the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-1: Gilbert Parker's The Seats of the Mighty presents the memoirs of Captain Robert Moray, of the Virginia Regiment and later Amherst's. This record's pages give the dedication to Madge Henley's memory and a contents list spanning four volumes. Volume one holds chapters one to six, ending with Moray telling the story of his life. Volume two adds the coming of Doltaire. Volume three reaches a chamber of torture, and volume four ends with the sacred countersign. No chapter text itself is present here, so Moray's narrative does not appear.
the-settlers-in-canada-1:
Captain Frederick Marryat's The Settlers in Canada is dated 1844. Its first chapter is called An Unexpected Fortune. In the year 1791, Marryat begins, an English family went out to settle in Canada. Emigration then was a very different affair, he warns. No steamboats stemmed the river currents and rapids. Indians still lived across Upper and much of Lower Canada. Wild animals infested the country, and French settlers held the best land.

The family is Mr. Campbell's, the chapter explains. Campbell was a surgeon with a fast-growing practice. He and his wife raised four boys, plus two orphaned nieces. His sister Mrs. Percival had died after her husband's business failed and fever killed him. Then a letter with a large black seal arrives one Christmas holiday. Sholto Campbell of Wexton Hall has died without a will. The entailed estates, worth 14,000 pounds a year, fall to Mr. Campbell as nearest of kin.
the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-entert: Only a Project Gutenberg header stands at the head of this record for volume one of George Meredith's The Shaving of Shagpat. The header gives the e-text number 4401. Its release date is September 2003, and it was first posted on December 21, 2001. Pat Castevans and David Widger produced it. The rest of the pages shown are the project's notices on copyright and donations. No title page, contents, or line of Meredith's Arabian entertainment itself appears. What the first volume contains therefore cannot be described from these pages.
the-sisters-volume-1:
Georg Ebers's The Sisters is labeled volume one in this record. Clara Bell translated it from the German. Its dedication and preface are the same ones carried by the record labeled complete. Ebers dedicated the book to Herr Eduard von Hallberger, his friend of twenty years. The novel was partly written under Hallberger's hospitable roof at Tutzing.

The preface tells how the story grew from archive fragments. Petitions in Greek survived from the Royal Archives of Memphis, Ebers writes. A Macedonian recluse in the Serapeum composed them for twin sisters. The twins served the god as pourers out of the libations. Closer study shows documents of great value, he argues. They reveal the internal life of Serapis's temple under Ptolemy Philometor. Ebers had visited the spot and searched every part of it, he adds.
the-star-chamber-an-historical-romance-v: W. Harrison Ainsworth, author of Windsor Castle, published this historical romance in two volumes with Bernhard Tauchnitz at Leipzig in 1854. For volume one, only the title page and contents are present here. The contents list twenty-six chapters. They open at the Three Cranes tavern in the Vintry. They move through Sir Giles Mompesson and a Star-Chamber victim. Jocelyn Mounchensey and King James the First follow. A forged confession closes the list. The narrative itself does not appear.
the-tatler-volume-1:
Volume one of The Tatler, edited with introduction and notes by George A. Aitken, was issued in 1899 by Hadley and Mathews in New York and Duckworth in London. The preface reprinted here looks back over the whole paper's run. Richard Steele acknowledges his debt to Dr. Swift, whose Bickerstaff writings created the town's taste for the disguise. He also describes Swift's uncommon turn of conversation as perfect training for treating common subjects in new ways.

Steele thanks unknown correspondents for many pieces and one nameless gentleman, a friend since childhood, for frequent help, meaning Addison. The preface is literary history from the inside. Readers meet the Tatler's makers explaining, with gratitude and pride, how a famous periodical was actually produced.
the-three-cities-trilogy-lourdes-volume-:
Émile Zola's Lourdes, first novel of his Three Cities trilogy, appears here in Ernest A. Vizetelly's translation, volume one covering the first day. Pilgrims and patients packed on hard third-class seats finish chanting a hymn as their train leaves Paris. Marie, raised on her couch of misery and feverish with impatience, spots the fortifications and cries that they are off at last. Her father, M. de Guersaint, smiles at her delight.

Beside them, Abbé Pierre Froment warns that Lourdes is still more than twenty-two hours away, with arrival at three-forty next morning. The contents promise Poitiers, miracles, and Bernadette herself. Zola loads a white train with the sick and the hopeful and watches faith, medicine, and suffering ride together toward the famous grotto.
the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volume-1:
Book One of Zola's Paris, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, opens with the same translator's preface that stands at the front of the complete edition elsewhere in this set. Vizetelly presents Paris as the end of the Three Cities trilogy begun at Lourdes and continued at Rome. Abbé Pierre Froment, the doubting priest, finishes here as Zola's opinions always required. The preface reads Froment as Man himself, struggling between the Catholic Church and Reason and Life.

Vizetelly then argues that Zola makes a remarkably good case for France, where the masses, he says, regard Catholicism as a religion of death condemning them to poverty. Because this volume's opening is the preface rather than the novel's first scene, readers start with the trilogy's thesis in hand. Pierre's Paris education in work, anarchism, and hope follows under that sign.
the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volume-1: Volume one of Zola's Rome, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, presents the title page and contents of its first three parts, with no narrative pages attached. The headings promise 'New Rome' and Froment's first impressions. They name the Boccaneras under the motto 'Black Mouth, Red Soul.' Cardinals Boccanera and Sanguinetti follow, then Romans of new Italy such as the Pradas and Saccos. Later headings reach the Vatican and Leo XIII. Readers hold the design of the Roman volume while its story waits outside this record.
the-tragic-comedians-a-study-in-a-well-k:
Volume one of George Meredith's Tragic Comedians, dated 1892, opens with the same Book One meditation on 'fantastical' found in the complete edition held elsewhere in this library. Nature pushes forth fantastically in sunlight, and human nature sails like a ship with drunken pilot, mutinous crew, and angry captain. Meredith asks readers to broaden sympathy and sharpen judgment by accepting the fantastical as part of ourselves.

He then introduces his historical pair, whose acts were incredible and whose last chapter was written in red blood. The man, a party leader venerated by followers and hated by enemies, fell through love; the woman joined hands with his slayer. Because both this volume and the complete record begin identically, they should be read as overlapping copies of Meredith's study of Lassalle's fatal romance.
the-trail-of-the-sword-volume-1: The record labelled volume one of Gilbert Parker's Trail of the Sword gives the novel's complete contents, all four epochs, rather than only its first quarter, and stops at the dedication heading. Epoch one brings an envoy, a renegade's threat, and a kidnapping; later epochs add the treasure house, Bucklaw the pirate, and the sheathing of the sword. A subtitle states the contents plainly: the history of Jessica Leveret, Pierre Le Moyne of Iberville, George Gering, and Edward Bucklaw, mutineer and pirate. No narrative page follows in this record.
the-translation-of-a-savage-volume-1:
Volume one of Gilbert Parker's Translation of a Savage carries the whole novel's contents, all three volumes' chapters, and the same introduction that fronts the complete edition in this library. Parker wrote the book at Hampstead Heath in the early autumn of 1893, in one concentrated effort, with letters delivered weekly and his whereabouts secret. Volume one's own five chapters are titled His Great Mistake, A Difficult Situation, Out of the North, In the Name of the Family, and An Awkward Half-Hour.

Those headings trace the premise: an English officer's impulsive northern marriage brings his Indigenous wife, Lali, south into his family's world. Because this record prints the full contents and shared introduction rather than volume one's scenes, readers meet Parker's method and map here. The 'translation' of Lali into an English lady, and the family's into kinder people, is the work ahead.
the-travels-of-marco-polo-volume-1: Volume one of The Travels of Marco Polo in the complete Yule-Cordier edition joins Henry Yule's annotated translation of 1903, revised by Henri Cordier, with Cordier's later notes. This record gives front matter only: a portrait plate of Yule and Amy Frances Yule's dedication, dated from Taradale, Ross-shire, in September 1902. She dedicates the volumes to Sir Roderick Murchison, who brought Yule and publisher John Murray together, and to his niece Harriet, under whose roof many proofs were read. Polo's narrative of Cathay begins beyond these leaves.
the-trespasser-volume-1:
Volume one of Gilbert Parker's Trespasser prints the novel's whole contents, all three volumes, and the same introduction that opens the complete edition held in this library. Parker recalls the commission arriving while he studied French Canada in 1892: Arrowsmith's Annual wanted fifty or sixty thousand words, and he cabled yes. At Audierne in Brittany he wrote most of it in a high-walled garden. Volume one's own chapters run from One in Search of a Kingdom through claims, a life story, his father's past, to finding his enemy.

Readers should treat the front matter here as shared with the complete record, not as a separate introduction. What belongs to this volume alone is Gaston's beginning: a young man of the Canadian wilds claiming an English heritage. The story itself starts beyond the introduction's garden recollections.
the-wits-and-beaux-of-society-volume-1:
Grace and Philip Wharton wrote The Wits and Beaux of Society, and volume one appears in an 1890 New York edition. Justin Huntly McCarthy wrote a preface for this new edition. H. K. Browne and James Godwin supplied the original illustrations. McCarthy dedicates the edition to Augustin Daly. Their shared interest, he says, is the people and periods covered.

The contents begin with the Comte de Grammont. His choice between church and army opens the story. His wit, love affairs, and visits to England follow. The court of Charles II comes into view. Readers get lively sketches of fashionable society and its celebrated talkers.
the-works-of-lord-byron-letters-and-jour: Rowland E. Prothero edited volume one of Byron's Letters and Journals for an illustrated edition dated 1898. What appears here is a numbered list of the letters. The earliest, from November 1798, goes to a Mrs. Parker. Letters to Byron's mother follow in 1799 and 1803. Many 1804 letters are addressed to his half-sister Augusta. The letters themselves do not appear in the pages present.
the-world-for-sale-volume-1: Volume one of Gilbert Parker's The World for Sale holds only a contents list and an empty introduction heading in this record. The same three-book, twenty-seven-chapter plan appears as in the complete record. Book one follows Ingolby, the two towns, and Jethro Fawe's coming. Book three ends with a chapter called The World for Sale. No chapter text follows the list in the pages present here.
their-silver-wedding-journey-volume-1:
Part I of William Dean Howells's novel appears here as the first volume of the 1899 three-volume edition. Its opening pages match the opening of the complete record exactly. Editor Basil March is told by his partner Fulkerson that he needs rest.

Fulkerson adds that March's wife and doctor agree, and that a sabbatical is already two years overdue. March can prepare issues ahead and leave the magazine to younger hands. The volume begins a travel story shaped by affectionate argument, editorial work, and a husband's reluctance to enjoy himself without a duty to blame.
theological-essays-and-other-papers-volu:
Thomas De Quincey gathered theological essays and other papers in two volumes, and volume one opens with Christianity as an organ of political movement. Other pieces treat Protestantism, Judas Iscariot, Hume on miracles, casuistry, and Greece under the Romans. The first essay dates from 1846.

De Quincey compares Christianity's political steps to growth and gravitation, forces too slow and hidden to watch directly. He argues its movement is stealthier still. Readers get dense, figurative prose from the author of Confessions of an English Opium-Eater, applied to church, scripture, and history.
theologico-political-treatise-part-1: Baruch Spinoza's Theologico-Political Treatise is divided here into a first part covering chapters one to five. A detailed contents list summarises the preface on superstition and the author's reasons for writing. Chapter one defines prophecy and chapter two examines the prophets. Spinoza holds that prophets perceived revelation through imagination, not knowledge of natural things. Later headings promise chapters on divine law and ceremonies. In this record the summary contents are what is present, so Spinoza's chapters themselves do not appear.
theophrastus-enquiry-plants-hort-vol-1:
Arthur Hort translated Theophrastus's Enquiry into Plants for the Loeb series in 1916. Volume one opens the founding text of botany in Greek and English. Theophrastus, Aristotle's successor at the Lyceum, wrote around 300 BCE.

He sorts plants by kinds, parts, growth, and habitats with care. Trees, shrubs, and herbs each receive systematic description and comparison. Theophrastus asks what distinguishes plants from one another and why. His teacher Aristotle had done the same for animals a generation earlier. Two thousand years of plant science begin on these pages. Hort's Loeb made the Enquiry handy for students. Modern botanists still honor Theophrastus as their science's founder.
thierry-norman-conquest-vol-1:
Augustin Thierry wrote his History of the Conquest of England by the Normans as epic. William Hazlitt put Volume 1 into English in 1847 for British readers. Thierry frames 1066 as a clash of races, Saxon against Norman.

Hastings and its harsh aftermath drive his heated, moving narrative. He sides with the crushed English against their foreign masters throughout. Facts serve feeling in his Romantic method, by his own design. The book made the Conquest a national tragedy for a generation. Readers meet history as epic poetry, vivid and frankly partisan. Its fire still warms debates about England's founding wound today.
thirlwall-history-greece-vol-1:
Connop Thirlwall, a Cambridge scholar and bishop, began his History of Greece in 1845. Volume 1 opens with the heroic age and the Dorian invasion. Legend slowly gives way to firmer ground as the book proceeds.

Thirlwall weighs myths with care, keeping what seems sound in them. Early tribes, kings, and colonies take shape under his calm hand. His work became the first modern scholarly history of Greece in English. He writes without heat, trusting proof more than fine phrases. Readers who want a steady start to Greek history start here. The eight volumes that follow build on this sober base.
through-forest-and-fire-wild-woods-serie: Edward S. Ellis wrote Through Forest and Fire as number one in the Wild-Woods Series, published at Philadelphia by Porter and Coates in 1891. Ellis also wrote the Deerfoot, Wyoming, and Log Cabin series. A cover caption shows Nellie praying for protection. Contents begin with a boy named Nick, school days, and a mathematical discussion, before a chapter called Lost. The front pages and opening contents are what is held in this record, so Ellis's frontier story itself does not appear.
tocqueville-democracy-in-america-reeve-v:
Alexis de Tocqueville, a young French aristocrat, toured the United States in 1831 and published the first volume of Democracy in America in 1835. Henry Reeve's English translation is the text here. Tocqueville came to study prisons; he stayed to study democracy itself.

Volume one maps how equality of conditions shapes American laws, towns, courts, and parties. He praises local self-rule and the jury, and warns of a tyranny of the majority. His eye for the habits under the laws made the book a classic at once. Americans still read it to see themselves as a sharp outsider saw them.
traditions-of-lancashire-volume-1: John Roby, M.R.S.L., collected Lancashire traditions in two illustrated volumes, and volume one appears here in a fifth edition from George Routledge at London in 1872. Steel and wood engravings illustrate the work. An epigraph from Verstegan anticipates a world of judges and sharp censures. A contents heading for volume one begins at the end of what is present, but its entries do not follow. The front pages are what is present here, so Roby's Lancashire tales themselves do not appear.
travels-in-morocco-volume-1:
James Richardson's Travels in Morocco appeared in two volumes, edited by his widow after his death. Richardson had already written on Central Africa and the Sahara desert. An introduction by another hand urges the book's value at a moment of crisis near Gibraltar.

The introduction reckons Morocco at 219,420 square miles and nearly eight million people. It sorts the population into Moors and Arabs, Berbers, Jews, and others, and weighs the emperor's small regular army. Every Arab, it notes, rides well, and the Berbers make strong foot soldiers. Volume one thus opens with the country sized up before Richardson's own journey begins.
troublous-times-in-canada-a-history-of-t: Capt. John A. Macdonald, a veteran of both campaigns, wrote Troublous Times in Canada as a history of the Fenian raids of 1866 and 1870. The opening pages give a detailed table of contents. Early chapters cover the Fenian Brotherhood and the Cincinnati convention that proclaimed an Irish republic. Later chapters follow the landing near Fort Erie and the battle of Ridgeway. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the history itself does not appear.
tuzk-i-jahangiri-rogers-vol-1:
Jahangir, the Mughal emperor, wrote his own memoirs in the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri. Alexander Rogers and Henry Beveridge put Volume 1 into English in 1909. His accession and early reign open this rare royal life story.

Jahangir records his court, his hunts, and his habits with frank ease. He praises fine art, weighs nobles, and owns up to his vices. Few kings anywhere left so personal a record of their rule. His voice sounds curious, vain, witty, and oddly honest across the pages. The volume opens the most human royal memoir of the Mughal age. Jahangir's candor about himself still startles modern readers today.
tylor-primitive-culture-1871-vol-1:
Edward Burnett Tylor published the first volume of Primitive Culture in 1871, the work that founded cultural anthropology. Tylor, later Oxford's first professor of the subject, gave 'culture' its technical meaning here. Volume one develops his doctrine of survivals and his theory of animism.

Survivals are customs carried by habit into a new age that has outgrown their meaning: children's games, sayings, and rites that fossilize older thought. Animism, the belief in souls and spirits, he makes the seed of all religion. Tylor builds his case from a mountain of traveler and missionary reports. The book's learning and sweep still command respect.
un-doc-united-nations-human-rights-counc:
Accountability in Sri Lanka after the civil war returned to the Human Rights Council in resolution 22/1, adopted in March 2013. The text followed up the Council's call of the year before. It noted that Colombo had still not held a full, trusted inquiry into wartime abuses.

The resolution asks Sri Lanka to act on the advice of its own inquiry and of the UN rights chief. It urges access for UN experts and steps to protect judges, lawyers, and reporters. Readers see how the Council kept steady pressure on one country file, year after year.

Sri Lanka faced its strongest Human Rights Council text yet in resolution 25/1, adopted in March 2014. By then the Council had pressed Colombo for two years over alleged war crimes at the end of the civil war in 2009. Promises of a home-grown inquiry had not satisfied most members.

The resolution goes further than the earlier texts. It asks the UN rights office to run its own international inquiry into alleged abuses by both sides. It also calls for protection of witnesses and minorities. The vote set up the inquiry whose report shaped later debates on Sri Lanka.

Days after Sri Lanka's civil war ended in May 2009, the Human Rights Council met in special session and adopted resolution S-11/1. The session was called to address the human cost of the final assault on the Tamil Tigers. Thousands of civilians had died in the last months of fighting.

The text praises Sri Lanka's victory and its plans for aid and rebuilding. It stresses that aid work and inquiries are matters for the state itself. Many rights groups attacked the outcome as a whitewash. The resolution remains a much-debated record of a divided Council.
un-ga-res-1:
Atomic energy forced its way onto the world stage with the very first vote the UN General Assembly ever passed. Resolution 1, adopted on 24 January 1946, sets up a commission to deal with the questions raised by the find of atomic power. The new body would report to the Security Council. Its reports would be made public, unless the Council, for the sake of peace, held them back.

The Council's prime duty for peace shapes the plan. In fit cases, it should pass the reports on to the Assembly, to member states, and to the UN's social and trade bodies. Born months after Hiroshima, the Atomic Energy Commission was the world's first bid to place the atom under joint rule.
un-ga-res-66-1: General Assembly Resolution 66 (I) dates to December 1946, the Assembly's first year of work, when the new world body was still setting its basic machinery in place. The record gives the number in the old first-session style and names no subject, so its contents are best taken from the official text itself. It stands as a formal decision of the full Assembly from the founding season of the United Nations, preserved in the official record. That session also handled the body's first budgets, sites, and rules.
un-ga-res-a-69-1:
Ebola's outbreak in West Africa in 2014 forced the General Assembly to act in Resolution A/69/1, the first vote of its sixty-ninth session. The text voices grave concern at the outbreak's new scale and speed. Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone were hit hardest. The Assembly fears the plague could undo years of gains in peace, stable rule, and roads, schools, and trade in those lands.

The need to contain the health crisis is pressed hard, for its human, trade, and social toll could be grave. The Assembly pledges a fast, strong, joint response. It names the World Health Organization as the lead body, backing the brave work of the states whose people stood in the plague's path.
un-ga-res-a-70-1:
Seventeen goals for the whole earth stand in Resolution A/70/1, the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted by the General Assembly in 2015. Its head calls it a plan of action for people, planet, and shared wealth. It seeks to strengthen world peace in greater freedom. The end of want in all its forms, the text holds, is the greatest test the world faces, and a must for growth that can last.

All lands and all who hold a stake pledge to work the plan as one. The human race is to be freed from the grip of want, and the planet healed and kept safe. Bold, deep steps are called for, to shift the world onto a path that can last. No one, the text vows, will be left behind. The 17 goals and 169 marks that follow shape world aid to this day.
un-ga-res-a-73-1:
World chiefs met at UN headquarters on 24 September 2018 for the Nelson Mandela Peace Summit, and Resolution A/73/1 adopts their pledge. The meet marked one hundred years since Mandela's birth. The text salutes his traits: his low pride, his grace to foes, his care for others, and his life of service to mankind. His work is praised across a wide field, from the settlement of wars to the rights of children.

The chiefs pledge to double their work for a just and peaceful world. Fair growth, the rights of women, and the lift of poor lands all stand in the text. The pledge casts Mandela's path, peace by talks and grace, as the path the whole UN should walk.
un-ga-res-es-11-1:
Days after Russian forces invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the UN General Assembly met in emergency special session and passed Resolution ES-11/1. The text recalls the Charter ban on the use of force against the land or freedom of any state. It also notes that the Security Council, blocked there, had called the Assembly into session under the Uniting for Peace rule.

The Assembly deplores the attack, backs Ukraine's right to its land and borders, and calls on Russia to halt its forces and pull them out at once. Passed by a wide margin, the vote showed how alone Russia stood, though Assembly votes guide rather than bind.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
At the seventeenth plenary meeting, on 24 January 1946, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 1. It was the Assembly's first resolution. It created a commission to deal with the problems raised by atomic energy. The new body was to report to the Security Council. The Council would direct it on security matters, because the Council held chief duty for world peace.

The commission's charge was wide. It was to propose wider sharing of basic science for peaceful ends. It was to propose control of atomic energy, so it served only peaceful uses. It was to propose removal of atomic and other mass destruction weapons from national armouries. It was also to propose safeguards, backed by inspection. The safeguards would catch cheating and guard states that kept the rules.

UN General Assembly Resolution 66 (1) — a 1946 General Assembly decision from the UN’s founding session. It preserves the young Assembly’s formal action as a primary diplomatic text. The 1946 founding session is the young: the Assembly’s early action preserved here.

General Assembly resolution 69/1, issued in September 2014, is the Assembly's response to the Ebola outbreak then spreading across West Africa. The text voices grave concern at the outbreak's unprecedented scale, at the rapid deterioration in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, and at the risk of undoing those countries' post-conflict recovery.

The Assembly welcomes the Secretary-General's intention to establish the United Nations Mission for Ebola Emergency Response and asks him to carry it out promptly and report in detail. It calls on all member states and United Nations bodies to support the mission fully. The resolution treated a fast-moving epidemic as a matter for the whole United Nations system, not only for health agencies.

Resolution 70/1, adopted at the United Nations summit in New York in September 2015, is the General Assembly's 'Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development'. The resolution adopts the outcome document agreed by heads of state and government meeting from 25 to 27 September 2015, as the United Nations marked its seventieth anniversary.

The Agenda sets 17 Sustainable Development Goals and 169 targets to be met by 2030, building on the unfinished business of the Millennium Development Goals. It treats ending poverty in all its forms as the greatest global challenge. It balances the economic, social and environmental sides of development. It pledges that no one will be left behind. Because the goals apply to every country, rich and poor alike, the Agenda became the main framework for global development policy. That held for the following fifteen years.

The General Assembly adopted Resolution 73/1 at its seventy-third session in 2018. It adopts the political declaration of the Nelson Mandela Peace Summit. Heads of state and government met in New York on 24 September 2018 to reflect on global peace in honour of the centenary of the birth of Nelson Mandela.

The declaration salutes Mandela's humility, forgiveness and work on conflict resolution, human rights and reconciliation. It commits governments to place human dignity at the centre of their actions. It reaffirms the Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the 2030 Agenda. It stresses prevention, mediation and the protection of women and children in conflict. It names the period from 2019 to 2028 the Nelson Mandela Decade of Peace.

UN General Assembly Resolution ES-11/1 — the landmark 2022 emergency-session resolution deploring Russia’s aggression against Ukraine. It demanded the invasion’s immediate reversal. The 2022 aggression deplored is the landmark condemnation: the Russian invasion’s immediate reversal formally demanded here in session.
un-sc-res-1:
Security Council Resolution 1, adopted on January 25, 1946, was the very first decision of the new council. It set up the Military Staff Committee, a body named in the UN Charter. Chiefs of staff from the five permanent members, or their deputies, were to form the group and hold their first meeting in London that February.

The committee's job was to advise the council on military needs for keeping peace, and to direct any forces placed at the UN's call. Cold War rivalry soon left it with little real work. Still, the short text marks the moment the wartime alliance tried to turn itself into a standing peace system.
un-un-res-united-nations-human-rights-co: UN Human Rights Council Resolution 22/1 — the Council's 2013 vote numbered 22/1. It put the 2013 stance on record. The 22/1 vote is the 2013 mark: the Council's word that year on file, filed here in full session today.

UN Human Rights Council Resolution 25/1 — the Council's 2014 vote numbered 25/1. It put the 2014 stance on record. The 25/1 vote is the 2014 mark: the Council's take that year on file, filed here in full session today.

UN Human Rights Council Resolution S-11/1 — the Council's 2009 crisis-session vote. It met in special session on Sri Lanka. The S-11/1 vote is the 2009 crisis mark: the Council's emergency word on file, filed here in full session today.
