vedanta-sutras-thibaut-vol-1:
George Thibaut translated the Vedanta Sutras with Sankara's commentary in 1890. The volume opened the Sacred Books of the East presentation of India's most debated philosophy. Badarayana's sutras compress Vedanta teaching into some five hundred terse aphorisms.

Aphorisms so brief need commentary, and Sankara supplies the classic reading. He argues that only Brahman is real and the world is its appearance. Liberation comes through knowledge of the self's identity with Brahman. Thibaut's first volume covers the opening portion of this system. The translation founded English study of Advaita Vedanta. Philosophers still begin with Thibaut when approaching Sankara in English.
visuddhimagga-pe-maung-tin-vol-1:
Buddhaghosa, the great fifth-century commentator, wrote the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purity, as the full manual of Theravada Buddhism. Pe Maung Tin's English translation appeared in 1923 for the Pali Text Society. Part one, this volume, covers virtue and the first stages of meditation.

The manual runs in three great parts: virtue, concentration, and wisdom. Here the reader gets the moral code in detail and the forty subjects of meditation, from breath to colored disks to corpses in a graveyard. Buddhaghosa writes with the patience of a teacher who has answered every question twice. The Visuddhimagga became the Theravada world's chief guide to practice.
vittoria-volume-1: A Project Gutenberg header identifies this file as volume one of Vittoria by George Meredith, number 41 in the Gutenberg series of his works. The pages present here are that old license header only, so no title page, contents, or novel text is shown. The header's rules urge readers to keep the file whole and check the copyright law of their own country before sharing it. A companion record gives the full contents of Vittoria, Meredith's novel of the Italian revolt, in place of story text.
voltaire-age-of-louis-xiv-1753-vol-1:
Voltaire published his Siècle de Louis XIV, The Age of Louis XIV, in 1751, and the English translation of 1753 fills volume one here. Rather than a life of one king, Voltaire wrote the portrait of an age. Louis XIV's France, in his telling, stood at a peak of power, art, and polish matched by few eras in history.

The book changed how history gets written: wars share its pages with manners, trade, letters, and science. Voltaire called this way of writing philosophical history, and it set the pattern for centuries. His style is quick, bright, and full of judgment. Volume one opens the age in his shining, opinionated voice.
vyse-operations-gizeh-vol-1:
Colonel Howard Vyse led a bold dig at the Gizeh pyramids in 1837. Volume One of his Operations records that season day by day. Vyse was a soldier with funds, workers, and few doubts.

His crews blasted into the Great Pyramid with gunpowder. They found chambers and marks that bear on who built it. Modern readers may wince at his rough methods. Yet his journal preserves finds and scenes no one else wrote down. The volume is a Victorian adventure in print: part logbook, part claim to fame, wholly firsthand. Bold hands left a bold record behind.
wacousta-a-tale-of-the-pontiac-conspirac:
Volume one of John Richardson's Wacousta, or The Prophecy, opens with a preface on Pontiac's rising after the cession of the Canadas. Pontiac, the great head of the Indian race of that day, had formed a federation of the tribes. It threatened the British western posts with ruin. Nine posts stood in all. His method was to seal one fort from the rest and offer terms. Once the terms were granted, he broke faith. Seven posts fell by trusting him.

Detroit and Michilimackinac, or Mackinaw, remained. The chief bent all his ingenuity on winning them. The same preface fronts the record that calls itself the complete novel. Its pages likewise head themselves volume one of three. The front matter of the two records is one and the same. From that ground the tale opens on the siege of Detroit. A strange prophecy hangs over the garrison and its foes.
waifs-and-strays-part-1:
O. Henry's Waifs and Strays, part one, gathers twelve stories. Among them stand The Red Roses of Tonia, Hearts and Hands, The Cactus, and The Snow Man. The first tale opens on a burned trestle of the International Railroad. The southbound train from San Antonio is cut off for forty-eight hours. On that train rides Tonia Weaver's Easter hat.

Espirition, a Mexican hand, has ridden forty miles in a buckboard from the Espinosa Ranch to fetch the hat. At the small station of Nopal he learns of the delay. He shrugs, lights a cigarette, and turns his ponies home, having no orders to wait. O. Henry adds that Easter cares as much for her loyal subjects at Cactus, Texas, as for the parade on Fifth Avenue. Ranch wives and daughters bloom in new hats as faithfully as anyone. A small mishap thus opens a warm Texas tale.
waverley-or-tis-sixty-years-since-volume:
Volume one of Sir Walter Scott's Waverley, in the Caledonian series of fifty books that hold all his works, opens with the publishers' statement of their ambition. They have long wished, they say, to give the public an ideal edition of Scott. Hazlitt wrote of that great poet and novelist that his works are almost a new edition of human nature.

An ideal edition of a classic, the note argues, must stand out in typography. It must present the best text to be had. Its pictures must please the eye and deepen the reader's hold on the book. The record named for the complete novel carries this same note, word for word, before its own Volume I heading. The front matter of the two records is shared. Volume one takes Edward Waverley from his English home into the Highlands, as the rising of 1745 gathers around him.
welles-diary-vol-1:
Gideon Welles, Lincoln's secretary of the navy, kept a sharp diary through the Civil War. Volume One, published in 1911, covers the war's opening years. Welles sat in the cabinet and trusted few of his colleagues fully.

He records the blockade of the South, the building of ironclads, and the hunt for Confederate raiders. Cabinet quarrels fill many pages, with Seward and Chase judged harshly. Lincoln appears throughout, growing in Welles's respect over time. Historians rank the diary among the best insider records of the Union government at war, candid and often acid in tone. He wrote for himself alone, which frees his pen in every entry.
what-s-mine-s-mine-volume-1:
George MacDonald opened What's Mine's Mine with a London dining room full of costly, dull goods. Volume one of three sets the scene there. The narrator says no thing in the room shows true personal choice. Fashion and class habits rule the whole house instead.

The contents then move the tale toward Scotland. Chapters name a village shop, a chief, plough bulls, and a fir grove. Hills, a lake, and wolves follow, then a clan Christmas dance. This record shares its opening pages word for word with the record named as the complete set. MacDonald's theme is plain early: real worth lies past show and wealth.
wieland-geschichte-des-agathon-teil-1:
Ancient Greece hosts the education of a young idealist in Wieland's Geschichte des Agathon, Part One, given here in German. Often called the first modern German novel, the book follows Agathon through love, philosophy, and disillusion. Wieland helped invent the Bildungsroman, the novel of formation, with this story.

Agathon begins as a dreamy Platonist and meets a world that mocks his purity. Sophists, courtesans, and tyrants each teach him something his books could not. The narrative pauses for debate, then moves on with new experience. German prose fiction learned to think and feel at once in these chapters. Readers meet a hero being educated by disappointment itself, volume by volume.
wild-youth-volume-1:
Volume one of Gilbert Parker's Wild Youth opens in Askatoon, a western town of sharp, original people. Parker says the town slept with one eye open and woke with both wide. Cleverness there was as natural as eating and drinking. Chapter one brings the Mazarine family into the town.

The chapter list for this record, like the complete record, prints the contents of both volumes. Nine chapters make up volume one, ending with The Stars in Their Courses. Louise, Orlando, and a bargain with two sides fill the early tale. This record and the complete record share the same first chapter, word for word. Young love stirs under the town's watchful eye.
yoga-vasistha-mitra-vol-1:
Vihari-Lala Mitra translated the Yoga-Vasistha Maharamayana into English across the 1890s, in four volumes of which this is the first. The Sanskrit work, ascribed to Valmiki, stages a vast dialogue on liberation. Prince Rama, sick of the world, is taught by the sage Vasistha.

Rama opens in despair: wealth, youth, and life itself all pass, so what is worth wanting? Vasistha answers that the world is a dream of the mind, and freedom comes from seeing through it. Stories within stories carry the teaching, of queens, demons, and worlds inside stones. Mitra's old-fashioned English keeps the epic's sweep. The work is a summit of Hindu philosophy in story form.
zibeline-volume-1: Philippe de Massa wrote this French romance, shown here as volume one of three. Pages present here hold only a publisher's header giving the title, his name, and an April 2003 release note. No title page, introduction, or story text appears in these pages. The header notes the series French Immortals Crowned by the French Academy. Which chapters this first volume holds cannot be told from what is present here.
